A1.title: Signal flow and gain staging
A1.sum: Where sound travels, and why the first stage decides everything after it.
cards: Every audio system is a chain. Capture (a microphone) → gain (the preamp) → processing (EQ, dynamics) → routing (buses and auxes) → reproduction (amplifiers, loudspeakers, the stream). A problem at one stage travels to every stage after it.

Headroom is the space between your loudest peak and a stage's ceiling. In digital audio the ceiling is 0 dBFS — full scale. A peak that tries to go higher is clipped: flattened, and permanently distorted.
Set gain for the real performance. Ask for the loudest line, sung at the real distance. A quiet line check sets the gain too high, and the chorus clips.
Fix it at the earliest stage you can reach. EQ comes after the preamp, so no EQ can undo clipping that already happened.
rv: RV-28: fundamentals content needs a subject-matter review before release.

A2.title: Decibels without fear
A2.sum: A decibel is a ratio. Learn the four numbers that matter.
cards: A decibel compares two things. It's a logarithmic ratio, so it needs a reference: dBFS (digital full scale), dBu (a voltage reference), dB SPL (sound pressure). A dB number without its reference is incomplete.
Four numbers to keep: for voltage or sound pressure, +6 dB ≈ 2×. For power, +3 dB ≈ 2× and +10 dB = 10×.
Distance. In open air, a small source loses about 6 dB per doubling of distance (the inverse-square law). Real rooms add reflections, so treat it as an estimate.

Louder usually wins. In a comparison, even a small level difference can make one version sound “better”. Match levels before you judge tone. [LEDGER: level-match comparisons before judging tonal or dynamic preference]
rv: RV-28; RV-25 for the level-matching claim.

A3.title: Frequency and wavelength
A3.sum: Why bass wraps around pillars and treble doesn't.
cards: Wavelength = speed ÷ frequency. λ = c / f, with c ≈ 343 m/s in air near 20 °C.
Real sizes: 100 Hz ≈ 3.4 m · 343 Hz = 1 m · 1 kHz ≈ 34 cm · 10 kHz ≈ 3.4 cm. Human hearing is nominally 20 Hz to 20 kHz, and the top end drops with age.
Big waves bend around things. Low frequencies wrap around pillars and people; high frequencies are more directional and easier to block.
An octave is a doubling. 250 Hz → 500 Hz → 1 kHz. Heuristics like “250–500 Hz is mud” name a region to look at, not a rule.
rv: RV-28: fundamentals content needs a subject-matter review before release.

A4.title: Microphones and polar patterns
A4.sum: What a microphone hears depends on its type, pattern and distance.
cards: Dynamic vs condenser. Dynamic mics are rugged and need no power. Condensers are more sensitive and need power — usually phantom power (commonly 48 V) sent from the console.
Polar patterns. Omni hears all around. Cardioid rejects sound from the rear — aim that rear null at a wedge or a loud source. Figure-8 hears front and back, rejects the sides.
Proximity effect. Directional mics gain low end when the source is very close. The same voice sounds heavier at 2 cm than at a hand's width.
Distance is a fader you can't see. Moving from 5 cm to 10 cm is roughly −6 dB (inverse square, as an estimate). Consistent distance = consistent sound.

V1.title: Frames and frame rates
V1.sum: Video is a stack of still pictures. Everyone in the chain has to agree how fast.
cards: Frames per second. Common rates: 23.976/24 (the film look), 25/50 (most former PAL regions), 29.97/59.94 (most former NTSC regions), and 30/60.
Why 29.97? When color was added to the NTSC system in 1953, the frame rate was lowered by a factor of 1.001: 30 ÷ 1.001 ≈ 29.97.
Period = 1 ÷ rate. At 50 fps each frame lasts 1/50 s = 20 ms.
Match end to end. Camera, switcher, recorder, wall processor and stream should agree. A mismatch shows up as judder, dropped or repeated frames, or no picture at all — an artifact, not a crash.
rv: RV-28: fundamentals content needs a subject-matter review before release.

V2.title: Resolution, aspect and scaling
V2.sum: Pixels, shapes, and why upscaling can't invent detail.
cards: 1920 × 1080 = 2,073,600 pixels ≈ 2.1 megapixels, a 16:9 shape.
UHD 3840 × 2160 has four times the pixels of 1080: twice as wide, twice as tall.
Scaling changes pixel count, not detail. Upscaling 720 to 1080 makes a bigger picture of the same information.
i vs p. 1080i is interlaced (alternate lines per field); 1080p is progressive (every line, every frame).
rv: RV-28: fundamentals content needs a subject-matter review before release.

V3.title: Cameras and LED walls
V3.sum: Two different problems look alike on camera. Learn to tell them apart.
cards: LED walls pulse. Each LED is driven on and off very fast to set brightness, and the wall is a grid of pixels.

Problem 1 · Refresh banding. Dark bands that roll or sit across the wall. Cause: the camera's shutter samples the wall's pulsing. It changes when you change the shutter (or the wall's refresh settings).

Problem 2 · Moiré. Wavy, shimmering interference patterns. Cause: the camera sensor's pixel grid beats against the wall's pixel grid. It changes with focus, distance, zoom and angle — not with shutter.
The test that separates them: change one thing. If the pattern responds to shutter, it's banding. If it responds to focus or position, it's moiré.

V4.title: White balance and color temperature
V4.sum: Telling the camera what white looks like.
cards: Light has a color temperature, measured in kelvins (K). Common references: tungsten stage light ≈ 3200 K (warm), daylight ≈ 5600 K (cool).
Lower K looks warmer (orange); higher K looks cooler (blue).
Set white balance under the real show light. A camera balanced for daylight, pointed at tungsten light, makes everything look orange.
Match every camera. If cameras are balanced differently, every cut jumps in color.
rv: RV-28: fundamentals content needs a subject-matter review before release.

L1.title: Key, fill and back
L1.sum: Three lights, one face, one feeling.
cards: Key is the main light that shapes the face. Fill softens the key's shadows. Back (rim) light separates the person from the background.
Ratio sets the mood. A low key-to-fill ratio (say 2:1) looks open and even; a high ratio (8:1) looks dramatic.
Angle matters. Light straight from above puts eyes in shadow. Front light from a moderate angle reads well on camera.
Light for the camera and the room. What looks fine to the eye can be too contrasty for a camera.
rv: RV-28: fundamentals content needs a subject-matter review before release.

L2.title: Color temperature and color rendering
L2.sum: Warm, cool, and why skin can look wrong under good-looking light.
cards: The kelvin scale (named for Lord Kelvin): candlelight ≈ 1900 K, tungsten ≈ 3200 K, daylight ≈ 5600 K. Values are approximate references.
Color rendering. A light can look white and still render skin badly if its spectrum is spiky. Metrics such as CRI and TLCI describe how faithfully a source shows colors.
Mixing. RGB fixtures make white by mixing three colors; the result can look white but render skin poorly. Fixtures with added white or broader spectra usually do better.
Pick a target and hold it across fixtures, and tell the cameras.
rv: RV-28: fundamentals content needs a subject-matter review before release.

L3.title: Beam, throw and brightness
L3.sum: How wide the light is, and how fast it fades with distance.
cards: Field width from the field angle θ and throw distance d: w = 2 · d · tan(θ/2). A 26° field at 10 m covers about 4.6 m.
Inverse square. Illuminance falls with the square of distance: E = I / d². Double the throw and you get a quarter of the light.
Units. Illuminance is measured in lux (lumens per square meter). 1 foot-candle ≈ 10.76 lux.
Trade-off. Wider coverage from the same fixture means less light per square meter.
rv: RV-28: fundamentals content needs a subject-matter review before release.

L4.title: DMX512 basics
L4.sum: The control language most stage lighting still speaks.
cards: One universe = 512 channels (slots), each carrying a value from 0 to 255.

Addresses and footprints. A fixture uses a block of channels starting at its address. A 16-channel fixture at address 1 uses 1–16; the next fixture starts at 17. Overlaps make fixtures copy each other.
A line, not a tree. DMX runs in a daisy chain. Splitting it needs a proper splitter, not a Y-cable, and the far end of the line is terminated.
Intermittent flicker is often physical: a damaged cable or connector, the wrong cable type, or a missing terminator. Find the first fixture that misbehaves — the fault is usually just upstream of it.

A5.title: Feedback and gain before feedback
A5.sum: Why a microphone starts to howl, and the four things that buy you more level before it does.
cards: Feedback is a loop. A loudspeaker's sound reaches the mic, gets amplified, comes out louder, reaches the mic again. When the loop gain at some frequency reaches unity (0 dB), that frequency rings and then howls.
Distance is the biggest lever. Halve the distance from the talker to the mic and the talker is about 6 dB louder at the mic, while the loudspeaker isn't. That's 6 dB more level before feedback.
Aim the nulls. A directional mic rejects sound from some directions. Point its least-sensitive direction at the wedge or loudspeaker. Keep loudspeakers in front of mics, not behind them.

Fewer open mics. Every doubling of open mics costs about 3 dB of gain before feedback. Mute what isn't in use. Narrow notch filters can buy a few dB at a ringing frequency — they're the last step, not the first.

A6.title: Digital audio: samples, bits and delay
A6.sum: What a sample rate, a bit depth and a millisecond really mean.
cards: Sample rate is how many times per second the level is measured. 48 kHz is the usual rate for live and video work. A system can represent frequencies up to half its sample rate (the Nyquist limit): 24 kHz at 48 kHz.
Bit depth sets the dynamic range: about 6 dB per bit. 16-bit ≈ 96 dB; 24-bit ≈ 144 dB in theory (real converters reach less).
Every stage adds delay. Conversion, processing and networks each add a little. Sound travels about 34 cm per millisecond in air, so 3 ms of processing is like moving the loudspeaker a meter back.
One clock. Digital devices that pass audio must agree on one clock. Two clocks drifting apart cause clicks, dropouts or silence — a timing fault that looks like a signal fault.
rv: RV-28: fundamentals content needs a subject-matter review before release.

A7.title: Wireless microphones
A7.sum: A wireless mic is a radio first and a microphone second.
cards: It's a radio link. Transmitter, air, receiver, antennas. Bodies, walls and metal absorb or reflect radio, and reflections can cancel each other at the antenna (multipath) — a dropout.
Diversity receivers use two antennas and keep the better signal moment to moment. Antennas belong in line of sight of the stage, not behind a rack or a wall.

Every channel needs its own coordinated frequency. Two transmitters can mix inside receivers and create new frequencies (intermodulation) that land on a third channel. Use a coordinated plan. Which bands are legal to use differs by country and changes over time.
Batteries are part of the system. Fresh or fully charged, logged, and checked from the stage position under real conditions — not at the booth.

V5.title: Getting the picture there
V5.sum: Cables, distance, and the one-cable failure.
cards: Consumer interfaces are short-range. A typical passive consumer display cable is reliable for a few meters to around 10–15 m; longer runs need active cables or extenders.
SDI runs over coax with locking connectors and is built for distance: roughly 100 m for 1080p at 3G rates with good cable. Higher-rate versions for UHD reach shorter distances.
Fiber goes much farther and carries no electrical connection between buildings. Twisted-pair extenders and video over IP use network-style cabling; IP video needs its bandwidth planned.
The one-cable failure. When one source goes black, carry a small monitor down the path. The fault is between the last point with picture and the first point without. [F-04]
rv: RV-28; RV-33 (cable-length values are typical, not specs).

V6.title: LED walls on camera: timing and standards
V6.sum: Why a wall that looks perfect in the room can band on camera — and how to line up the timing.
cards: Frame-rate families. 25/50 is one family; 29.97/59.94 another; 24/23.976 and 30/60 are others. Everything feeding one show should live in one family. A rented processor can arrive set for a different one.

Expose for whole light cycles. The wall pulses its LEDs many times a second. If each camera frame catches a whole number of those pulses, every frame gets the same light. A shutter equal to the frame period (1/60 at 59.94p) is a common starting point; shorter shutters can work when the wall refreshes at a high multiple of the frame rate.

Refresh and sync. Walls refresh at a multiple of their input rate. A higher multiple and a shared sync reference (genlock) between wall and cameras make banding much less likely. Test at the brightness you'll really use: dimmed walls can band more.
Moiré is separate. It's spatial, not timing: change focus, zoom, distance or angle. Fixing the timing won't touch it.

V7.title: Streaming: codecs, bitrate and delay
V7.sum: What happens between the program output and a phone at home.
cards: The encoder compresses. A codec throws away what viewers are least likely to notice to fit a target bitrate. A 1080p stream might run at a few megabits per second (illustrative).

Leave upload headroom. Your internet upload must carry the stream steadily, with margin, alongside everything else on that connection. A plan that needs 100% of the upload fails when anyone else uses it.
Hard pictures cost bits. Haze, confetti, fast motion and LED walls are hard to compress; at a fixed bitrate they turn blocky.

Streams are late. Viewers are seconds — sometimes tens of seconds — behind the room. Never feed an overflow room from the stream without telling people; never monitor it in the room with the sound up.

L5.title: Mixing light and color
cards: Additive mixing (light). Red + green + blue light make white. Red + green = yellow; green + blue = cyan; red + blue = magenta.
Subtractive mixing (filters). A color filter (gel) removes the colors it doesn't pass. A deep red gel passes red and absorbs most of the rest — so the fixture gets much dimmer.
Multi-emitter fixtures mix colored LEDs (RGB, or RGB plus white, amber or lime) to make many colors and better whites.
Saturated color on camera. Very saturated blues and reds can overload one color channel of a camera and look flat or blocky on the stream. Check big color moments on camera.
rv: RV-28: fundamentals content needs a subject-matter review before release.

L6.title: Lighting for the camera
L6.sum: The eye forgives. The camera doesn't.
cards: Cameras see less range than eyes. A contrast that looks gentle in the room can crush shadows or clip highlights on camera. Light faces evenly across the stage and keep the background from outshining them.
Measure, don't guess. A light meter (lux) or the camera's exposure tools (waveform, zebras) show whether key light is consistent from spot to spot.

Flicker. Some LED fixtures and dimmers pulse their output. At certain frame rates and shutters the pulsing shows up as flicker or bands. Many fixtures offer higher-frequency or camera-friendly modes. Test at the real frame rate, shutter and intensity.
Color temperature. Pick one white for faces, hold it across fixtures, and white-balance the cameras to it.
rv: RV-28; RV-29 (flicker behavior varies by fixture).

L7.title: Lighting control over networks
L7.sum: When one DMX line isn't enough.
cards: Universes over Ethernet. Larger rigs carry many DMX universes over a network using DMX-over-Ethernet protocols. Nodes turn the network back into ordinary DMX lines near the fixtures.
Count before you patch. Universes needed = total channels ÷ 512, rounded up. 30 fixtures × 40 channels = 1,200 channels → 3 universes.
RDM (Remote Device Management) lets the console discover, address and check fixtures over the DMX line itself — if every splitter in between supports it.
The lighting network is a network. It has an owner, an address plan and a switch. Don't put it on the office switch.

N1.title: Networks for AV
N1.sum: Bandwidth, multicast, and who owns the switch.
cards: Bandwidth is a budget. A port has a speed (e.g., 1 Gbit/s). Uncompressed or lightly compressed video can use hundreds of Mbit/s; a stream needs a few. Add it up before you plug it in.

Unicast, multicast, broadcast. Unicast goes to one device. Multicast goes to devices that ask for it — if the switch knows who asked (IGMP snooping on a managed switch). An unmanaged switch floods multicast to every port. That's season 1.
VLANs separate traffic logically on shared switches: AV, office, guests. Managed switches also keep counters — the measurements you'll want during an incident.
Every network has an owner. Change it with them, not around them.

P1.title: Power for AV
P1.sum: Watts, amps, earth, and what a UPS is for.
cards: P = V × I. Power (watts) = voltage × current (amps). A circuit and its breaker are rated for a current; add up nameplates before adding load. Continuous-load rules vary by code and place.
A breaker that trips is doing its job. Only the person authorized to open the panel resets it.
Protective earth is a safety path, never a hum fix. Hum lives in the signal path; fix it there.
Power sequencing and UPS. Amplifiers on last and off first to avoid thumps. A UPS carries critical gear through short outages and gives minutes to shut down cleanly — it is not a generator.

FB1.title: One signal, four disciplines
FB1.sum: An AV system is four crafts acting as one experience. Route every signal on purpose, and check it where people receive it.
cards: An AV system is four disciplines working as one experience. AV engineering covers sound, picture, light and the signal flow between them. Computer engineering is the machines that play, stream and control. Networking is the switches, addresses and internet. Infrastructure is power, cabling, racks and cooling. A weak link in any one of them breaks the experience for everyone.

Signal flow is the path from a source (a microphone, a camera, a laptop) to a destination (a loudspeaker, a screen, the stream), including every box and setting in between. The Fieldbook rule: every source needs an owner, a destination and a reason.
One signal, two destinations. The same microphone feeds the room and the stream, but each needs different processing. A shared source doesn't mean a shared mix.

Verify the last mile. A moving meter only proves the signal reached the console. Confirm it at the loudspeaker, the display, the confidence monitor and the stream return — where people actually receive it.

Control vs media. A switch connects devices on one network; a router connects networks. Control messages are small, while media (audio and video) is large and continuous, so a full link hurts media first. How full is a link? % = traffic ÷ link speed × 100.
rv: FB-01: Fieldbook module — starting points are rules of thumb and numbers are illustrative; subject-matter review before release.

FB2.title: What sound is — and why it gets quieter
FB2.sum: Sound is a pressure wave. Frequency, wavelength and distance explain most of what a room does to it.
cards: Sound is vibration traveling as pressure waves through air at about 343 m/s at 20 °C. Frequency (in hertz, Hz) is how many waves pass each second — you hear it as pitch. Amplitude is how big the pressure swing is — you hear it as loudness, measured in decibels (dB).

The five fundamentals are frequency, wavelength, amplitude, phase and time. Wavelength is how long one wave is: λ = v ÷ f. A 50 Hz wave is about 6.9 m long; a 5 kHz wave is about 7 cm. Long waves bend around objects and fill rooms. Short waves beam straight and are easily blocked.

Hearing decibels. +3 dB is just noticeable, +6 dB is clearly louder, and +10 dB sounds about twice as loud. For voltage or sound pressure, the decibel is 20·log₁₀ of the ratio; for power, it's 10·log₁₀. (The Fieldbook's power line used 20·log₁₀ — corrected here.)

The inverse-square law. A small source in open air loses about 6 dB each time the distance doubles. The Fieldbook's example: 95 dB at 10 ft becomes about 83 dB at 40 ft. Distance, not just volume, decides what people hear. The front rows are always louder, and the booth is rarely a typical seat.

Direct vs reflected. The same sound can reach one seat by two paths, one of them off a hard surface. The reflection arrives a little later and cancels some frequencies. That is the hollow sound of CASE-001.
rv: FB-01: Fieldbook module — starting points are rules of thumb and numbers are illustrative; subject-matter review before release.

FB3.title: The frequency spectrum and EQ
FB3.sum: EQ removes what doesn't belong before it adds anything. Know the map, make small moves, and check with the EQ bypassed.
cards: EQ (equalization) turns specific frequency ranges up or down. It changes the tone of a signal, not how hard the signal hits the input.

The map (Fieldbook ranges, approximate): sub bass 20–60 Hz (felt more than heard); bass 60–250 Hz (weight); low mids 250–500 Hz (mud, boxiness); mids 500 Hz–2 kHz (body, honk); high mids 2–6 kHz (presence and consonants — ears are most sensitive around 2–5 kHz); highs 6–20 kHz (air, sibilance). An octave is a doubling of frequency: fup = 2 × f.

Cut before you boost. Start with a high-pass filter, which lets frequencies above a cutoff pass and removes rumble below it (around 80–120 Hz on a voice). Then make a small cut at 200–400 Hz for mud. Add a little 2–4 kHz presence only if the voice still needs it. Keep moves small (2–3 dB), and compare with the EQ bypassed.
Mix rescue (CASE-003): buried vocals, boomy drums and a chest-heavy mix came from low-mid build-up, effects that were too wet and gain problems, not from a lack of volume.
Protect the ears doing the work. Mix at moderate levels (roughly 75–85 dB SPL, illustrative) and take breaks. Tired ears make bad EQ decisions.
rv: FB-01: Fieldbook module — starting points are rules of thumb and numbers are illustrative; subject-matter review before release.

FB4.title: Gain structure, noise and hum
FB4.sum: Set gain at the preamp, leave headroom, keep the signal well above the noise, and cure hum without ever touching the safety earth.
cards: Gain structure is the level at every stage of the chain. Source (acoustic) → microphone (a few millivolts, called mic level) → preamp (raises it to line level, about +4 dBu in pro gear) → mixer/DSP → amplifier (speaker level: volts and watts) → loudspeaker → room → people.

Gain vs volume. Gain sets the level going into the system; the fader sets how loud it comes out. Too little gain means noise, and too much means clipping at 0 dBFS, the digital ceiling. The Fieldbook's targets (illustrative) are an average around −18 dBFS with peaks around −12 dBFS. The space above your peaks is headroom.

Pre-gain in five steps: set the fader to unity (0 dB) and turn processing off. Have the performer sing or speak at their real loudest. Raise the gain until peaks reach the target with no clip light. Then mix with faders. G = Ltarget − Lin.

SNR (signal-to-noise ratio) is how far the signal sits above the noise floor. The Fieldbook lists these noise sources: RF interference, EMI from LED walls and dimmers, damaged or unbalanced cables, and ground loops, which cause hum when equipment powered from different grounds is connected. Fix a ground loop with isolation (a DI box or signal isolator) and the right power plan from the electrician. Never lift or defeat a protective earth.

Balanced cables (XLR, TRS) carry the signal twice, one copy inverted. The receiver flips it back and adds the two, so noise picked up along the way cancels. Unbalanced cables (TS, RCA) can't do this. A DI box turns an unbalanced source into a balanced one. A bad cable can sound like a bad microphone.
rv: FB-01: Fieldbook module — starting points are rules of thumb and numbers are illustrative; subject-matter review before release.

FB5.title: The channel strip, the stagebox and the label
FB5.sum: Learn the console the way the signal travels through it, and treat every label as evidence that has to be true.
cards: The digital console is the brain of front-of-house. It turns many inputs into controlled mixes for the room, the stage monitors and the stream at the same time, and it can save each setup as a scene.

The channel strip, in signal order: input select (which source feeds this channel) → preamp gain → phantom power (48 V for condenser mics) → polarity (flips the waveform to fix a phase problem) → high-pass filter → gate/compressor → EQ → sends → fader. The channel meter reads after the preamp and before the EQ, so a CLIP light means the gain is too hot.

The stagebox puts the mic inputs on stage and converts them from analog to digital. It sends up to 32 channels over one network cable (a digital snake) and returns outputs for wedges and in-ears. If every input drops at once, check the digital link first.

Scribble strips and labels. Clear channel names make mixing faster and more confident. For cable discipline, the Fieldbook says: label both ends, keep power and signal apart, coil over-under, use strain relief, and leave no trip hazards. A label only counts as evidence if it's true, so verify it before you trust it.
rv: FB-01: Fieldbook module — starting points are rules of thumb and numbers are illustrative; subject-matter review before release.

FB6.title: Electricity basics — and whose panel it is
FB6.sum: Voltage, current, resistance and power, the safety earth, and the line you don't cross: the panel belongs to the electrician.
cards: Voltage (V) is electrical pressure; current (A) is flow; resistance (Ω) opposes the flow; power (W) is how fast energy is used. V = I × R (Ohm's law) and P = V × I.

AC (alternating current) changes direction many times a second — 120 V at 60 Hz in the U.S. (it varies by country). DC flows one way, as in batteries and inside equipment. A power supply transforms, rectifies and regulates AC into DC. Inrush current is a surge at switch-on, which is why big systems are powered up in sequence.
Short circuit: a path with almost no resistance, so the current becomes very high and the breaker trips. The breaker is there to protect the wiring. Open circuit: a broken path, so no current flows.
Protective earth gives fault current a safe path and gives equipment a shared 0 V reference. It exists to protect people's lives. Never defeat, lift or bypass it; hum is solved another way.

The boundary. Maya can work out a load: I = P ÷ V. Only a licensed electrician opens a panel, resets a breaker on a doubtful circuit or adds circuits. The math is for the conversation, not for the screwdriver.
rv: FB-01: Fieldbook module — starting points are rules of thumb and numbers are illustrative; subject-matter review before release.

FB7.title: Microphones and mic technique
FB7.sum: A microphone is a transducer with a direction. How close it is decides how much the room has to be turned up.
cards: A transducer converts one form of energy into another: a microphone turns air pressure into voltage, and a loudspeaker does the reverse. Dynamic mics use a coil moving in a magnetic field; they're rugged and handle loud sources (vocals, drums, amplifiers). Condenser mics use a diaphragm and backplate that form a capacitor; they're detailed and sensitive (choir, acoustic instruments) and need phantom power.

Polar pattern is where a mic listens. Cardioid hears the front and rejects the rear; it's the most common live. Supercardioid is narrower, with a small rear lobe. Omni hears all around (conference tables, choirs). Figure-8 hears front and back. Point the dead side at the monitors.

Distance is gain. The Fieldbook says 2–3 inches from the mouth, aimed at the mouth. Every doubling of distance loses about 6 dB of voice: ΔL = 20·log10(d2 ÷ d1). The preamp has to make that up, which also turns up the room and the loudspeakers — and brings feedback closer.
Technique for readers and speakers: don't cover the mic head, keep it close, face it, and speak consistently. Teach this before the service, kindly. It's part of the system too.
Mic level is tiny (millivolts). The Fieldbook's common mistakes: mics pointed at monitors, unused mics left open, mics too far away, and the wrong mic for the job.
rv: FB-01: Fieldbook module — starting points are rules of thumb and numbers are illustrative; subject-matter review before release.

FB8.title: Video basics — frames, formats and the house standard
FB8.sum: Video is a language made of frames and pixels. Everything in the chain has to speak the same dialect.
cards: Video is a sequence of still images shown fast enough to look like motion. Frame rate is frames per second: 24 (cinematic), 30 or 29.97 (broadcast style), 60 or 59.94 (smooth motion). Each frame lasts T = 1 ÷ fps. Resolution is pixels wide × high: 1920 × 1080, 3840 × 2160. Aspect ratio is width to height: 16:9 today, 4:3 for older material, 9:16 for phones.
Progressive (p) draws every line of each frame at once. Interlaced (i) draws odd lines, then even lines, at slightly different moments, so moving edges comb. Interlaced is a legacy format.

Standards must match. In CASE-010 a new camera showed black on the switcher. The camera was fine: it sent 1080p at 60.00 while the switcher expected 1080p at 59.94. Video is a language; every device has to speak the same one. Write the house standard down.

Moiré is a false pattern that appears when a camera's pixel grid and an LED wall's pixel grid beat against each other. Fixes: change the angle or distance, soften focus on the wall slightly, match the shutter to the wall's refresh, and reduce sharpening.
Connections: HDMI for short runs, SDI for long runs with a locking connector, and IP over the network. Keep every display on the same resolution and frame rate.
rv: FB-01: Fieldbook module — starting points are rules of thumb and numbers are illustrative; subject-matter review before release.

FB9.title: Readiness — maintenance, computers and the register
FB9.sum: Preventive maintenance, an honest asset register and healthy booth computers turn surprises into scheduled work.
cards: Preventive maintenance is small planned care, so failures don't get to choose their moment. The Fieldbook's schedule: weekly, a visual check of cables, power and gear; monthly, review the logs and firmware notes; quarterly, deep clean and check batteries, spares and documentation; yearly, replace worn parts, review the design and confirm the asset records.

Asset register: a list of every device with where it lives, its age, serial number, firmware, license and expiry dates. Budget conversations start here, because you can't plan to replace what you haven't listed.

Computers in the booth. The CPU does the thinking; RAM is short-term working memory; storage keeps files (leave 15–20% free); the GPU draws graphics. Good habits: approved updates (never an hour before service), protection left on, only trusted software, backups you've actually restored from, a locked screen, and strong unique passwords with MFA.
Batteries are maintenance too. t = C ÷ I gives the ideal runtime. Fit fresh batteries before every service anyway.
What “ready” looks like. The best Sunday isn't the one with the most heroic rescue. It's the one where the team removed preventable uncertainty before the service started.
rv: FB-01: Fieldbook module — starting points are rules of thumb and numbers are illustrative; subject-matter review before release.

FB10.title: Lighting basics and DMX addressing
FB10.sum: What light does in a room, and how DMX tells each fixture what to do — one universe, one chain, one address at a time.
cards: What lighting does: visibility, focus, mood, depth and story. Terms: intensity (how bright); color temperature in kelvin (about 2,700–3,200 K is warm, 5,600 K is daylight, 6,500 K+ is cool); beam angle (how wide); wash vs spot vs beam; a cue (a saved look with timing); and a fade.

DMX512 is one-way digital control sent down a daisy chain from fixture to fixture. It uses RS-485 differential signaling, which resists noise, and the last fixture is terminated. DMX carries control, not power.

A universe is 512 channels. Each fixture has a start address and uses N channels; its mode (personality) sets N. last = start + channels − 1, and the next free address is last + 1. fixtures = ⌊512 ÷ channels⌋.
CASE-004: one worn connector that wouldn't lock made every fixture after it flicker or freeze. One loose connection affects everything downstream, so check the chain in order.
rv: FB-01: Fieldbook module — starting points are rules of thumb and numbers are illustrative; subject-matter review before release.

FB11.title: Something broke during the service — now what?
FB11.sum: The Fieldbook's decision tree, its golden rules and the pre/during/post checklist: calm first, source first, one change at a time.
cards: The decision tree: stay calm → identify the symptom (what is happening?) → isolate it (where is it failing?) → check the signal path from source to destination → fix it or work around it, then test → communicate (tell the team). Keep the service flowing while you do it.

Golden rules: start at the source and work forward. Check the simplest things first (power, mute, cable). Make one change at a time. Use your eyes, ears and meters. Keep a backup plan ready. A working workaround beats perfection. Write it all down afterwards.

The reliability mindset: live systems fail at interfaces — connectors, power, grounding, RF, the network, protocols, routing and human hand-offs. Physics comes first: software can't repeal the physical layer. Trace energy. Trace data. Trace control.

Pre / during / post. Pre: mics, batteries, frequency scan, gain, monitors, stream mix, comms, a walk of the room. During: watch levels, RF and meters, and talk on comms. Post: mute, power down in order, charge, note the issues, reset.
Roles: the technical director leads, supported by audio, stream, cameras, video, graphics, lighting and stage. Different roles, one mission. Hand-offs are part of the system.
rv: FB-01: Fieldbook module — starting points are rules of thumb and numbers are illustrative; subject-matter review before release.

FB12.title: How wireless works
FB12.sum: A wireless mic is a tiny radio station. The air is shared, so you coordinate it, scan it, and give your antennas a clear view.
cards: RF (radio frequency): a transmitter turns audio into a radio signal and the receiver turns it back into audio. The air is shared with other users and local services. You coordinate it; you don't own it.

Frequency coordination means scanning each venue, choosing clean frequencies that don't interfere with each other (including intermodulation products), and labeling every channel. A plan belongs to one place and one day.

Line of sight and antennas. Keep antennas where they can see the transmitters, away from LED walls, Wi-Fi routers and power cables. Use external antennas at the proper height. A simple quarter-wave antenna is L = λ ÷ 4 long, where λ = c ÷ f with c ≈ 300,000,000 m/s for radio.
Care: fresh batteries checked before every show, bodypacks worn upright, spares ready, and firmware kept current — but never updated on show day.
rv: FB-01: Fieldbook module — starting points are rules of thumb and numbers are illustrative; subject-matter review before release.

FB13.title: Phase and time — when two copies meet
FB13.sum: Two copies of the same wave add or cancel depending on timing. Distance is delay, in air and on the radio.
cards: Phase is where a wave is in its cycle. Two copies that are in phase add together (up to +6 dB); copies 180° apart cancel. Common causes: different distances, polarity reversed (pins 2 and 3 swapped), or two mics on one source. If it sounds thin, check phase.

Time and delay. Sound travels about 343 m/s — roughly 2.9 ms per meter, or 0.88 ms per foot. Distance is delay: t = d ÷ c. A delay speaker is delayed to line up with the sound arriving from the mains, and subs are aligned with the mains the same way. (1,000 ft of air takes about 0.89 s.)

Multipath is the same idea on the radio. A direct wave and a reflected wave meet out of phase at one spot and cancel, leaving a dead zone. A diversity receiver uses two antennas because they're unlikely to sit in a null at the same moment.
The Fieldbook's example: a delay speaker 30 ft from the mains needs about 30 × 0.883 ≈ 26.5 ms. Measure, calculate, align — then listen from the seats.
rv: FB-01: Fieldbook module — starting points are rules of thumb and numbers are illustrative; subject-matter review before release.

FB14.title: Fixtures, angles, and key, fill and back
FB14.sum: Choose the right fixture and the right angle for faces. Choosing a position is design; hanging it is rigging — and that's somebody else's call.
cards: Fixture types: the PAR (simple, soft-edged wash); the Fresnel (very soft, natural light); the ellipsoidal or profile (hard edge, gobos, precise shaping); moving heads in wash, spot and beam versions; and LED bars. Wash covers an area, spot picks out a subject, and beam is a visible shaft of light.

Key, fill and back. The key light sits about 45° in front — high enough to shine down, not so high it hollows the eyes. The fill is softer, from the other side. The back or rim light separates the subject from the background. The Fieldbook's mistakes: top light only (raccoon eyes), back light only (a silhouette), front light only (flat).
Beam width at a distance: w = 2 × d × tan(θ ÷ 2). A wider angle gives a wider, dimmer pool of light.

Overhead is a boundary. Picking a position is design. Hanging a fixture there is rigging, owned by the rigger and the structural engineer, with a load plan and a rating. Nobody improvises a position, and nobody climbs during a show.
rv: FB-01: Fieldbook module — starting points are rules of thumb and numbers are illustrative; subject-matter review before release.

FB15.title: Scenes, snapshots and the change freeze
FB15.sum: Saved states make shows repeatable. Know what a recall changes, keep control and signal apart in your head, and don't change anything on show day.
cards: Scene: a saved snapshot of a console's settings. Cue: a saved lighting look with its timing. Safes protect chosen channels from being changed by a recall. The Fieldbook's common mistakes: recalling a scene without knowing what it changes, and not saving before a big edit.

Control plane vs signal plane. In CASE-012 the switcher kept switching video after its control software lost contact. Control and signal travel on different paths, so know which one you've lost before you touch anything.
Change freeze: no updates before an event. Update afterwards with a rollback plan and a known-good version kept, and test before the next show.
Fallbacks: a hardware panel, a second control computer, a console preset or the house lights — a way to keep light and sound up that doesn't depend on software.
rv: FB-01: Fieldbook module — starting points are rules of thumb and numbers are illustrative; subject-matter review before release.

FB16.title: Buses, sends and DCAs
FB16.sum: Bus = send it somewhere. Group = process and mix. DCA = control the volume of many channels without changing their sends.
cards: Bus: a mix sent somewhere — a wedge, in-ears, a recorder, the stream. An aux send sets how much of a channel goes to a bus. Pre-fader sends ignore the channel fader (use them for monitors); post-fader sends follow it (use them for effects).

Group = processing plus mixing, e.g. a vocal group with its own compressor. DCA = remote volume control for many channels that doesn't change their sends. The Fieldbook's rule: DCA = volume, group = processing, bus = send it somewhere. DCAs don't fix a bad mix; they make a good one easier to control.
Mix-minus is a mix of everything except the person listening, so a remote presenter doesn't hear their own voice come back late (see lesson A10).
The Fieldbook's structure: two paths, one mission — the room and the stream. Keep peaks in the groups around −12 to −6 dBFS (illustrative).
rv: FB-01: Fieldbook module — starting points are rules of thumb and numbers are illustrative; subject-matter review before release.

FB17.title: Room physics — the room is part of the signal chain
FB17.sum: Reflection, absorption, room modes and reverberation. Measure several seats before you believe one.
cards: Five things a room does to sound: reflection (it bounces), absorption (carpet and people soak it up), diffusion (it scatters), diffraction (bass bends around objects) and transmission (it passes through walls).
Room modes. A room's dimensions favor some bass notes: f = c ÷ (2 × L) along each dimension, plus whole-number multiples. That's why one note booms and another disappears.
RT60 is the reverberation time — how long sound takes to fall by 60 dB. Sabine's formula: RT60 = 0.161 × V ÷ A, with volume in m³ and absorption in m². A short RT60 helps speech.

Low end builds where the sources stack up. In Building the Room (CASE-002) the bass amp, keys amp, drums, left sub and left main all sat on one side, so the room leaned left before the mix even started. Measure several seats. Graphs are evidence, not the mix.
RTA (real-time analyzer): shows level across frequency. Measurement turns opinion into fact.
rv: FB-01: Fieldbook module — starting points are rules of thumb and numbers are illustrative; subject-matter review before release.

FB18.title: The livestream audio journey
FB18.sum: The stream is a different room with different listeners. Give it its own mix, leave headroom, and let the platform do its normalizing.
cards: The chain: stream mix → audio interface (A/D) → streaming computer → encode (compress) and upload → the platform re-encodes and normalizes loudness → phones, laptops and TVs.

The myth that no processing is better. Raw audio online sounds harsh, uneven and muddy. What to do: a separate stream mix, healthy gain, headroom (peaks around −6 dBFS), control of the low end, vocals first, and gentle compression. Don't over-compress, because the platform compresses again.

LUFS (loudness units relative to full scale) measures loudness over time the way ears hear it. Many platforms normalize to about −14 LUFS integrated; it depends on the platform, so check yours. The Fieldbook's “−12 to −6 LUFS” is louder than typical platform targets. The correction is G = Ltarget − Lmeasured.
Record clean stems separately from the processed stream mix (CASE-008): 48 kHz / 24-bit, with peaks around −12 dBFS.
Bass on phones. Small speakers can't reproduce deep bass. Controlled low end plus some harmonic detail lets the bass line translate.
rv: FB-01: Fieldbook module — starting points are rules of thumb and numbers are illustrative; subject-matter review before release.

FB19.title: Getting the picture there — HDMI, SDI, IP, fiber
FB19.sum: Choose the transport for the distance and the stakes. Digital video fails off a cliff, so test the path one segment at a time.
cards: Transport choices: HDMI (common, short runs); SDI (75-ohm coax with a locking BNC connector — long runs, live production); IP (video, audio and control over the network); fiber (very long runs, immune to electrical noise).

The cliff effect. Digital video works perfectly until it suddenly doesn't, with no gradual fade to warn you. In CASE-009 one damaged BNC connector took out the main camera. The camera itself was fine.
Method: test the path segment by segment, keep certified spares, secure and label every run, and respect bend radius and length limits.
Uncompressed video is huge: R = W × H × fps × b × s. That's why IP video is often compressed — and compression adds delay.
rv: FB-01: Fieldbook module — starting points are rules of thumb and numbers are illustrative; subject-matter review before release.

FB20.title: Addresses, subnets and the IP plan
FB20.sum: Every device needs an address in the right range. Critical gear gets addresses that don't move, and the plan gets written down.
cards: IP address: a device's address on the network (e.g. 198.18.0.21). Subnet mask: which addresses count as local (/24 = 255.255.255.0). Gateway: the router that leads to other networks. DNS: turns names into addresses. MAC address: a hardware address burned into the device.
DHCP vs static. DHCP hands out addresses automatically. Critical AV gear gets a static address or a DHCP reservation so it doesn't move between shows.
How many hosts? hosts = 2(32 − prefix) − 2: a /24 has 254 usable addresses.

Topology and plan. A star (every device back to a switch) is best for AV; avoid daisy chains. Use separate VLANs for audio, video, lighting, control and management. Keep a consistent scheme — and write it down. When something won't talk: is it powered? Are there link lights? Is it in the right subnet? The right protocol and port? Simplify, isolate, test one piece at a time.
rv: FB-01: Fieldbook module — starting points are rules of thumb and numbers are illustrative; subject-matter review before release.

FB21.title: Dynamics — compressors, gates, limiters and effects
FB21.sum: Dynamics control movement, not personality. Effects come after clarity — if the reverb hides the consonants, it's too much.
cards: Compressor: turns down signal above the threshold by a ratio. Attack is how fast it acts; release is how fast it lets go; makeup gain restores the level. Lout = T + (Lin − T) ÷ R. Starting points for a vocal (illustrative): 3:1–4:1, attack 10–30 ms, release 50–150 ms, 3–6 dB of reduction.
Limiter: a very high ratio — a ceiling that protects streams and recordings from clipping. Gate: closes below its threshold to cut bleed between hits. De-esser: tames harsh “s” sounds around 5–8 kHz.
The Fieldbook's mistakes: threshold too low (lifeless), attack too fast (kills the punch), release pumping. Compare with the compressor bypassed.
Effects come last. Reverb has decay and pre-delay (10–30 ms keeps words clear). Delay includes slapback at 80–120 ms. If reverb hides the consonants, it's too much.
rv: FB-01: Fieldbook module — starting points are rules of thumb and numbers are illustrative; subject-matter review before release.

FB22.title: Computers in AV — accounts, updates and habits
FB22.sum: The room computer is part of the system. Treat its accounts, updates, storage and backups like any other signal path.
cards: The parts: the CPU thinks, RAM is working memory, storage keeps files, and the GPU draws. The ports matter too: display outputs, Ethernet, USB-C, audio.
Hygiene: keep the operating system patched on a schedule, leave the firewall and antivirus on, install only approved software, keep 15–20% of storage free, and lock the screen when you step away.

Accounts and identity: use strong unique passwords and MFA. A room signs in with its own room account, not a person's account — a policy written for people can sign a room out. H = L × log2(N) shows why length beats cleverness.

The quick fixes, in order: restart the app, then the computer; check cables and power; check the audio and display output devices; report early. Organize files consistently, and back up to more than one place.
rv: FB-01: Fieldbook module — starting points are rules of thumb and numbers are illustrative; subject-matter review before release.

FB23.title: DSP fundamentals — filters, Q and slopes
FB23.sum: DSP is math. Filters shape the spectrum, Q sets how narrow, slopes set how steep, and some filters trade latency for phase.
cards: Time domain vs frequency domain. A waveform shows level over time; a spectrum (from an FFT) shows level across frequency. They're the same sound seen two ways.

Filters: a low-pass keeps what's below the cutoff and a high-pass keeps what's above it. A band-pass keeps a band; a notch removes a narrow band (a feedback tone, a whine); a shelf gently lifts or lowers everything above or below a point.
Q is how narrow a filter is: Q = f0 ÷ BW. A high Q is surgical; a low Q is broad and musical. Slope (dB per octave) is how steeply a filter cuts beyond its cutoff.
IIR vs FIR. IIR filters are efficient; FIR filters can be linear-phase but add latency. DSP is math — small changes make a big difference.
rv: FB-01: Fieldbook module — starting points are rules of thumb and numbers are illustrative; subject-matter review before release.

FB24.title: A meeting room is four disciplines
FB24.sum: A small room holds a computer, a network, infrastructure and AV devices. Most of its failures live at the seams between them.
cards: The room: a room computer and its conferencing app (computer engineering); a switch with PoE, VLANs, QoS and DNS (networking); power, cabling and mounting (infrastructure); and a USB camera, microphones, speakers, displays and a touch panel (AV).
What the Fieldbook found: USB devices not recognized, network misconfiguration (DNS, VLAN, QoS), and rooms configured slightly differently from one another.
What helps: a written room standard so every room is the same, remote device management, and health monitoring that checks what users actually experience.
Right tools, right roles. Separate machines for separate jobs when the stakes are high — the Fieldbook splits live streaming and control from playback and graphics.
rv: FB-01: Fieldbook module — starting points are rules of thumb and numbers are illustrative; subject-matter review before release.

FB25.title: The OSI model, AV style
FB25.sum: Seven layers from the cable to the app. Troubleshoot from the bottom up, and name the layer before you name the fix.
cards: The layers, top down: 7 Application — what people use (the conferencing app, lyrics software, switcher control); 6 Presentation — how data is formatted (resolution, frame rate, codec, encryption); 5 Session — starting and keeping a conversation going (logins, a stream session); 4 Transport — getting data there (TCP is reliable but slower; UDP is fast with no retries, which suits live media).

3 Network — finding the path (IP addresses and routing); 2 Data link — moving across the local network (MAC addresses, switch ports, VLANs); 1 Physical — the real wires and signals (cables, connectors, light, radio).
What goes wrong where: a bad cable (1), the wrong VLAN (2), the wrong subnet (3), a blocked port or lost UDP packets (4), an expired login (5), a codec or format mismatch (6), an app setting (7).
Troubleshoot bottom-up. The top layers are the user's experience; the bottom layers are the infrastructure. You can't fix layer 7 on a dead layer 1.
rv: FB-01: Fieldbook module — starting points are rules of thumb and numbers are illustrative; subject-matter review before release.

FB26.title: Latency — every stage adds some
FB26.sum: Total delay is the sum of every stage's delay. Find the biggest term before you try to shrink anything.
cards: Latency is the delay between an input (an action) and its output (the result). Every stage adds some: mic and DSP processing, the encoder, the network, the decoder, and display or speaker processing.
Total latency Ltotal = L1 + L2 + … + Ln.
One-way vs round-trip. One-way is input to output (live sound, lip sync, IMAG). Round-trip is there and back (video calls, intercom), and it decides whether people talk over each other.
How to reduce it: fewer processing stages, wired rather than wireless, lower-latency settings, local processing, and proper network QoS. Measure first — a green dashboard doesn't measure delay.
rv: FB-01: Fieldbook module — starting points are rules of thumb and numbers are illustrative; subject-matter review before release.

FB27.title: Everything becomes numbers — binary, control and macros
FB27.sum: Sound, pictures and button presses all become numbers. Macros automate many actions at once — including the wrong ones.
cards: Everything becomes binary. Sound is sampled into numbers; the more bits per sample, the more precise each number and the lower the noise: DR ≈ 6.02 × b. Video is pixels, each one a number; resolution is how many pixels, and frame rate is how many pictures per second.
Compression and bitrate. Encoding shrinks media into a stream, and decoding rebuilds it. Too low a bitrate gives blocky, soft artifacts.

Control is data too. A touch-panel button sends a command to the control processor, which tells devices what to do. The control software for a switcher handles sources, transitions, graphics, audio levels, camera control and macros, which automate several actions with one press.

Macros are powerful and fragile. A macro replays exactly what it was built for, whatever state the room is really in. Name them, document them, and test them against the states the room can actually be in.
rv: FB-01: Fieldbook module — starting points are rules of thumb and numbers are illustrative; subject-matter review before release.

FB28.title: Coverage and intelligibility — point it at people
FB28.sum: Aim loudspeakers at ears, not surfaces. Reflections comb-filter speech. Accessibility is part of the design, not an extra.
cards: Direct vs reflected. It's the same sound by different paths, with different results. A proper center fill is aimed at people (the front and middle center seats) and works together with the mains.

The upward center fill (CASE-001, recomputed): a fill aimed at the ceiling sends a strong early reflection. With about 6 m of extra path the reflection arrives around 17.5 ms late, putting the first notch near 29 Hz and a new notch every ~57 Hz through the speech range. f1 = 1 ÷ (2 × Δt). Hear the speaker, not the ceiling.
Can it reach the seat? SPL = S + 10·log10(W) − 20·log10(d) is a free-field estimate before you aim, buy or turn anything up.

Intelligibility. Speech clarity (STI, with a common target above 0.6 — illustrative) drops with reverberation, noise and comb filtering. Accessibility means a listening system, captions and readable screens, designed in from the start.
rv: FB-01: Fieldbook module — starting points are rules of thumb and numbers are illustrative; subject-matter review before release.

FB29.title: Operations — roles, hand-offs and “write it down”
FB29.sum: Clear roles, calm communication and documentation turn heroics into a system other people can run.
cards: Roles, one mission. The technical director leads, aligns and removes blockers. Audio, stream, cameras, video, graphics, lighting and stage each own their part, and the hand-off between them is part of the system.
Communication: calm, concise and respectful — on comms and in tickets. Say what you saw, what you did, and what the next person needs.
Documentation: Do it once. Do it right. Write it down. If it's not documented, it doesn't exist. A ticket closed with no record of the cause is a ticket that will reopen.
Culture: humility, growth, accountability and gratitude. Leaders help by giving inputs early (the run of show and the music the night before). Better preparation makes for a calmer service.
rv: FB-01: Fieldbook module — starting points are rules of thumb and numbers are illustrative; subject-matter review before release.

FB30.title: Network reliability for AV — VLANs, QoS and multicast
FB30.sum: Separate the systems, prioritize what's live, tame multicast — and change nothing on a network you don't own without its owner.
cards: VLANs by system: audio, video, lighting, control and management each get their own. That means less congestion, better security and easier troubleshooting.
QoS (quality of service) sets priorities: live audio first, then video, then lighting and control, then general traffic. It only works if every switch on the path honors the same plan.

Multicast sends one stream to many listeners. Without IGMP snooping (and a querier) a switch floods it to every port, and everything slows down. Also watch PoE budgets, port errors and link utilization: % = traffic ÷ link speed × 100.
Ownership: the network belongs to its owner. Bring evidence — utilization, errors, a diagram — and ask. Simplify, isolate, test one piece at a time.
rv: FB-01: Fieldbook module — starting points are rules of thumb and numbers are illustrative; subject-matter review before release.

FB31.title: Picture and light on camera
FB31.sum: Exposure, lenses and light have to agree with the camera. Good technology disappears behind the person speaking.
cards: The exposure triangle: aperture (f-stop — a lower number lets in more light and gives a shallower depth of field), shutter (motion blur; start at ts ≈ 1 ÷ (2 × fps)) and ISO/gain (brighter, but noisier — use the lowest that works). Match white balance and settings across every camera.
Lenses: focal length sets the field of view (wide, normal, telephoto). Optical zoom keeps the quality; digital zoom only enlarges pixels. Depth of field is how much of the scene is in focus.

Light for the camera. Lumens is the total light a source emits; candela is how intense it is in one direction; lux is how much lands on a surface (1 fc = 10.76 lux). A small fixture follows the inverse-square law: E2 = E1 × (d1 ÷ d2)2. Match color temperatures, and check CRI/TLCI for skin tones.
Flicker: LEDs dimmed by PWM switch on and off quickly, and low PWM frequencies band on camera. Test with the real cameras before the event.
The Fieldbook's closing: the goal isn't more gear — it's a clearer message, a calmer team and a more confident experience. Protect the moment without becoming the story.
rv: FB-01: Fieldbook module — starting points are rules of thumb and numbers are illustrative; subject-matter review before release.

A8.title: RF basics for touring
A8.sum: A wireless plan that worked in one city is a hypothesis in the next.
cards: Key idea. A wireless mic is a radio link with a budget: transmitter power, antennas, the path through air, bodies and steel, and the receiver. What keeps it clean is margin: margin (dB) = received signal − noise floor. Lose the margin and the audio drops.

Every city is a new radio environment. Local services use parts of the spectrum, and what was empty last month in one city can be occupied in the next. So a touring plan is: a coordinated list, a scan on arrival, and a per-city adjustment with spares ready. Which bands are allowed differs by country and changes over time.

Coordinate as a set. Transmitters can mix inside receivers and create new frequencies (intermodulation) that land on another channel. Sixteen channels are one plan, not sixteen choices. Keep a few spare frequencies per city.

Size matters. λ = c ÷ f. At an illustrative 600 MHz, λ ≈ 0.5 m, so a quarter-wave antenna is about 12.5 cm. Antennas need line of sight to where performers really stand. A plan without a walk test is a guess.

P2.title: Temporary power: who connects what
P2.sum: On the road, power arrives through an interface — and every piece of it has an owner.
cards: Key idea. Show power comes from the venue's service or a generator, through a connection made by a qualified person (the tie-in), into a distribution box (a distro), and only then into your circuits. The AV team plugs into what it is handed.
Advance it in writing. What service, where, how far from the stage, whose electrician, and the date on the drawing. A ten-year-old drawing is a question to ask, not a fact to plan from.

The boundary. The tie-in, any panel, generator earthing and anything wet belong to the venue's electrician or the power vendor. You bring a load list: P = V × I for each circuit, with your assumptions written down (numbers illustrative).
Alarms belong to their owner. If a generator or distro alarms, you tell the power vendor and protect the show; you don't reset or open their equipment. Never defeat a protective earth.

A9.title: Antennas and diversity
A9.sum: Two antennas beat one — unless both are standing behind the same steel.
cards: Key idea. A diversity receiver listens through two antennas in different places and uses the better signal moment to moment. Reflections that cancel at one spot (a multipath fade) rarely cancel at the other at the same instant. It builds on lesson A7.
What diversity can't fix. If both antennas lose line of sight — behind a steel frame, a wall, a truck of cases — both see a weak signal. Choosing the better of two bad signals is still a bad signal.

The body is mostly water. A performer's body absorbs radio. Standing between the transmitter and the antennas can cost a large share of the margin (how much varies; every figure here is illustrative).

Test like the show. Walk the performer's real path, facing the way they face, at show level, with a meter. Log before-and-after readings at each position. Antennas go where the show will be, not where the space is.

S1.title: Overhead is a boundary
S1.sum: What a rating is, what a rigging plan contains, and who signs — so you know what to ask for, not how to do it.
cards: Key idea. A structural rating is a number a qualified engineer stands behind — for a specific point, beam or truss, in a specific configuration, on a specific date. “It held before” is history, not a rating. A photo is not a rating. Confidence is not a rating.

A rigging plan is a document, not a feeling. It says what hangs where, how much it weighs, what it hangs from, the rating of each point, and who checked and signed it. This lesson tells you what to ask for. It is not a procedure.

Who signs. The venue supplies the building's structural data. A structural engineer approves loads on the structure. The head rigger owns the plan and the hang. Everyone else — A1, LD, PM, the local crew chief — can ask, and can stop, but can't make it safe by being sure.

When there's no number, change the design, not the rules. Ask for the data; meanwhile use approved positions, ground-supported structures an engineer has checked, or cut the position — and write down honestly what the show lost. Stop-work is normal, not an insult.
rv: RV-28; RV-41 (non-instructional; reviewed by a qualified rigger and a structural engineer).

N2.title: Show networks on the road
N2.sum: The same network, rebuilt in a new building every few days, is only as good as its labels and its test.
cards: Key idea. A touring show carries its own network — lighting control, audio, video, intercom — in road cases, and rebuilds it every city. The design doesn't change; the building, the cable runs and the people plugging things in do.

Distance is part of the design. Common copper network cable is limited to about 100 m per run between active devices. Longer runs use fiber or an extra switch. A run that worked in one venue can be too long in the next.
Redundancy you haven't tested is a hope. Primary and backup paths, a spare switch, a backup console: know what happens when one fails, and try it during setup, not during the show.

Keep the show network the show's. Don't patch it into the house network; the house network has an owner. Managed switches keep counters and logs — the evidence you'll want when someone says “it's the network”.

C1.title: Room combining and control states
C1.sum: A divisible room is one system with more than one shape. Know which shape it thinks it is.
cards: Key idea. A ballroom with an airwall is one system with several states — COMBINED, DIVIDED, sometimes more. Each state has its own routing: which inputs feed which loudspeaker zones, and which panels control what. The same wall plate can be live in one state and ignored in another.

Key idea. The system has to be told where the wall is. Usually a partition sensor on the wall track reports it; a panel may request a state; often an interlock refuses DIVIDED while the sensor says the wall is open. If the sensor and the real wall disagree, the system is confidently wrong.

Key idea. Wrong states give predictable symptoms. COMBINED while the wall is closed: one room plays the other room's inputs and its own plates are ignored. DIVIDED while the wall is open: half the room goes quiet. So read the state before you re-patch — the panel, and your ears in both rooms.

Key idea. A state change is a change. It moves many routes at once, with no fade. Plan it: feed both paths first (make before break), count it in with the system's owner, then verify in every room — including the one you weren't working in.

V8.title: Streaming tap points and A/V sync
V8.sum: Where the stream listens decides what the world hears — and when.
cards: Key idea. A console channel is a chain: input → preamp → processing (gate, EQ, compressor) → mute → fader → the room's mix. A send to the stream can be tapped at different points: at the input (raw, before everything), pre-fader (after processing; whether it obeys the mute depends on the console and its setting), or post-fader (it follows the room's balance).

Key idea. A stream mix is its own output. It should obey mutes and gates — what's muted in the room stays muted online — but keep its own balance, because a room mix leans on sound the stream can't hear: a loud band in a small room barely needs the PA. Tap pre-fader, post-mute, after processing, then balance for headphones.

Key idea. Pictures are late. Switchers, frame synchronizers and graphics each add frames; audio usually arrives first. Measure it (a clap or a slate on camera), then delay the audio to match: audio delay = video latency − audio latency. At 59.94 fps one frame ≈ 16.7 ms. Audio arriving early is usually more noticeable than late.

Key idea. Prove the stream where the viewers are: a second listener on an independent path — a phone on cellular, headphones, the real stream — for longer than a song. The booth confidence monitor and the encoder's “Healthy” share the path you're trying to prove.

L8.title: Show control, cue lists and change freezes
L8.sum: A show is a program. Show day is not the day to rewrite it.
cards: Key idea. A cue list is a numbered sequence of states — lights, video, sound, sometimes more — each fired by a GO. Show control links systems so one GO fires several departments at once. That's powerful, and it means one untested cue can go wrong in three places at the same moment.

Key idea. The stage manager calls the show: “standby,” then “go.” The booth doesn't fire cues on its own and never improvises a scenery or fly move. If something's wrong, you tell the stage manager the facts; holding or stopping is their call.

Key idea. A change freeze: after a set time (often doors), the show file is frozen. New requests go in a log with a name and a time. They wait for tomorrow — unless the stage manager holds and there's a way to test them. An untested show-day change is how opening nights go wrong.

Key idea. The pre-show checklist — comms, every source on the switcher, every mic at show level, the first cues, the floor — runs after the last change to the room, not before. A check before a change proves the room you had, not the room you've got.

N3.title: Addressing, DHCP and fixed addresses
N3.sum: Every device needs an address nobody else is using — and one server answering the question.
cards: Key idea. On an IP network every device needs an address, a subnet (which addresses are local) and a gateway (the door to other networks, like the internet). Two devices with the same address make both unreliable. A wrong gateway makes a device look connected and reach nothing.

Key idea. DHCP: a server hands out addresses from a pool, with the gateway and name servers to use, on a lease. One network, one DHCP server — unless the servers are deliberately coordinated. Two independent servers give two different answers, and each device believes whichever arrived first.

Key idea. Fixed (static) addresses suit gear you must always find: consoles, encoders, processors. Put them outside the pool, or reserve them in the server. A fixed address inside an unreserved pool works until the server hands the same number to someone else — which may be months later, somewhere bigger.

Key idea. Private ranges (10.x.x.x · 172.16–31.x.x · 192.168.x.x) are reused everywhere, so two networks you join may already overlap. Joining networks is a design change with an owner: keep them separate, route between them, or plan one range together — and write it down.

A10.title: Mix-minus, IFB and in-ear monitoring
A10.sum: What performers hear is a system too — and in a crisis, it's the one that has to keep working.
cards: Key idea. In-ear monitors give each performer their own mix, usually over a wireless link, straight into earpieces. They isolate a performer from a loud stage — which means the in-ear mix is almost all they hear. Its failures are private and intense. Levels are the performer's and their audiologist's business.

Key idea. A mix-minus is a return feed of everything except the listener's own voice. IFB (interruptible foldback) lets a producer or stage manager cut into a presenter's earpiece. Any delayed path carrying a performer's own voice back into their ear is deeply disruptive.

Key idea. In a hold, the stage manager needs two things from audio: a working announce mic to the audience and a way to talk into the performers' ears. Keep both on the most local, most reliable path you have — and test them before the show, not during the hold.

Key idea. A local fallback mixer at the stage can take over monitor control when the link from FOH is unreliable, so a network drop can't take a performer's ears. It belongs in the written fallback plan, set up and tested at soundcheck — a branch you planned, not a trick you improvised.

C2.title: Identity and room accounts
C2.sum: A meeting room signs in like a person. Policies written for people can sign it out.
cards: Key idea. A meeting room is a user. To read its calendar and join calls, the room computer signs in with its own room account — often called a resource or service account. If the account can't sign in, the room can't join, however healthy the camera and microphones are.

Key idea. Policies written for people break rooms. A room can't answer “change your password”, approve a sign-in on a phone, or read an email. Room accounts need their own policy: unique credentials, rotation managed by the identity team, and sign-in limited to the room's own device.

Key idea. A shared password is a shared key. One password for every room means one leak opens every room's calendar, camera and microphones. Unique credentials shrink the blast radius: one leak = one room.

Key idea. Identity belongs to its owners. AV brings evidence — which rooms, which error, when, what changed — and verifies rooms after the change. The identity or security team decides and changes access. Symptom: Control (won't join). Cause: Dependency (identity).
rv: RV-28; RV-60: identity mechanics are generic and simplified.

A11.title: Acoustic echo cancellation
A11.sum: Why remote people hear themselves, and why one canceller is better than two.
cards: Key idea. In a meeting room the far end's voice comes out of the loudspeakers, bounces around the room and goes back into the microphones. Without help, the far end hears itself — late, because it traveled there and back across the network.

Key idea. An echo canceller keeps a copy of exactly what it sent to the loudspeakers (the reference), learns how the room changes that sound, and subtracts its prediction from the microphones. No true reference, no cancellation: far-end audio played through any device the canceller can't see comes straight back.

Key idea. One canceller per path, nearest the microphones, with the true reference. A second canceller in series sees an already-cleaned signal, keeps re-learning, and can leak bursts or chop the room's voices during double-talk (both ends talking at once). Updates can quietly switch the second one back on.

Key idea. The person who hears the echo is not the one causing it. If remote people hear themselves, look in your room. If your room hears itself, the leak is in theirs. Test from the far end, in silence and in double-talk.
rv: RV-28; RV-61: echo cancellation is simplified for teaching.

V9.title: USB, cameras and room computers
V9.sum: Why a USB camera can leave a call without anyone touching it.
cards: Key idea. Enumeration. When a USB device connects, the computer asks what it is, loads a driver and gives it an identity for this session. If the device drops and reconnects, it can come back as a new instance — and software that remembers “that exact camera” may keep looking for the old one.

Key idea. Power budget. A port supplies a limited current at 5 V (textbook values: about 500 mA for USB 2.0, 900 mA for USB 3.x). P = V × I: 5 V × 0.9 A = 4.5 W. An unpowered hub shares one port's budget among everything plugged into it; a camera's motors at start-up can tip it over.

Key idea. Power states. Computers save energy by suspending idle USB devices. Laptops love it; room computers shouldn't. A camera that sits idle while someone presents can be put to sleep, and not every device or extender wakes cleanly.

Key idea. Distance. A passive USB 2.0 cable is good for roughly 5 m. Rooms use extenders (often over category cable, sometimes powered from a network switch) — and the extender must carry data, power and the sleep/wake conversation. Test the whole chain under the condition that fails: idle, then wake.
rv: RV-28; RV-62: USB values are textbook figures; behavior simplified.

N4.title: Segments and VLANs for AV
N4.sum: Why a device can be “reachable” and still not hear a thing.
cards: Key idea. A VLAN (a network segment) is a separate logical network running on shared switches. Each switch port is assigned to one. Two devices on different segments can't talk directly, even if their cables end a meter apart. Builds on N1.

Key idea. AV gets its own segment because media is different: networked audio and video often use multicast streams, need steady timing, and shouldn't share a crowd with office traffic — or be reachable by everything in the building.

Key idea. Traffic between segments passes a router or firewall with rules. Control commands (one device to another) may be allowed across; media streams usually stay inside their segment. So a camera can be reachable for control while its audio or video never arrives: reachable ≠ receiving.

Key idea. A move is a change. Re-patching a wall port or moving a desk can put a device on another segment. The network owner assigns ports and records it; AV brings evidence — the device, its address, the port, when it moved — and verifies the outputs afterward.
rv: RV-28; RV-63: segmentation simplified; addresses invented.

M1.title: Measuring what matters
M1.sum: Why every tile can be green while the help desk is on fire.
cards: Key idea. Every metric is a proxy. Write down the outcome it stands for. “Green” here meant “the room controller answered a ping.” The outcome people care about is “my meeting started, and everyone could see and hear it.” Those can disagree all day.

Key idea. Data has an age. If a failed poll leaves a tile at its last color, the dashboard shows the past as the present. Show “last heard” on every tile and gray it out when it's too old — stale green is a lie of omission.

Key idea. A dashboard only sees what's in its inventory. Missing rooms never go red; absence of alarms isn't health. Check coverage against an independent list: coverage = monitored rooms ÷ real rooms.

Key idea. Measure user outcomes and triangulate: call logs, calendars and tickets together. Tickets under-report — people stop filing when they stop expecting things to work. And when a measure becomes a target, people start serving the measure instead of the outcome.
rv: RV-28; RV-64: monitoring practice simplified; figures illustrative.

C3.title: Control systems as state machines
C3.sum: A room is always in exactly one state. Events move it. Guards decide whether they should.
cards: Key idea. A room controller is a state machine: at any moment the room is in exactly one state — OFF, WARMING, READY, IN CALL, COOLING — and it changes state only when an event arrives: a button, a booking starting or ending, a device reply, a timer.

Transitions need guards. An event should move the room only if a condition holds: SHUTDOWN only if no call AND nobody in the room AND no booking soon. A transition without a guard fires in situations nobody imagined — like between two meetings.

Races. When two events can arrive at almost the same moment, the result depends on which lands first. A delay only moves the race to a new time. Handling events one at a time, with guards on every transition, removes it.

The panel must tell the truth. Drive what the panel shows from device feedback (display power, call status, occupancy), not from a variable a macro set optimistically. And make buttons safe to press twice: Start in a room already in a call must never hang up the call.

A12.title: Speech intelligibility and microphone coverage in meeting rooms
A12.sum: Remote people hear only what the microphones hear. Make every seat count.
cards: Key idea. Intelligibility depends on the speech-to-noise ratio at the listener, not on loudness. Remote participants hear only what the microphones pick up — the talker, plus the air handling, the projector fan and the room's reflections.

Distance costs you. Each doubling of talker-to-microphone distance loses about 6 dB of direct speech (inverse-square estimate), while noise and reverberation stay put. near seat 1 m vs far seat 4 m ≈ 12 dB less direct speech — the far seat sounds distant and roomy to the far end.

Coverage is a map, seat by seat. Ceiling and table microphones each cover a zone. Seats outside every zone go quiet or hollow for remote listeners. Check coverage with a real talker at every seat, listening from the far end — not with one meter reading at the center of the table.

Every listener, every path. A listening system (a loop or receivers) needs its own feed: far-end audio plus room speech, not room microphones alone. And the echo canceller needs the far-end audio as its reference. Prove it with the people who use it.

M2.title: Incident, problem and change
M2.sum: Restore it. Remove the cause. Change things safely, on the record.
cards: Key idea. An incident is an unplanned interruption — the goal is to restore service fast. A problem is the underlying cause of one or more incidents — the goal is to remove it. A change is any controlled addition, modification or removal that could affect service.

Repeats are a signal. same symptom + same fix + again = a problem. Link the incidents to one problem record with an owner. Closing nine tickets fast is good incident work; nobody owning the tenth is a process failure, not a person's.
Known error and workaround. While the problem is open, record what's known about the cause and the fastest safe workaround, so the desk stops rediscovering it every morning.

Change safely. A standard change is pre-approved and low risk (pausing one room's schedule for a day); a normal change is assessed and approved; an emergency change is fast-tracked but still recorded. Every change has an owner, a rollback and a test. Close the problem only when the fix is verified at the moment it used to fail.

S2.title: Least privilege for AV devices
S2.sum: Every account, person and tool gets only the access the job needs, for only as long as it needs it.
cards: Key idea. Least privilege: every person, account and tool gets only the access the job needs, for only as long as it needs it. In AV, every processor, room computer, touch panel and camera with a management interface is a door.
