Named, not shared. A shared admin account makes every action anonymous: the log says “someone.” Named accounts with a second factor make the log say who. Change default passwords at installation, and keep credentials in the organization's approved store — not in a notebook.

Remote help through an approved path. named + approved + time-limited + one device + recorded + endable. An always-on inbound agent running as administrator is a door left open, whoever installed it and however well they meant.

Who decides. Security owns access decisions. AV owns what the work needs. Vendors propose. If you find something unexpected — an old agent, a shared account — keep the evidence, touch nothing, and report it. (generic and non-instructional).

M3.title: Update rings and exception registers
M3.sum: Roll changes out in stages that look like your fleet — and write down every room that doesn't.
cards: Key idea. Update rings roll a change out in stages: ring 0 (a lab), ring 1 (a few representative rooms), ring 2 (a slice of the fleet), ring 3 (everyone) — with a watch period, a check where the users are, and a pause or rollback at every step.

Representative means every shape. A ring of five standard rooms tests one room five times. A failure that needs two inputs, a divisible wall or an unusual computer can't appear in it. ring 1 = one room of every configuration, not five of the commonest.

The exception register. Every room that differs from the standard gets a row: what differs, why, who owns it, the compensating control, a review date — and whether it's in the test ring. An exception nobody recorded is invisible to inventories, dashboards, scans and rings.

Pin what matters; query the fleet. Set critical settings explicitly (which input carries content) instead of trusting a default a vendor may change. After any failure, query the whole fleet for the same shape. Keep a 30-second fallback card in every room.

V10.title: Sync, genlock and timing references
V10.sum: Why a studio needs one clock — and what happens when it loses the sky.
cards: Key idea. Every camera, switcher and converter in a studio has to agree on when a frame starts. They follow a shared timing reference: in older plants a signal called black burst; in IP plants a network clock. Following it is called genlock.

Key idea. The master reference usually locks to satellite time. If it loses its antenna it goes into holdover — it keeps running on its own oscillator and slowly drifts. Drift grows with time: drift = ppm × 10⁻⁶ × t.

Key idea. Tolerant devices follow a drifting reference smoothly. Strict ones — often older converters — drop out when the reference moves outside their lock range. The symptom looks random: a picture that tears “every few seconds.”

Key idea. A backup reference is only a backup if it is independent. If it follows the main, one failure takes both. Write the fallback where the operator's eyes land: on the rack, not in someone's head.

V11.title: Measuring A/V sync
V11.sum: Lips and voice arriving together — and how to prove it where viewers watch.
cards: Key idea. Every processing step delays picture or sound. Scalers, graphics, frame synchronizers and encoders delay video by whole frames; audio paths usually add much less. If nothing compensates, sound arrives early.

Key idea. Measure with a sync clip: a flash and a beep at the same instant. Record the output where viewers watch and count the gap: offset = audio delay − video delay. Negative means the sound is early.

Key idea. People notice sound that's early sooner than sound that's late — in real life, sound always arrives after light. Planning windows are lopsided: a little early is already wrong; a little late is forgivable.
Key idea. Compensate in the audio path by a measured amount: delay = frames × (1000 ÷ fps) ms. Then label the reason next to the setting, or the next careful person will remove it.

A13.title: Loudness and metering
A13.sum: Why a peak meter can't tell you what viewers hear — and what a loudness meter does.
cards: Key idea. A peak meter shows the highest instant. A loudness meter averages how loud a program feels over time, weighted toward how ears hear. A heavily compressed promo can peak lower than the news and still sound much louder.
Key idea. Broadcasters aim programs at a loudness target, measured in LUFS (loudness units relative to full scale). 1 LU = 1 dB. The correction is simple: gain = target − measured.
Key idea. Every path to the viewer needs the same treatment: programs, breaks, promos, inserted ads. A path that bypasses the loudness processor is where complaints come from.
Key idea. Loud is not the same as noticed. About every +10 LU sounds roughly twice as loud — and the loudest item on a channel is the one people mute. Make important messages clear, not hot.

V12.title: Captions and accessible media paths
V12.sum: Why captions can be perfect on air and missing on the stream.
cards: Key idea. Live captions are typed or respoken by a captioner and inserted into the video signal as data, alongside the picture. Every box in the path has to pass that data through untouched.
Key idea. A converter, scaler or transcoder that doesn't know about caption data may drop it silently. The picture and sound look perfect; the captions are simply gone.
Key idea. Each output is a separate promise: broadcast, stream, apps, archive. Monitor caption presence on every output, and check from where viewers watch.
Key idea. Access isn't a feature. For a deaf or hard-of-hearing viewer, the captions are the audio. Missing captions during an emergency bulletin is a missing bulletin.

R1.title: Microwave links and fade margin
R1.sum: How a beam across a valley loses to rain — and why margin is a budget.
cards: Key idea. A studio-to-transmitter link (STL) is often a microwave hop: two dishes in line of sight. The receiver needs a minimum signal; everything above it is fade margin — the budget you spend on bad days.
Key idea. Heavy rain absorbs microwaves. Extra loss grows with rain rate and path length: A = γ × d. A link with a thin margin fails first in the storm you most need it for.
Key idea. Line of sight isn't a line — it's a fat ellipse called the Fresnel zone. Ridges, trees or buildings inside it cost signal even when you can see the far dish.

Key idea. A second path is only a backup if it doesn't share the failure: a different carrier, a different route, a different conduit. Check the map, not the label. Towers are for certified crews, in calm weather.

N5.title: Contribution over cellular
N5.sum: Bonding, buffering and why a fixed bit rate breaks in a crowd.
cards: Key idea. A bonded cellular kit splits one video stream across several modems and reassembles it at the station. More links, more capacity — shared with everyone else's phones.
Key idea. Each link's capacity depends on bandwidth and signal quality: C = B × log₂(1 + S/N). Twenty thousand phones raise the noise and lower S/N — every link shrinks at once.

Key idea. A fixed bit rate can't bend; when capacity drops below it, the stream breaks. Adaptive bit rate lowers quality to fit, with a floor below which you'd rather cut away. A bigger buffer trades delay for stability.
Key idea. The reporter's earpiece needs a mix-minus: the studio and cues, never her own voice and never the delayed program return. Test it with the reporter talking, not with meters.

N6.title: Addressing plans, reservations and exclusions
N6.sum: Why a fixed address inside the automatic range is a time bomb.
cards: Key idea. On most networks a service hands out addresses automatically (DHCP) from a range. Devices that need a known address get a fixed one — which must never be handed out automatically to someone else.
Key idea. Two safe patterns: put fixed devices outside the automatic range, or reserve their addresses in the service so it never offers them. free = last − first + 1 tells you how much room is left.
Key idea. A fixed address inside the range works until the range fills up or someone widens it — then a laptop is handed the same address and both stop working. It's a fuse with a delay.
Key idea. Addressing lives in two places: the network owner's configuration and the documents that tell installers what to do. A change to either must check the other.

S3.title: Shared accounts, sessions and resets
S3.sum: Why one password for twenty-two people is twenty-two ways in — and no way to know who.
cards: Key idea. A shared account means everyone who knows the password is the same person to the system. When it's misused you can't tell who, and you can't remove one person's access without resetting everyone.
Key idea. Named accounts with only the access each job needs (least privilege) contain the damage: one captured login opens one person's door, not the newsroom's.
Key idea. Segmentation keeps the air chain alive when the office is compromised: playout and master control on their own network, with their own accounts, never depending on newsroom logins.
Key idea. In an incident, security owns access: locks, resets and exceptions. Operations keeps the service running without the locked systems — paper, offline copies approved by security, and calm.

M4.title: Failover drills and runbooks
M4.sum: How to find out your backup doesn't work — before you need it.
cards: Key idea. A backup you've never used is a hope. A drill moves the real service to the backup on purpose, on a quiet night, for a set time, with everyone told.
Key idea. Write rollback criteria before you start: what, if it fails, sends you straight back (captions, audio, emergency alerts). Then rolling back is following the plan, not panic.
Key idea. Everything must be locked to the right reference at the backup too — including timecode. Free-running clocks drift: drift = ppm × 10⁻⁶ × t.
Key idea. A runbook is the notebook, typed, tested and owned by more than one person. Every drill finding goes into it the same night.

M5.title: Emergency information: relay, verify, make it accessible
M5.sum: What a station's job is — and isn't — on the worst night.
cards: Key idea. Relay, don't originate. Forecasts, warnings and evacuation orders belong to the agencies that issue them. Read them word for word, name the source, and repeat them on a schedule.
Key idea. Verify before you air. A caller's “the bridge is open” may be true, wrong or an hour old. Route it to the emergency manager; air what officials confirm.
Key idea. Make it accessible. Captions on every output, a second-language feed, plain words, the same wording every time. The people most at risk are often the least able to catch a paraphrase.
Key idea. Keep people out of it. Evacuation orders apply to the station too; field crews pull back under the field safety plan. The backup exists so nobody has to stay.

M6.title: Monitoring outcomes at scale
M6.sum: Four hundred rooms you will never visit: what to watch, and how to prove a fix from a distance.
cards: Heartbeat vs outcome. A heartbeat check asks “is the device answering?”. An outcome check asks “did the user get the result?” — a recording with sound, a call that connects, a picture on the screen. Heartbeats stay green while outcomes fail.

Scale changes proof. You can't stand in 400 rooms. Prove a fix remotely with the same path the user uses: a test recording played back from the student portal, a test call answered on a phone, a screenshot of what the display shows.
How big is the problem? % = part ÷ whole × 100 — 22 of 400 rooms is 5.5%. How long to prove it? T = Σ (count × time each) — 22 rooms × 6 min = 132 min. Plan the proof before you promise a time.
Rings. Updates go to a small ring of pilot rooms first, then wider. A ring defined by a wildcard (“every room whose name starts ENG”) isn't a pilot — it's a building. Use explicit room lists.

N7.title: Clinical video on a shared network
N7.sum: Why the same cart works in one room and freezes in the next: VLANs, QoS and per-device caps.
cards: Segments. A VLAN keeps different kinds of traffic apart on the same switches. A hospital might keep clinical video, staff PCs and visitors' phones on separate VLANs, each with its own rules.
Priority. QoS marks live video and audio so switches send them first when links are busy. A guest network usually gets no priority and a per-device cap.
How close to the edge? % = traffic ÷ link speed × 100 — traffic in Mb/s, link speed (or cap) in Mb/s. A 3.8 Mb/s consult under a 4 Mb/s cap runs at 95%: any spike freezes it.

Boundaries. The network belongs to its owner: bring the evidence (the device's VLAN, port and a graph), and the owner makes the change. Clinical calls belong to the clinicians: test with a training manikin, never by watching a patient's consult.

A14.title: Hearing loops: field, coverage and honest signs
A14.sum: How a loop reaches a hearing aid — and how to prove it reaches every seat.
cards: How it works. A loop is a wire around (or under) the seating, driven by an amplifier with the room's program sound. It makes a magnetic field; a hearing aid's telecoil picks it up — clean speech, no room noise.

Field strength is measured in mA/m at each seat. Compare with the reference: L = 20·log10(H ÷ Href) — H is the reading at the seat (mA/m), Href the target (400 mA/m here, illustrative). −12 dB is a quarter of the field: a dead zone.
Metal eats the field. Steel in floors, platforms and seating frames can soak up much of the field. Anything added later — a platform, a steel riser — needs a re-test.

Proof is two things. A seat-by-seat field map, and a listening test by telecoil users. And a sign is a promise: say where the loop works and what to do where it doesn't. The installer and facilities own the wiring and the floor.

P3.title: PoE budgets and port priority
P3.sum: Why adding a camera can switch off a microphone three rooms away.
cards: Power over Ethernet sends power and data down the same cable. Each switch has a PoE budget — the total watts it can hand out across all its ports.

Add it up. Pused = Σ Pport · headroom = Pbudget − Pused — Pport is each device's draw in watts, Pbudget the switch's budget. Use the worst-case draw: a camera with its infrared on, a heater in winter.
When headroom goes negative the switch has to shed load. It cuts ports by port priority — and when nobody set one, the default decides for you.
Boundaries. The switch belongs to the network owner; cameras and their schedules to security; you bring the numbers and a plan, and each owner decides for their own equipment.

A15.title: Echo cancellation and its reference
A15.sum: Why remote people hear themselves — and why the canceller needs the right reference.
cards: The loop. In a hybrid room, remote people's voices play from the room's speakers, the ceiling mics hear them, and — unless something removes them — send them straight back. The remote person hears themselves one round trip later.
How late? techo = 2 × tone-way — tone-way is the delay in one direction (ms). 150 ms each way is a 300 ms echo: long enough to trip up anyone speaking.

The canceller (AEC) subtracts from the mics whatever it hears on its reference input. The reference must be the far-end audio — what the speakers play. Feed it the wrong signal and it removes the wrong thing.
Change safely. A preset that reaches forty rooms is a big change: a change record, a pilot room, a test call, then batches. Room-specific settings shouldn't live inside a global preset.

A16.title: Auto-mixers, coverage and open microphones
A16.sum: Why a presenter who walks can vanish from a recording — and how to cover the room without feedback.
cards: Coverage. A ceiling array forms lobes — zones it listens to. Walk out of every lobe and you're only in the room's noise.

Distance costs level. ΔL = 20·log10(d2 ÷ d1) — d1 and d2 in meters. From 1 m to 4 m the direct sound is 20·log₁₀(4) ≈ 12 dB quieter. In a real room the reverberant sound doesn't fall away like that, so the level drops a little less — but the microphone hears more room and less talker, which is what makes speech muddy and trips the gate.
The auto-mixer opens the channels that hear speech and turns the others down. If a presenter is 12 dB down, the mixer may decide he isn't there.
Open mics cost headroom. ΔGBF = −10·log10(Nopen) — each doubling of open microphones costs about 3 dB of gain before feedback. Add a lobe where people stand, not everywhere.

N8.title: Alert paths and latency budgets
N8.sum: Why the same alert reaches a phone in five seconds and a sign in a minute and a half.
cards: A chain of stages. An alert passes through the emergency manager's console, a notification hub, each channel's delivery system and the screen itself. Each stage adds time.
Add them up. Ltotal = L1 + L2 + … + Ln — each L in seconds. The biggest term is where to look first.

Push vs poll. A push path sends the alert the moment it exists. A polling player asks ‘anything new?’ every so often — on average it waits half its interval, at worst the whole interval. Plan for the worst case: an alert budget has to hold every time, not on average.
Boundaries. The emergency manager owns every word and every hold time. AV and IT measure and carry the message; the network owner changes the network. You never write, edit or send an alert.

V13.title: Time, clocks and drift
V13.sum: Why a clock that's slightly fast becomes a second out by breakfast — and how to keep many clocks honest.
cards: Every clock drifts. A clock's error is measured in ppm — parts per million. Left alone, the time error grows: drift = ppm × 10−6 × t — ppm the clock error, t the elapsed time in seconds.
In frames. frames = drift × fps — fps is frames per second. 50 ppm for an hour is 0.18 s: about 5 frames at 30 fps. Lips and voice visibly part at one or two.

Following a reference keeps clocks together — but if everyone follows one reference, they all go wrong together. Use several independent sources that vote, so a liar is outvoted: three at the very least, four so that one can fail and the rest can still outvote a liar.

Correct gently. Stepping a clock jumps every recording in progress. Slewing speeds or slows the clock slightly — typically no more than about half a millisecond per second — so a one-second error takes over half an hour to remove. The network owner runs the time servers.

M7.title: Failure rates and lifecycle plans
M7.sum: How to turn a pile of tickets into a replacement plan you can defend.
cards: Rate, not count. λ = failures ÷ (units × years) — λ (lambda) is failures per unit per year; units is how many devices; years is how long you watched.
Expected failures. expected = λ × units × years — for next year, years = 1. It's an estimate: say so, and say what it assumes.
Split before you plan. One average can hide a cluster: one model, one building, one kind of room. Compute λ for each group.
Weigh the impact. cost = tfixer + people × tdelay — a failure in a 240-seat hall costs far more than one in a seminar room. Plans are about risk, not age.

A17.title: Feeds for interpreters, captioners and streams
A17.sum: Every listener at a big event needs a different mix — and a stream needs room on the link.
cards: Different people, different mixes. The room hears the PA. The stream hears a broadcast mix. An interpreter needs a clean feed of whoever is speaking — without crowd noise — and a captioner needs the same, early.
Second-language channel. The interpreter's voice goes to its own bus, then to the stream's alternate audio and to headsets in the room. Never mixed over the main language.
Room on the link. % = traffic ÷ link speed × 100 — traffic is every stream you send (Mb/s), link speed the uplink (Mb/s). 8 + 1 + 8 on 100 Mb/s is 17%: plenty of headroom.
Outcome checks. Watch the stream the way viewers do, with captions and the second language — a clean program in the truck isn't proof.

D1.title: Drawings, coordination and conduit fill
D1.sum: How a line on an AV sheet becomes a box in a floor — and what has to agree before it can.
cards: The set. Architectural, electrical, structural, mechanical and AV sheets describe one building. Each discipline draws on the others' latest sheets as a background. An old background is an old building.
Coordination means overlaying the sheets and finding the clashes: a floor box with no conduit, a projector under a beam, a loudspeaker in a sprinkler's spray.

Conduit fill. fill = Σ Acable ÷ Aconduit × 100 — Acable is each cable's cross-section area and Aconduit the conduit's internal area, both in mm². For three or more cables the electrical code's usual limit is 40%.
Who signs what. The engineer of record sizes and signs conduit; the architect owns the room layout. The AV designer supplies the cable list, the fill numbers and the intent — and asks.

D2.title: Throw distance, lenses and sections
D2.sum: Where a projector can sit is decided by its lens — and by everything else in the ceiling.
cards: Throw ratio. D = TR × W — D is the lens-to-screen distance, TR the lens's throw ratio, W the image width. A 6 m image needs 9 m with a 1.5:1 lens and 4.8 m with a 0.8:1.
Zoom lenses have a range (say 1.5–1.9:1), so a position works if the needed ratio falls inside it. Lens shift moves the image without moving the projector.
Plans aren't enough. Beams, catwalks, ducts and sightlines live on the sections — cut-through drawings. Draw the projection cone on the latest section before you promise a position.
Who decides what. The AV designer proposes the lens and the position with numbers; the architect owns the booth and sightlines; the structural engineer owns the beam and anything hung from it.

D3.title: Availability and redundancy
D3.sum: Why two of something is only better than one if they can't fail together.
cards: Availability — the fraction of time something works: A = MTBF ÷ (MTBF + MTTR). MTBF is mean time between failures, MTTR mean time to repair, both in hours.
Two in parallel — if either one is enough: Apair = 1 − (1 − A)². One recorder at 0.994 is down about 52 hours a year; two independent ones, about 20 minutes.

The catch: independence. The pair formula only holds if nothing is shared. A shared UPS, a shared mixer, a shared network switch or the same software bug means both fail together — and a copy of one recorder's file is not a second recorder.
Who decides. For a court, what the official record must survive is the court's rule. Value engineering is the owner's call. The designer's job is the function statement and the numbers.

D4.title: Specs, submittals and 70 V lines
D4.sum: How a design becomes a product on site — and how to check the product is the design.
cards: Specification — what the building must have. Submittal — the contractor's proposed products. The designer reviews each submittal for conformance: does it meet the spec?
“Or equal” lets a contractor offer an alternative. It only works if the spec lists the salient characteristics — the measurable things that make a product equal.
70 V lines. Each loudspeaker has a transformer tap (3, 6, 10 W …). The amplifier channel must carry the sum: Ptaps = Σ Ptap ≤ 0.8 × Pamp — the 0.8 is a common design margin.
Who does what. The contractor chooses the products; the designer reviews against the spec; formal responses go back through the architect. The designer doesn't buy the product.

D5.title: Reverberation, speech and finishes
D5.sum: Why a beautiful room can swallow the words — and how to fix it without spoiling the room.
cards: Reverberation time. RT60 = 0.161 × V ÷ A — V is the room volume in m³, A the total absorption in m² (sabins: each surface's area × its absorption coefficient). RT60 is how long a sound takes to fall 60 dB.
Speech needs less. Long reverberation smears one syllable into the next. A playhouse for drama usually targets roughly 0.8–1.1 s at speech frequencies; music rooms run longer.
Where matters. Reflective surfaces near the stage send early reflections that help actors be heard; absorbers on the rear and upper walls kill late reflections and echoes.
Who owns what. The architect owns finishes; the fire engineer owns fire ratings; the acoustician and the director agree the target. Prove it by measurement after installation.

D6.title: Frequency coordination and RFIs
D6.sum: Why moving one wireless mic can break two others — and what an RFI answer owes the site.
cards: Intermodulation. Two transmitters near each other make new signals at fIM3 = 2f₁ − f₂ and 2f₂ − f₁ (third order). If one lands within about 0.1 MHz of another carrier, that mic hisses or drops.
A plan is a system. Change one carrier and every product that involves it moves. Recompute them all against every carrier — including the in-ear monitors.
Occupied spectrum — a TV service, a new local transmitter — is off-limits, with a guard band either side. What's usable is the regulator's and the venue coordinator's to say.
RFI. A Request for Information from site is answered by the designer. An answer is a design decision: numbers attached, second checker, filed with the drawings.

D7.title: Multicast, VLANs and IGMP
D7.sum: Why an audio network can make lights stutter — and the two settings that stop it.
cards: Multicast sends one stream to many receivers. Unless the switch knows who asked for it, it floods the stream to every port in the VLAN.
Link use. % = traffic ÷ link speed × 100. Forty audio flows at 6 Mb/s is 240 Mb/s — 240% of a 100 Mb/s lighting node's port.
IGMP snooping lets switches send each stream only to ports that joined it. It needs a querier — one device that keeps asking who's listening — or memberships time out and many switches flood again.
VLANs are boundaries: flooding stays inside its VLAN. Lighting control and audio streams on separate VLANs can't swamp each other. The network is the venue IT team's; the design says what's needed.

E1.title: Standards, variants and drift
E1.sum: Why a forty-site estate needs a standard — and why a standard alone can't tell design from drift.
cards: A room standard says what every room must do and how. It lets forty sites be supported as one — the same spares, the same training, the same fixes.

A regional variant is a recorded, approved difference: 230 V power, 50 Hz camera settings, a hearing loop a local code requires, a second language on the panel. It has a reason, an owner and an approval.
Drift is a difference nobody decided: a setting changed on a visit, a part swapped in a hurry, a preset added and never recorded. It has no reason on file, no owner, no end date.

Measure the right thing. % = part ÷ whole × 100 — but choose the part. Rooms working as designed (standard or recorded variant) over all rooms is conformance; unrecorded differences over all rooms is drift. That's the number to shrink.

E2.title: Update rings, inventories and exposure
E2.sum: How forty sites stay current — and how a whole region can fall off the map without a single failure.
cards: Update rings roll firmware out in stages: a pilot, then a site, then everything. Each ring is a list of devices — usually a query against the asset inventory.

A query that matches nothing fails silently. ‘0 targeted, 0 failed’ looks like success. Every rollout report should show how many devices it targeted, and every estate should report the devices in no ring.
Exposure. E = N × t — devices at risk times days at risk, in device-days. It turns ‘behind on updates’ into a number security can weigh against the risk of a hurried rollout.
A pause is a decision. Stopping updates because a release broke something can be exactly right — if it's recorded with a reason, an owner and an end date. Unrecorded, it becomes an island.

E3.title: Licenses, renewals and payback
E3.sum: Why one renewal date can take down forty sites — and how to argue for the fix in finance's own units.
cards: Co-terming puts many licenses on one renewal date. It can earn a discount and simplify paperwork. It also turns hundreds of small renewals into one payment that must not fail.
A grace period is a countdown, not a safety net: features switch off when it ends, wherever you are in the approval queue.
Reconcile against the inventory. Licenses outlive rooms. Matching every license to a room that exists finds the ones you pay for and nobody uses.

Payback. years = one-off cost ÷ savings per year — a reconciliation costing $18,000 that stops $43,500 a year of waste pays back in about 0.41 years, five months. Finance approves; you bring the numbers.

E4.title: Follow the sun: handovers and UTC
E4.sum: How three desks in three time zones keep one problem owned — and how a single ‘9:00’ can lose it.
cards: Follow the sun hands open work to the next region's desk as each working day ends, so someone awake always owns the problem. It only works if ownership moves with the note.

UTC. tlocal = tUTC + offset — Tahvara is UTC+8, Valmera UTC+1, Harrowmere UTC−5. 09:00 in Tahvara is 01:00 UTC and 20:00 the evening before in Harrowmere. Write the UTC time, with the customer's local time beside it.
A good handover names a person (not a desk), the state, the evidence, the next action and when it's due — and the receiver reads it back.
Status words matter. ‘Awaiting customer’ pauses most SLA clocks. If we owe the customer a call, we're not waiting on them — they're waiting on us.

E5.title: Sampling, polling and scheduled jobs
E5.sum: Why a monitor can report 100% while rooms fail every hour — and how to choose what it must see.
cards: Polling is sampling. A monitor that asks every T minutes sees only those instants. An outage shorter than T can fall between two polls.
How likely? P = min(1, d ÷ T) for an outage of length d if polls land at random times. An 8-minute outage and a 15-minute poll: about 53%. If T ≤ d, every outage is caught.

Phase lock. If the fault is scheduled (a job at five past every hour) and the polls are too (on the quarter hour), the monitor can miss it every single time. Event-driven alerts — the device reporting a restart the moment it happens — don't have that blind spot.
Start from a requirement. ‘See any outage of five minutes or more’ sets T ≤ 5. The server's budget sets the other side: devices × 60 ÷ T polls an hour. Then add an outcome check where the users are.

E6.title: Shared credentials, jump hosts and vendor lock-in
E6.sum: Why one convenient password is a risk to forty sites — and why you fix reach before keys.
cards: One password on 740 devices means one leak opens all of them, nobody can tell who used it, and nobody can revoke one person's access. % = part ÷ whole × 100 — 740 of 1,150 devices is 64% of the estate.

Reach first. A password only matters to someone who can reach the login. Put device management on its own VLAN, reachable only through a jump host where every person logs in with a named account and every session is recorded.

Then keys. Find everything that uses the password before you change it — integrations and scheduled scripts included. Give each a least-privilege service account from a secrets vault, then rotate to unique credentials site by site.

Lock-in is when only your supplier can log in, change or explain your systems. The contract should say the owner owns every credential and configuration — and there's an exit plan. Security owns access decisions; the story shows no attack technique.

E7.title: Fifty hertz, flicker and regional variants
E7.sum: Why kit and settings that are right in one country can be unsafe or wrong in another — and who decides.
cards: Mains differs by country: 120 V at 60 Hz in Harrowmere, 230 V at 50 Hz in Valmera and Tahvara (invented, but typical pairs). Many power supplies accept both; many don't. The rating plate says which.

Never improvise power. Converters and step-down transformers are the electrician's decision — sized, listed and installed by them. The fix for the wrong-voltage part is the right part. I = P ÷ V — the same 3,400 W is 14.8 A at 230 V and 28.3 A at 120 V.

Lights on mains flicker at twice the mains frequency — 100 Hz on 50 Hz power. fflicker = 2 × fmains. A camera exposure that holds a whole number of pulses (1/100 s, 1/50 s) averages them out; 1/60 s holds 1.67 and shows bands.
Regional variants are design. 230 V parts and a 50 fps profile for 50 Hz sites are recorded, approved differences — and the scanner should read them, not flag them.

E8.title: Interpretation, relay and captions
E8.sum: How three languages share one room and one stream — and why the captioner needs a clean channel too.
cards: Simultaneous interpretation. Interpreters in booths hear the floor through headphones — clean and undelayed — and speak into their own channel. Listeners in the room and on the stream pick a channel. Their working conditions (breaks, booth, feeds) are set with them.

One channel, one language. Stream tracks and the captioner's feed come from clean buses. R = channels × fs × b — an uncompressed mono channel at 48 kHz, 24-bit is 1.152 Mb/s; three compressed stream tracks at 128 kb/s add 384 kb/s.

Relay and retour. When the floor speaks a language a booth can't work from, that booth takes relay from another booth (a pivot language, usually English). That only works if a booth can work back into English — retour — and the system has a path for it.

Captions are a listener. A human captioner (CART) writes the English channel. Feed them two languages and the captions show both — or neither. Captions are an access requirement owned by the accessibility lead.

E9.title: Requirements, preferences and the exception register
E9.sum: How a standard for forty sites stays short, testable and honest about its exceptions.
cards: A testable requirement states an outcome and its test: ‘a remote participant can join from the panel in 60 s or less, 19 attempts in 20’. It can pass or fail in any room, whatever the brand.
A preference names a product, a color or a habit. It may be good advice — in guidance, not in the rule that decides pass or fail.

The register is part of the standard. Every exception has an owner, a reason and an end date (or is a permanent regional variant, approved). % = part ÷ whole × 100 — 38 of 96 exceptions past their date is 40% of the register quietly turned to drift.
Owned and versioned. A change board — regional leads, security, accessibility and the standard's owner — releases versions on a schedule; accessibility and security clauses belong to their owners.

E10.title: Cutovers, thresholds and alarm floods
E10.sum: How to move forty sites to one operations center without drowning the one alarm that matters.
cards: A cutover has a way back: checkpoints, rollback criteria written in advance, and the old system running in parallel until the new one has seen the same world for long enough.
Thresholds carry design. Ttimeout ≥ k × Tinterval — a device that sends a heartbeat every 120 s, allowed three misses, needs a timeout of at least 360 s. A 60 s timeout calls every gap a death.
Never mute everything. Silence the specific false alarm (one rule, one owner, an expiry) and keep everything else live. A bulk mute is how real alarms disappear.
Give owners countdowns. t = Ebatt × η ÷ Pload — a rough UPS runtime in minutes lets facilities decide what to shed. The UPS is theirs; the figure is rough.

F1.title: Backbones, loss budgets and bulletins
F1.sum: How a fiber route is chosen, proved — and kept in step with a building that's still changing.
cards: A backbone links the equipment rooms. Single-mode fiber loses about 0.4 dB per kilometer at 1310 nm and reaches kilometers; multimode reaches only a few hundred meters at 10 Gb/s.

The loss budget. L = α × d + nc × Lc + ns × Ls — fiber, connectors and splices add up in dB. Margin = the optics' budget − L. A spec asks for spare margin because connectors get dirty and repairs add splices.
Prove it with an OTDR trace (every joint, by distance) and a loss test, witnessed by the commissioning agent.
Bulletins change the drawings mid-build. The general contractor's document control sends them to every trade whose work they touch; a trade that never got one builds the old building.

F2.title: Temporary power, loads and switch-on surges
F2.sum: Why a breaker trips at seven every morning — and why the fix is a conversation with the electrician, not a reset.
cards: Temporary power is the electrician's: sized for a plan, protected by breakers, inspected. Using it for anything new starts with a load schedule — each load, its watts, its hours.
Running current. I = P ÷ V — 2,000 W at 120 V is 16.7 A, already over a 20 A breaker's 80% planning line (16 A).
Switch-on surge. Ipeak ≈ n × k × Irun — twelve LED drivers switched together can draw many times their running current for a few milliseconds. Staggering them is the electrician's usual fix.
Permanent isn't available until it's released. A new panel energized for one test isn't inspected or released for use. Only the electrician and the engineer of record decide when it is.

F3.title: Sequence, hold points and hatch schedules
F3.sum: Why the order of trades decides what can be fixed later — and how a value-engineering answer can open a hole in coverage.
cards: Sequence is the general contractor's: which trade works where, and when. Change it to save time, and every trade behind a surface must agree first.
Hold points stop work until a check is signed — ‘no ceiling closes until AV, electrical, mechanical and fire have signed above it’.
Hatch schedules follow the equipment. When an RFI moves or deletes a loudspeaker, the hatches must move with it — or someone opens a hatch onto nothing.

Coverage. D = 2 × (Hc − He) × tan(θ ÷ 2) — a 90° loudspeaker 3.8 m above ears covers a circle 7.6 m across (3.8 m radius). Delete one from a 5 m grid and the seats under it are 5 m from the nearest: a hole.

F4.title: Cable certification, crosstalk and pulling tension
F4.sum: What a PASS report proves — and what it can't, if the cable was damaged going in or the test never happened.
cards: Certification tests every installed link — length, loss, crosstalk — against a standard. The report is evidence only if each result belongs to the link it names: keep the tester's raw files.
NEXT (near-end crosstalk) is signal leaking between pairs. It's the first thing to fail when the pairs' twists are disturbed — by a kink, a crush or an over-hard pull.
Pulling tension has a limit (around 110 N for a typical 4-pair cable — check the data sheet). ratio = A ÷ B — 400 N on a 110 N cable is more than 3.6 times its rating.
Witness a sample. The commissioning agent watches a share of the tests live. % = part ÷ whole × 100 — five failures in a sample of twelve is about 42%. Installation methods stay the installer's.

F5.title: Heat loads, cooling and N+1
F5.sum: Why every watt in a rack becomes the mechanical engineer's problem — and how many cooling units ‘enough’ really is.
cards: Every watt becomes heat. QBTU/h = PW × 3.412 — 12,800 W of racks puts about 43,700 BTU/h into the room.
The heat schedule lists each rack's load (and what's expected to grow) so the mechanical engineer can size cooling. It's the AV designer's to issue — and to confirm received.
N+1. C × (N − 1) ≥ Q — with one unit out for maintenance or failed, the rest must still carry the load. Two 7 kW units can't; three can.
Whose decision: the mechanical engineer of record sizes and selects cooling; the GC sequences it; a fire-rated MER door is never propped open to cool a room.

F6.title: Firmware at scale: versions, staging and update paths
F6.sum: How to bring four hundred endpoints onto one firmware without touching the show network — or bricking the first twenty.
cards: Know the split before you touch it. % = part ÷ whole × 100 — 180 of 400 decoders on 3.8 is 45% of the fabric. The controller's inventory tells you which ones, by shipment.
Stage, don't push. Devices being updated go on a staging VLAN, away from the production network and anything else sharing it — here, the lighting console that should never have been on VLAN 60.

Read the update path. Release notes often say which versions must be passed through. Update one endpoint first; then batches you can verify. T = Σ (count × time each) — 9 batches × 2 hops × 6 min = 108 min.

Whose decision: the AV contractor updates the endpoints; the network contractor changes switches and VLANs; the lighting contractor owns the lighting network. Maya specifies the version and the method.

F7.title: Overhead: owners, loads and what you do from the ground
F7.sum: Why a loudspeaker cluster goes up only when three other people say so — and what a design lead does meanwhile.
cards: Three owners overhead. The structural engineer approves what a hang point may carry; the rigging contractor installs and flies the load; the general contractor controls access to anything unfinished. None of them is Maya.

Your number starts their work. The cluster's weight — boxes, frame and cables — goes to the structural engineer on the coordination register. Change it and the review re-opens: % = part ÷ whole × 100 — 480 kg to 640 kg is a third heavier.

Meanwhile, from the ground. A ground-stack on the deck, placed by the AV contractor to the maker's instructions, is a rehearsal system, not the design. ΔL = 20·log10(d2 ÷ d1) — 30 m instead of 22 m is about 2.7 dB quieter at the back.
Never: anyone on an unfinished catwalk, anyone under a load, or a ‘quick look’ at height. And no tuning the room on a temporary system.

F8.title: Fire alarm interfaces: sequence, fail-safe wiring and re-tests
F8.sum: How a fire alarm tells the AV system to get out of the way — and why nobody ever ‘just jumpers it’.
cards: The sequence of operations is the fire alarm designer's: what every system does in alarm. Here, program audio mutes so the voice evacuation message is heard. The fire marshal accepts it by watching it work.

The interface: a relay in the fire alarm system (the fire alarm contractor's) opens a contact; the DSP (the AV contractor's) watches that input and mutes. Normally closed means a cut wire looks like an alarm — the failure is safe and obvious.
Time it. T = Σ stage times — relay 0.05 s + DSP input scan 0.1 s + ramp 0.5 s = 0.65 s, inside the sequence's 2 s (illustrative).
Never: jumper, bypass or ‘temporarily’ disable anything in a life-safety interface. Any change in the chain — a re-patch, a firmware update, a tidy-up — re-opens the test.

F9.title: Punch lists: rate, risk and what ‘closed’ means
F9.sum: How to finish a building that won't all be finished — and tell the truth about which parts.
cards: Rate first. rate = count ÷ time — crews closing 15 a day for 19 days close 285. Against 412, that's 127 short. Say it on day one, not day nineteen.

Order by risk, not by ease. Life safety and accessibility are commitments. Then the show. Then what the people running the building will need — verified work and true drawings. Cosmetics last. The owner decides what is deferred, and to when.
‘Closed’ means seen. A trade's own sign-off isn't verification. Sample it: % = part ÷ whole × 100 — 3 of 10 not fixed is 30%, so about 18 of 60 ‘closed’ items are still open.
As-builts are part of the building. Drawings three revisions behind are a punch item, not paperwork: the venue's technicians will run the building from them.

F10.title: Opening under conditions: everything at once, in order
F10.sum: How to spend ninety minutes when everything the season taught arrives together — and half of it isn't yours.
cards: First what gates everything. Life safety gates occupancy: no marshal's signature, no audience. The fire alarm contractor repairs their circuit; you prove the mute with a timed retest before the marshal does.
Use what the design promised. L = α·d + nc·Lc + ns·Ls — the spare south pair loses 1.92 dB of a 6.2 dB budget. You knew that in week one.
Give owners numbers, not hands. I = P ÷ V — a preheat group of 16 × 108 W on 120 V is 14.4 A. Tove staggers it; you never touch the panel.
Contain, don't cure, tonight. The foyer decoders go to staging and show a still slide; the show doesn't need them. % = traffic ÷ link speed × 100 — the truck's feed takes the uplink to 77%.
Prove it where people are: the marshal's test, the back row, the hearing loop. Then write down every gap you're opening with — owned and dated.

G1.title: Remote access: accounts, owners and offboarding
G1.sum: Why the most dangerous account in a building is the one everyone forgot — and how to close it without cutting off the people who need it.
cards: Four kinds of account. Named (one person), shared (several people, one password), service (software, not people) and orphaned (its owner has gone). Only named and service accounts belong in a working building.
Measure the exposure. % = part ÷ whole × 100 and E = N × t — nine people who know a password for ninety days is 810 person-days; two of the nine have left (22%).
Build the new door before closing the old one. Named accounts through a jump host, each session approved and recorded, then the shared account is disabled — so nobody loses the ability to fix a show.
Whose decision: security (Solveig) owns accounts, credentials and any investigation. Maya brings the facts; she never uses someone else's login or deletes an account herself.

G2.title: Emergency messages: who starts them, who repeats them
G2.sum: Why a false ‘evacuate’ is dangerous in itself — and how to design signage that can help in an emergency without ever starting one.
cards: One origin. Evacuation messages come from the fire alarm's voice system and the incident commander's staff — the channels the fire alarm designer specified and the marshal accepted. Signage may repeat; it never originates.
A false alarm is a hazard. People move fast on stairs and at exits. % = part ÷ whole × 100 — 90 of 620 people moving is 14.5% of the lobby, on a false message.
Design the repeat, not the start. A read-only relay from the fire panel can put one fixed slide — ‘follow staff instructions’ — on the exit screens. No template library, no publish button.

Whose decision: the duty manager (incident commander) decides whether people move or stay and what paging says; the marshal accepts life-safety messaging. Nobody counter-messages on a channel that just lied.

G3.title: Roles and least privilege
G3.sum: How to turn one shared admin password into named people with the right buttons — without locking anyone out of their job.
cards: Shared means untraceable. A log that says ‘admin’ can't tell you who. % = part ÷ whole × 100 — five of fourteen people who know it no longer work here: 36%.

Roles, not people. Operator (recall show states), technician (levels, EQ, the loop), two named administrators (accounts, firmware), the integrator through security's jump host, and no access for everyone else.

Design the panel for the role. If an operator needs ‘Rehearsal’, it goes on the operator panel — and ‘Show’ always puts the room back, loop included. Borrowed passwords are a symptom of a missing button.
Check what matters. L = 20·log10(H ÷ Href) — a loop measuring 280 mA/m against a 400 mA/m reference is about 3 dB low. Security owns the accounts; Maya designs the roles.

G4.title: Independent paths for messages that must get through
G4.sum: Why ‘paging has priority’ isn't the same as ‘paging will be heard’ — and what independence means on a shared network.
cards: Count the load. % = traffic ÷ link speed × 100 — 900 guests × 1.2 Mb/s = 1,080 Mb/s on a 1,000 Mb/s uplink is 108%. Past 100%, something gets dropped; it doesn't ask what.
Priority is inside a box; independence is the path to it. The DSP ducks the program for paging, but packets lost on a saturated uplink never reach the DSP.
Separate, then prioritize. Paging on its own VLAN, guests on an isolated guest VLAN, priority queuing for paging on the uplinks and a cap on guest traffic — the network owner's design and change.
Whose decision: the network and every change to it are Raffa's; what paging says in an incident is the duty manager's. The fire alarm's voice evacuation system is separate again.

G5.title: Records as evidence
G5.sum: What a commissioning record is for — and what to do when you find your own signature on one that isn't true.
cards: A PASS needs a file. % = part ÷ whole × 100 — 30 of 48 lines with test files is 62.5%. The other 18 are claims.
Patterns tell on made-up data. Real measurements scatter; eighteen results that all equal the design value to a tenth of a decibel weren't measured.
Own your part first. If your name is on a summary you didn't check, say so in writing before anyone asks. Then fix the record: retest, re-issue with exceptions, honest data to the manufacturer.
Plan the retest. rate = count ÷ time — 18 channels at 6 an hour is 3 hours, witnessed by the commissioning agent.

G6.title: Logs, clocks and evidence
G6.sum: How to turn three disagreeing logs into one timeline — without destroying what you're trying to read.
cards: Evidence first. Don't reboot, restore or ‘tidy’ a device you're investigating. Security exports logs and configuration read-only and records who handled them (chain of custody).
Convert every clock to UTC. tlocal = tUTC + offset — 07:10 UTC at UTC−5 is 02:10 local.
Measure the drift. drift = ppm × 10−6 × t — a clock 685 s slow after 120 days (10,368,000 s) is running about 66 ppm slow. Correct for it, then fix the time source.
Whose decision: the investigation and the evidence are security's; the time server and the network are Raffa's. Maya builds the timeline from the facts.

G7.title: Segmentation and allowed flows
G7.sum: How to split a flat AV network by purpose without breaking the show — and who owns each piece.
cards: Measure how flat it is. % = part ÷ whole × 100 — 212 of 340 ports on the default VLAN is 62%: everything can reach everything.
Segments by purpose. Control, signage, paging, guest, a vendor landing that reaches only the jump host. Devices that don't need to talk don't share a segment.

Then the doors. Every flow the system needs between segments goes on a written list — from, to, what, why, owner. Everything not on the list is blocked. Missing one breaks a feature; that's why it's tested in a window with a rollback.
Whose decision: Raffa owns the network and every rule; security approves access policy; Maya names what the AV systems need.

G8.title: Tabletop exercises and incident roles
G8.sum: How to find the gaps in an incident plan around a table, before a full house finds them for you.
cards: One incident commander. The duty manager decides whether people move or stay and what paging says. Everyone else brings facts and owns a lane: security the account and evidence, facilities the power, communications the public words, AV the systems.

Time the plan. T = Σ (count × time each) — detect 60 s + decide 90 s + blank the screens 45 s + page the house 30 s = 225 s. The exercise took 780 s, mostly arguing about who could reach the off switch.
Injects find the gaps. A video going viral, a chief executive demanding every plug pulled, a second screen group — each tests who decides and who acts.
Write by role, two deep. A step that names one person fails the night they're away. Name the role, train two per shift, rehearse twice a year.

G9.title: Blameless reviews, owners and risk
G9.sum: How to turn a season of findings into owned, funded fixes — without making anyone the scapegoat.
cards: Count the ownerless. % = part ÷ whole × 100 — seven of nine findings (78%) had no named owner. That, not any one person, is the finding.
RACI. For every system: who is Responsible for the work, who is Accountable for the outcome, who is Consulted, who is Informed. ‘I thought that was yours’ ends here.
Score the risks. R = L × I — a shared vendor login is likely (4) and severe (5): 20. A scuffed cover plate: 1. Fund by score, inside the budget.
Accept the rest in writing. What isn't funded goes on the risk register, accepted by its owner — here the board and Odile — with a date to look again.

G10.title: When every screen lies: trusted paths and incident command
G10.sum: How the season's quiet fixes decide a loud night — and what each person does in the first five minutes.
cards: First, what can be trusted. The screens are lying; paging and the fire interface are independent and clean. Tell the incident commander that — she decides and speaks.
Darken the liar at its power, not its brain. Facilities cut the signage controllers on her instruction; the CMS server stays untouched because it's evidence.

Close the door through its owners. Security keeps the logs, then disables the account with the vendor; the network owner blocks one route — never a pulled plug. T = Σ stage times — detect 30 s + decide 40 s + page 30 s = 100 s.
The review starts the same night. Blameless, in UTC, with owners — beginning with the account nobody inventoried.

T1.title: Clocks: one leader, everyone follows
T1.sum: Why two clocks that are ‘both perfectly good’ still click — and how to read a fault that keeps time.
cards: Every sample happens on a tick. A converter takes 48,000 samples a second because a clock tells it when. When two devices pass audio between them, they must share that clock — one leader, every other device a follower.

Two good clocks are still two clocks. No two crystals run at exactly the same rate. A difference of a few parts per million means one device slowly gets ahead; a small buffer hides it, until it fills and a block of samples is dropped or repeated — a sample slip, heard as a click.

A fault that keeps time is a clue. Clicks at a regular interval point at clocks, not cables. The reference has the relationship between buffer size, sample rate and clock difference t = B ÷ (fs × Δ) — choosing it, and saying why, is the skill.

Warnings are evidence. A lock warning means a device can't follow its leader. Silencing it by switching the device to its own clock hides the fault and keeps it. Whose decision: the studio and its gear are Hollis's; Esme's performance is hers — nobody asks her to sing shorter to dodge a fault.

T2.title: Rooms: modes, nulls and where you sit
T2.sum: Why a room can hide the bass from exactly one chair — and why an EQ can't give it back.
cards: Between two parallel walls, bass stands still. At certain frequencies sound bouncing between two walls reinforces itself into a standing wave — an axial mode. The first is set by the distance between the walls; the rest are whole-number multiples.

Where you sit decides what you hear. Each mode's pressure is highest at the walls. The odd ones (first, third …) cancel on the center line, so a chair in the exact middle hears holes in the bass. The reference has the relationship fn = n × c ÷ (2 × L) — which one you reach for, and why, is the skill.

EQ can cut a peak. It can't fill a null. A cancellation eats whatever you feed it: boosting it makes the rest of the room boom and works the woofers hard, while the chair stays hollow. Move the listener or the speakers; treat the room.

Ears and meters, together. Measure at the chair and a few spots around it, then check every mix on other systems and against reference tracks at matched loudness. Whose decision: the room and its purchases are Hollis's; wall and ceiling work is the builder's, to the acoustician's design.

T3.title: Phase and polarity at the drum kit
T3.sum: Why several good microphones on one drum can add up to a worse drum — and how to line them up.
cards: Polarity is a flip, not a delay. A mic under a snare faces the opposite way to the one on top: when the skin moves toward one, it moves away from the other. Added together they cancel at every frequency they share. Flipping one channel's polarity makes them push together.

Distance is a delay. Sound takes about 2.9 ms to travel a meter. A mic further away hears the same hit later; added to the close mic it makes a comb filter — notches at regular spacing. The reference has t = d ÷ c and f1 = 1 ÷ (2 × Δt). Which one first, and why, is yours to say.

Fix the geometry first. Make the overheads the same distance from the snare with a tape measure; keep other mics at least three times further from the snare than from their own drum (the 3:1 rule); only then delay close mics to line them up — and check everything in mono.
The player judges the sound. The kit and its sound are the drummer's. Ask before moving his drums; ask him to listen when you're done.

T4.title: Latency: what a performer can feel
T4.sum: Why milliseconds in the headphones change how someone sings — and how to take the computer out of the loop.
cards: The round trip. A singer's voice goes into a converter, waits in the computer's input buffer, goes through any plug-ins, waits in the output buffer and comes back out to her ears. Each piece adds time; the sum is the round-trip latency.

Choose the relationship that fits. The reference has buffer, sample rate and plug-in delay together t = 2 × B ÷ fs + tconv + tplug, and plain time-of-flight for a speaker across the room. Say which you need, and why.

Early and late at once. A singer hears herself instantly through her own head. A few milliseconds more in the headphones and the two copies comb — hollow; tens of milliseconds and she sounds late to herself. A player a meter from a wedge is used to about 3 ms.

Take the computer out of the loop. Direct monitoring — the mic to the cue mixer before the computer — gives a millisecond or two, however big the buffer is. Lookahead belongs on a master, never in a performer's ears. Record dry. Whose decision: who sings on the album is the artist's; stopping for her voice is hers too.

T5.title: Archives: formats, fixity and migration
T5.sum: Why a recording you can't open is the same as a recording you don't have — and what keeps one openable.
cards: A session file is instructions, not audio. It tells one program where each piece of audio goes. When that program retires, the instructions go with it. The safest thing to leave is every track exported as a plain Broadcast WAV, from bar 1, all the same length.
Know what you're looking for. The reference has the size of uncompressed audio S = N × fs × (b ÷ 8) × t and a plain share for what's missing. Which one answers which question is the skill.

Proof beats labels. ‘FINAL’ on a disc is a claim. A checksum recorded when a file is made proves later that a copy is bit-for-bit the same. Work on read-only copies, never the originals, and list what you couldn't recover rather than quietly replacing it.

Archives need a calendar. Three copies, one elsewhere; a fixity check every year; media and formats migrated before they die. Whose decision: the archive is Hollis's; reissue rights are the label's to clear with the artists; what happens to a lost part is the artist's call.

T6.title: Gain staging and loudness for delivery
T6.sum: Why ‘louder’ stops meaning louder on a playlist — and how to record and deliver with room to spare.
cards: Services normalize. A playback service measures each track's integrated loudness in LUFS and turns it to its own target. A master pushed louder is simply turned down further — keeping its squashed drums, losing nothing but dynamics.

Compare fairly. Louder always sounds ‘better’ for a moment, so compare versions at matched loudness. The reference has G = Ltarget − Lmeasured and the peak-headroom relationship; which one answers which question is yours to say.

True peaks and the encoder. Samples can sit below full scale while the waveform between them goes above it; lossy encoding can push peaks higher still. Delivery specs often ask for true peaks at −1 dBTP or below.

Record with room. At 24 bits there's roughly 144 dB between full scale and the noise — record with peaks around −10 dBFS and nothing is lost; a take clipped at 0 dBFS is damaged for good. Whose decision: the master's sound is the mastering engineer's and the artist's; the delivery spec is the label's.

T7.title: Hum, earth and safety
T7.sum: Where studio hum comes from, what you may fix yourself — and the one thing nobody ever touches.
cards: Two earths, one cable. Gear on different circuits can sit at slightly different earth potentials. Join them with an audio cable's shield and a small current flows along it — a ground loop, heard as hum at the mains frequency and its harmonics. A hard buzz means strong odd harmonics.
Choose the relationship that fits. The reference has harmonics fn = n × f0 for naming the buzz and current I = P ÷ V for the circuit plan. Say which you're using, and why.

What you may touch. A DI box's ground lift breaks the audio shield at one end — audio only. An isolation transformer in the audio line does the same. The mains protective earth is never lifted, bypassed or adapted away: it is what keeps a metal case from becoming live.

Whose decision. Circuits, outlets and earthing are the licensed electrician's; a mains-powered amp with a fault is repaired by a qualified technician. And a hum that stops with nothing changed is evidence — test the earth before anyone plays.

T8.title: Consent and custody of recordings
T8.sum: What a studio holds in trust, who decides what leaves the building — and how to keep a copy from becoming a leak.
cards: A performance belongs to the performer. Her contract says what the label may do with it. Anything beyond that — stems to a remixer, clips online, raw takes, training a voice model — needs her own yes, in writing, for that use (not legal advice).

The studio holds custody. That means choosing how files travel: links for named people, view-only where possible, with an expiry; watermarked review copies; a log of who opened what; and nothing raw leaving the building without the consent recorded.

Measure what's out of your hands. The reference has shares and rates — % = part ÷ whole × 100 — for how much of a leak you can account for. Which relationship tells the artist the truth, plainly, is yours to choose.

Whose decision. The performance and every new use of it: the artist's. The release and its delivery: the label's, under her contract. The studio's policies and file shares: the owner's. Chasing a stranger who has a copy: the label's lawyers — never the studio.

T9.title: Backups: 3-2-1, versions and restores
T9.sum: Why a mirror isn't a backup, why the upload can't keep up, and why nothing counts until it's been restored.
cards: 3-2-1. Three copies of anything that matters, on two kinds of storage, with one somewhere else. A fire, a flood or a thief takes everything in one building.

A mirror copies mistakes. Two drives holding the same data survive a dead drive — and delete a file on both the instant you delete it. Versioning keeps what was there before, for as long as you choose.

Can the copy keep up? The reference has the size of uncompressed audio and the transfer relationship t = S ÷ r (and so S = r × t). Which answers ‘will the upload keep up?’ and which answers ‘how long to restore?’ is the skill — with bits and bytes kept straight.

Restore, on a calendar. A green tick says a job finished. A restore test — a whole session brought back to another computer, opened, played and timed — says you have a backup. Whose decision: the studio's systems and spending are Hollis's; the files are the artists' work in his care.

T10.title: The last night: trust, time and whose call
T10.sum: How to run the worst night of a project calmly — by trusting what was built and tested, and handing each decision to its owner.
cards: Trust what you tested. On a loud night, the only systems you can rely on are the ones you proved on quiet days: the versioned backup you restored, the one clock you measured, the consent log the artist signed.

Size the danger before you act. A failing drive: stop writing, find what exists only on it, copy that first. The reference has t = S ÷ r and time budgets; which one tells you how long the danger lasts is the skill.
The performer decides about her voice. Show her the evidence — the comp sheet, what's already covered — and make stopping easy. Whether she sings again is hers.
‘She said yes on the phone’ isn't a yes. If the consent log has no entry, the answer is no until she writes one. Deliver with a checksum manifest, and ask the receiver to confirm it matches.

U1.title: Operations rooms: change windows and handovers
U1.sum: Why a room that runs around the clock needs changes on a calendar the director signs — and a handover that survives a dark screen.
cards: A room with no quiet hour. An operations center in an activation never sleeps. Any automatic update, restart or ‘maintenance’ has to happen in a change window the room's owner approves — and never during an activation.

Clocks tell stories. A device may keep UTC while people think in local time. The reference has tlocal = tUTC + offset and a plain time budget; choosing which one explains a daily 07:00 restart, and which one sizes its cost, is the skill.

The handover is the most fragile moment. Two shifts, one picture, a few minutes. If the picture lives only on the wall, a dark wall loses the handover. A written handover brief — situation, pending actions, resources, hazards, who's who — survives anything.
Whose decision. The room, its procedures and its change windows: the director of emergency management. The wall controller and the network: county IT. Maya brings the evidence and the design.

U2.title: Failover, flapping and shared risk
U2.sum: Why automatic failover can make an outage worse — and why two carriers can still be one path.
cards: Detection is a trade. A router that declares a link dead after a few missed heartbeats fails over in seconds. The reference has Ttimeout ≥ k × Tinterval for detection; choosing it — rather than the availability sum — is the first judgment.

Flapping. A link that keeps dropping and returning drags an eager failover back and forth. Every switch costs the sessions riding on it. A hold-down timer keeps traffic on the backup until the main path has stayed clean for minutes, not seconds.
Two only counts if they fail separately. Apair = 1 − (1 − A)2 assumes independence. Two carriers in one conduit over one bridge share a single risk — the flood that takes one takes both.

Whose decision. The network and its timers: the county's network owner. The carriers' cables: the carriers. A new radio path: the radio shop, under license, with a certified tower crew — nobody else climbs. The money: the director.

U3.title: Radio interoperability: patches, plans and intermod
U3.sum: Why agencies that each work perfectly can't hear each other — and how two transmitters can make a third.
cards: Every agency owns its channels. Fire, law, EMS and public works each have their own channels or talkgroups. An interop patch joins them through a gateway when a plan says so — and a net control dispatcher runs the joined channel so it doesn't become everyone at once.

Transmitters on one mast mix. Strong signals meeting in anything non-linear make new ones. The reference has fIM3 = 2f1 − f2 and 2f2 − f1; choosing it is how you find a frequency nobody transmitted. A product on a receive frequency means desense.
A patch in one head isn't a plan. The plan is written: which talkgroups join for which incident, who's net control, how it's tested and when. It lives in the radio room and the EOC plan.

Whose decision. Frequencies, licenses, transmitters, the gateway and the mast: the radio systems manager — towers only with a certified crew. Each talkgroup and who speaks on it: its agency. Which patch runs in an activation: the director, through the plan.

U4.title: Verbatim: warnings, relays and languages
U4.sum: Why an official warning must arrive in its owner's words — in every language — and where the county's own voice belongs.
cards: The words are the warning. ‘Move to higher ground now’ and ‘flooding possible’ are different instructions. An agency's warning is relayed verbatim, with the agency's name and time. The county's own guidance goes in a separate, labeled message.

Time the chain. Receive, check the source, relay, caption, translate. The reference has a time budget T = Σ (count × time each) and plain differences; choosing them shows where minutes go — and which step changed the meaning.

Every language, prepared before the storm. Translating a warning in the moment — by machine or by a busy colleague — changes it. Qualified translators write templates for every standard warning in advance; the director approves them; a live interpreter covers briefings.

Whose decision. The warning: the issuing agency. Evacuations: the director of emergency management. The county's own words: the PIO. Captions and interpretation: the accessibility lead. The relay system and its templates: Maya's design.

U5.title: Backup power: tests, transfer and time
U5.sum: How long a room really has when the mains goes — and why the test that causes a blip is the one that saves the day.
cards: Three parts, one chain. The UPS carries the room for the seconds (or minutes) until the generator runs and the automatic transfer switch moves the load. Any link can fail; only a load test proves all three together.
Runtime shrinks quietly. Loads grow and batteries age. The reference has t = Ebatt × η ÷ Pload and plain power sums; choosing them tells you what the room really has today, not what the label said.
Plan to shed. A load-shed plan lists what switches off first — break room, printers, half the wall — so the UPS carries what matters for longer.

Whose decision. The generator, the transfer switch and the UPS: facilities. When a test runs: the director, with facilities. Maya checks the numbers, writes the load-shed plan with the room and never touches the power.

U6.title: Public briefings for everyone
U6.sum: What a live briefing needs so that everyone it's for can follow it — and how to check it before the camera light goes red.
cards: Every audience is an audience. A second language on its own channel, the sign-language interpreter always in the picture, captions carrying the words, partners fed at their loudness, speech in time with lips. Missing any one of them shuts someone out.
Choose the relationship. The reference has G = Ltarget − Lmeasured for partners' loudness and Daudio = Lvideo − Laudio for lip sync; which answers which complaint is the skill.

Fix live, then fix the system. Keep a live briefing live — routes and framing can be corrected on air. Then make it impossible to repeat: a pre-briefing checklist, run by a trained operator, signed off by the accessibility lead.
Whose decision. Captions, interpretation and how they're shown: the accessibility lead. What the county says: the PIO, with the director. The stream path, the delays and the levels: Maya's design.

U7.title: Fatigue, rosters and the only one who knows
U7.sum: Why the person who stays longest isn't the safest — and how an operation stops depending on any one of them.
cards: Judgment wears out. Past a long shift, people make the errors they would catch in others: the wrong channel, the wrong number, the step skipped. A roster exists to stop that before it happens.

Put a number on it. The reference has shares and time budgets — % = part ÷ whole × 100 and T = Σ (count × time each). Which tells you how far past the limit you are, and which tells you how long a proper handover takes, is the skill.
The only one who knows is a single point of failure. If a system can only be run by one person, the system is broken — however good the person is. Runbooks and two trained people per shift fix it.

Whose decision. The roster and who works when: the director of emergency management. The gateway: the radio systems manager, run by trained people. Going home at the end of a shift: not heroic — the job.

U8.title: Partners, visitors and the operations network
U8.sum: How a room full of agencies, contractors and visitors keeps its operations network for operations — without making anyone's work harder.
cards: Every port is a door. A live network port at a desk lets whatever is plugged into it onto that network. Unused ports are switched off; used ones check what's connected; a new device raises an alert.

Make the right path the easy one. Partners need the internet and a way to share files. A partner network — internet only, marked jacks at every desk — and a scanned file-transfer service mean nobody needs the operations network.
Size it honestly. The reference has t = S ÷ r for the transfer and shares for the exposure. Choosing them tells you what the contractor actually saved — and how many doors were open.

Whose decision. The operations network and its ports: county IT. Access and any review of what the laptop did: county IT's security officer. A partner's laptop: its owner. Maya asks, records and designs — she doesn't seize anyone's device.

U9.title: After-action: from findings to owners, money and signatures
U9.sum: How to turn two storms' worth of lessons into a plan that actually changes the next storm.
cards: Blameless, one timeline. Put every finding on one timeline, in one clock, and ask what the system made easy to get wrong — not who got it wrong.
Owners and dates. A finding without an owner is a finding nobody will fix. Each one gets a person, a department and a date.
Money by risk. The reference has R = L × I to rank and shares to show what a budget retires; choosing them is how you explain the plan to people who control the money.
Accept the rest, in writing. What isn't funded goes on the risk register, and its owner signs the acceptance. Whose decision: the plan, the spending and every acceptance are the director's.

U10.title: The mission room: everything at once, and you are a node
U10.sum: How a room holds when every part of it is under stress — and why the person running it is part of the system.
cards: Trust first. Tell the director what can be trusted and what can't — the separate path, the written plans, the templates. She decides; you bring facts.

Use the separate path before the shared one fails. A crossing under water in half an hour is a deadline, not a forecast: t = d ÷ v. Wendell routes; the radio shop owns the link; nobody goes near the bridge or the tower.
Words belong to owners. The agency's warning goes out verbatim, in both languages, captioned; a rumor is answered with the owner's facts in the PIO's words; evacuations are the director's.

You are a node. Fatigue is a failure mode the roster manages. Know your minutes — t = E × η ÷ P for the UPS, T = Σ stage times for the handover — and hand the room over in writing, read back and signed, before the hour you know you make mistakes.

W1.title: Exceptions: record, expire, escalate — or promote
W1.sum: How a principal reads the differences between a standard and its rooms, and turns each one into a decision someone owns.
cards: Every difference is evidence. A room that differs from the standard tells you something: the standard doesn't fit, someone was in a hurry, or someone found a better way. The reference has % = part ÷ whole × 100 to size the gap and rates to compare rooms fairly; choosing which, and saying why, is the skill.
Owner, reason, risk, expiry. An exception without an expiry is drift with paperwork. Each one is renewed on purpose, brought back to standard, or changes the standard.
Some differences are boundaries. A disabled fire-alarm mute input isn't a preference. It goes to the site's facilities team and its fire-alarm contractor the same day — nobody else re-enables it.
Some differences are better. When an exception outperforms the standard, promote it: test it elsewhere, then take it to the change board. The standard is the CIO's.

W2.title: Lifecycle: reserves, cliffs and one page
W2.sum: How to turn the age of an estate into a decision the board can make before anything fails.
cards: Every room has a birthday. Install date, replacement cost, planned life and each part's end-of-support date. Without them, ‘is the budget enough?’ has no answer.
The reserve. The reference has R = C ÷ L: replacement cost over life gives what to set aside each year. It's an average — and averages hide cliffs.
Cliffs and staggering. Equipment bought in one wave ends in one wave. Bringing some forward and deferring some — with the risk accepted in writing by its owner — flattens the bill.
One page. Age, cost, risk and a schedule, every year. The money and every acceptance are the CIO's and the board's.

W3.title: Staged rollouts and the right to stop
W3.sum: Why every change reaches one room before sixty — and why the most junior person must be able to say no.
cards: Blast radius. A change pushed to everything at once can break everything at once. The reference has % = part ÷ whole × 100 to size what a change can reach, and T = Σ stage times to plan how long a staged rollout takes.
Stages. A lab room, then one room per region, then 10%, then all — each stage soaked and checked before the next. Slow is the point.
Stop-work authority. Anyone can stop work they believe is unsafe or unapproved. It only exists if it's written into the standard, built into the tools, and backed by leaders when it's used.
Blameless. The senior who relayed the pressure isn't the villain; a tool that made the dangerous thing one click is the finding. The standard and the change board are the CIO's.

W4.title: Runbooks that work without their author
W4.sum: Why the best runbook is the one a junior has already run — and why it names roles, never people.
cards: Time to restore. The reference has T = Σ stage times: detect, diagnose, restore, added together. Each stage is a design choice — an alert, a decision tree, a tested backup.
Drilled by the users. A runbook written by an expert has steps the expert skips without noticing. Juniors running it in a drill find them. Fix what the drill finds within a week.
Roles, not names. ‘Call Tobin’ fails the day Tobin is on leave. ‘Call the Tahvara on-call engineer’ works as long as the rota does.
Keep the backup warm. A backup path tested monthly is a step in a runbook; a spare in a cupboard is a project at 3 a.m. The event is the producer's; the network is its owner's.

W5.title: Knowledge coverage and decision records
W5.sum: How to measure what would break if someone left — and how to keep the ‘why’ from leaving with them.
cards: List the tasks, count the people. For each critical task: who can do it unaided today? The reference has % = part ÷ whole × 100 to turn a list into a number the CIO can track down to zero.
Count yourself. The architect is on the list. Tasks only you can do are the first to hand off.
Pairs, proven by doing. A second person is trained and signed off by doing the task — with the expert credited, not replaced.

Decision records. What was decided, why, what else was considered, who owns it — kept with the standard. The next person can change a decision; they shouldn't undo one by accident. Succession is the CIO's to require.

W6.title: Outcome monitoring and synthetic tests
W6.sum: How to know a room is failing before the people in it tell you — and who should find out.
cards: Devices vs outcomes. A ping proves a device is on. It doesn't prove a meeting can start, or that the far end can hear. Outcome monitoring tests what people experience.

Synthetic tests. A scheduled test call in an empty room: join, play a tone out and hear it back, check the far end, check captions. The reference has t̄ = T ÷ 2 — a failure waits on average half the interval — and % = part ÷ whole × 100 for the share users find first.
Alerts to roles. An alert goes to the regional on-call role on the rota — someone who can act now — never to the architect's inbox.
One number that matters. Track the share of incidents users report first, every week. When monitoring works, it falls. The network is its owner's; the change board the CIO's.

W7.title: Weighted decisions and the loudest voice
W7.sum: How to rank competing claims so the answer comes from evidence, not volume — and who decides.
