LAB-SF-01.title: Rebuild the stream mix before doors
LAB-SF-01.brief: The stream mix is empty and the pulpit mic is barely there. Patch the three sources into the stream bus, then set the pulpit preamp so every source arrives at −18 dB. Both outputs must land between −18 and −10 dB.

math.q: The pulpit mic arrives at −50 dB. How much preamp gain puts it at −18 dB?
Three equal sources at −18 dB each are summed on a bus. What level does the bus read? (1 decimal)
math.why: Equal uncorrelated sources add as powers: +4.8 dB for three.

LAB-SF-01.success: Pulpit preamp at +32 dB, all three sources into the stream bus: the stream and the room both read about −13 dB. The stream now has its own complete mix.
LAB-SF-01.timeoutWhy: Do the gain math first (target − source), then patch one source at a time and watch the stream meter.

LAB-SF-02.source: S01E06 · Nobody Could Hear the Reading
LAB-SF-02.title: Give the listening system its own mix
LAB-SF-02.brief: SPOKEN WORD mutes AUX 4 — and the listening transmitter hangs off AUX 4. Build AUX 6 from all four sources, feed the transmitter from AUX 6, and set AUX 6's gain so the transmitter reads −12 dB (±1).

math.q: AUX 6 sums four sources at −20 dB each. What does the bus read before any gain? (1 decimal)
How much AUX 6 gain brings that to −12 dB?

LAB-SF-02.success: AUX 6 carries speech and music, is never muted by a scene, and hits the transmitter at −12 dB. An output with its own intent.
LAB-SF-02.timeoutWhy: Tap a source, then AUX 6, for each of the four; then AUX 6 → Listening TX; then the gain.

LAB-SF-03.title: Gain-stage the chorus
LAB-SF-03.brief: The vocal's chorus peaks hit the preamp at −24 dB — and the preamp is set for a whisper. Set the preamp so chorus peaks sit at −6 dB (6 dB of headroom), then use the fader to put the main at −12 dB. Nothing may clip.

math.q: Chorus peaks arrive at −24 dB. What preamp gain puts them at −6 dB?
With the preamp output at −6 dB and a flat EQ, what fader setting gives −12 dB at the main?

LAB-SF-03.success: Preamp +18 dB, fader −6 dB: the chorus has headroom and the room hears the same level. Fix it at the earliest stage, then match with the fader.
LAB-SF-03.timeoutWhy: Headroom is set at the preamp. The fader only sets how loud it is in the room.

LAB-SF-04.title: Build the presenter's mix-minus
LAB-SF-04.brief: The presenter's earpiece carries her own voice — late, off the stream return. Rebuild her feed so she hears the host and the video playback, and never herself or the delayed return. Keep the earpiece between −20 and −10 dB.

targets.whyNot: Hearing yourself late breaks fluent speech (delayed auditory feedback).

math.q: The stream return arrives 0.4 s late. How many samples is that at 48 kHz?

LAB-SF-04.success: Mix-minus: everything the presenter needs, minus herself and anything late. The template now has a rule, not an assumption.
LAB-SF-04.timeoutWhy: Remove the two wires that shouldn't be there (tap the line), then add the host.

LAB-SF-05.title: Choose the stream's tap point
LAB-SF-05.brief: Input taps ignore the room's mutes (the hot wings mic is on air); post-fader taps follow the room's faders (the band vanishes online). Build the stream stems from after processing and after the mutes, but before the faders. Stream between −18 and −12 dB.

targets.whyNot: A mic the room muted must never reach 4,000 people.
targets.whyNotVia: The room's faders balance the room, not the stream; input taps skip the mutes.

math.q: After processing, the presenter is at −18 dB and the band at −16 dB. What does the stems bus read? (1 decimal)
On the input tap the band was at −12 dB and the presenter at −24 dB. How many times louder (voltage) was the band? (2 decimals)

LAB-SF-05.success: Pre-fader, post-mute, after processing: the room's mutes count online; the room's faders don't. The stream finally has a mix someone approved.
LAB-SF-05.timeoutWhy: Cut INPUT TAP → Stream. Feed STREAM STEMS from the processing blocks, then STEMS → Stream.

LAB-SF-06.title: Thirty seconds: get the CEO's slides to the far end
LAB-SF-06.brief: An overnight update switched the capture device to input 1 (the room computer's blank desktop). Ray's label says IN 2 = TABLE CUBBY. Patch the CEO's laptop through the capture device so the far end sees it.

targets.whyNot: The investors are staring at a blank desktop.

LAB-SF-06.success: IN 2 through the capture device: the far end sees the deck. A five-year-old label beat a three-minute reboot.
LAB-SF-06.timeoutWhy: Tap IN 1 → Capture to cut it, then IN 2 → Capture.

LAB-EQ-01.title: Notch the ringing wedge
LAB-EQ-01.brief: A wedge is ringing. The analyzer's peak is in bin 116 of a 2,048-point measurement at 48 kHz. Find the frequency, then place a narrow cut that brings the ring down to ≤ +3 dB without cutting more than 3 dB an octave away.

math.q: FFT bin to frequency: bin × sample rate ÷ N. What frequency is bin 116? (Hz)
Q = center frequency ÷ bandwidth. What Q gives a 300 Hz-wide cut at that frequency? (1 decimal)

LAB-EQ-01.success: A narrow cut exactly on the ring. The rest of the voice is untouched — physics first, then a surgical notch.
LAB-EQ-01.timeoutWhy: Do the bin math, type the frequency into the band, pull the gain down, then raise Q until only the ring moves.

LAB-EQ-02.title: Seat 13: two arrivals, one delay
LAB-EQ-02.brief: At seat 13 the fill's reflection arrives 1.7 m of path after the direct sound. Watch the comb filter, then dial the delay that lines the two arrivals up at this seat. (In the story the real fix was a re-aim — a delay only aligns one seat. That's the lesson.)

math.q: Path difference 1.7 m at 343 m/s. What is the time difference in ms? (2 decimals)
Before alignment, where is the first notch? (Hz)

LAB-EQ-02.success: Aligned at seat 13 — and only seat 13. Seat 12 has a different path difference, so no single delay or EQ fixes ten seats. Geometry problems need geometry fixes.
LAB-EQ-02.timeoutWhy: Convert meters to milliseconds first; then set that exact delay.

LAB-EQ-03.source: S02E10 · Festival in the Rain (delay towers)
LAB-EQ-03.title: Time the delay tower
LAB-EQ-03.brief: The delay tower is 30 m behind the main PA. Without delay, people near it hear everything twice. Set the tower's delay so it lines up with sound arriving from the stage.

math.q: How long does sound take to travel 30 m? (ms, 2 decimals)

LAB-EQ-03.success: The tower now fires when the stage's sound arrives: one show, not an echo.

LAB-CAM-01.title: Clean the LED wall on camera
LAB-CAM-01.brief: Bands roll across the wall and the zoomed shot swims with moiré. The presenter stands 2.3 m in front of the wall; the wall is 11.8 m from the camera. Fix focus, iris, shutter and the wall's frame-rate family. The system runs 59.94p.

math.q: How far from the camera is the presenter? (m)
Wall at 59.94 Hz with an 8× refresh, shutter 1/60: how many refresh cycles fit in one exposure? (3 decimals)

LAB-CAM-01.success: Wall in the building's family, a whole-cycle shutter, focus on the person and an open iris so the wall goes soft. Two problems, two different fixes.
LAB-CAM-01.timeoutWhy: Timing first (wall family + shutter), then space (focus on the person, open the iris).

LAB-CAM-02.title: The rental camera that stutters
LAB-CAM-02.brief: The rental IMAG camera came from a 50 Hz tour: it judders on the 59.94p switcher and the presenter is soft. The presenter is 2.4 m in front of a scenic wall that is 16.4 m away. Match the system and pull focus.

math.q: Presenter distance from the camera? (m)
At 59.94p, how long is one frame? (ms, 2 decimals)

LAB-CAM-02.success: One frame-rate family across every source, focus on the person. The switcher stops repeating and dropping frames.
LAB-CAM-02.timeoutWhy: Camera frame rate must equal the system's. Then shutter and focus.

LAB-CAM-03.title: The meeting-room camera that looks wrong
LAB-CAM-03.brief: The room camera wakes in a default mode: wrong frame rate for the room system (29.97) and focused on the back wall. The presenter sits 3.1 m from the camera; the display wall behind her is 5.6 m away.

math.q: How far behind the presenter is the display wall? (m)

LAB-CAM-03.success: Room system rate, focus on the person, wall soft. The camera finally matches the room it lives in.
LAB-CAM-03.timeoutWhy: Match the room's frame rate first, then focus on the person, then fix the wall banding with a whole-cycle shutter.

LAB-NET-01.title: Stop the flood on the booth switch
LAB-NET-01.brief: The overflow video (multicast, 400 Mb/s) shares VLAN 10 with the stream encoder, and the switch floods it everywhere. Isolate it on VLAN 30 (valid 198.18.2.x fixed addresses outside the auto range) or turn on multicast snooping — and keep the office network (Priya's) out of it.
forbid: The office network runs door locks and kiosks; it isn't ours.

math.q: On a 1,000 Mb/s port, what percentage does the 400 Mb/s flood use?

LAB-NET-01.success: Video on its own VLAN (or snooped), the encoder hears only what it asked for, and the office network stays Priya's.
LAB-NET-01.timeoutWhy: Either tick multicast snooping for VLAN 10, or move both video devices to VLAN 30 and give them 198.18.2.x addresses.

LAB-NET-02.title: Gates at nine: untangle the festival network
LAB-NET-02.brief: Someone patched the ticket scanners into the AV network, and the stream encoder's fixed address sits inside the automatic range. Put scanners back on the ticket VLAN, keep AV and tickets separate, and give the encoder a fixed address the automatic range can never hand out.
forbid: AV and ticketing are separate networks with separate owners.

math.q: How many usable host addresses are in a /24?
Automatic assignment hands out .10–.250. How many usable addresses are left above it (.251–.254)?

LAB-NET-02.success: Scanners home, AV separate, and the encoder on .251–.252 — above the automatic range, so nothing can collide with it. (In the story nobody wrote this down. You just did.)
LAB-NET-02.timeoutWhy: Scanners → VLAN 50 first. Then move the encoder out of .10–.250 to an unused .251–.252.

LAB-NET-03.title: Nineteen minutes: the moved port
LAB-NET-03.brief: A desk move put the conferencing computer's port on the workstation VLAN, and the audio bridge was given an address outside its /26. Get the DSP → bridge → conferencing computer path onto the AV audio VLAN with valid addresses.

math.q: How many usable hosts in a /26?
What is the last usable address's final number in 198.18.1.0/26?

LAB-NET-03.success: Port 14 back on AV AUDIO, the bridge inside .1–.62: the CEO's voice reaches everyone outside the room. And the move gets a change record.
LAB-NET-03.timeoutWhy: Two fixes: the conferencing computer's VLAN, and the bridge's address (must be .1–.62 and not already used).

LAB-DMX-01.title: Clear the phantom flicker
LAB-DMX-01.brief: Eight fixtures on one line. Fixture 6 is an 18-channel fixture; the rest use 16. There's an address overlap, a microphone-cable extension and no terminator. Fix all three.

math.q: Fixture 6 starts at 81 and uses 18 channels. What is its last channel?
Fixture 7 (16 channels) moves to 99. Where must fixture 8 start at the earliest?

LAB-DMX-01.success: No overlaps, data cable on every link, a terminator at the end: the line is clean, and Elias can sign against evidence.
LAB-DMX-01.timeoutWhy: Do the address math, then fix the cable type and the terminator.

LAB-PWR-01.title: Plan the Easter rebalance for the electrician
LAB-PWR-01.brief: Everything is on stage-left circuit C3 and it tripped. Plan a spread across C3, C5 and C7 that keeps each circuit under 80% of its 20 A breaker at 120 V. This is a worksheet for Andre (the licensed electrician) — he does the actual work.

loads.label: Keyboard rig
loads.onlyWhy: its cable only reaches stage left

loads.label: Monitor amps
loads.onlyWhy: they sit downstage

loads.label: Pedalboards
loads.onlyWhy: stage left

math.q: Total load is 2,600 W at 120 V. How many amps? (1 decimal)
What is 80% of a 20 A breaker?
How many watts is 16 A at 120 V?

LAB-PWR-01.success: Every circuit under 16 A. Hand the plan to Andre; he moves the loads and resets the breaker. You did the arithmetic; he opens the door.
LAB-PWR-01.timeoutWhy: Keyboard and pedals must stay on C3. Put bars where they fit under 1,920 W per circuit.

LAB-RF-01.title: Coordinate six wireless channels for city 3
LAB-RF-01.brief: Six transmitters in an illustrative 520–536 MHz window. The scan found two occupied ranges. Keep every carrier ≥ 0.4 MHz from the others, ≥ 0.1 MHz from any two-transmitter intermod product (2a − b), and off the occupied ranges.

math.q: Transmitters at 522.0 and 523.5 MHz: what is 2 × 522.0 − 523.5?

LAB-RF-01.success: Six clean carriers: no collisions, no intermod hits, off the occupied ranges. Now save the plan somewhere other than your laptop.
LAB-RF-01.timeoutWhy: Evenly spaced carriers make intermod land on each other. Spread them unevenly and watch the amber ticks.

PHY-S01E01.title: Two speakers, one seat
PHY-S01E01.brief: Main and fill both reach row 8. Slide along the row and change the frequency until the two arrivals cancel (−15 dB or lower). That's the hollow sound Dolores heard.

math.q: If the path difference is 1.7 m, where is the first notch? (Hz, 1 decimal)

history.title: Thomas Young and interference
history.body: In 1801 Thomas Young showed that light passing through two slits makes bands of bright and dark — waves adding and canceling. Sound from two loudspeakers obeys the same arithmetic. The hollow seats are Young's fringes, in air.

PHY-S01E01.success: Where the path difference is half a wavelength, the two arrivals cancel. Move a seat, and the notch moves.

PHY-S01E02.title: Why a wedge starts to howl
PHY-S01E02.brief: Every lap around mic → amp → wedge → mic multiplies the sound by the loop gain. Set a loop gain that is stable with at least 3 dB of margin (−6 to −3 dB).

math.q: At +1 dB per lap, how many times louder after 10 laps? (2 decimals)

history.title: Harold Black's feedback and Harry Nyquist's rule
history.body: Harold Black invented the negative-feedback amplifier on a ferry in 1927. Five years later Harry Nyquist published the rule for when a feedback loop stays stable. Every howling wedge is a loop that broke Nyquist's rule.

PHY-S01E02.success: Below 0 dB per lap the loop dies away; above it, it grows into feedback. Margin is safety.

PHY-S01E03.title: Hum is a chord
PHY-S01E03.brief: Hum is not one tone: it's the mains frequency plus harmonics. Build a buzzy square-ish wave from the 60 Hz fundamental by setting the 3rd, 5th and 7th harmonics to 1/3, 1/5 and 1/7.

math.q: What frequency is the 3rd harmonic of 60 Hz hum?

history.title: Joseph Fourier's sums of sines
history.body: In 1822 Joseph Fourier argued that any repeating wave is a sum of sine waves. That is why a hum that 'sounds like 60 Hz' can still ring at 180, 300 and 420 — and why a filter at one frequency rarely kills it.

PHY-S01E03.success: Odd harmonics at 1/n make the harsh, buzzy shape. Hum is a family of tones, not one.

PHY-S01E05.title: Current, heat and a 20 A breaker
PHY-S01E05.brief: At 120 V, find the largest load you can plan for one 20 A circuit without passing the 80% line (16 A). This is a planning number for the electrician, not a procedure.

math.q: 16 A at 120 V is how many watts?

history.title: Ohm's law and Joule heating
history.body: Georg Ohm published the relation between voltage, current and resistance in 1827. In 1841 James Joule showed that current heats a wire in proportion to the current squared — the heat a breaker is built to notice before the wire does.

PHY-S01E05.success: About 1,900 W is the planning ceiling for that circuit. Above it, the breaker is doing its job.
PHY-S01E05.goalWhy: the most you can plan under 16 A (80% of 20 A)

PHY-S01E06.source: S01E06 · Nobody Could Hear the Reading
PHY-S01E06.title: Reaching row 8
PHY-S01E06.brief: The listening transmitter needs 20 dB of margin at the receiver. Find how far away a receiver can sit with a person's body in the way.

math.q: Free-space loss at 50 m and 72 MHz: 20·log10(0.05) + 20·log10(72) + 32.44 = ? (1 decimal)

history.title: Maxwell predicts, Hertz proves
history.body: James Clerk Maxwell's equations of 1865 predicted invisible electromagnetic waves traveling at the speed of light. In 1887 Heinrich Hertz made sparks jump a gap across his lab and proved them. Dolores's receiver lives on that discovery.

PHY-S01E06.success: With the body in the way, stay within the distance that keeps 20 dB of margin.

PHY-S01E07.title: Why cameras see what eyes don't
PHY-S01E07.brief: A camera samples the world 30 times a second. Find a wheel speed where the camera sees the wheel frozen — the same trick that makes LED walls band.

math.q: A 6-spoke wheel filmed at 30 fps looks frozen if it turns one spoke-gap per frame. How many revolutions per second is that?

history.title: Nyquist, Shannon and the wagon wheel
history.body: Harry Nyquist (1928) and Claude Shannon (1949) showed that you must sample at least twice as fast as the fastest change or you'll see something false. Film audiences had already seen it: stagecoach wheels spinning backwards on screen.

PHY-S01E07.success: Sampling can freeze or reverse motion. The LED wall's pulses are a wheel the camera samples.

PHY-S01E09.title: Mix Sofia's warm white
PHY-S01E09.brief: The new fixtures make white from red, green and blue. Mix a warm white that matches the target.

math.q: On the mired scale (1,000,000 ÷ K), what is 3,200 K? (1 decimal)

history.title: Three colors make them all
history.body: Thomas Young proposed in 1802 that the eye senses color with three receptors; Hermann von Helmholtz developed the idea. In 1861 James Clerk Maxwell used three filtered photographs — red, green, blue — to make the first color photograph, of a tartan ribbon.

PHY-S01E09.success: Warm white: lots of red, less green, little blue. The eye adds light the way the fixtures do.

PHY-S01E10.title: Counting the storm
PHY-S01E10.brief: The storm's thunder travels to the sanctuary. On a 25 °C night, how long does sound take to cover 1 km? Set the air temperature, then check the time.

math.q: How long does sound take to travel 1,000 m at that speed? (s, 2 decimals)

history.title: Measuring the speed of sound
history.body: Marin Mersenne timed echoes and cannon fire in the 1630s. Newton calculated a speed in 1687 that came out too slow; in 1816 Pierre-Simon Laplace fixed it by realizing sound compresses air too fast for heat to escape. Warmer air carries sound faster.

PHY-S01E10.success: About 2.9 seconds per kilometer on a warm night: count from the flash to the rumble.

PHY-S02E02.title: Behind the steel frame
PHY-S02E02.brief: At the drop-out spot, the singer turns her back and stands behind the LED wall's steel frame. Turn both losses on and find the largest distance that still keeps 15 dB of margin.

math.q: Body (10 dB) plus frame (15 dB) together cost how many dB?

history.title: Hedy Lamarr and frequency hopping
history.body: In 1942 actress and inventor Hedy Lamarr and composer George Antheil patented a frequency-hopping scheme to keep radio-guided torpedoes from being jammed. The idea resurfaced decades later in the radios that surround every stage.

PHY-S02E02.success: Obstacles eat margin fast. Line of sight to the antenna is worth more than any new frequency.

PHY-S02E03.title: Why the beam's number matters
PHY-S02E03.brief: A 400 kg load hangs on a 6 m beam between two supports rated (illustratively) 250 kg and 200 kg. Find where the load can sit so neither support is overloaded. Real hangs are the rigger's and the engineer's decision.

math.q: If the load sits 2 m from the left support, how much does the right support carry? (kg, 1 decimal)

history.title: Archimedes and the lever
history.body: Archimedes worked out that a lever balances when weight times distance is equal on both sides — 'give me a place to stand and I will move the Earth.' Every structural rating Ben asks for is that same balance, with a safety factor added by an engineer.

PHY-S02E03.success: Where a load sits decides who carries it. Without the beam's rating, nobody can say it's safe.

PHY-S02E04.title: Cue 14's stage blue
PHY-S02E04.brief: The update changed cue 14's color. Rebuild Sofia's deep stage blue from the rehearsal video.

math.q: In an 8-bit channel (0–255), what fraction of full is 64? (3 decimals)

history.title: Newton's prism
history.body: In 1666 Isaac Newton split sunlight with a prism and then recombined the colors into white, showing that white light is a mixture. A lighting console mixing red, green and blue is running Newton's experiment backwards, every cue.

PHY-S02E04.success: Deep blue: almost no red, a little green, lots of blue. Cues store numbers; the eye sees mixtures.

PHY-S02E05.title: How late is too late?
PHY-S02E05.brief: Noor heard herself through a return that was 400 ms late — like hearing a wall 69 m away echo her voice. Set a temperature so sound crosses 137 m in 398–401 ms.

math.q: How far does sound travel (round trip) to make a 400 ms echo at 343 m/s, one way? (m)

history.title: Delayed auditory feedback
history.body: In 1950 engineer Bernard Lee found that hearing your own voice delayed by a fraction of a second makes fluent speakers stumble and stutter. Broadcasters built mix-minus feeds for decades before anyone could explain why they mattered so much.

PHY-S02E05.success: Hundreds of milliseconds of delay is an echo off a distant building — and it breaks speech.

PHY-S02E06.title: Two rooms, two reverbs
PHY-S02E06.brief: Half the ballroom (2,400 m³) rings for a keynote. Add absorption (drapes, audience) until RT60 is 0.9–1.1 s.

math.q: RT60 for V = 2,400 m³ and A = 250 m²? (2 decimals)

history.title: Symphony Hall
history.body: Boston's Symphony Hall, opened in 1900, was the first hall designed with Sabine's formula. Hotel ballrooms, built for dinners and dancing, rarely get that care — which is why every keynote in one sounds like a lecture in a swimming pool.

PHY-S02E06.success: People, drapes and carpet are acoustic treatment. A full room sounds different from a soundcheck.

PHY-S02E10.title: How far the PA reaches
PHY-S02E10.brief: The main PA makes 130 dB at 1 m (illustrative). Where in the field has it fallen to 94 dB — the point a delay tower must take over?

math.q: 130 − 94 = 36 dB. How many doublings of distance is that?
So how far from the PA? (m)

history.title: Faraday and the loudspeaker's ancestor
history.body: Michael Faraday showed in 1831 that a moving magnet makes current flow in a wire — and that current in a wire makes a magnet move. Every loudspeaker on a festival tower is Faraday's experiment, turned into air pressure.

PHY-S02E10.success: Sixty-four meters out, the PA has lost 36 dB. Past that, towers take over — timed to the stage.

PHY-S03E01.title: How strong is a room password?
PHY-S03E01.brief: Every room account got a new password policy. Choose a length and character set that give at least 60 bits of entropy (random passwords only).

math.q: Entropy = length × log2(set size). 10 characters from 62 symbols ≈ ? bits (1 decimal)

history.title: Shannon on secrecy
history.body: In 1949 Claude Shannon published the mathematics of secret communication, treating a key's strength as the number of possibilities an attacker must try. Every password policy that locked twelve rooms out on a Monday is a descendant.

PHY-S03E01.success: Length beats cleverness: each character multiplies the attacker's work.

PHY-S03E02.source: S03E02 · The Room That Hears Twice
PHY-S03E02.title: Echo is a loop
PHY-S03E02.brief: The far end's voice leaves the room speakers, enters the room mics and goes back: a loop. Set the loop's total gain so echoes die away quickly (−30 to −20 dB per lap), the job of an echo canceller.

math.q: Speakers make 70 dB at the mic position; the echo reaches the mic at 52 dB. What's the echo return loss? (dB)

history.title: Echo cancellers for the long line
history.body: When phone calls began bouncing off satellites in the 1960s, the extra delay made echoes unbearable. Engineers at Bell Labs built adaptive echo cancellers that learned the echo and subtracted it — the same job the room's processor does, and why two of them fight.

PHY-S03E02.success: Each lap the echo must shrink a lot. One canceller that has learned the room beats two that fight.

PHY-S03E03.title: The camera that looks at the back wall
PHY-S03E03.brief: The meeting-room camera (4 mm lens) woke up focused on infinity. Focus it on a person 3.1 m away.

math.q: For f = 4 mm and do = 3,100 mm, di = ? (mm, 3 decimals)

history.title: Kepler explains the eye
history.body: In 1604 Johannes Kepler showed that the eye's lens forms an upside-down image on the retina — the eye is a camera. Small meeting-room cameras use tiny focal lengths so that almost everything is in focus; the math is Kepler's.

PHY-S03E03.success: Tiny lenses barely move to focus, which is why room cameras seem 'always sharp' — until they aren't.

PHY-S03E04.title: The ceiling mic and the CEO
PHY-S03E04.brief: A ceiling mic hears the CEO from 0.8 m when she leans in, and from farther when she stands back. Find the distance where her level is 12 dB below the 1 m reference (86 dB → 74 dB).

math.q: 12 dB is how many doublings of distance?

history.title: Bell's first sentence
history.body: On 10 March 1876 Alexander Graham Bell spoke into his transmitter: 'Mr. Watson — come here — I want to see you.' The first words carried electrically needed him to lean close to the mouthpiece. Distance still decides who is heard in a town hall.

PHY-S03E04.success: Twice the distance, a quarter of the intensity: a CEO who steps back from the mic loses 6 dB per doubling.

PHY-S03E05.title: The dashboard that blinks at the wrong time
PHY-S03E05.brief: Monitoring samples each room every few minutes; a fault that comes and goes at the same rate can look like nothing at all. Freeze the wheel on camera to see how sampling hides motion.

math.q: A room is checked every 15 minutes. How many checks per day?

history.title: Nightingale's diagrams
history.body: In 1858 Florence Nightingale used her 'coxcomb' charts to show that soldiers were dying of preventable disease, not wounds. The data changed policy. A dashboard is only honest if it samples what actually hurts people, often enough to see it.

PHY-S03E05.success: Sample too slowly and a recurring failure disappears. Measure what people feel, as often as it changes.

PHY-S03E07.title: The room hearing-aid users struggle in
PHY-S03E07.brief: A glass-walled meeting room (180 m³) rings too long for hearing-aid users. Add absorption until RT60 is 0.4–0.6 s.

math.q: RT60 for V = 180 m³ and A = 20 m²? (2 decimals)

history.title: Georg von Békésy and the cochlea
history.body: Georg von Békésy won the 1961 Nobel Prize for showing how the cochlea sorts sound by frequency along a traveling wave. Hearing loss often narrows that sorting — which is why long reverberation, a nuisance for most, can make speech unreadable for some.

PHY-S03E07.success: A dry room helps everyone and rescues some. Accessibility starts in the physics.

LAB-SF-07.title: Move the gateway to an independent reference
LAB-SF-07.brief: The video gateway follows Reference A, which is drifting in holdover. Cut the gateway's reference from A and feed it HOUSE REF B (black burst) instead, so CAM 2 reaches program on a stable clock. Reference A must not reach the gateway.

targets.whyNot: The gateway still follows the drifting reference — CAM 2 will keep tearing.

math.q: Reference A has been in holdover 47 minutes at about 20 ppm. How far has it drifted? (ms, 1 decimal)

LAB-SF-07.success: Gateway on house black: CAM 2 and the return stop tearing. The drifting reference no longer reaches the one device that can't tolerate it.
LAB-SF-07.timeoutWhy: Tap REF A → Gateway reference input to cut it, then HOUSE REF B → Gateway reference input.

PHY-S04E01.title: How bad can a clock be?
PHY-S04E01.brief: A free-running clock slips a little every second. Find the WORST clock error you could live with for one hour before the picture slips a quarter to half a frame.

math.q: How many frames does a 20 ppm clock slip in one hour at 29.97 fps? (2 decimals)

history.title: Clocks that count atoms
history.body: In 1949 the U.S. National Bureau of Standards built a clock regulated by ammonia molecules; in 1955 Louis Essen and Jack Parry at Britain's National Physical Laboratory built the first accurate caesium clock. Satellite time — the time a studio reference locks to — descends from them.

PHY-S04E01.success: Around 2–4 ppm keeps an hour's slip under half a frame. A satellite-locked clock is thousands of times better — which is why losing the sky matters.

LAB-EQ-04.title: Put the five frames back
LAB-EQ-04.brief: The stream's video path is five frames late (29.97 fps); its audio isn't delayed at all, so Omar's voice arrives before his lips. Set the stream audio delay to match the video path.

math.q: How many milliseconds is five frames at 29.97 fps? (2 decimals)

LAB-EQ-04.success: Stream audio delayed 166.8 ms: lips and voice arrive together at the viewer's end. Now label it.
LAB-EQ-04.timeoutWhy: Frames × (1000 ÷ fps) = milliseconds. Set the delay to that, not to what sounds right.

PHY-S04E02.title: When is sound 'too early'?
PHY-S04E02.brief: The stream's picture is 167 ms late. Set the audio path delay so the offset (audio − video) lands inside the window viewers accept: no more than 15 ms early, no more than 45 ms late.

math.q: Sound travels 343 m/s. How far from a stage are you when its sound arrives 45 ms after the light — the edge of 'late but fine'? (m, 1 decimal)

history.title: Sound printed on the picture
history.body: In 1923 the inventor Lee de Forest showed short films with sound recorded as an optical track on the film itself, beside the pictures. Because sound and image were on the same strip, they could never drift apart — the same problem studios now solve with measured delays.

PHY-S04E02.success: Anywhere from about 152 to 212 ms of audio delay puts the offset inside the window. Real life taught us to accept a little late — never early.

LAB-SF-08.title: Put the breaks back through the loudness processor
LAB-SF-08.brief: The break path skips the loudness processor, so the PSA reaches air at −14 (loudness, LUFS ≈ dB here) while the news sits at −24. Route the PSA through the loudness processor and set its gain so the break output lands at −24 (±1). The news path must stay at −24.

math.q: The PSA measures −14 LUFS and the target is −24 LUFS. What gain does the loudness processor need?

LAB-SF-08.success: The PSA reaches air at −24: as loud as the news, not ten LU louder. People stop muting it.
LAB-SF-08.timeoutWhy: Cut PSA → Break bus, wire PSA → Loudness processor → Break bus, then set the processor's gain to target − measured.

PHY-S04E03.title: How much louder does it sound?
PHY-S04E03.brief: The PSA sits ten LU above the news. Trim it back to the target line and watch the jump disappear.

math.q: By the rule of thumb, a 10 LU jump sounds about how many times as loud?

history.title: Measuring how loud things feel
history.body: In 1936 the psychologist S. S. Stevens proposed the sone, a scale of how loud a sound seems rather than how strong it is. People reported that a sound about 10 dB stronger felt roughly twice as loud. Loudness meters today still try to measure what listeners feel, not just what the needle sees.

PHY-S04E03.success: At −24 the PSA matches the news. Viewers stop reaching for the remote — and hear the message.

LAB-SF-09.title: Route the stream through a profile that keeps captions
LAB-SF-09.brief: The stream transcoder is on profile SPORTS TEST, which discards caption data. Re-route the program so the stream passes through the NEWS profile (captions kept) — never SPORTS TEST — and keep captions on broadcast too.

targets.whyNotVia: SPORTS TEST throws the caption data away.

LAB-SF-09.success: Stream through the NEWS profile: captions arrive on the stream and on broadcast. Now check it from a phone — and roll the test profile back for good.
LAB-SF-09.timeoutWhy: Tap Caption inserter → SPORTS TEST to cut it, then Caption inserter → NEWS, then NEWS → Stream.

LAB-SF-10.title: Get program to the mountain by a path that doesn't share the failure
LAB-SF-10.brief: The microwave STL has faded out in the rain, and the 'backup' internet runs through the same Old Mill conduit as the main internet. Get program to the transmitter over the IP link on the other carrier — not through the faded STL and not through the Old Mill conduit.

targets.whyNotVia: The Old Mill conduit carries both 'diverse' paths — one event takes both.

math.q: Rain costs about 0.25 dB/km on this 18 km hop. How much extra loss is that? (dB, 1 decimal)
The hop had only 8 dB of clear-sky margin since March. How much is left in this rain? (dB, 1 decimal)
math.hint: 8 − 4.5 = 3.5 dB — and gusts took the rest.

LAB-SF-10.success: Program reaches the transmitter over the other carrier through a two-second buffer. Now confirm it on the off-air receiver, not the studio monitor.
LAB-SF-10.timeoutWhy: Wire Program → IP link · other carrier → Receive buffer → Transmitter input. Leave the Old Mill path alone.

PHY-S04E05.title: Rain, a ridge and a beam
PHY-S04E05.brief: The hop crosses a ridge 9 km out. In a 30 mm/h storm, keep at least 3 dB of fade margin by clearing the ridge out of the Fresnel zone.

math.q: First Fresnel radius at the midpoint: r = 17.32 × √(9 × 9 ÷ (7 × 18)). What is r? (m, 1 decimal)

history.title: Waves that bend around edges
history.body: Augustin-Jean Fresnel explained in 1818 how light spreads and interferes around obstacles — the zones that carry his name. Seventy years later Heinrich Hertz showed radio waves obey the same optics. A microwave beam across a valley is still Fresnel's light, just longer.

PHY-S04E05.success: Raise both dishes until the ridge sits below about 60% of the Fresnel radius: the diffraction loss vanishes and the storm leaves enough margin.

LAB-SF-11.title: Give the reporter a clean mix-minus
LAB-SF-11.brief: The reporter's earpiece is fed the program return from the station — two seconds late — so she hears herself and stumbles. Build her feed from the studio anchor and the director's cues only: never her own mic, never the program return.

targets.whyNot: Hearing yourself two seconds late stops fluent speech.

LAB-SF-11.success: Her earpiece: anchor and cues, nothing of herself, nothing late. She talks through the fourth quarter without a stumble.
LAB-SF-11.timeoutWhy: Cut Program return → IFB. Wire Studio anchor → IFB and Director cues → IFB. Never her own mic.

PHY-S04E06.title: Twenty thousand phones and four modems
PHY-S04E06.brief: The crowd has pushed each link's signal-to-noise down to 2 dB. Bond enough links to carry the 8 Mb/s the encoder needs.

math.q: Per link: C = 5 × log₂(1 + 1.58). What's C? (Mb/s, 2 decimals)

history.title: The limit of a channel
history.body: In 1948 Claude Shannon, at Bell Labs, published a mathematical theory of communication. It showed that every channel has a maximum rate for error-free information, set by its bandwidth and its signal-to-noise ratio. No clever encoder can beat it — which is why a stadium full of phones changes what a truck can send.

PHY-S04E06.success: Three bonded links carry about 10 Mb/s usable at this noise level — enough, with room to adapt.

LAB-NET-04.title: Move the room devices out of the automatic range
LAB-NET-04.brief: Priya widened the automatic range to .10–.250. Section 5.3 put three room controllers at .240–.242, and an exception room's controller was hand-typed on the wrong subnet. Give all four valid fixed addresses OUTSIDE the automatic range so each reaches the room scheduler — and nothing collides.

math.q: The automatic range ends at .250. How many usable addresses are left above it in the /24 (.251–.254)?

LAB-NET-04.success: Four controllers on .251–.254, outside the automatic range, all reaching the scheduler. The laptops can have everything else. This is what section 5.3 should have said.
LAB-NET-04.timeoutWhy: Give Rowan, Harbor, Forum and 30-East the addresses .251, .252, .253 and .254 on 198.18.0.

LAB-NET-05.title: Keep the air chain out of the newsroom
LAB-NET-05.brief: In the scramble, the prompter laptop and the graphics playout PC were plugged into newsroom ports. Security has the newsroom locked down. Put both back on the PLAYOUT segment with valid fixed addresses so they reach the playout server — and keep the newsroom PCs separate.
forbid: The air chain must never share a segment with the compromised newsroom.
The prompter copy was approved as isolated.
LAB-NET-05.success: Graphics and prompter back on PLAYOUT (198.18.1.x), reaching the server; the newsroom stays walled off. The show never needed a newsroom login.
LAB-NET-05.timeoutWhy: Set both devices to VLAN 70 and give them unused 198.18.1.x addresses, e.g. .21 and .22.

PHY-S04E08.title: Twenty-two people, one password
PHY-S04E08.brief: Replace the shared login with named accounts and long passphrases. Choose a length and symbol set that give at least 60 bits of entropy (random choices only).

math.q: A passphrase of 5 words chosen at random from a 7,776-word list. H = 5 × log₂(7,776) ≈ ? bits (1 decimal)

history.title: When one program met thousands of computers
history.body: In November 1988 a self-spreading program slowed thousands of early internet computers in a day, partly by guessing weak passwords from a short list. The response led to the first computer emergency response team. Password strength stopped being theory that week.

PHY-S04E08.success: Length and randomness beat cleverness — and a named account beats any password shared by twenty-two people.

LAB-SF-12.title: Make the backup MCR carry everything
LAB-SF-12.brief: At the backup MCR, the timecode generator free-runs and the stream bypasses the caption inserter. Lock the timecode generator to REF B and feed it to both outputs; route the captions through the inserter to broadcast AND stream.

math.q: The backup's timecode drifted 2 frames in 7 hours at 29.97 fps. What's the clock error in ppm? (1 decimal)

LAB-SF-12.success: Timecode locked to REF B on both outputs; captions through the inserter to broadcast and stream. The backup can carry a real night.
LAB-SF-12.timeoutWhy: Wire REF B → Timecode generator → both outputs; Caption encoder → Caption inserter → Stream; cut Program → Stream.

PHY-S04E09.title: A night is a long time for a clock
PHY-S04E09.brief: The backup's timecode free-runs overnight. Find the worst clock error you could live with for an eight-hour night before it slips half a frame to a whole frame.

math.q: At 20 ppm, how many frames does a clock slip in 8 hours at 29.97 fps? (1 decimal)

history.title: The second, redefined
history.body: In 1967 the international definition of the second changed from a fraction of the Earth's orbit to 9,192,631,770 oscillations of a caesium atom. From then on, the best clocks on Earth disagreed with the planet — and every studio's reference traces back to that count.

PHY-S04E09.success: About 0.6–1.2 ppm keeps an eight-hour night within half a frame to a frame. Locked to a reference, the drift is zero.

LAB-SF-13.title: Route the second-language feed at the backup
LAB-SF-13.brief: 11:52 p.m. At the backup MCR, the second-language channel is carrying a copy of the main audio, and the stream's alternate audio is empty. Feed the interpreter's second-language audio to both the broadcast second-language channel and the stream's alternate audio — and keep main audio on the main channel.

targets.whyNot: The second-language channel is carrying Omar again, not the interpreter.

LAB-SF-13.success: Omar on the main channel; the interpreter on broadcast's second-language channel and the stream's alternate audio. The runbook said page 17 — it was right.
LAB-SF-13.timeoutWhy: Cut Main audio bus → 2nd-language channel. Wire Interpreter → Second-language bus → both second-language outputs.

LAB-SF-14.title: Give the recording its sound back
LAB-SF-14.brief: ENG-214 sounds fine in the room, but the capture appliance is recording its empty USB input. Route the room DSP's line out into the capture appliance so the recording carries the lecturer — and not through the empty USB input.

targets.whyNotVia: The USB input has nothing on it — that's the silence.

math.q: 22 of the campus's 400 rooms were hit. What percentage is that? (%, 1 decimal)
Each room needs a 6-minute test recording and playback. How long for all 22? (min)

LAB-SF-14.success: The recording carries the room DSP's line out: the lecturer, not an empty USB port. Now prove it the way a student hears it — play the test recording from the portal.

LAB-SF-17.brief: Grant is at the whiteboard. He reaches the lectern lobe 12 dB down (4 m instead of 1 m), under the auto-mixer's gate. history.title: The first public-address systems
history.body: In the early 1920s, amplified public-address systems let a single speaker be heard by crowds of thousands — as long as he stayed at the microphone. Step back and the sound fell away, exactly as the inverse square predicts. A hundred years later, lecturers still walk out of their microphones' reach.

LAB-SF-18.brief: Campus time servers follow only the hub's time service, which has been drifting since 2:14. Feed them from the arena's satellite-disciplined clock and the national time servers instead, take the hub out of the vote, and keep the cameras and door logs on campus time.

PHY-S05E08.title: A one-hour lecture and a clock that's a little fast
PHY-S05E08.brief: A lecture lasts an hour. Find the largest clock error that keeps a one-hour recording between half a frame and one frame of drift at 29.97 fps — lips and voice still together.

history.title: One clock for the world
history.body: In 1884 delegates to the International Meridian Conference in Washington agreed on Greenwich as the prime meridian — so the world's clocks could share one reference. Railways had been running on dozens of local times. A shared reference made timetables possible; a single one, with nothing to check it, makes shared failures possible too.

PHY-S05E08.success: Under about 9 ppm, a one-hour lecture stays within a frame. Locked to honest sources, the drift is zero.

history.title: The magic lantern's arithmetic
history.body: Nineteenth-century lantern shows already worked the same sum: lecturers moved the lantern back to grow the picture, and makers sold objective lenses of different focal lengths so the image fit halls of any size. The throw ratio is that old arithmetic, printed on a data sheet.

history.title: Sabine's cushions
history.body: In 1895 Harvard asked a young physics instructor, Wallace Sabine, to fix a lecture hall nobody could understand. history.title: Fifty thousand people and one voice
history.body: In September 1919, President Woodrow Wilson spoke to a crowd of about 50,000 in San Diego's stadium through an early electric public-address system — among the first times a crowd that size heard a speaker through loudspeakers. The engineers placed horns to cover the crowd, and the parts of the stands between them heard less. Coverage has been geometry ever since.

PHY-S07E05.title: See every outage that matters
PHY-S07E05.brief: The rooms fail from :05 to :13 every hour. Set the polling interval so any outage of five minutes or more is seen whatever its timing — without going over the monitoring server's budget of 12,000 polls an hour for 600 devices.

history.title: Nyquist, Shannon and the space between samples
history.body: In 1928 Harry Nyquist worked out how many independent pulses a telegraph line of a given bandwidth can carry. In 1949 Claude Shannon set the idea down as the sampling theorem: sample often enough, or lose what happens between the samples. A monitor that polls is a sampler too — and an outage shorter than its interval is a signal it can't see.

PHY-S07E05.success: Polling every 3–5 minutes sees any outage of five minutes or more, whatever its timing, inside the server's budget. Event-driven alerts see it sooner still.

history.title: Fifty and sixty
history.body: In the 1890s the companies building the first alternating-current systems tried many frequencies. North America settled on 60 Hz; most of Europe, and much of the world after it, on 50 Hz — choices made by competing manufacturers and engineers, not by physics. More than a century later, every camera that crosses between them has to be told which one it's in.

history.body: In 1970 a team of three researchers drew the first optical fiber that lost less than 20 decibels per kilometer — the threshold engineers had said would make light a practical way to carry calls. history.title: Weather made to order
history.body: In 1902 a young engineer designed a system to control the humidity in a printing plant in Brooklyn, so paper wouldn't swell between one color and the next. LAB-NET-10.title: Stage the update off the show network
LAB-NET-10.brief: Everything sits on VLAN 60 (AV-PROD). Prepare the change the network contractor will make: the production controller keeps reaching the working 4.1 decoders; the 3.8 decoders and Dario's update tool go to the staging VLAN, where the tool can reach them and nothing else; the lighting console and its nodes go to VLAN 70, as drawn. One row stands for each group of decoders.

devices.label: Firmware update tool
devices.note: Dario's · updates only what it can reach

forbid: The update tool must never reach the working 4.1 decoders.
The 3.8 decoders stay off production until they're updated.
Lighting control belongs on its own VLAN, as drawn.

math.q: 180 of 400 decoders are on 3.8. Share? (%)
Batches of 20, 6 minutes a batch, one hop. Time for all 180? (min)

LAB-NET-10.success: Production keeps the working 220; the 180 and the update tool sit on staging where nothing else can be touched; lighting has VLAN 70 back, as drawn. The network contractor makes the change in tomorrow's window, with the lighting contractor told.
LAB-NET-10.timeoutWhy: Move the 3.8 decoders and the update tool (198.18.61.20) to VLAN 61; move the lighting console (198.18.70.40) and its nodes (198.18.70.41) to VLAN 70; leave the controller and the 4.1 decoders on 60.

LAB-NET-11.title: Give paging its own path
LAB-NET-11.brief: Everything in the lobby sits on VLAN 20. Prepare the change Raffa will make: both paging stations and the DSP's paging input on the paging VLAN, reachable to each other; both guest access points on the guest VLAN with the guest gateway; the lobby control panel stays on LOBBY, away from guests. One row stands for each device or group.

devices.label: DSP · paging input
devices.note: gives paging priority — once it arrives

forbid: Guests never share a segment with paging.
Guests never share a segment with paging.
Guests don't belong on the venue's control segment.

math.q: 900 guests at about 1.2 Mb/s each. Load? (Mb/s)
1,080 Mb/s on a 1,000 Mb/s uplink. Utilization? (%)

LAB-NET-11.success: Paging and its DSP input on their own VLAN; guests isolated with their gateway; the lobby panel on LOBBY. Raffa adds priority queuing for paging and a cap on guest traffic in the same window.
LAB-NET-11.timeoutWhy: Move both paging stations (198.18.30.31, .32) and the DSP paging input (198.18.30.10) to VLAN 30; move both guest access points to VLAN 90; leave the lobby panel on 20.

LAB-NET-12.title: Split the flat network by purpose
LAB-NET-12.brief: Everything below sits on VLAN 1. Prepare the segmentation Raffa will build: control processor, DSP control and the jump host's device side on CONTROL; the signage server and players on SIGNAGE; the jump host's vendor side and the integrator's landing on VENDOR. The jump host reaches control; the integrator reaches only the jump host; signage never shares a segment with control. The show-mode flow between control and signage is a documented rule on Raffa's firewall — not a shared VLAN.

devices.label: Control processor
devices.note: sends show mode to the players

forbid: Signage never shares a segment with control — show mode crosses as one documented firewall rule.
The integrator reaches control only through the jump host.
The integrator reaches signage only through the jump host.
Signage has no business on the DSP's segment.

math.q: 212 of 340 ports on VLAN 1. Share? (%, 1 decimal)
The show-mode flow: 40 players × 1.2 kb of commands a second. Rate? (kb/s)

LAB-NET-12.success: Control, signage and vendor each on their own segment; the jump host between vendor and control; signage and control apart, with show mode crossing as one owned rule. Raffa builds it in two windows with a rollback.
LAB-NET-12.timeoutWhy: Control processor (198.18.40.21), DSP control (198.18.40.22) and the jump host's device side (198.18.40.5) to VLAN 40; signage server (198.18.50.30) and players to VLAN 50; the jump host's vendor side (198.18.95.6) and the integrator landing to VLAN 95.

LAB-SF-23.title: One leader for Studio A
LAB-SF-23.brief: Hollis chose the interface as the one leader. The converter still runs on its own internal clock. Cut the converter's clock from its internal oscillator and feed it the interface's word-clock output; the stage boxes and cue mixers keep following the network. Nothing may follow the converter's internal clock.

targets.whyNot: The converter still runs on a clock nobody else follows — the clicks stay.

math.q: Two clocks 20 ppm apart at 48 kHz: how many samples apart do they drift each second? (2 decimals)
The interface's input buffer absorbs 64 samples. Seconds between clicks? (1 decimal)

LAB-SF-23.success: One leader: the converter follows the interface over word clock, the network follows it too, and the generator stays out of the chain. The next ten-minute take is silent.
LAB-SF-23.timeoutWhy: Tap Converter · internal clock → Converter clock select to cut it, then Interface word-clock out → Converter clock select.

LAB-SF-24.title: Take the computer out of Esme's ears
LAB-SF-24.brief: Esme hears her own voice after a round trip through the recording computer (about 27 ms). Feed her vocal and the band playback to her headphones through the personal cue mixer instead, and take the computer's monitor output off her headphones. The vocal still records, dry.

targets.whyNotVia: Her own voice still goes round the computer — about 27 ms late.

math.q: 2 × 512 samples at 48 kHz: round-trip buffer delay? (ms, 1 decimal)
Add 1 ms of converters and 5 ms of lookahead. What was Esme hearing? (ms, 1 decimal)

LAB-SF-24.success: Her voice reaches her ears in about 1.5 ms through the cue mixer; the band comes from the computer as before; the vocal records dry. The buffer can stay where the mix needs it.
LAB-SF-24.timeoutWhy: Cut Recording computer → Esme's headphones; wire Esme's vocal → Personal cue mixer, Band playback → Personal cue mixer, and Personal cue mixer → Esme's headphones.

LAB-SF-25.title: Play both masters the way the playlist will
LAB-SF-25.brief: Before anyone argues, hear the masters as the service plays them. Route each through its own normalizer and set the gain so each lands at the service's −14 LUFS target (±1).

math.q: The hot master measures −7 LUFS; the service's target is −14 LUFS. Normalizer gain? (dB)
Its true peak is +0.8 dBTP and the spec asks for −1.0 dBTP. How far must the peaks come down? (dB)

LAB-SF-25.success: Both play at −14. The hot master is turned down 7 dB and sounds flatter; the dynamic one, down 2 dB, keeps its drums. Now the argument can be about the sound.
LAB-SF-25.timeoutWhy: Cut each master's direct wire; route hot → Normalizer A → Playlist · hot master at −7 dB and dynamic → Normalizer B → Playlist · dynamic master at −2 dB.

LAB-PWR-06.source: S10E07 · The Hum That Went Away
LAB-PWR-06.header: AMPS PER 120 V CIRCUIT · dashed line = the electrician's 80% planning line · ILLUSTRATIVE
LAB-PWR-06.title: Plan the backline onto technical power, for Bea
LAB-PWR-06.brief: Bea has added a technical outlet in the live room on T2. Plan where every load goes: all audio gear on the technical circuits (T1, T2), nothing audio on the kitchen circuit K3, every circuit under 16 A. Bea checks the plan and does the work.

loads.label: Console and control surface (400 W)
loads.onlyWhy: audio gear goes on technical power

loads.label: Racks: converters and interface (900 W)
loads.onlyWhy: audio gear goes on technical power

loads.label: Recording computer (450 W)
loads.onlyWhy: audio gear goes on technical power

loads.label: Monitor power amps (600 W)
loads.onlyWhy: audio gear goes on technical power

loads.label: Studio valve amp (280 W)
loads.onlyWhy: backline goes on technical power — the kitchen circuit is where the hum came from

loads.label: Bass amp (350 W)
loads.onlyWhy: audio gear goes on technical power

loads.label: Cue mixers (160 W)
loads.onlyWhy: audio gear goes on technical power

loads.label: Kitchen fridge (150 W)
loads.onlyWhy: the fridge stays on the kitchen circuit

loads.label: Kettle (1,500 W)
loads.onlyWhy: the kettle stays on the kitchen circuit

math.q: T1 carries the console, racks, computer and monitor amps: 2,350 W at 120 V. Current? (A, 1 decimal)
math.hint: I = P ÷ V = 2,350 ÷ 120 ≈ 19.6 A — over the 16 A line.

math.q: The electrician's planning line on a 20 A breaker? (A)

LAB-PWR-06.success: All audio on technical power, T1 at 1,750 W (≈ 14.6 A), T2 at 1,390 W (≈ 11.6 A), the kitchen circuit left to the kitchen. Bea checks it, does the work and signs her schedule.
LAB-PWR-06.timeoutWhy: Studio valve amp → T2 and monitor power amps → T2: T1 = 1,750 W ≈ 14.6 A, T2 = 1,390 W ≈ 11.6 A.

LAB-SF-26.title: Spanish on its own channel, partners at their loudness
LAB-SF-26.brief: The stream's audio 2 carries a copy of the English program and the partners get the program at −14 LUFS. Route the interpreter to stream audio 2 and to the partners' second-language feed; send English to the partners' main feed; put both partner feeds through their loudness processors so they land at −24 (±1). Stream audio 1 stays English.

targets.whyNot: Channel two is still carrying the English program.

math.q: The partner feeds leave at −14 LUFS; partners take −24. Processor gain? (dB)
The picture runs 200 ms behind the audio after the encoder. Audio delay to add? (ms)

LAB-SF-26.success: English on audio 1 and the partners' main feed; the interpreter on audio 2 and the partners' second language; both partner feeds at −24. Amara hears it on a phone and signs it off.
LAB-SF-26.timeoutWhy: Cut Program bus → audio 2 and → Partner feed · main; wire the interpreter → Second-language bus → audio 2 and → Partner loudness · SAP → Partner feed · SAP; Program bus → Partner loudness · main → Partner feed · main; both processors at −10 dB.

R-01.title: Build the stream audio path
R-01.brief: Doors in ten minutes. The stream has no audio at all. Rebuild the path from the pastor's mic to the stream computer, stage by stage.

why.Room loudspeakers: That's the room's output. The stream has its own mix.
why.Office switch: Not ours — it runs the door locks and giving kiosks. Using it without the owner is an authorization failure.
why.Lobby TV: That's the overflow room's display, downstream of the stream, not part of it.
why.Preamp: Gain comes right after capture, before any processing.
why.Stream mix (aux): The stream gets its own mix after processing.
why.Network audio link: Transport carries the finished mix to the stream computer.
why.Stream computer: Encoding is the last stage in the building.

R-01.success: Capture → gain → process → mix → transport → encode. When the stream fails, walk this path from the first stage.
R-01.timeoutWhy: Start at the source and move one stage at a time. You don't need the whole map to place the first chip.

R-02.title: Feed the listening system
R-02.brief: Receiver users hear the songs but never the readings. Route a listening feed that no scene can mute.

why.AUX 4 · band wedges: The SPOKEN WORD scene mutes the wedges — that's exactly why the readings went silent.
why.Main mix: It works, but it's shaped for a big room, not an ear an inch away — and it follows every room change.
why.Stream mix: The stream's mix serves people at home, with its own processing and delay.
why.Listening transmitter: That's the output — the last stage.
why.AUX 6 · listening: A dedicated bus, saved in every preset, never muted by a scene.

R-02.success: Its own bus, fed by speech and music, never muted by a scene. The output now has an owner and an intent.

R-03.title: Camera to stream
R-03.brief: Camera 2 sits 40 m from the booth. Build its path to the stream.

why.HDMI cable (40 m): HDMI is designed for short runs; 40 m needs a transport built for distance (SDI or fiber, or extenders).
why.LED wall processor: That feeds the wall in the room, not the stream.
why.Lobby TV: An overflow display, not part of the stream path.

R-03.success: Source → long-run transport → switcher → program → encoder → uplink. Each stage is a place to measure.

R-04.title: Wire the DMX line
R-04.brief: Three 16-channel fixtures on stage left. Build the line from the console, with correct addresses, and finish it properly.

why.Fixture B · address 16: Fixture A uses 1–16, so address 16 overlaps its last channel. The next free address is 17.
why.Y-cable to stage right: DMX is a line, not a tree. A branch needs a proper splitter.
why.Microphone cable extension: It may fit the connector, but it isn't built for data; use cable rated for DMX.
why.Terminator: It belongs at the far end of the line.

R-04.success: Console → A(1) → B(17) → C(33) → terminator. Addresses don't overlap, and the line ends properly.

F-01.title: The heavy vocal
F-01.brief: The lead vocal sounds heavy and crushed on every chorus. You have one reading at each stage.

stages.name: Mic
stages.reading: Signal present, normal tone at rehearsal level
stages.why: The capsule is fine; the problem appears only when she sings loud.

stages.name: Preamp
stages.reading: Red clip light on every chorus peak
stages.why: Clipping at the input. Everything after inherits it.

stages.name: EQ
stages.why: A downstream change. It can't undo clipping.

stages.name: Fader
stages.why: Louder, not cleaner.

stages.name: Room
stages.why: That's the symptom, not the first failure.

F-01.success: Fix at the earliest stage you can reach: lower the preamp gain, then match the level with the fader.

F-02.title: Gaps in the stream
F-02.brief: People at home lose audio every 20–60 seconds. Pick the first stage where a MEASUREMENT shows the problem.

stages.name: Console stream mix
stages.why: Healthy output. The problem is downstream.

stages.name: Booth switch
stages.reading: All port lights busy (observed; unmanaged, no counters)
stages.why: Suggestive, but busy lights aren't a measurement and this switch has no counters to read.

stages.name: Stream computer network in
stages.reading: Receiving hundreds of Mbit/s; needs a few (measured)
stages.why: The first measurement that shows the failure: the port is being flooded.

stages.name: Stream software
stages.why: It reports its own view — after the damage.

stages.name: Viewers
stages.why: The symptom where the users are.

F-02.ask: Tap the earliest stage where a measurement — not a hunch — shows the failure.
F-02.success: Busy lights made you suspicious; the receive rate made it evidence. Keep that history — restarting the computer erases it.

F-03.title: The phantom flicker
F-03.brief: During acceptance, several fixtures flicker at random. The console output is steady. One reading per point on the DMX line.

stages.name: Console output
stages.why: Data leaves the console clean.

stages.name: Fixture 1
stages.why: Receiving good data.

stages.name: Fixture 2
stages.why: Still good.

stages.name: Fixture 3
stages.reading: Flickers when the cable is touched
stages.why: The first fixture that misbehaves — the fault is at or just upstream of its input.

stages.name: Fixtures 4–8
stages.why: Downstream of the fault, so they inherit it.

F-03.success: Everything downstream of a bad link fails too. Check the cable and connector between fixture 2 and fixture 3 first.

F-04.title: No picture on input 3
F-04.brief: Camera 3 shows black on the switcher. You carry a small field monitor and check each point.

stages.name: Camera viewfinder
stages.why: The camera is working.

stages.name: Camera SDI out
stages.why: The camera's output is good.

stages.name: Wall plate (stage)
stages.why: The cable from camera to plate is good.

stages.name: Patch panel (booth)
stages.why: The first point with no picture: the run between the wall plate and the patch.

stages.name: Switcher input 3
stages.why: Downstream of the break.

F-04.success: The fault sits between the last good reading and the first bad one: the wall-plate-to-patch run. One cable, one camera — the classic one-cable failure.

C-01.title: Ten hollow seats
C-01.brief: Rows 7–9, center, have sounded hollow for two years.

clues.t: The same recording sounds clean from other seats
clues.why: Rules out the mic and EQ: they'd be wrong everywhere.

clues.t: The notches move from one seat to the next
clues.why: Position-dependent: geometry, not a setting.

clues.t: Fill alone clear, mains alone clear, both together hollow
clues.why: Needs two arrivals: points straight at interference.

clues.t: Complaints cluster in rows 7–9
clues.why: Useful for WHERE, but doesn't separate the explanations.

clues.t: The pastor switched microphones last year
clues.why: The problem started two years ago, and other seats are fine.

clues.t: Dolores is 81
clues.why: Her age isn't evidence about the room, and her hearing isn't ours to judge.

clues.t: EQ the fill to see if it helps
clues.why: Changes the system before you've measured it: your baseline is gone.

clues.t: There's a vent above row 8
clues.why: Testable (switch it off), but a vent doesn't explain notches that move.

C-01.success: Three clues that separate the explanations: the room, two arrivals, geometry.

C-02.title: Forty-five minutes to doors
C-02.brief: The stream drops audio every 20–60 seconds; the room is fine.

clues.t: Console stream meters are steady during gaps
clues.why: The source is healthy: the failure is downstream.

clues.t: Stream computer receiving hundreds of Mbit/s
clues.why: It's being flooded — it isn't broken.

clues.t: The picture keeps moving during every audio gap
clues.why: A dead internet would take picture and sound together.

clues.t: The switch is warm to the touch
clues.why: Worth noting, but it's just as warm after the fix.

clues.t: An update prompt is waiting on screen
clues.why: Nothing was updated. It's a suspect, not evidence.

clues.t: Sofia is running haze
clues.why: Haze affects the picture, not the audio path.

clues.t: Restart the stream computer and see
clues.why: It erases the receive history — the one measurement that proves the cause.

clues.t: It stopped when Ray leaned in
clues.why: A bursty pattern pausing by chance.

C-02.success: Healthy source, flooded receiver, picture unaffected: the network, not the computer.

C-03.title: WORSHIP opens the wrong mics
C-03.brief: The touch panel's WORSHIP button opens the lectern and mutes Marisol.

clues.t: Talking into each mic: the vocal lands on CH 7, the lectern on CH 3
clues.why: Measured: the inputs are crossed before the console.

clues.t: Priya's photo from a month ago shows the original patch
clues.why: A before-state to compare against.

clues.t: Change log: rack tidy-up on Tuesday
clues.why: Answers “what changed?”.

clues.t: The touch panel's software is old
clues.why: Old isn't broken. The panel did exactly what it was told.

clues.t: Marisol's mic battery
clues.why: Her mic works — it just arrives on the wrong channel.

clues.t: Re-save the WORSHIP preset to match today
clues.why: It hides the patch change and leaves every other preset wrong.

clues.t: The panel restarted fine
clues.why: Restarting proved nothing and cost time.

C-03.success: Measured crossing + a before-state + a known change: the patch moved, not the panel.

M-01.title: Symptom vs cause
M-01.brief: The failure is rarely where the symptom appears. Classify each CAUSE.

items.s: Stream audio drops — video traffic floods the booth switch
items.why: The cause is traffic on the network.

items.s: Room hums — two safely grounded systems disagree about “zero”
items.why: Reference potential between power systems.

items.s: Wrong mics on WORSHIP — two patch cables were swapped
items.why: A setup changed; the control did what it was told.

items.s: Ten seats sound hollow — a ceiling reflection arrives late
items.why: The room's geometry.

items.s: Breaker trips — twelve fixtures added without checking the circuit
items.why: A change made without coordination.

items.s: Stream fails — the platform account's key expired
items.why: Something outside the building.

items.s: Panel shows System Off during a live meeting — two schedules race
items.why: The system's own commanding logic.

items.s: Vocal crushed — preamp gain too high for the real performance
items.why: The signal itself, at the gain stage.

M-01.success: Symptoms cluster in Signal; causes live everywhere.

O-01.title: Service triage
O-01.brief: A live incident. Put the method in order.
items: Make it safe (stabilize; nothing unsafe)
State the broken outcome in one sentence
Classify by path before touching anything
Gather evidence before changing anything
Predict, then change one reversible thing
Restore service
Verify where the users are (two conditions + one neighbor)
Record it and hand it off
why: Safety first, always.
One observable sentence focuses everyone.
Which path carries the broken function?
Evidence you don't keep, you don't get back.
One change, with a prediction that could prove you wrong.
Service comes back — but you're not done.
Proof is where the people are, not at the booth.
Leave a record another person can use.
O-01.success: Stabilize, classify, gather, test one thing, restore, verify, document.

O-02.title: A rack change done right
O-02.brief: Next Tuesday a crew will tidy the rack again. Order Imani's checklist.
items: Write the patch plan
Photograph the before-state
Print labels for both ends
Make the change
Log it before you leave
Press every preset and watch the right channels
Compare against the photos and the drawing
why: Know what you intend before touching anything.
A before-state makes the change provable.
Labels are how the building remembers.
Only now touch the cables.
Not Thursday. Before you leave.
Every preset, not just the one you care about.
Close the loop against the record.
O-02.success: Plan, photograph, label, change, log, test, compare.

O-03.title: Acceptance, step by step
O-03.brief: Elias won't sign until the evidence is in order. Order the acceptance work.
items: List the requirements
Give each one a method and a pass/fail threshold
Test under stated conditions
Record results and where the evidence lives
Write the punch list
Fix and retest
Sign — or don't
why: What must be true?
How will you know, and what counts as pass?
Conditions make results repeatable.
Evidence someone else can check.
Every failed item, owned.
Retest the same way.
A signature is a claim about evidence.
O-03.success: Requirement, condition, method, result, threshold, evidence. Then sign.

C-04.title: Bands on the stream
C-04.brief: Christmas Eve, 3:52 p.m. Dark bands roll up the LED wall on the stream. The room sees nothing wrong.

clues.t: The bands change speed when the shutter changes
clues.why: Shutter-dependent: a timing effect, not a spatial one.

clues.t: The processor status reads IN: 50 Hz; every camera is 59.94
clues.why: A standards mismatch: two frame-rate families in one show.

clues.t: Rental tech: “factory reset at 2 p.m.”
clues.why: Answers “what changed?” — and why the December 10 fix is gone.

clues.t: Rainbow ripples change when Cam 2 zooms
clues.why: Real, but that's moiré — a separate spatial effect. It doesn't explain rolling bands.

clues.t: The stream software says “Healthy”
clues.why: The encoder reports its own view. The bands exist before it.

clues.t: Both cameras show the bands
clues.why: Makes one faulty camera unlikely, but doesn't separate timing from anything else.

clues.t: Reboot the processor and watch
clues.why: Ninety seconds of black wall in the room, and the status screen that proves the mismatch is gone.

clues.t: The room's eye sees an even wall
clues.why: Consistent with a camera-sampling effect, but it doesn't say which one.

C-04.success: Shutter-dependent, a 50 Hz processor in a 59.94 building, and a factory reset: a timing mismatch that arrived with the rental's defaults.

F-05.title: Back from the dip, but silent
F-05.brief: A two-second power dip mid-service. Everything seems to come back — and the room is silent. One reading per stage.

stages.name: Console (on its UPS)
stages.why: The source side survived. The failure is downstream.

stages.name: Network link to the processor
stages.why: Transport is fine.

stages.name: Loudspeaker processor
stages.reading: Rebooted 3 min ago; preset 00 SAFE START; all outputs muted (observed on its panel)
stages.why: The first stage where the signal stops: it came back in its power-on safe preset.

stages.name: Amplifiers
stages.why: Healthy, starved: downstream of the failure.

stages.name: Loudspeakers
stages.why: The symptom where the people are.

F-05.success: The processor rebooted into a muted safe preset — by design, years ago. Recall the service preset from the documented procedure, then verify every output.

M-02.title: Season review: where did the cause live?
M-02.brief: Late-season failures. Classify each CAUSE, not the symptom.

items.s: Bands on camera — a rented wall processor arrived set to the 50 Hz family
items.why: A setting that disagreed with the building's standard.

items.s: Receivers silent in readings — the listening feed rode a bus a scene mutes
items.why: Routing and scene setup.

items.s: Flicker on fixtures 3–8 — a mic cable used as a DMX extension
items.why: The physical data link itself degraded the control signal.

items.s: Room silent after a dip — processor rebooted into its power-on safe preset
items.why: The event that started it was a power disturbance on unprotected gear.

items.s: Recovery stalled — the processor password lived only in one person's notebook
items.why: Knowledge held by one person is a workflow failure.

items.s: Stream dies Sunday — the platform's account key expired
items.why: Outside the building.

items.s: Faint band at 10% brightness — the wall's dimming pulsed differently on camera
items.why: A borderline call: the show's lighting state (a dimmed room) exposed it. Many reviewers would also accept Configuration.

items.s: Stage outlets dead — twelve fixtures added without checking the circuit
items.why: A change without coordination.

M-02.success: Causes spread across every class. The symptom only tells you where to start looking.

O-04.title: Two seconds of dark
O-04.brief: Mid-sermon the power dips, the emergency lights flash, and the room comes back silent. Put the AV team's moves in order.
items: People first: follow the building's plan and the person in charge; nothing electrical is ours to open
Tell the person in charge what the booth can and can't do right now
Read the state without changing it: what's up, what rebooted, what's muted
Stop the thump risk: keep amplifiers muted until their input is sane
Recall the service preset from the documented recovery card
Bring outputs back one at a time, listening where the people are
Verify every output: room, stream, listening system, lobby
Log times and states; hand the building questions to facilities
why: Life safety belongs to the building; the booth supports it.
The pastor and ushers need facts, not guesses.
Evidence before action, even in a hurry.
A sudden full-level return can hurt ears and equipment.
A written procedure beats memory under pressure.
One path at a time, so you hear what each does.
Every output has people on the other end.
Facilities owns the power; you own the record.
O-04.success: People, then facts, then evidence, then careful recovery, then proof and a record.

T-01.title: One budget line
T-01.brief: The roof repair came in high. The AV line is now $6,000 (illustrative). Fund the plan that retires the most risk. Some items are commitments you can't skip.

items.name: Replace 4 failing listening receivers
items.why: People who rely on them are excluded right now. A commitment, not an option.

items.name: Booth network redesign (DEBT-009)
items.why: The stream shares a temporary switch; every new device competes with it. Hundreds of homes, most weeks.

items.name: Equipment-room UPS for processor + amps
items.why: Rare, but a power dip mid-service could silence the room.

items.name: Documentation day: drawings, labels, credentials (DEBT-002)
items.why: Cheap. Takes knowledge out of one person's notebook.

items.name: Balcony-front loudspeaker (DEBT-010)
items.why: Certain and weekly, but mild: forty seats hear a little less clearly.

items.name: Dedicated stage circuit (electrician)
items.why: E05's rebalance holds for now; more headroom for growth.

items.name: New wireless microphones
items.why: The current ones work. A want, not a risk.

items.name: Buy the rented LED wall
items.why: Exciting, and far beyond the line. It retires no risk.

items.name: Four moving-head lights
items.why: Shiny. Retires no risk.

T-01.success: Risk = likelihood × impact. Commitments first, then the most risk retired per dollar — and say out loud what you're choosing not to fund.
T-01.timeoutWhy: Start with what you can't skip, then compare risk per dollar. You don't need a perfect plan to have a defensible one.

O-F02.title: Balance a room that leans
O-F02.brief: The left side is boomy, the right side thin, the vocals buried. Put the work in the order that finds the cause before it polishes the symptom.
items: Walk and measure several seats with the same material — left, center, right, front, back
Map the stage: which sources stack up on one side?
Mix the source: agree stage amp levels with the players
Check each monitor's aim — is one feeding the room?
Check sub polarity and alignment, one change at a time
Re-measure the same seats and log what changed
why: A single seat is an opinion; several seats are evidence.
Energy piles up where the sources do.
No fader can turn down an amp on stage.
A wedge pointed at a wall is a loudspeaker for the room.
Two subs out of polarity cancel; one change keeps the cause visible.
Proof, then a record for the next person.
O-F02.success: Measure, map, fix the source, check the monitors, align the subs, prove it. The room becomes an instrument instead of an accident.

O-F05.title: Every pixel carries a purpose
O-F05.brief: One module of the LED wall has gone dim mid-set, in the rain. Put the response in order. (Who and what — nobody opens the wall during the show.)
items: Identify: which module, since when, does it follow the content?
Check the wall processor's status for that module: data, power, temperature
Move critical graphics away from the dim square
Tell the wall's vendor, with a photo and the module's position
After the weather hold lifts and under the vendor's plan, they swap or reseat the module
Measure brightness against its neighbors and log the cause
why: Name the symptom exactly before you guess.
Evidence without touching anything.
Protect the message while you wait.
The wall has an owner.
Physical work in the rain belongs to the owner's safety plan.
Proof and a record.
O-F05.success: Identify → understand → measure → fix, through the wall's owner. The show kept its message while one square waited.

O-F11.title: Fifteen percent of a stage
O-F11.brief: Mid-service, the lighting software and the interface both say “license expired.” Put the moves in order. Nobody climbs.
items: Tell the technical director: stage control is lost
Bring the house lights up to a safe, readable level from the wall station
Use any console or hardware preset that doesn't need the software
Leave the software alone until the service ends
After the service: renew, update from a known-good installer, and test
Add every license and expiry date to the asset register, with reminders sent to two people
why: Communicate first; the service needs to know.
People need to see — from the ground.
A fallback that doesn't depend on software.
Rebooting or reinstalling mid-sermon gambles the rest of the service.
Fix it when there's time to prove it.
An expiry nobody tracks is a failure with a date on it.
O-F11.success: Tell, light the room safely from the ground, use the fallback, wait, fix, register. The climb in the old story is the one move you never make.

R-11.title: The touring patch
R-11.brief: LANTERN tours with its own stage boxes. One vocal mic has to reach three worlds: front of house, the monitor desk and the broadcast truck. Build channel 7's path.

why.Venue house patch (unlabeled): You'd be trusting a patch you didn't build, differently wired in every city. The tour carries its own path so it's the same every night.
why.Y-cable from the stage box: A Y-cable joins three consoles' inputs together; one fault or one phantom-power choice affects all three. A proper splitter gives each world its own feed.
why.RF file on the laptop: That's the plan for the frequency — not part of the audio path. (Where it lives is a different problem.)
why.Broadcast feed (isolated split): The broadcast world gets its own isolated output so its problems can't reach the stage.
why.Splitter (one input, three outputs): One source, three independent feeds: FOH, monitors, broadcast.

R-11.success: Source → stage box → splitter → three worlds, each with its own feed. When a channel dies, you can now ask: in one world, or in all three?
R-11.timeoutWhy: Start at the source: the receiver. Everything else is downstream of it.

O-11.title: Advance a venue
O-11.brief: Venue 3 sent a packet that contradicts itself. Put the advance in an order that ends in a plan everyone can sign.
items: Read every page's title block, date and building name
List what's missing or contradictory
Send the venue specific written questions (drawing date, ratings, power service, contacts)
Escalate anything overhead to the head rigger, who escalates to the structural engineer
Plan a fallback that needs no missing data
Confirm the plan in writing with the venue and the crew
Store the plan where the whole tour can find it
why: You can't trust a page until you know which building and which year it describes.
Name the gaps before you fill any of them.
A specific question gets a specific answer; 'is it fine?' gets 'sure'.
Overhead decisions belong to qualified people.
If the data never comes, the show still needs a safe version.
A plan nobody confirmed is a wish.
A plan on one laptop is one spilled coffee from gone. (DEBT-004)
O-11.success: Read, list, ask, escalate, fall back, confirm, share. The last step is the one the printed story skips.

C-11.title: Same song, same spot
C-11.brief: Marisol's wireless drops at the same bar of song eleven, three shows running, in two cities. Pick the three clues that best separate the explanations.
hypotheses: interference from phones or local signals
a blocked radio path at one position

clues.t: RF scan: nothing new near channel 7, in either city
clues.why: Rules out interference: nothing is shouting over the channel.

clues.t: At bar 30 she walks to the downstage-right lip and turns upstage
clues.why: Same position, same moment, every time: points at the path, not the gear.

clues.t: Walk test: signal falls into the noise at the lip — and only there
