clues.why: A measurement at the exact position. Weak signal, not interference.

clues.t: A new batch of batteries went in at the Wexley
clues.why: City 2's drop happened on an old-batch battery.

clues.t: The front row films song eleven on phones
clues.why: The scan shows no new signals, and phones don't film only bar 32.

clues.t: The receiver is two years old
clues.why: Old isn't broken; it works everywhere else on stage.

clues.t: Change channel 7's frequency and see if it stops
clues.why: No interference was measured. Changing frequency changes the comparison across three shows and fixes nothing.

clues.t: It started the week the tour began
clues.why: True of everything on this tour.

C-11.success: No interference, one position, a measured weak signal there: the radio path is blocked at the lip.

F-11.title: Where does channel 7 die?
F-11.brief: Walk test at bar 30's position, one reading per stage from the transmitter to the console. Tap the first stage where the signal is lost.

stages.name: Transmitter + battery
stages.reading: Fresh battery; full output at the booth (measured)
stages.why: The source is healthy.

stages.name: Belt pack on the body
stages.reading: Worn as in the show; fine everywhere else on stage
stages.why: The pack isn't the problem by itself.

stages.name: Air path at the DSR lip
stages.reading: Steel frame + her body between pack and antennas; signal falls into the noise (measured)
stages.why: The first place the signal is lost: the path.

stages.name: Receiver antennas
stages.reading: Both behind the LED frame; both branches low at the lip
stages.why: Downstage of the loss — and the reason it happens. Diversity can't choose between two bad signals.

stages.name: Receiver + console ch 7
stages.reading: Receiver mutes when the signal drops; console hears silence
stages.why: The symptom where the people are.

F-11.ask: Tap the earliest stage where a reading — not a hunch — shows the signal is lost.
F-11.success: The loss happens in the air at one position. Move the antennas to line of sight, then prove it with the same walk.

T-11.title: A look inside the load budget
T-11.brief: Kim's check of Ben's ground-supported truss plus what's left on house pipe 4 gives Sofia a combined overhead budget of 240 kg (illustrative). Here “risk” means what the Act 2 moment loses if a piece is missing: likelihood the audience feels the gap × impact on the story. Faces must be lit.

items.name: Front key light for the lantern speech (ground truss)
items.why: If the audience can't see faces, the moment is gone. A commitment.

items.name: Four-unit halo, downstage (ground truss)
items.why: The heart of Sofia's idea, lower and wider than she drew — but there.

items.name: Two extra halo units upstage (ground truss)
items.why: A fuller ring. Lovely; heavy for what it adds.

items.name: Backlight row on pipe 4 (what's left of its rating)
items.why: Separates the actors from the dark. Cheap for what it gives.

items.name: Texture unit on pipe 4
items.why: Leaves on the floor. Small weight, small but real effect.

items.name: LED tape on the truss face
items.why: Hides the truss in the dark. Light, cheap.

items.name: Strobe pair for the storm cue
items.why: A different scene. Nice, not needed for this moment.

items.name: Spare moving head “just in case”
items.why: A want, not a need.

items.name: Camera platform on the truss for the tour video
items.why: Marketing. Retires nothing for the audience tonight.

T-11.success: Faces first, then the most story per kilo: the halo, the backlight, the cheap texture and tape. Say out loud what the look gave up.: figures illustrative.
T-11.timeoutWhy: Start with the commitment (faces), then compare what each kilo buys. A defensible look beats a perfect one you never present.

O-12.title: When there's no number
O-12.brief: A venue can't supply a rating for the beam your design needs. Put the people and documents in order. (Who and what — not how.)
items: Stop: nothing goes up; everyone knows why
Ask the venue in writing for drawings and ratings, and who issued them
Give the structural engineer the facts: photos, drawings, what you want to hang and its weight
The engineer approves, refuses, or offers an alternative
The head rigger turns an approved option into a written rigging plan
The designer adapts the look within the approved loads
Record the decision, who made it, and what the show lost
why: Stop-work first: normal, calm, no blame.
The data belongs to the venue; ask its owner.
An engineer can only judge what they're shown.
The engineer's call — not the loudest voice's.
Plans are documents people can check.
Art adapts inside the safe envelope.
Honest reports make the next venue ask earlier.
O-12.success: Stop, ask, escalate with facts, engineer decides, rigger plans, designer adapts, report honestly. Nobody is made safe by being confident.

C-12.title: Cue 14
C-12.brief: Press night. Cue 14 snaps instead of fading, and the moving heads aim low. Pick the three clues that best separate the explanations.
hypotheses: a change to the console after rehearsal

clues.t: Only cues with no fade time of their own run fast; cues with explicit times are perfect
clues.why: A pattern in the show's defaults — not random, not the network.

clues.t: Every moving head is off by the same angle; all other fixtures are right
clues.why: One fixture type, one consistent offset: something about how that type is defined.

clues.t: Console log: update installed 14:06 — after the last rehearsal
clues.why: What changed, and when. The pattern began after it.

clues.t: The network switch's lights are blinking fast
clues.why: That's normal control traffic; the conventional fixtures on the same network are perfect.

clues.t: Conventional fixtures on the dimmers look exactly right
clues.why: Clears the dimmers, but doesn't point at the cause by itself.

clues.t: Sofia's GO on cue 12 looked a beat late
clues.why: The rehearsal video shows her GO right on Rosa's call. Timing isn't the fault.

clues.t: Reboot the console at intermission and see if it clears
clues.why: Risks a dark stage, and the event log that proves the cause could scroll away. It won't undo an update anyway.

clues.t: It's press night and everyone's nervous
clues.why: True and irrelevant to the file.

C-12.success: Default-timed cues only, one fixture type only, starting after a 14:06 update: the console changed, not the network, the dimmers or the operator.

O-13.title: Show-day change freeze
O-13.brief: Write the rule that would have saved press night. Put the freeze in order, from the day before to after the curtain.
items: The day before: install and test any updates, then save a dated show file off the console
Morning call: declare the freeze — no updates, no new files, no new devices
Defer automatic update prompts on every show-critical device
Pre-show: sample key cues against the rehearsal record
During the show: work around problems by hand; the stage manager holds or stops the show
After the house empties: fix, test cue-to-cue against the record, log it, then lift the freeze
why: Changes happen when there's time to test them — and there's always a copy to go back to.
Everyone hears the rule at the same time.
A 2 p.m. pop-up shouldn't be able to ask the question at all.
Verify before doors, against something recorded.
The booth adapts; the SM decides. Fly and scenery cues run only as rehearsed.
Proof, then record, then the freeze ends.
O-13.success: Test the day before, freeze on the day, verify before doors, adapt by hand during, fix and prove after. Nobody should be asked “install now?” at 2 p.m. on press night.

F-12.title: Her own voice, late
F-12.brief: Noor heard herself about a third of a second late in her in-ear. One reading per stage of the path. Tap the first stage where the signal becomes wrong for its listener.

stages.name: Noor's mic → console
stages.why: The source is fine.

stages.name: Program mix → video truck
stages.why: Sending program to the truck is correct.

stages.name: Video truck processing
stages.reading: Adds ~0.32 s for frame sync and the encoder (measured, illustrative)
stages.why: Normal for video: viewers see and hear it in sync. Not a failure by itself.

stages.name: RTN 1 → Noor's IFB (template)
stages.reading: Program return, including her own mic, mixed into her in-ear (routing snapshot)
stages.why: The first place the signal is wrong for its listener: her own voice, delayed, into her ear.

stages.name: In-ear transmitter
stages.why: Downstream of the mistake.

stages.name: Noor's ear
stages.reading: Echo of her own voice, late
stages.why: The symptom where the person is.

F-12.ask: Tap the earliest stage where the signal stops being right for the person hearing it.
F-12.success: A delay that's normal for viewers becomes a failure the moment it's routed into the talker's ear. The fix is the routing: a true mix-minus.

M-11.title: Season so far: where did each cause live?
M-11.brief: Five episodes, one tour. Classify each CAUSE, not the symptom.

items.s: Last tour's RF plan hit local services in two cities — each city's radio environment differs
items.why: The surroundings changed from city to city.

items.s: Venue 3's rigging page was copied from another building
items.why: Information supplied from outside, and wrong.

items.s: Channel 7 dropped at the lip — antennas moved for a riser and nobody told RF
items.why: An undocumented change during load-in.

items.s: Cue 14 snapped — the update reset the show's default fade time
items.why: A setting changed under the show.

items.s: Press night had no rule against show-day updates
items.why: A missing process, not a missing part.

items.s: Noor heard herself late — a template routed a delayed return into her in-ear
items.why: Routing that was right in one place and wrong in another.

items.s: Moving heads aimed low — a new fixture profile gave stored values new meanings
items.why: The definition of the device changed.

items.s: The stream truck's return is ~0.32 s late — frame sync and encoding
items.why: A property of the signal path itself; normal for viewers, harmful in an ear.

M-11.success: Most of this season's causes are workflow and configuration: things people changed, copied or assumed. The parts mostly worked.

R-21.title: Room A, after the flip
R-21.brief: The airwall is closed. The keynote is in Room A. Build the path from the lectern to Room A's ceiling — including the state the house system must be in.

why.Plate B · tie-in (Room B): In DIVIDED, plate B feeds only Room B. Your keynote would land in the sponsors' lunch.
why.House processor · COMBINED: COMBINED ignores Room A's plates and plays Room B's inputs everywhere — exactly why Room A went silent.
why.Room B ceiling zones: That's the lunch room's output, not the keynote's.
why.Airwall sensor lead: It sets the state, but it carries no audio. It's control, not signal.
why.Plate A (Room A): The plate that belongs to the keynote's room.
why.House processor · DIVIDED: The state that matches a closed wall.
why.Halyard console: The mix comes after the mic.
why.Room A ceiling zones: The last stage: where the 400 people are.

R-21.success: Mic → console → the plate that belongs to the room → the state that matches the wall → that room's zones. The state is part of the signal path.
R-21.timeoutWhy: Start at the lectern and move one stage at a time. The only trap is the state: which one matches a closed wall?

F-21.title: Room A is silent
F-21.brief: 12:50 p.m. Maya's keynote walk-in music plays in no part of Room A. One reading at each stage.

stages.name: Halyard console
stages.why: The source is healthy. The failure is downstream.

stages.name: Cable to plate A
stages.reading: A tester at the plate end reads the signal (measured)
stages.why: The cable is fine — this isn't the missing cable.

stages.name: House processor
stages.reading: Input A meter moving; panel says COMBINED · WALL OPEN, Room A plates not routed (observed)
stages.why: The first stage where your signal stops: it arrives, and the state throws it away.

stages.name: Room A amplifiers
stages.reading: Powered; playing whatever the processor sends — right now, Room B's lunch mic
stages.why: Healthy, and busy reproducing the wrong room.

stages.name: Room A speakers
stages.reading: No walk-in music; the lunch emcee, faintly
stages.why: The symptom where the people are.

F-21.ask: Tap the earliest stage where the evidence shows your signal being lost.
F-21.success: The signal reached the processor and the state discarded it. That rules out cables, amplifiers and speakers — and points at the wall sensor.

C-21.title: The mix nobody approved
C-21.brief: 2:16 p.m. Online viewers hear the band too loud and a wings mic the room never heard. The room sounds perfect.
hypotheses: the stream's tap point is before the room's mutes and faders
the room mix is too hot

clues.t: Devon's mute on the wings mic doesn't move the stream's meter
clues.why: The stream hears the channel before the mute: a tap-point clue.

clues.t: Devon pulls the band down in the room; the stream's band stem doesn't budge
clues.why: The stream ignores the fader too: it's tapped upstream of it.

clues.t: The vendor's patch sheet: STREAM STEMS · TAP: INPUT (PRE)
clues.why: The record says where the stream listens.

clues.t: The joke was only heard online
clues.why: True and alarming, but it doesn't say where the stream taps.

clues.t: The co-presenter's wireless battery reads 20%
clues.why: The mic worked perfectly. That was the problem.

clues.t: The encoder shows “Healthy”
clues.why: It reports its own view; it's faithfully encoding the wrong mix.

clues.t: Restart the encoder to reset its audio
clues.why: Four thousand viewers lose the stream for a minute, and the stem meters' history goes with it.

clues.t: Chat complaints spike during the band's second song
clues.why: Useful for WHEN, not WHERE.

C-21.success: Mute ignored, fader ignored, and a sheet that says INPUT: the stream was listening upstream of everything the room engineer did.

R-22.title: Build the stream's speech path
R-22.brief: Rebuild the co-presenter's path to the stream so that what's muted in the room stays muted online, and the stream keeps its own balance.

slots.label: 7 · SYNC
slots.answer: Audio delay to match the picture

pool: Audio delay to match the picture

why.Input tap (before everything): That's the vendor's template: it ignores the mute, the gate and the fader. It's how the joke got online.
why.Post-fader send: Follows the room's balance — and the room barely needs the band in the PA. The band vanishes online.
why.Room main L/R: The room's mix, shaped for a room that hears the band acoustically. Wrong balance, wrong EQ for headphones.
why.Channel mute (Devon's): The mute comes after processing and before the tap you want.
why.Stem send · pre-fader, post-mute: Obeys the mute, ignores the room's fader.
why.Audio delay to match the picture: Video is late; the audio waits for it.

R-22.success: Mic → gain → processing → mute → a pre-fader, post-mute tap → the stream's own mix → delay to the picture → encoder.
R-22.timeoutWhy: Start at the mic. The only hard slot is the tap: after the mute, before the fader.

T-21.title: Sixty minutes before doors
T-21.brief: 6:00 p.m. Doors at 7:00. Graham wants his new product-reveal cue tonight; the only hour is the pre-show checklist hour. Build the plan that retires the most risk. Times and scores are illustrative.

items.name: Comms + stage manager channel check
items.why: Nobody can call a show — or a hold — without comms. Not optional.

items.name: Every source on the switcher, full screen
items.why: The room flipped for dinner an hour ago. Camera 2 is the CEO's IMAG.

items.name: Every mic line-checked at show level
items.why: Batteries, packs and the CEO's headset — each one a live failure if skipped.

items.name: Run cues 1–4 at the top of show
items.why: The first minutes are the ones everyone remembers.

items.name: Program the new reveal cue (light + video + sting)
items.why: Skip it and the client relationship takes a certain, moderate hit.

items.name: Rehearse the reveal once with Rosa
items.why: An unrehearsed show-control cue is a gamble in three departments. Only useful if it's programmed.

items.name: Stream: second listener on cellular
items.why: This afternoon proved why.

items.name: Walk the floor: pockets, ramps, cable paths
items.why: Carts, catering and chairs just moved over every cable in the room.

items.name: Full dress rehearsal of the whole show
items.why: Thorough, and it eats the hour.

items.name: Install the console's “recommended” update while you wait
items.why: Retires nothing and adds a new risk on show day.

T-21.success: Commitments first, then risk per minute: comms, every source, every mic, the floor — and the reveal, programmed and rehearsed once, frozen at doors. Say out loud what you're not checking.
T-21.timeoutWhy: Start with what you can't skip, then the cheap high-risk lines. You don't need the perfect hour, just a defensible one.

F-22.title: Camera 2 is black
F-22.brief: 6:07 p.m. The switcher shows camera 2 black. The router is correct. You carry a field monitor down the path.

stages.name: Camera 2 viewfinder
stages.why: The camera is working.

stages.name: Camera SDI out
stages.why: The camera's output is good.

stages.name: Floor pocket · camera side
stages.why: The run from the camera to the pocket is good.

stages.name: Floor pocket · house side
stages.why: The first point with no picture: the connection through the pocket.

stages.name: Router input 2
stages.why: Downstream of the break.

stages.name: Switcher
stages.why: The symptom.

F-22.success: Last good reading, first bad one: the fault is the connection through the floor pocket. One cable, one camera.

F-23.title: The scanner that can't check a ticket
F-23.brief: 12:58 a.m. A gate scanner shows OFFLINE. Its Wi-Fi bars are full. One reading per stage of its path to the ticketing service.

stages.name: Wi-Fi link
stages.why: The radio link is fine.

stages.name: Address
stages.why: It has an address nobody else is using.

stages.name: Gateway
stages.reading: 198.18.20.1 — the AV router, which has no internet (observed vs. the site sheet: .254)
stages.why: The first failure: it was handed the wrong door out.

stages.name: Name lookup
stages.why: Downstream: nothing beyond the wrong gateway answers.

stages.name: Ticketing service
stages.why: The symptom.

F-23.ask: Tap the earliest stage where the evidence shows the failure.
F-23.success: Connected, addressed — and pointed at the wrong gateway. A second DHCP server gave it a different answer.

M-22.title: Where did the festival network fault live?
M-22.brief: Faults from a festival night. Classify each CAUSE, not the symptom.

items.s: Half the scanners offline — two DHCP servers on one joined network
items.why: Two answers to one question on the network itself.

items.s: Stream drops — the encoder's fixed address sat inside the pool the site server hands out
items.why: An address plan that disagreed with the server's pool.

items.s: Networks joined at midnight by a team that then went home
items.why: A change without its owner around to own it.

items.s: Tickets won't validate — the ticketing company's cloud service was down
items.why: Outside the site.

items.s: Gate Wi-Fi drops every time the catering truck parks in front of the access point
items.why: A physical obstruction in the radio path.

items.s: The gate tent switch is dead — its extension lead was unplugged for a kettle
items.why: No power, no switch.

items.s: Encoder audio clicks every few seconds — two devices don't share one audio clock
items.why: A timing fault inside the signal itself.

M-22.success: Symptoms showed up as “the network.” Causes lived in seven different places.

O-24.title: Rain, lightning, hold, restart
O-24.brief: An outdoor show and a storm. Put the AV team's part in order. The hold itself is the weather plan's and its named person's — never the booth's.
items: Before doors: know the weather plan — who calls a hold, what triggers it, where people shelter
Rain starts: protect the show with reversible moves (wired backup mic, local monitor fallback)
Power or structure problems go straight to their owners (power vendor, riggers)
When the plan's person calls a hold: support it — stop work, nobody at wet power or overhead
Keep the announce mic and performer talkback alive for the stage manager; move to shelter
Use the hold: gather evidence from shelter — logs, photos, scans — and plan the fixes
After the all-clear, owners make their areas safe; then fix one thing at a time
Prove it: a monitored stable period, an RF walk test, the vendor's sign-off
Report facts to the stage manager — restart is production's call — then write the report
why: The plan decides; you need to know it before the sky does.
Service first, with changes you can undo.
Not yours to reset, re-seat or climb.
The hold is the plan's call. Your job is to make it easy.
During a hold, communication is the show.
The hold is the best troubleshooting time you'll get.
Nothing before the all-clear, and nothing before the owner says it's safe.
Proof, not hope, before the crowd comes back.
Facts to the person who decides. Then write it down — somewhere that isn't one laptop.
O-24.success: Know the plan, protect the show reversibly, support the hold, use it, fix after the all-clear, prove it, report facts.

C-22.title: Control drops in the rain
C-22.brief: 9:26 p.m. FOH loses stage-box control for two or three seconds at a time. Four explanations are on the board.
hypotheses: water at a ground-level network junction

clues.t: Control drops line up with bursts of heavier rain, minute by minute
clues.why: Correlated with rainfall intensity, not with anything the console does.

clues.t: Switch log: the stage-left junction port flaps 23 times; every other port is steady
clues.why: One physical link, not the console or the whole network.

clues.t: Imani's 8:40 walk photo: the junction's rain boot hanging off, the box on the ground
clues.why: The mechanism: a connector with no rain protection at ground level.

clues.t: The console took a software update last week
clues.why: True, and it passed a full show since. Recent isn't evidence.

clues.t: Twelve thousand phones in the crowd
clues.why: Phones don't flap a wired network port — and the RF scan showed nothing new.

clues.t: The stage box is five years old
clues.why: Old isn't broken; the box answers fine between drops.

clues.t: Reboot the console during the hold to “clear” it
clues.why: It wipes the drop log that lines up with the rain — and proves nothing about a wet connector.

clues.t: The drops started at 9:21, when the rain started
clues.why: Suggestive, but onset alone is weaker than intensity lining up with every drop.

C-22.success: Drops that follow the rain, one flapping port, and a photo of a bootless junction on the ground: the water, not the console.

M-23.title: Season 2 review: where did the cause live?
M-23.brief: Season 2's failures, one line each. Classify each CAUSE, not the symptom.

items.s: Opening night fades wrong — a console update installed that afternoon, never tested
items.why: A show-day change without verification. Configuration is also defensible.

items.s: Presenter hears herself late — a template sent a delayed return into her in-ear mix
items.why: A routing template built for a different show.

items.s: Half the ballroom silent — airwall sensor unplugged, processor stuck in COMBINED
items.why: The system's state logic acted on a wrong belief.

items.s: Stream carried a muted mic — stems tapped before the channel mute
items.why: A send's tap point.

items.s: Camera 2 black — a connector crushed at a floor pocket
items.why: The physical signal path itself.

items.s: Scanners offline — two DHCP servers on one joined network
items.why: Addressing on the network.

items.s: Control drops in the rain — a junction connector sitting in water
items.why: Weather reached a connector that had lost its protection.

items.s: Generator alarm mid-set — a fault in the power vendor's machine
items.why: The power source itself.

items.s: Next month's RF plan lost — it lived on one laptop
items.why: A single point of failure made of habit (DEBT-004).

M-23.success: Nine failures, six classes. The symptom tells you where to start; the evidence tells you where it lived.

C-31.title: Twelve rooms, one cause
C-31.brief: Monday 8:55. Twelve meeting rooms on six floors refuse to join calls. Pick the clues that separate the explanations.
hypotheses: a network outage on those floors
the room accounts can't sign in

clues.t: A personal laptop in the same room joins the same call fine
clues.why: The meeting service is up and the room's network path works. That clears two suspects at once.

clues.t: Every panel shows the same error: sign-in failed · password expired
clues.why: Twelve rooms, one identical message about an account — not about a network or a panel.

clues.t: Change calendar: Friday 18:00 · passwords older than 90 days must change at next sign-in
clues.why: Answers “what changed?” — and it touches accounts, which is what the error names.

clues.t: All twelve are pilot-ring rooms that restarted at 02:00 Sunday
clues.why: Keep this one: it explains WHEN they tried to sign in. On its own it doesn't separate the causes.

clues.t: The rooms are on six different floors and five different switches
clues.why: Makes one floor's switch unlikely, but the laptop test says more, faster.

clues.t: The touch panels are three years old
clues.why: Old isn't broken. The panels are reporting an account error faithfully.

clues.t: Renata says the rooms “always break on Mondays”
clues.why: A pattern worth writing down (the Monday Ghost) — not evidence about this cause.

clues.t: Restart all twelve rooms and see what happens
clues.why: They sign in with the same expired password and fail again — and the panels' sign-in logs are gone.

C-31.success: Service fine, network fine, one account error, one Friday change: the rooms are signed out by an identity policy. The fix belongs to the account's owner.

O-31.title: Before two a.m.
O-31.brief: 277 more rooms restart at 02:00 and will hit the same wall. Put the day's work in the order a professional would take it.
items: State the broken outcome in one sentence: rooms can't sign in; 277 more restart at 02:00
Bring the evidence to the accounts' owner (identity / security) — not a fix
The owner moves room accounts to a room-account policy with unique, managed credentials
Prove it on the pilot ring: restart the twelve and watch each one sign in
Test a real call from a pilot room to a far end outside the building's network
Let the fleet restart on schedule and watch the sign-in failure count
Walk three occupied rooms when the first meetings start
Fix the change template so “impacted systems” must list room accounts
why: One observable sentence, with the deadline in it.
Identity isn't yours to change; evidence is yours to bring.
The owner makes the access decision and the change.
Twelve rooms is a safe ring: small, known, already broken.
A panel saying READY isn't a working meeting.
The schedule is the test the fleet was always going to run.
Proof is where the people are.
Close the gap that let this through, or the next policy change does it again.
O-31.success: Outcome, owner, change, pilot, real call, fleet, people, template. The rooms never saw Tuesday.

F-31.title: Where does the echo get through?
F-31.brief: Remote participants hear themselves about half a second late, only from the Harbor Room. One reading per stage of the conferencing audio chain.

stages.name: Far-end audio arriving
stages.reading: Clean and on time at the room (measured)
stages.why: The far end's voice arrives intact. Nothing wrong yet.

stages.name: Room processor · echo canceller
stages.reading: On; reference = the exact signal sent to the loudspeakers; tested alone, no echo returns (measured)
stages.why: The canceller nearest the mics, with the true reference, does its job.

stages.name: Conferencing software processing
stages.reading: Its own echo cancellation and noise suppression ON — re-enabled by Sunday's update; echo bursts return (observed)
stages.why: The first stage where echo gets through that shouldn't: a second canceller fighting the first.

stages.name: Network to the far end
stages.why: Transport carries whatever it's given — including the echo.

stages.name: Far-end ear
stages.why: The symptom, where the user is. Not the cause.

F-31.ask: Tap the first stage where the echo gets through.
F-31.success: One canceller per path, nearest the mics, with the true reference. The second one — switched back on by an update — was fighting it.

R-31.title: One canceller, the right reference
R-31.brief: Rebuild the Harbor Room's conferencing audio so exactly one echo canceller works on the room, with the true loudspeaker reference.

slots.label: 2 · PLAYBACK = REFERENCE
slots.answer: Processor output to the room loudspeakers

pool: Processor output to the room loudspeakers
Software echo canceller on as well

why.Display's built-in speakers: Sound that doesn't pass through the processor has no reference in its canceller — that's a classic way to CREATE echo.
why.Software echo canceller on as well: Two cancellers in series fight: the second keeps re-adapting to a signal the first already cleaned.
why.Microphone gain down 10 dB: Everyone gets quieter, the far end and the echo together. The path is unchanged.
why.Processor echo canceller: It needs the exact signal that went to the loudspeakers as its reference.
why.Conferencing software (its canceller off: The software still carries the call; it just stops re-processing a signal the room already cleaned.

R-31.success: Far end → loudspeakers (the reference) → mics → ONE canceller with that reference → software → far end. One job, one place.

M-31.title: Where did the camera go?
M-31.brief: Camera-missing tickets from across the fleet. Classify each CAUSE, not the symptom.

items.s: Camera vanishes after ten idle minutes — the computer suspends idle USB devices
items.why: A device power state: the computer put it to sleep.

items.s: Camera comes back as a new device; the software keeps looking for the old one
items.why: The software was set to one exact instance, not “the room camera”.

items.s: Thirty-seven camera tickets closed as “user error” for months
items.why: A recurring fault hidden by how tickets were closed.

items.s: The extender doesn't carry the wake-up signal cleanly over its long cable
items.why: The link itself mishandles part of what it must carry. Some reviewers would say Configuration.

items.s: Camera and speaker bar share an unpowered hub; the camera drops when its motors home at start-up
items.why: The port's power budget, shared and exceeded.

items.s: Last month's room image set an energy-saving power plan on every room computer
items.why: A standard setting that disagreed with what a room needs.

items.s: No camera because the room account was signed out of the meeting service
items.why: Something outside the room (identity) — season 3's ghost.

items.s: Camera picture too dark after facilities removed the blinds
items.why: The room's light changed, not the system.

M-31.success: One symptom — “the camera's gone” — with causes in power, configuration, signal, dependency, environment and workflow.

T-31.title: Fifteen rooms, eight hours
T-31.brief: The Studio Room is fixed. Fourteen more rooms share the extender, with 37 tickets closed as user error. You have Sam's eight hours this week (480 minutes, illustrative). Commitments first.

items.name: Profile fix on the pilot ring + idle-share test
items.why: Nothing else is safe to roll out until the fix is proven on a ring.

items.name: Reopen the 37 tickets and call the 14 users: it wasn't you
items.why: People were told they caused it. Correcting that is a commitment, not an option.

items.name: Roll the profile to the 14 extender rooms, with a test in each
items.why: Known-broken rooms, weekly impact, cheap per room.

items.name: Write a problem record: camera tickets closed as user error
items.why: So the pattern has an owner and doesn't get closed away again.

items.name: Add the extender model to the room inventory
items.why: Next time, one query finds every affected room.

items.name: Replace “replug here” stickers with “call us with the time”
items.why: Turns a workaround into evidence.

items.name: Roll the profile to the rest of the fleet by ring
items.why: Worth doing — next week, after the extender rooms are proven.

items.name: Replace every extender with a new model
items.why: Expensive, slow, and the profile fix already removes the trigger.

items.name: Buy new cameras for all fifteen rooms
items.why: The cameras were never broken.

items.name: Zip-tie the table cables so nobody can unplug them
items.why: Blocks the users' only workaround and fixes nothing.

T-31.success: Commitments first (prove the fix, tell people it wasn't them), then the most risk per minute: the known-broken rooms, a problem record, the inventory. Say out loud what waits for next week.
T-31.timeoutWhy: Start with what you can't skip. Then compare risk per minute.

R-32.title: Six thousand people need to hear her
R-32.brief: Rebuild the town-hall audio path from Dana's microphone to remote staff. Every stage must be on the right network.

why.Encoder audio card · office segment: That's exactly Thursday's fault: the stream lives on the AV segment and doesn't cross to the office one.
why.Guest Wi-Fi: Not allowed for production media, and not yours to decide. The network owner sets that rule.
why.Confidence monitor: It shows the room what the camera sees. It proves nothing about remote audio.
why.Room loudspeakers: The room's output. The room was never the problem.
why.Network audio stream · AV segment: The processor puts Dana's audio on the AV segment as a stream.
why.Encoder audio card · AV segment (CR-12): The receiver has to be on the same segment as the stream.

R-32.success: Mic → processor → AV-segment stream → encoder card on the AV segment → encoder → platform. One wrong segment and six thousand people hear nothing.

T-32.title: Twelve minutes to ten
T-32.brief: 9:48. You've found where the audio stops. Twelve story-minutes remain. Choose what the team does before Dana walks on (figures illustrative).

items.name: Listen stage by stage to confirm where audio stops
items.why: Without it, every other move is a guess.

items.name: Priya moves the encoder's port to the AV segment (logged)
items.why: The fix, by the person who owns the network.

items.name: Priya checks all four re-patched ports
items.why: The ticket said four. You found one.

items.name: Outside-network phone check, interpreter included
items.why: Proof where the remote staff are.

items.name: Calibrated status to Ines and Dana
items.why: The CEO needs facts to decide whether to wait.

items.name: Patch the processor's analog backup into the encoder
items.why: A fallback inside AV's own kit — good if there's time.

items.name: Full sound check of all eight audience mics
items.why: Nice. The Q&A is in forty minutes.

items.name: Reboot the room processor “to be safe”
items.why: It's healthy; rebooting erases its state and silences the room.

items.name: Re-test the confidence monitor
items.why: It was never broken.

items.name: Rebuild the webcast layout
items.why: Pretty; retires no risk.

T-32.success: Find it, fix it by its owner, check every port the ticket touched, prove it from outside, and tell the CEO the truth. The fallback if there's room.
T-32.timeoutWhy: Start with what you can't skip — finding and fixing — then add proof.

C-33.title: Where does the Monday Ghost live?
C-33.brief: Ten Mondays of room failures, a different cause each time. Pick the clues that separate the explanations.
hypotheses: rooms outside the inventory miss every fleet fix
people are rougher with rooms after weekends

clues.t: Six of last Monday's seventeen tickets came from rooms with no dashboard tile
clues.why: Those rooms are invisible to monitoring — they can never go red.

clues.t: The inventory lists 289 rooms; facilities lists 300 bookable rooms
clues.why: Eleven rooms exist that the systems don't know about.

clues.t: Every fleet fix this season was scoped by an inventory query
clues.why: Identity, echo and USB fixes all skipped the eleven — so they keep failing the next Monday.

clues.t: Ghost tickets cluster on Mondays
clues.why: It tells you WHEN (after weekend changes), not WHERE the failures keep landing.

clues.t: Mondays have the most meetings
clues.why: True, and it doesn't explain why the same rooms keep failing.

clues.t: The boardroom belongs to the CEO
clues.why: Who uses a room says nothing about why it fails.

clues.t: 14-East is green and no longer exists
clues.why: Damning for the metric, but it's about what green means — not which rooms are missing.

clues.t: Reimage the eleven rooms to standard tonight
clues.why: It wipes out whatever made each room an exception — the evidence of why — and may break the boardroom.

C-33.success: Missing rooms, an inventory that's short, and fixes scoped by that inventory: the ghost lives in the rooms nobody can see.

M-32.title: Why the dashboard lied
M-32.brief: Telemetry failures from Nora's reconstruction. Classify each CAUSE.

items.s: Harbor's tile is green but last heard nine days ago — failed polls keep their last color
items.why: The data is stale; the display hides its age.

items.s: Eleven rooms never appear — nobody added hand-configured rooms to the inventory
items.why: A recording habit that never happened.

items.s: “Green” is defined as “the controller answered a ping”
items.why: The monitoring was set up to measure the box, not the meeting.

items.s: Floor 30's controllers can't be polled — a firewall rule blocks the poller
items.why: The telemetry path itself is broken.

items.s: Every room fails at once because the meeting service is down
items.why: Outside the building.

items.s: 14-East was turned into a mail room, but its controller stayed in the inventory and plugged in
items.why: A decommission nobody finished.

items.s: A room's ceiling mics go dead because their switch is unplugged by the cleaning crew each night
items.why: The devices lose power; the controller never notices.

items.s: Sunday's update resets room audio settings to defaults
items.why: A setting changed underneath the room.

M-32.success: A dashboard can be wrong about coverage (workflow), about age (data), and about meaning (configuration) — all while every tile is green.

C-41.title: System Off, mid-meeting
C-41.brief: Six tickets: the touch panel shows SYSTEM OFF while a meeting is live. Sam closed all six as “user pressed End”.

clues.t: The controller log shows no button press before any of the six
clues.why: Rules out users: nobody pressed anything.

clues.t: Every event lands within seconds of the hour, right after a back-to-back booking
clues.why: On the hour, between two meetings: schedules colliding.

clues.t: Device feedback says display ON and call live while the panel says OFF
clues.why: The panel shows a belief the devices contradict — the state variable was set wrong.

clues.t: The panel hardware is three years old
clues.why: Old isn't broken, and a faulty panel wouldn't pick the exact second of the hour.

clues.t: The interviewer was new to the company
clues.why: Six tickets, six different people. It isn't them.

clues.t: It only happens in rooms on the new template
clues.why: Useful for WHERE to look, but it doesn't separate the explanations.

clues.t: Reboot the controller to clear it
clues.why: The event log that shows the sweep firing at 14:00:00.6 is gone — and the call may drop.

clues.t: The display has a firmware update waiting
clues.why: Nothing was updated. A suspect isn't evidence.

C-41.success: No press, on the hour, and a panel that disagrees with its own devices: two scheduled events racing, and a state variable that lies.

O-41.title: Fix a race the right way
O-41.brief: The Cedar Room's shutdown sweep races the calendar's wake on the hour. Order the work that removes the race instead of moving it.
items: Write down the states and events the room really has
Reproduce the race on purpose in the test room (back-to-back bookings)
Add a guard to every transition that can end a meeting
Handle events one at a time, in a queue
Drive the panel from device feedback, and make Start safe in a call
Raise a change request with the test evidence
Prove it in one room: many transitions, including a live call across the boundary
Roll out in small batches, watching each
why: You can't fix a machine you haven't drawn.
A fault you can trigger on purpose is a fault you can prove fixed.
Guards make order irrelevant: “is it safe right now?”
One transition finishes before the next begins.
The panel must tell the truth, and a second press must never hurt.
Production code changes go through change control — with evidence.
Test the condition that failed, not an empty room at night.
Small batches keep one surprise from becoming forty.
O-41.success: Draw it, reproduce it, guard it, queue it, make the panel honest, change it properly, prove it where it failed, roll it out carefully.

R-41.title: Every voice to every ear
R-41.brief: The Rowan Room's listening loop carries room microphones only; the hearing-aid participant hears nothing from remote people. Build the listening feed.
pool: Loudspeaker output after the volume knob

why.Room mics only: That's today's fault: loop users hear the room and miss every remote voice.
why.Loudspeaker output after the volume knob: Anyone who turns the room down turns the loop down too — and it carries the room's echo.
why.Laptop headphone jack: One person's laptop isn't the room. It leaves when they do.
why.Far-end audio from the call: Remote voices must reach the loop, not just the loudspeakers.
why.Listening mix · far end + room: Its own mix, with its own intent and owner.
why.Loop driver / listening transmitter: The output, last in the chain.

R-41.success: Covered capture, processing with an echo reference, far-end audio, a dedicated listening mix, then the loop. Every voice, every ear.

T-41.title: What goes into version 1
T-41.brief: The room standard's version 1 gets $25,000 per room type for changes beyond the base kit (illustrative). Two accessibility items are commitments. Fund the version that retires the most risk.

items.name: Table panel within seated reach + lowered wall panel
items.why: Participant 2 couldn't reach the door panel. A room someone can't operate isn't finished.

items.name: Listening feed = far end + room
items.why: Loop users miss every remote voice today. A commitment, not an option.

items.name: Share shows progress within about a second
items.why: Every first-time user, every day: six seconds of black looks like failure.

items.name: Mic coverage verified at every seat
items.why: Far seats sound distant to remote people in most rooms.

items.name: 30-second fallback card in every room
items.why: Cheap, and it turns a failure into a minute instead of a meeting.

items.name: Guarded state-machine template (from Cedar)
items.why: E06's race, removed in every room from day one.

items.name: Occupancy sensors for energy saving
items.why: Worth doing; retires little risk to meetings.

items.name: Largest display size in every room
items.why: Impressive. Retires no risk.

items.name: Voice-controlled room assistant
items.why: Untested with these users. A want, not a risk.

items.name: Ambient accent lighting strip
items.why: Pretty. Retires no risk.

T-41.success: Commitments first, then the most risk per dollar: feedback, coverage, the fallback card, the guarded template. Say out loud what version 1 leaves out.
T-41.timeoutWhy: Start with what you can't skip, then compare risk per dollar. Version 1 only has to be defensible, not perfect.

C-42.title: Nine times, one cause
C-42.brief: The Garden Room's display is on the wrong input most mornings. Nine tickets, nine “Resolved”. Which clues separate the explanations?

clues.t: The display's info screen: last input change 07:00:00, source CONTROL (network)
clues.why: A command did it, not a hand and not a fault — at an exact time.

clues.t: All nine tickets were opened between 07:02 and 07:55, weekdays only
clues.why: A weekday morning pattern: a schedule, not people at random.

clues.t: Switching to HDMI 1 fixes it every time — until the next morning
clues.why: A setting being changed, not hardware failing: rules out the display and the cable.

clues.t: The cleaning crew uses the room at 6 a.m.
clues.why: They leave by 6:30, and cleaners don't change inputs at 07:00:00 exactly.

clues.t: Nothing is plugged into HDMI 2
clues.why: Explains the “No Signal”, not what selected HDMI 2.

clues.t: Factory-reset the display to clear it
clues.why: Wipes the input-change history — the only record that names the source.

clues.t: The display is five years old
clues.why: Old isn't broken. It's doing exactly what it's told.

clues.t: Every ticket note says “Resolved”
clues.why: True, and exactly the problem — but it doesn't point at a cause.

C-42.success: An exact-time control command, a weekday-morning pattern, and a fix that holds until the next morning: something scheduled is switching the display.

O-42.title: From nine incidents to one problem
O-42.brief: Sam's Garden Room tickets. Put the work in order — from the meeting at 7:52 to the day the problem closes.
items: Restore service: switch the input, keep the meeting
Record what you saw before you changed it (photo of the display's info screen)
Link the repeat tickets to one problem record with an owner
Find the pattern: time, room, same fix
Catch the cause in the act — with the network's owner doing the capture
Publish the known error and the workaround to the desk
Raise a change to remove the cause: owner, rollback, test
Verify at the moment it used to fail, then close the problem
why: People first: the meeting starts at eight.
Evidence you don't keep, you don't get back.
Nine tickets are one story. Give it a name and an owner.
The pattern is the first real clue.
Measure on a network you're allowed to measure — through its owner.
Stop the desk rediscovering it every morning.
Finding a cause doesn't authorize removing it.
Proof at 07:00:00, not at noon.
O-42.success: Restore, record, link, pattern, catch, publish, change, verify. Incident work keeps meetings alive; problem work makes the next ticket unnecessary.

C-43.title: Who approved this?
C-43.brief: An old remote-support agent is running on the boardroom computer under a shared account. Where did it come from?

clues.t: Its install date matches the boardroom's commissioning week, five years ago
clues.why: Installed with the room — not recently, not later.

clues.t: It runs under the shared account the original installer created
clues.why: Points at the install team's habits, not an outsider.

clues.t: The boardroom isn't in the inventory: an exception room, never scanned
clues.why: Explains why five years passed without anyone seeing it.

clues.t: Its last inbound session was three weeks ago at 23:40
clues.why: Important for security — but it fits every explanation on the board.

clues.t: The agent's icon looks old-fashioned
clues.why: Style isn't evidence.

clues.t: Ray is annoyed at the delay
clues.why: Feelings aren't evidence either, in either direction.

clues.t: Uninstall it now to be safe
clues.why: The install record, the account and the session history go with it — and it's security's call.

clues.t: The vendor recommends always-on agents
clues.why: Explains why an installer might add one; doesn't show this one was.

C-43.success: Commissioning-week date, the installer's shared account, and a room nobody scanned: an old convenience nobody recorded. It still goes to security, untouched.

O-43.title: A supervised vendor session
O-43.brief: The processor's maker needs an hour in the boardroom before Monday. Put Mei's safe path in order.
items: Write down exactly what the vendor must touch, and for how long
Security decides the access path
Create a named, time-limited vendor account with a second factor
Open the session through the approved path, to that one device only
Watch the session live and keep the recording
Verify the result where the users are
End the session and confirm the access has expired
Record who, what, when, and who approved it
why: Scope first: one processor, one hour.
AV says what the work needs; security says how anyone gets in.
One person, one login, a log that can say who.
Least privilege: not the room network, not the computer, one device.
Supervision you can replay.
The board preset, tested from the far end.
Access that outlives the job is a door left open.
The record is what makes it approved rather than tolerated.
O-43.success: Scope, decide, name, narrow, watch, verify, expire, record. A yes with edges.

F-41.title: Where does the content stop?
F-41.brief: Monday 9:00. The CEO shares; the local display shows the chart; the far end sees a blank window. One reading per stage.

stages.name: CEO laptop
stages.why: The source is fine.

stages.name: Table HDMI → IN 1
stages.why: The cable works — the local display proves it.

stages.name: Switcher → room display
stages.why: The local path is healthy.

stages.name: Capture device → room computer
stages.why: The first stage where the far end's path goes wrong: the update pointed content at the empty input.

stages.name: Far end
stages.why: The symptom, downstream of the wrong selection.

F-41.ask: Tap the earliest stage whose reading explains the blank window.
F-41.success: Local path fine; the room computer captures the wrong input. Move to the labeled input or join from the laptop — then find out why the input changed.

O-44.title: The 30-second fallback card
O-44.brief: The card taped under every boardroom table since season 3. Put its steps in order.
items: Keep the meeting going — the room is still working
Check the far-end view (the assistant's tablet or a phone on the call)
Try the other labeled table input
If that fails: join the call from the presenter's laptop and share
Confirm with one remote person, on their own screen
Note the time and what you did
After the meeting: report it — never change the room's software mid-meeting
why: People first: the room, the call and the presenter are fine.
See what the far end sees before you touch anything.
Seconds, and nothing restarts.
The documented fallback: a second path that doesn't depend on the room computer's capture.
Proof where the people are.
The week that follows starts from this note.
Rollbacks and fixes are changes. Changes wait for the change process.
O-44.success: Keep going, look from the far end, try the labeled input, fall back to the laptop, confirm, note, report. Thirty seconds, nothing broken.

M-41.title: Season 3 review: where did the cause live?
M-41.brief: Season 3's failures, E01 to E10. Classify each CAUSE, not the symptom.

items.s: Twelve rooms won't join — a password policy change signed their accounts out
items.why: Identity is something the rooms depend on, outside the room.

items.s: Remote people hear themselves — echo cancellation applied twice
items.why: Two processors both set to do the same job.

items.s: A camera “randomly” leaves calls — the room computer puts its USB ports to sleep
items.why: A device power state. Many reviewers would also accept Configuration.

items.s: The town hall is silent remotely — a desk move put a port on the wrong segment
items.why: Segmentation. The move without a change record is a Human-workflow cause behind it.

items.s: The dashboard is green while rooms fail — rooms missing from the inventory
items.why: Nobody recorded the exceptions, so nothing measured them.

items.s: The panel says System Off mid-meeting — two scheduled events race
items.why: The control logic itself.

items.s: The display changes input at 7:00 — an orphaned job on an unowned server
items.why: An old scheduled configuration still running. Human workflow (no owner) is also defensible.

items.s: The far end sees a blank window — an update changed the default capture input
items.why: A setting changed underneath the room. Dependency is also defensible.

M-41.success: Season 3's symptoms all looked like “the room is broken.” The causes lived in identity, settings, power, networks, schedules — and records nobody kept.

F-51.title: Where does the timing go wrong?
F-51.brief: 5:08 p.m. CAM 2 and the program return tear every few seconds. One reading per stage — tap the earliest stage that explains it.

stages.name: Satellite antenna (roof)
stages.why: The first wrong reading: the reference lost the sky. The roof is facilities' — report it; don't go up.

stages.name: Reference A
stages.why: Downstream of the antenna: doing what it's designed to do.

stages.name: Reference B
stages.why: It follows A, so it drifts too. A backup that isn't.

stages.name: Video gateway
stages.why: The strict device shows the symptom first.

stages.name: Program output
stages.why: The symptom the viewers would see.

F-51.ask: Tap the earliest stage whose reading is wrong.
F-51.success: The antenna lost the sky; everything after it is consequence. You can't fix the roof (not yours) — so you move the strict device to an independent reference.

O-51.title: Prove the lips match
O-51.brief: Put the lip-sync check in order, the way you'd run it on a quiet morning.
items: Play the flash-and-beep sync clip into the program
Watch the stream on a phone off the station network
Record the phone screen and count the frames between flash and beep
Compare with the broadcast output
Set the stream audio delay to the measured value
Re-measure at the viewer's end
Label the delay with its reason
why: A known event on both tracks.
Measure where viewers are, not on the studio monitor.
Numbers beat opinions about lips.
Stream-only or both? That tells you where to look.
Compensate by a measured amount, not by ear.
Proof after the change.
So the next careful person doesn't remove it.
O-51.success: Measure at the viewer's end, compensate by the measurement, prove it again, and label the reason.

M-51.title: Where did the loudness go wrong?
M-51.brief: Match each observation from the afternoon to where its cause lives.

items.s: The PSA measures −14 LUFS; news −24 — mastered hot on purpose
items.why: A producer's choice, made in good faith, with no delivery rule.

items.s: Breaks skip the loudness processor since Tuesday — a preset reloaded
items.why: A setting, not a device fault.

items.s: The peak meter shows the PSA lower than the news
items.why: The signal is what it is; the peak meter measures the wrong thing for this question.

items.s: Complaints only mention the stream and the late news
items.why: Only the paths with the old preset.

items.s: Nobody owns 'delivery specs' for promos
items.why: A missing owner.

M-51.success: A producer's good intention, a reloaded preset, and a meter measuring the wrong thing. Three causes, three owners.

C-51.title: Where did twelve minutes of captions go?
C-51.brief: Captions vanished on the stream from 22:14 to 22:26 during the Route 9 bulletin. Pick the clues that tell the explanations apart.
hypotheses: The stream path dropped caption data

clues.t: June's encoder log shows every word sent, 22:14–22:26
clues.why: The captions left her encoder.

clues.t: Broadcast recordings show captions throughout
clues.why: Everything upstream of the split is fine.

clues.t: The stream transcoder switched to profile SPORTS TEST on Saturday
clues.why: A new box setting on the stream path only.

clues.t: Complaints came from app and web viewers
clues.why: Consistent with the stream — but doesn't say which box.

clues.t: Captions have been flaky before, people say
clues.why: A feeling, not a reading.

clues.t: The bulletin was about a road closure
clues.why: It's why it mattered, not why it failed.

clues.t: Restart June's encoder to 'clear it'
clues.why: It wipes the log that proves the captions were sent.

C-51.success: Captions left June's encoder and reached broadcast; the stream profile changed Saturday. The stream path dropped them.

T-51.title: The storm hour
T-51.brief: 11:50 p.m. The transmitter is on its slate. You have 20 minutes of Felix's attention and the station's. Choose what to do (figures illustrative).

items.name: Move program to the other carrier's IP link
items.why: Gets the valley back on air tonight.

items.name: Confirm on the off-air receiver at the studio
items.why: The only proof of what viewers get.

items.name: Check the utility map for shared routes
items.why: Finds the conduit both 'diverse' paths share.

items.name: Read Felix's STL margin log
items.why: Explains why this storm, this link.

items.name: Book daylight realignment with a certified crew
items.why: The real fix, by the right people, on a calm day.

items.name: Ask the tower crew to go up 'just to look'
items.why: Never in wind. Not a trade-off.

items.name: Ask Felix to raise transmitter power
items.why: The transmitter isn't the problem; its input is.

items.name: Wait for the rain to stop
items.why: The valley stays dark for hours.

items.name: Reboot the STL radios
items.why: Rain isn't a software fault; you'd lose the logs.

T-51.success: Back on air over a truly different path, proven off-air, with the real fix booked for daylight — and nobody on the tower.
T-51.timeoutWhy: On air first (IP link + off-air proof), then the map and the margin log.

R-51.title: Stadium to living room
R-51.brief: Rebuild the remote chain from the sideline reporter to viewers — and back to her ear.

why.Encoder · fixed 12 Mb/s: Tonight's fault: it can't bend when the crowd arrives.
why.Program return → reporter's earpiece: Two seconds late: she hears herself and stops talking.
why.Stadium fan Wi-Fi: Not yours, and shared with twenty thousand phones.

R-51.success: Adaptive encoder over bonded cellular into a buffered receiver; the reporter hears a clean mix-minus, never the program return.

O-52.title: Unwind section 5.3
O-52.brief: Sixty rooms are dark from address conflicts. Put the recovery in order.
items: Say what you know on the bridge: 5.3 put fixed addresses inside the range
Priya excludes the block from the automatic range (her change, logged)
Rooms recover their addresses; check the conflict list
Find the rooms that aren't on the list (exception register)
Correct the standard: reserved block outside the range
Sam opens the problem record
Add a 'standards touched?' check to the change template
why: The owner of the cause speaks first.
The network owner changes her network.
Measure the recovery.
The register finds what the list missed.
Fix the document that spread it.
Someone owns the whole problem.
So the next reviewed change knows what it touches.
O-52.success: Speak, let the owner fix her network, verify, look beyond the list, fix the document, own the problem, change the process.

M-52.title: What kind of risk was that?
M-52.brief: Classify where each cause from the morning lives.

items.s: 22 people share the 'newsdesk' login
items.why: An account design choice.

items.s: A producer forwarded the fake email to all staff
items.why: A helpful act with no safe path to take instead.

items.s: Playout on its own segment with its own accounts
items.why: Segmentation — and it's why the show went on.

items.s: The backup MCR runbook lists the shared login
items.why: A dependency waiting for the worst night.

items.s: The rundown system is unavailable after the lockout
items.why: The show depended on a system security had to lock.

M-52.success: Shared accounts and a helpful forward caused it; segmentation contained it; a runbook would have spread it to the backup. Fix all three.

O-53.title: Run the drill
O-53.brief: Put the 2 a.m. failover drill in order.
items: Tell the newsroom, Vera and the emergency manager's office the drill window
Write rollback criteria: captions, audio, alerts
Check the backup's references and timecode lock
Move program to the backup MCR
Verify every output off-air and on a phone, captions included
Roll back the moment a criterion fails
Fix, retry, and write every finding into the runbook
why: Nobody should be surprised at 2 a.m.
Decide the exits before you're in the room.
Clocks first — everything follows them.
The actual failover.
Proof where the audience is.
Following the plan is not failure.
The drill's real product is the runbook.
O-53.success: Tell, decide the exits, check the clocks, fail over, prove every output, roll back by the plan, write it all down.

T-61.title: The last hour before the crest
T-61.brief: 10:40 p.m. You have 30 minutes of the team's attention before the order you expect. Choose what to do (figures illustrative).

items.name: Agency forecast read word for word every 15 min, captioned
items.why: Relay, repeat, accessible.

items.name: Backup MCR confirmed ready (named accounts, captions, timecode)
items.why: So nobody has to stay.

items.name: Confirm field crews' positions against the safety plan
items.why: Vera's plan, Vera's call.

items.name: Check the second-language feed on every output
items.why: The people least able to catch a paraphrase.

items.name: Ask Hank for the generator's status
items.why: Know your power without touching it.

items.name: Route viewer reports to the emergency manager's desk
items.why: Verify before you air.

items.name: Build the station's own crest forecast graphic
items.why: Not ours. The agency's forecast is the forecast.

items.name: Send the crew to the bridge for a live shot at the crest
items.why: Against the field safety plan.

items.name: Redesign the lower-thirds for the big night
items.why: Pretty; retires no risk.

T-61.success: Relay and repeat, have the backup ready, keep crews where the plan says, make every language and caption work, and route reports to officials.
T-61.timeoutWhy: Start with what saves people: relay, backup, crews.

F-71.title: Silent since Saturday
F-71.brief: ENG-214's recordings have been silent since Saturday; the room itself sounds fine. One reading per stage — tap the earliest stage that explains it.

stages.name: Ceiling mics
stages.why: The room hears the lecturer — the mics are fine.

stages.name: Room DSP
stages.why: The DSP is sending program to the capture appliance.

stages.name: Capture input
stages.why: The first wrong reading: the appliance is listening to an empty USB input, not the DSP line.

stages.name: Encoder
stages.why: It records exactly what it's given — silence.

stages.name: Student portal
stages.why: The symptom Kai reported.

F-71.ask: Tap the earliest stage whose reading is wrong.
F-71.success: The capture input changed from LINE to USB. Everything after it faithfully records nothing.

O-71.title: Proving a fix in rooms you'll never visit
O-71.brief: The corrected capture profile is ready for all 22 rooms. Put the rollout in an order you could defend to Nadia.
items: Fix one room (ENG-214) and make a 30-second test recording
Play it back from the student portal, as a student would
Push the corrected profile to the other 21 rooms
Make and play back a test recording in each room
Add an audio-level check to the dashboard
Tell students which lectures were silent and what replaces them
why: One reversible change first.
Prove it where the people are — the portal, not the appliance.
Scale only what you've proven.
Each room is its own proof.
So the next silence turns a tile red.
Honest, specific, with a replacement — not a vague apology.
O-71.success: One room, proven; then all rooms, each proven; then monitoring that would have caught it; then the people who were affected.

C-72.title: Only weekday mornings
C-72.brief: Telehealth carts freeze in C-104, C-106 and C-110 — never in the afternoon, never in C-108. Pick the three clues that best separate the explanations.
hypotheses: the carts' network path (VLAN and cap)

clues.t: Freezes happen only 9–11 a.m. on weekdays
clues.why: Matches something busy on the network at that time — not the hardware.

clues.t: C-104's cart page: VLAN 300 · GUEST · cap 4 Mb/s
clues.why: The cart is on the visitors' network with a cap — that's the mechanism.

clues.t: The same cart moved to C-108 never freezes
clues.why: Rules out the cart; points at the room's port.

clues.t: Camera firmware updated in January
clues.why: The C-108 cart has the same firmware and never freezes.

clues.t: Some doctors call in from home
clues.why: True of every room, including C-108.

clues.t: Reboot the core switch to 'clear it'
clues.why: Not yours — and it would drop every clinical call in the building.

C-72.success: Mornings only, a guest VLAN with a cap, and a cart that works in another room: the path, not the cart.

O-72.title: Commission a loop you can trust
O-72.brief: The installer has added the supplementary segment for rows 8–12. Put the commissioning steps in an order that would have caught this in the first place.
items: Set the loop amplifier to the reference level with program sound
Survey field strength seat by seat across every row
Map the readings and mark anything below −3 dB
Run a listening test with telecoil users in the weakest seats
Record the map and the test in the acceptance file
Re-test whenever anything metal changes under or around the seating
why: Measure a calibrated system.
Every seat is its own proof.
Turn numbers into a picture anyone can read.
The people who rely on it are the real test.
Evidence the next person can check.
A later platform broke this one.
O-72.success: Level, survey, map, listen, record — and re-test after changes. PASS means something again.

F-72.title: Where does the power story go wrong?
F-72.brief: 4:03 p.m. The microphone arrays in rooms 201–204 keep rebooting. One reading per stage — tap the earliest stage whose reading is wrong.

stages.name: Camera schedule
stages.why: Doing what it was set to do — by itself, not wrong.

stages.name: Camera draw
stages.reading: 25 W each at night (13 W by day)
stages.why: Normal for these cameras with infrared on.

stages.name: Switch AV-2F budget
stages.reading: 490 W asked of a 370 W budget
stages.why: The first wrong reading: the switch was asked for more than it has.

stages.name: Port priority
stages.why: Downstream: it only decides who loses.

stages.name: Microphone arrays
stages.why: The symptom.

stages.name: Proctor's announcements
stages.why: What the students experience.

F-72.ask: Tap the earliest stage whose reading is wrong.
F-72.success: The budget is where it breaks. The cameras are doing their job, the mics are doing theirs — the switch was asked for 120 W it doesn't have.

O-73.title: Push a preset you can stand behind
O-73.brief: HYBRID v8 is ready: v7's better levels with the correct echo-canceller reference. Put the steps in the order that would have kept Friday quiet.
items: Write the change record: what changes, which rooms, how to undo it
Snapshot every target room's current settings
Load v8 in one pilot room
Make a test call to the pilot room from the remote test account
Have a second person review the result and the record
Roll out in batches of ten, with a test call per batch
why: Say it before you do it.
Each room's own undo — including its local settings.
Small blast radius.
Prove it the way remote students will hear it.
Reviews go both ways.
Stop at the first batch that fails.
O-73.success: Record, snapshot, pilot, test, review, batches. Forty rooms, one at a time until it's proven.

M-54.title: Proxy or outcome?
M-54.brief: Sort each check: does it tell you about the device (a proxy) or about what the person actually got (the outcome)?

items.s: Microphone array reports ONLINE
items.why: The device is on. Grant could still be inaudible.

items.s: Recording file exists and is larger than zero
items.why: A file full of room noise passes.

items.s: Speech level in the recording stays within 6 dB of the lectern level
items.why: What students actually hear.

items.s: A walk test recording with the presenter moving around the room
items.why: The real use, measured.

items.s: Average audio level over the whole hour is above −40 dB
items.why: Loud minutes hide silent ones: an average stands in for the outcome.

items.s: Students can hear the end of every sentence in a sample recording (with consent)
items.why: The person's experience.

M-54.success: Four proxies can be green while the outcome is failing. Keep the proxies — and add the outcome.

R-52.title: From her console to the quad
R-52.brief: Rebuild the alert path to the outdoor kiosks the way it runs after Friday's fix.

slots.label: 2 · HOLD
slots.answer: Notification hub · 5 s signage hold (her setting)

slots.label: 5 · PROVE
slots.answer: Timestamped TEST log, stage by stage

pool: Notification hub · 5 s signage hold (her setting)
Timestamped TEST log, stage by stage

why.Content server · poll every 60 s: The slow fallback the kiosks were stuck on.
why.Building Systems VLAN: Where the kiosks couldn't reach the gateway — and where building controllers must stay isolated.

R-52.success: Her words, her hold, a push path, an override layer — and a stage-by-stage log that proves nine seconds.

F-73.title: Where does time go wrong?
F-73.brief: 7:00 a.m. Lecture recordings show lips a second behind voices. One reading per stage — tap the earliest wrong one.

stages.name: Hub satellite antenna (400 km away)
stages.why: The first wrong reading. It's the hub's — you report it; you can't touch it.

stages.name: Hub clock
stages.why: Downstream: doing what holdover does.

stages.name: Campus time servers
stages.why: Following a liar faithfully.

stages.name: Room cameras
stages.why: Consequence: they follow campus time.

stages.name: Recordings
stages.why: What students see.

F-73.ask: Tap the earliest stage whose reading is wrong.
F-73.success: The hub lost the sky at 2:14. Everything after it followed faithfully. The fix on your side: stop following one clock.

T-52.title: Sixty thousand for 140 projectors
T-52.brief: Friday. The provost's budget for next year is $60k (illustrative). Choose what to fund — risk score = likelihood × impact.

items.name: Claim Varro-series driver boards under the extended warranty (labor only)
items.why: The cluster, fixed for almost nothing — before 30 June.

items.name: Replace the 12 projectors in halls over 200 seats
items.why: Where a failure costs 60 person-hours, not 5.

items.name: Spares pool: 6 projectors ready to swap in 20 minutes
items.why: Turns any failure into a short one.

items.name: Projector hours and lamp alerts on the dashboard
items.why: See the next cluster before the tickets do.

items.name: Lamp stock for the other 100 projectors
items.why: Cheap, boring, useful.

items.name: Replace all 40 Varro-series outright
items.why: Over budget — and the warranty fixes the cause.

items.name: Convert all 140 to laser
items.why: A good idea for a five-year plan, not this budget.

items.name: Refresh the quad signage casings
items.why: Not this problem.

T-52.success: The cluster fixed under warranty, the expensive rooms protected, a spares pool and monitoring — inside $60k, defended by rates, not ages.

C-74.title: Is it us?
C-74.brief: 10:42. Tess: “Your feed is tearing on our air.” Pick the three clues that best separate ‘campus stream’ from ‘hub gateway’.
hypotheses: the hub's gateway following the hub's clock

clues.t: Campus viewer monitor (as viewers see it): clean
clues.why: The campus output is fine where it matters.

clues.t: Campus time: three sources agree, offset 0.000 s
clues.why: Rules out campus time — the E08 fix holding.

clues.t: Tess: hub SYNC alarm since 10:41
clues.why: The hub's clock, again — its gateway follows it.

clues.t: It's the busiest moment — the names
clues.why: Busy, not broken: the uplink is at 17%.

clues.t: Uplink at 17%
clues.why: True, and it rules out the link — but not the others.

clues.t: Restart the campus encoder to ‘reset’ the feed
clues.why: Drops 9,000 viewers during the names.

C-74.success: Clean at our viewer, honest campus time, a hub alarm: the tearing is on the hub side. Offer the direct path.

M-61.title: Whose line is it?
M-61.brief: Sort each decision on the courtroom drawings to the person who owns it.

items.s: Where the counsel tables sit, and the wheelchair turning space around them
items.why: The room layout is Odile's.

items.s: The conduit size and route to each floor box
items.why: Varga sizes and signs it.

items.s: Which cables each floor box must carry, and how many
items.why: Maya's cable list — the input to the fill calculation.

items.s: How the conduit is actually cut into the slab on site
items.why: Means and methods belong to the builder.

items.s: Whether the court's recording inputs are at the witness box
items.why: Intent and requirements — agreed with the court.

M-61.success: Four owners, one room. The AV designer's job is the cable list, the numbers and the question — not someone else's line.

F-602.title: Where did the projector go wrong?
F-602.brief: The Playhouse projector lands in a steel beam. One document per stage — tap the earliest one that's wrong.

stages.name: Owner's brief
stages.reading: 6 m image for the proscenium screen
stages.why: The requirement. Fine.

stages.name: Specification 27 41 00
stages.why: A real choice for a ceiling position — but nobody told the calc.

stages.name: Throw calculation
stages.why: The first wrong document: it used a lens the spec doesn't call, so the position it produced belongs to a different design.

stages.name: Architect's section, rev C
stages.why: Correct for the architect — the beam carries the new catwalk.

stages.name: Projector position on AV-301
stages.why: Faithfully follows the wrong calc.

F-602.ask: Tap the earliest document that's wrong.
F-602.success: The calc used the wrong lens. Everything after it inherited the mistake; the beam only made it visible.

T-604.title: Farah's review, with a small change budget
T-604.brief: Courtroom 3's design review returned eight comments. The change budget is 40 (thousand, illustrative). Access requirements aren't optional — fund them first, then what's worth it.

items.name: Assisted listening at the witness box (receiver and neck-loop, IR coverage)
items.why: The person whose words matter most must hear the questions.

items.name: Touch panel's top control down to 1.2 m, second control at the clerk's desk
items.why: Inside the reach range — and not dependent on someone else.

items.name: Interpreter position in the sightlines, with face-and-hands lighting
items.why: A deaf juror has to see the interpreter; so does the remote-interpreting camera.

items.name: Real-time captions to the jury box display
items.why: Helps deaf and hard-of-hearing jurors — and everyone in a noisy moment.

items.name: Assisted-listening signage at the entrance
items.why: People can't use what they don't know exists.

items.name: Gold-plated connectors throughout
items.why: No measurable benefit here.

items.name: A second 98-inch display on the gallery wall
items.why: Nice, not needed.

items.name: Color-changing mood lighting for the jury room
items.why: Not an access item.

T-604.success: Every access requirement first — witness box, reach and the interpreter — then captions and signage, inside 40.

O-606.title: Treat a room without spoiling it
O-606.brief: The Playhouse is too live for speech. Put the steps in an order you could defend to Odile and the director.
items: Agree the reverberation target with the director and the acoustician
Measure the room and calculate the absorption needed (Sabine)

Re-specify the panels as fire-rated absorbers, with Odile
Measure again after installation, with the room set as for a show
why: The goal first — it's theirs.
Numbers before products.
Where matters as much as how much.
The cheapest absorber is the one already paid for.
Finishes are the architect's; fire ratings the fire engineer's.
Prove it where the audience sits.
O-606.success: A target, the numbers, the right surfaces, the panels already in the budget re-specified with the architect, and a measurement to prove it.

C-607.title: The jurors can't hear the witness
C-607.brief: In the mock-up of Courtroom 1, two jurors say the witness sounds ‘far away’. Everyone else is fine. Pick the three clues that best separate the explanations.
hypotheses: a lower ceiling over the jury box

clues.why: Position-specific drops point at coverage, not at a source or an amplifier.

clues.why: A lower ceiling shrinks the coverage circle right there.

clues.t: The loudspeakers are on a 6.0 m square grid; coverage at ear height is 6.0 m across
clues.why: Edge-to-edge on a square grid leaves holes between every four.

clues.t: The witness sounds fine in the gallery
clues.why: True — and exactly why it isn't the mic.

clues.t: The amplifier is new
clues.why: New tells you nothing; the level is fine elsewhere.

clues.t: Turn everything up 6 dB and see
clues.why: The gallery gets too loud and the holes are still holes.

clues.t: The jurors are older
clues.why: Maybe — but the survey drops at the same spots for everyone.

C-607.success: Holes in a 6 m grid and a bulkhead over the jury box: the coverage, not the sound source.

F-609.title: Where did the port map go wrong?
F-609.brief: Clinic room 4's record drawing shows twelve ports; the room has six. One document per stage — tap the earliest one that's wrong.

stages.name: Contractor's redlines
stages.why: Recorded right — and never used.

stages.name: Record drawings
stages.why: Faithfully copied the wrong schedule instead of the redlines.

F-609.ask: Tap the earliest document that's wrong.
F-609.success: It started with a copied schedule in Maya's second week. The contractor built it right and even redlined it right — and the record set ignored the redlines.

M-701.title: Design or drift?
M-701.brief: Six differences from the HQ room standard, found by the conformance scan. Sort each one: a recorded design decision, or drift.

F-702.title: Where did Tahvara fall off?
F-702.brief: Security release 7.6 never reached Tahvara, and nothing reported a failure. One stage per step of the rollout — tap the earliest one that's wrong.
