T-703.title: Sixty thousand before the cliff
T-703.brief: 10 April. The CFO can approve up to $60k this week without the board (illustrative). Features stop at 00:00 UTC on 15 April; the AGM streams to forty sites fifteen hours later. The other licenses can follow under the normal order if procurement gets an extension. Fund what protects the AGM — and what stops this happening again.

items.name: AGM auditorium: room, stream encoder and live-captioning licenses
items.why: The meeting itself — with captions, which the access policy requires.

items.name: One AGM viewing room per site (40 room licenses)
items.why: Forty sites watch the AGM together.

items.name: The twelve executive boardrooms (≈ $1.8k)
items.why: Cheap, and the week after the AGM is board week.

items.name: License reconciliation against the room inventory (one-off)
items.why: Finds the ghosts, pays back in about five months, and keeps the list true.

items.name: Service-desk and training rooms (180 licenses)
items.why: Useful — and covered by the extension if procurement gets it.

items.name: Signage player licenses (220)
items.why: Nice for the AGM foyer screens; evacuation messages come from the fire alarm, not signage.

items.name: The 290 licenses for decommissioned rooms (≈ $43.5k)
items.why: Rooms that don't exist.

items.name: Everything — all 1,200 licenses at once
items.why: Three times the approval limit, ghosts included.

T-703.success: The AGM path first, the boardrooms, and the reconciliation that stops the next cliff — inside $60k, with the rest under the extension.

O-704.title: A handover that survives three time zones
O-704.brief: You're handing a P2 ticket from your desk to the next region's. Put the steps in an order you could defend at 3 a.m.
items: Confirm the ticket's current state yourself — what works, what doesn't, what's been tried
Write every time in UTC, with the customer's local time beside it
Name the next action, who does it and when it's due
Name the receiving owner — a person, not a desk
Hand over live: the receiver reads the note back
The new owner tells the customer who has it now
why: Hand over what's true now, not what was true this morning.
One clock for the desks, the customer's clock for the customer.
A next step without a time is a wish.
Desks don't answer phones; people do.
Read-back catches ‘9:00’ before it becomes three different nines.
The customer should never have to guess who has it.
O-704.success: State, times with their zones, the next action, a named owner, a read-back — and the customer told. Nothing left for the next desk to guess.

C-705.title: Eight minutes, every hour
C-705.brief: Valmera's training rooms go dark for about eight minutes, over and over. The dashboard says 100%. Pick the three clues that best separate the explanations.
hypotheses: a scheduled task restarting the rooms

clues.t: Every complaint starts between five and seven minutes past the hour
clues.why: A clock-locked pattern points at something scheduled.

clues.t: The codecs' logs show a restart at hh:05 every hour since the rooms opened
clues.why: The devices themselves record the event.

clues.t: The monitor polls at :00, :15, :30 and :45 — never between :05 and :13
clues.why: Explains why a real fault shows 100%.

clues.t: The displays are a new model
clues.why: True, and irrelevant: the codec restarts, not the display.

clues.t: The switch shows no errors
clues.why: Useful, but it only rules one thing out.

clues.t: Reboot all eighteen rooms now to clear it
clues.why: Wipes the running state and proves nothing.

clues.t: Teachers say it happens ‘all the time’
clues.why: Real frustration, imprecise time.

C-705.success: Complaints locked to :05, restarts in the codec logs at :05, and polls that never look between :05 and :13. A scheduled job — hidden by a sampler.

M-709.title: Requirement or preference?
M-709.brief: Eight clauses proposed for Standard v3. Sort each one: a testable requirement, or a preference that belongs in guidance.

items.s: Speech transmission index (STI) ≥ 0.60 at every seat, measured at handover
items.why: An outcome with a test, any brand.

items.s: Touch panel: model TP-7 with the blue bezel
items.why: Names a product. The outcome it serves can be written instead.

items.s: A remote participant can join from the panel in 60 s or less, 19 attempts in 20
items.why: What people need, and how it's checked.

items.s: Racks painted corporate gray
items.why: Taste.

items.s: Assisted listening meeting the local accessibility code, checked with a field-strength meter
items.why: A legal and human requirement, with a test.

items.s: Every device administered through named accounts via the jump host
items.why: Security's requirement, auditable.

items.s: Status lights should be blue
items.why: Nice; untestable against any outcome.

items.s: Rooms should feel ‘premium’
items.why: A wish, not a test.

M-709.success: Four requirements with tests, four preferences for the guidance. v3 gets shorter and stricter at the same time.

T-710.title: The first hour after cutover
T-710.brief: 03:25 UTC. Yuki and one colleague have about 60 operator-minutes before the next checkpoint. Fund what matters — real risk first.

items.name: Call Tahvara facilities: HQ auditorium UPS on battery since 02:20 UTC, with the runtime
items.why: A real alarm, a real countdown, and the owner of the power.

items.name: Replace the bulk ‘all Tahvara’ mute with a suppression for heartbeat flaps only
items.why: Everything real becomes visible again.

items.name: Apply each site's heartbeat timeout from its design file (360 s for the 120 s sites), with a rollback
items.why: Ends the flood at its cause.

items.name: Status note to Henrik and the regional leads, in UTC and local times
items.why: People who need to know, in their own clocks.

items.name: Look into a Valmera codec firmware notice
items.why: Real, and not tonight's.

items.name: Acknowledge all 212 alarms one by one
items.why: An hour of clicking that fixes nothing.

items.name: Roll the whole cutover back to three systems
items.why: The old systems are already running in parallel; the rollback criteria aren't met.

items.name: Rename the alarm categories in the new center
items.why: Tidy. Not now.

T-710.success: The real alarm to its owner, the mute narrowed, the thresholds fixed at the cause, and the people told — inside the hour.

R-801.title: Reroute the backbone
R-801.brief: The backbone has to leave the dock wall before Tuesday. Rebuild the route the way it's pulled and proved after the RFI response.

slots.label: 2 · PATHWAY
slots.answer: South pathway · empty conduit on the drawings

slots.label: 3 · JOINT
slots.answer: One fusion splice at the south pull box

pool: South pathway · empty conduit on the drawings
One fusion splice at the south pull box
North riser · 390 m, four connectors, two splices
Check the link light comes on

why.East dock wall (demolished Tuesday): Where it is now — and why it has to move.
why.North riser · 390 m, four connectors, tw: Passes the budget, fails the spec's 3 dB margin.
why.Check the link light comes on: A lit link can still be one dirty connector from failing. Measure it.

R-801.success: MER → south pathway → one splice → stage rack, proved with an OTDR trace and a witnessed loss test.

O-803.title: Open a finished ceiling without making it worse
O-803.brief: The studio theater ceiling closed before the loudspeaker supports went in. Put the recovery in an order you could defend at the next OAC meeting.
items: Ask the general contractor to stop any further ceiling closure in the studio theater
Mark every loudspeaker position against the latest RFI log and hatch schedule
Issue an RFI response restoring S-9 and correcting the hatch schedule
The ceiling contractor opens the panels — their crew, their lift
The AV contractor installs supports and backboxes to the engineer's support detail
The ceiling contractor closes to the corrected hatch schedule; coverage is measured at ear height
why: Stop the problem growing first — and through its owner.
Positions from the latest documents, not memory.
Fix the design while it's cheapest to fix.
Their work and their equipment at height.
Supports are designed, not improvised.
Close once, then prove the room.
O-803.success: Stop, check against the latest documents, fix the design, let each trade do its own work in order, and measure the result.

C-804.title: Forty-eight passes, eleven twins
C-804.brief: The certification report shows 48 of 48 links passing. Some results look too alike. Pick the three clues that best separate the explanations.

clues.t: Eleven reports on different runs share the same length — 61.4 m, to the centimeter
clues.why: Different runs are never identical to the centimeter.

clues.t: Their timestamps fall within 90 seconds of each other
clues.why: Testing eleven outlets in different rooms takes much longer than that.

clues.t: The tester's raw file for those IDs holds one measurement, saved eleven times
clues.why: The raw data settles it.

clues.t: The cable is a brand the installer hasn't used before
clues.why: True, and irrelevant to eleven identical results.

clues.t: The installer has twenty years' experience
clues.why: Experience isn't evidence.

clues.t: Delete the eleven odd reports and ask for new ones by email
clues.why: Throws away the evidence and invites another copy.

clues.t: All 48 summaries say PASS
clues.why: That's the claim being tested.

C-804.success: Identical lengths, impossible timestamps, and one raw measurement saved eleven times: those links were never tested.

F-805.title: Where did the MER lose its cooling?
F-805.brief: The MER was cooled for 2 kW and is carrying 12.8. One document per step — tap the earliest one that's wrong.

stages.name: Owner's program
stages.reading: MER houses the AV and IT core
stages.why: The requirement. Fine.

stages.name: AV and IT equipment list
stages.why: Correct and up to date.

stages.name: AV heat schedule to the mechanical engineer
stages.why: The first wrong step — on the design team's side. The load existed; the person sizing the cooling never got it.

stages.name: Mechanical basis of design
stages.why: Right for what she was told.

stages.name: MER cooling unit
stages.why: Faithfully follows the basis of design.

F-805.ask: Tap the earliest step that's wrong.
F-805.success: The numbers existed; they never crossed from one discipline to the other. Everything after followed the old list faithfully.

M-807.title: Whose is it?
M-807.brief: Seven things stand between Thursday's rehearsal and a flown cluster. Sort each to the person who owns it.

items.s: Approving that the hang points can carry the cluster's new 640 kg
items.why: Loads on the structure are the structural engineer's to approve.

items.s: Installing the hoists and flying the cluster
items.why: The rigging contractor hangs it — after approval, with their own crew and method.

items.s: Who may go on the unfinished catwalk section, and when
items.why: Unfinished areas are the general contractor's to open — Bram's tape, Bram's call.

items.s: When the rigging crew's work fits the site sequence
items.why: Sequence is the GC's.

items.s: The circuit that will power the hoist motors
items.why: Power is the electrician's — Tove's.

items.s: The cluster's weight, aiming and coverage
items.why: Maya's number — the one everyone else starts from.

items.s: Sending the new weight to the structural engineer when a design change adds two subwoofers
items.why: The owner of the number sends it — and gets it acknowledged.

M-807.success: Two for the GC, one each for the structural engineer, the rigging contractor and the electrician — and two for Maya, both about her own number.

F-808.title: Where did the mute get lost?
F-808.brief: The alarm sounded and the program kept playing. One stage per step — tap the earliest one that's wrong.

stages.name: Manual pull station → fire alarm panel
stages.why: The panel knew. Fine.

stages.name: AV-shutdown relay K3 (the fire alarm contractor's)
stages.why: The relay did its job. Fine.

stages.name: Relay wiring at the DSP rack
stages.reading: Pair on logic input 7 · input 3 jumpered ‘TEMP — punch 188’
stages.why: The first wrong step: the signal lands where nothing listens, and a jumper holds the watched input closed for ever.

stages.name: DSP logic
stages.why: Right — but input 3 can never open with a jumper across it.

stages.name: Program audio in the hall
stages.reading: Keeps playing under the evacuation message
stages.why: The symptom, not the cause.

F-808.ask: Tap the earliest step that's wrong.
F-808.success: The panel and the relay were right. The wiring at the rack was wrong — and a jumper hid it. Everything after followed faithfully.

T-809.title: Forty crew-days
T-809.brief: Nineteen days to opening. The AV contractor has about 40 crew-days left (illustrative). Fund what protects opening night and the people who will run the building; the owner will schedule the rest after opening.

items.name: Life-safety interfaces: re-test all nine racks touched during the punch list
items.why: Occupancy depends on it — and punch 188 shows why.

items.name: Accessibility: hearing loop, assistive-listening receivers and the caption display
items.why: People depend on it from the first night; it's a commitment, not a nicety.

items.name: Show-critical: main-hall PA, stage monitors, intercom and show control
items.why: Without it there's no show.

items.name: As-built drawings brought up to date, life-safety racks first
items.why: The venue's technicians will run the building from them.

items.name: Verify the 60 ‘closed’ items: sample every trade, re-check any group that fails
items.why: Nkechi's first sample: 3 of 10 not fixed.

items.name: Operator training for the venue's technicians
items.why: Needed — and it can run in the first month under the contract.

items.name: Broadcast room fit-out
items.why: Not used until the spring broadcast season.

items.name: Lobby video wall content and scheduling
items.why: Nice on opening night; the wall works with a still slide.

items.name: Cosmetic: cover plates, cable dressing in back-of-house
items.why: Visible to crew, invisible to the audience. After opening.

T-809.success: Life safety and access first, the show, then verified work and true drawings — inside forty crew-days, with the rest scheduled by the owner after opening.

O-810.title: Ninety minutes, in order
O-810.brief: Everything the season taught, at once. Put the moves in the order that protects the most — starting with what gates everything else.
items: Life safety: the fire alarm contractor repairs their circuit; retest with Nkechi timing, before the marshal
Contain the fabric: foyer decoders to the staging VLAN, left out of tonight's push
Restore the core: the spare south pair, checked against its loss budget
Power with its owner: Tove staggers the lighting preheat
The extras: a program feed to the truck — signal from Dario's crew, power from Tove
Prove it where people are: the marshal's test, the back row, the hearing loop
why: Without the marshal's signature, nobody comes in — everything else waits behind it.
Fence off the fault so it can't spread; the show doesn't need the foyer tonight.
Use the path the design promised, proved on paper first.
The electrician's panel, the electrician's sequence — you bring the numbers.
Nice to have, and only once the must-haves hold.
Believing it works isn't the job. Proving it, where the audience sits, is.
O-810.success: Life safety, containment, the core, power with its owner, the extras — and proof where the people are.

M-901.title: Named, shared, service or orphaned?
M-901.brief: Seven accounts from the control processors' account list. Sort each one.

items.s: ext-support: the integrator's on-call technicians all use it
items.why: One password, several people — nobody can say who did what.

items.s: maya.k: Maya's own login
items.why: One person, one account.

items.s: booking-svc: the room-booking integration reads room status
items.why: Software, not a person — it needs only read access and a named owner.

items.s: t.hallan: a commissioning technician who left the integrator in the summer
items.why: The owner has gone; the account hasn't.

items.s: techs: the venue's own technicians, one password on the wall
items.why: A shared login, however friendly.

items.s: k.okafor: Kit's login
items.why: One person, one account.

items.s: demo: created for the opening-week demo, never used since
items.why: Nobody owns it; nobody needs it.

M-901.success: Two named, one service, two shared and two orphaned. Only the named and the service accounts should survive the review.

F-902.title: Where did ‘EVACUATE’ come from?
F-902.brief: Forty seconds of a false evacuation message. One step per row, from the fire panel to the wall — tap the earliest one that's wrong.

stages.name: Fire alarm panel
stages.why: The life-safety system never alarmed. Fine.

stages.name: CMS set-up (commissioning)
stages.reading: Emergency templates in the general library; every marketing account can publish them
stages.why: The first wrong step: a channel nobody accepted could originate a life-safety message, from any account.

stages.name: The template
stages.reading: ‘DRILL’ banner is a separate layer that falls off the 32:9 lobby canvas
stages.why: A second fault — it only mattered because the first one let the template be published.

stages.name: The schedule
stages.why: The trigger, not the cause. Anyone can leave a default.

stages.name: Players and lobby wall
stages.why: Doing their job.

F-902.ask: Tap the earliest step that's wrong.
F-902.success: The panel was right. The set-up let a channel nobody accepted start a life-safety message — from any account. Everything after was just the order things went wrong in.

M-903.title: Which role?
M-903.brief: Seven things people need to do on the DSP and control system. Give each the smallest role that can do it.

items.s: Recall ‘Show’, ‘Rehearsal’ or ‘Talk’ for the evening
items.why: Show states belong on the operator panel.

items.s: Raise the hearing loop level after a field-strength test
items.why: Levels, EQ and the loop are technicians' work.

items.s: Change a zone's EQ after a complaint about the balcony
items.why: Tuning is a technician's job, logged by name.

items.s: Create or remove user accounts
items.why: Two named administrators, with security's approval.

items.s: Install a firmware update the manufacturer recommends
items.why: A supervised, recorded session, approved by security.

items.s: A lighting contractor who needs nothing on the audio system
items.why: Least privilege: if the job doesn't need it, the account doesn't exist.

items.s: A former member of staff
items.why: Offboarding — the day they leave.

M-903.success: Operator for show states, technician for levels and the loop, two named administrators, the integrator only through the jump host — and nothing for anyone who doesn't need it.

C-905.title: Which PASS lines are real?
C-905.brief: The record says 48 PASS; there are 30 test files. Pick the three clues that best separate the explanations.
hypotheses: the 18 were tested and the files were lost
the amplifiers were replaced after testing

clues.t: The tester's own memory holds 30 sessions, not 48
clues.why: The instrument never ran the other 18 — the files weren't lost, they never existed.

clues.t: All 18 unlinked PASS lines equal the design value to a tenth of a decibel
clues.why: Real measurements scatter. Identical design values were typed, not measured.

clues.t: The 30 real files span five days; none is from handover eve — when the 18 lines were typed
clues.why: The dates separate testing from typing.

clues.t: All twelve amplifiers are the same model
clues.why: True, and it explains nothing about the missing tests.

clues.t: The record is printed on the integrator's letterhead
clues.why: Letterhead isn't evidence either way.

clues.t: The technician who typed them left the integrator in the summer
clues.why: It tells you who; it doesn't tell you whether tests happened.

clues.t: Retest everything today and overwrite the old record with the new results
clues.why: The old record is evidence of what was claimed. Retest — but keep the original and issue a corrected one.

C-905.success: Thirty sessions in the tester, eighteen identical design values, and dates that never touch handover eve: the eighteen were never tested.

O-906.title: A change nobody expected
O-906.brief: The lobby processor's configuration changed overnight. Put the steps in the order you could defend to security and to the show.
items: Touch nothing; write down what you see and when
Tell security — they own the evidence and the investigation
Security exports the logs and the configuration read-only and records who handled them
Note each log's time source and offset
Build one timeline in UTC
Restore the service through change control
why: Every touch changes the thing you're about to read.
It's their investigation, and the evidence is theirs to keep.
A copy nobody can alter, with a record of who held it.
Three clocks disagree until you know what each one is measuring.
One clock for the story.
Then fix it — and record the fix like any other change.
O-906.success: Hands off, security, a read-only copy, the clocks, one timeline — and only then the fix.

M-907.title: Allow or deny?
M-907.brief: Eight flows between the new segments. Which go on the allowed list?

items.s: Control processor → signage players: the show-mode command, one port
items.why: The show needs it. One port, one direction, an owner.

items.s: Guest Wi-Fi → DSP control
items.why: Guests have no business near the DSP.

items.s: Integrator VPN landing → control processors directly
items.why: Vendors reach devices only through the jump host.

items.s: Integrator VPN landing → jump host (vendor side)
items.why: That's the one door vendors have.

items.s: Jump host (device side) → control processors
items.why: Named, recorded sessions reach the devices from here.

items.s: Signage server → paging stations
items.why: Signage never touches the paging path.

items.s: Signage players → the control processor's admin page
items.why: Show mode flows one way. Players never manage control.

items.s: The time server → every AV device
items.why: One clock for every log.

M-907.success: Four doors — show mode, the vendor landing, the jump host and the time — and everything else blocked.

M-908.title: Whose decision?
M-908.brief: Eight moments from the tabletop. Whose is each one?

items.s: Whether the audience moves or stays
items.why: The duty manager decides, to the venue's emergency plan.

items.s: What paging says to the house
items.why: Her words, on paging.

items.s: Disabling the account that posted the message
items.why: Access and the investigation are security's.

items.s: Keeping the logs and the signage server untouched
items.why: Evidence is security's.

items.s: The holding statement for the video going round online
items.why: Public words are communications'.

items.s: Cutting power at the signage controllers
items.why: Building power is facilities' — on the incident commander's instruction.

items.s: Blanking all screens from the CMS
items.why: Two named AV staff can do it in software — on the incident commander's instruction.

items.s: Telling the incident commander which systems are safe to rely on
items.why: The facts about the systems are AV's to bring.

M-908.success: One incident commander; security, communications, facilities and AV each in their lane — and every action on her instruction.

T-909.title: Seventy thousand for next year
T-909.brief: The board can fund about $70k of remediation next year (illustrative). Fund what retires the most risk; whatever you don't fund goes on the risk register for the board to accept in writing.

items.name: Named accounts and the jump host for every system — signage, lighting, control
items.why: The door this season kept finding.

items.name: Signage approval workflow and the fire-relay slide on every exit screen
items.why: Screens repeat; they never originate.

items.name: Quarterly access reviews, and offboarding clauses in every contract
items.why: Stops the next forgotten account.

items.name: An inventory of vendor accounts built into products — the logins inside the software
items.why: Accounts nobody created, nobody reviews.

items.name: The commissioning evidence standard for all future work
items.why: Every line links its file.

items.name: Tabletop twice a year; two trained people per shift
items.why: The plan works without its author.

items.name: Time server for every device; a year of logs kept
items.why: One clock for every investigation.

items.name: Segmentation for lighting and the room-booking panels
items.why: Useful — and lower risk than the rest this year.

items.name: New 4K lobby displays
items.why: Nice. Not a security fix.

items.name: An outside consultant's report on ‘culture’
items.why: The season's findings already are the report.

T-909.success: Accounts, signage, reviews, the vendor-account inventory, the evidence standard and the tabletops — inside $70k, with segmentation of lighting on the register for next year.

O-910.title: Every screen at once, in order
O-910.brief: Seven moves for the first half hour. Put them in the order that keeps people safest — and keeps the evidence.
items: Tell the incident commander what can be trusted: paging and life safety are clean; the screens aren't
The incident commander pages the house in her own words
Facilities darken the screens at their power controllers, on her instruction
Security keeps the CMS state and logs
Security and the vendor disable the account; the network owner blocks its route to control
Communications post a holding statement
Check the show systems are clean, then curtain
why: She can't decide without knowing which voice is safe.
People on stairs need one trusted instruction first.
Stop the lie at its power — the server stays untouched.
Before anything else changes, the evidence is kept.
Close the door through its owners, with one targeted rule — not a pulled plug.
The video is spreading; true words, fast.
The show goes up only on systems you've checked.
O-910.success: Trust, voice, darkness, evidence, the door, the public — then the show.

M-1001.title: Leader, follower or free-running?
M-1001.brief: Studio A's clocked devices as Maya found them on Monday. Sort each one.

items.s: The network audio interface: the clock leader for the audio network
items.why: It sets the time for everything on the network.

items.s: The stage boxes in the live room: locked to the network's clock
items.why: They follow the interface.

items.s: The converter frame: set to its own internal clock since the spring
items.why: It follows nobody — and its audio goes into a device that does.

items.s: The personal cue mixers on the network
items.why: They follow the network's leader.

items.s: The recording computer: runs on whatever clock the interface gives it
items.why: It follows the interface.

items.s: The old word-clock generator in the rack: switched on, nothing connected to its outputs
items.why: A clock nobody follows — harmless, until someone plugs it in as a second leader.

M-1001.success: One leader, three followers, and two devices running on their own. The converter is the problem: its audio crosses into a device on a different clock.

M-1002.title: Cut, move or treat?
M-1002.brief: Seven findings from Studio A's measurements. What actually fixes each one?

items.s: A 6 dB bump at 80 Hz at the chair
items.why: A peak can be cut — gently, after the chair has moved.

items.s: A 14 dB hole at 40 Hz — the chair sits on the room's center line
items.why: A cancellation at one spot: move the listener.

items.s: A 9 dB hole at 120 Hz at the same chair
items.why: The third mode cancels on the center line too.

items.s: The left monitor is 40 cm closer to the chair than the right
items.why: An unequal triangle: move the speaker.

items.s: Bass keeps ringing for a long time after each kick drum, everywhere in the room
items.why: Long low-frequency decay needs absorption — the acoustician's design.

items.s: Bass piles up in the corners behind the monitors
items.why: Corners are where modes are strongest — where traps work best.

items.s: A 3 dB bump at 2.5 kHz that measures the same at every spot
items.why: Position-independent: it's the speaker, not the room.

M-1002.success: Position-dependent holes: move. Long decay and corner build-up: treat. Only what's the same everywhere, or a peak, is the EQ's.

O-1003.title: Line up a drum kit
O-1003.brief: Seven steps to find and fix phase problems on a close-miked kit. Put them in the order that finds the cause fastest and changes the least.
items: Listen to each mic alone, then add the others to the snare one at a time
Check polarity on mics that face each other — snare top and bottom, kick in and out
Tape-measure each overhead to the center of the snare
Make the overheads the same distance from the snare
Keep the other mics at least three times further from the snare than from their own drum
If the body is still thin, delay the close mics to line up with the overheads
Check the whole kit in mono, then ask the drummer to listen
why: Hear where the body disappears before you change anything.
A flip is the cheapest fix and the commonest fault.
Numbers, not guesses.
Equal distances keep the snare centered and the overheads from combing with each other.
The 3:1 rule keeps spill about 9 dB down.
Delay is the last resort — it lines up one drum and can shift others.
Mono exposes cancellation; the drummer owns the sound.
O-1003.success: Listen, flip, measure, equalise, space, align — then mono and the drummer's ears.

M-1004.title: Where does the delay come from?
M-1004.brief: Six things between a singer's mouth and her ears. Sort each by what kind of delay it adds.

items.s: The computer's 512-sample input buffer at 48 kHz
items.why: About 10.7 ms, waiting for a block to fill.

items.s: The computer's 512-sample output buffer
items.why: Another 10.7 ms on the way out.

items.s: A limiter with 5 ms of lookahead on her vocal
items.why: It delays the audio so it can see peaks coming.

items.s: A ‘vintage tape’ plug-in that reports 8 ms of delay
items.why: Plug-ins can add their own delay.

items.s: The converters in and out, about half a millisecond each
items.why: Small, and there even on the direct path.

items.s: Standing one meter from a monitor wedge
items.why: About 2.9 ms of air — what players are used to.

M-1004.success: Two buffers, two plug-ins, the converters and a meter of air. Only the buffers and the plug-ins are worth removing from her headphones.

O-1005.title: Rescue a session
O-1005.brief: Seven steps to rescue a ten-year-old album session. Put them in the order that risks the least and proves the most.
items: Copy every drive read-only before opening anything
Record a checksum for every file on the copies
List what each session expects and what's actually there
Recover missing files from other copies, logging every one that fails
Decide between conflicting copies with the paperwork and the people who were there
Export every track as Broadcast WAV from bar 1, the same length, named from the track sheet
Store three copies with a checksum manifest and a readme; book the next fixity check
why: Opening an old session can write to it.
Proof of what you started with.
Know the size of the hole.
Every failure logged, none hidden.
Dates and labels disagree; track sheets and memories don't lie in the same way.
Plain files anyone can line up.
An archive needs a next date.
O-1005.success: Copy, prove, list, recover, decide, export, store — and a date to check again.

F-1006.title: Where did the single go wrong?
F-1006.brief: The single sounds small and a little distorted on phones. One step per row, from the choir take to the listener — tap the earliest one that's wrong.

stages.name: Choir overdub
stages.reading: Peaks at 0 dBFS on two takes — clipped
stages.why: The first failure: a clipped take is damaged for good, before any mastering.

stages.name: Mix
stages.why: Fine — but it inherited two clipped takes.

stages.name: Master
stages.why: A second problem: pushed loud, and over the delivery limit.

stages.name: Encoder
stages.reading: Overs become distortion on the phone stream
stages.why: Doing what encoders do with overs.

stages.name: Service
stages.reading: Turns the track down 7 dB to its target
stages.why: Normalizing, as designed.

F-1006.ask: Tap the earliest step that's wrong.
F-1006.success: The choir take clipped first; the loud master and the encoder made it worse. The service only did its job.

O-1007.title: A safe hum hunt
O-1007.brief: Seven steps for a hum in the live room. Put them in the order that finds it without ever putting anyone at risk.
items: Leave every protective earth exactly as it is
Find when the hum appears — each connection on its own, then together
Try the DI box's audio ground lift
Ask the electrician which circuit each piece of gear is on
The electrician moves the audio gear onto the technical circuits
If a hum changes with nothing changed, have the gear's earth tested
Tag out anything with a failed earth until a qualified technician repairs it
why: The earth is the safety; it's never part of the hunt.
Find the loop by its connections.
Breaks the loop in the audio path, where it's safe to.
Two earths means two circuits — map them.
Their circuits, their work.
Silence can be a fault.
Nobody plays it until it's safe.
O-1007.success: Earths untouched, the loop found by its connections, the audio lift, the electrician's circuits — and a test when the hum ‘fixes itself’.

M-1008.title: Whose decision?
M-1008.brief: Seven questions that came up this week. Sort each by who decides it.

items.s: Whether her raw vocal takes may train a voice model
items.why: A new use of her voice: hers to agree to, in writing.

items.s: Sending her unreleased stems to a remix producer
items.why: Beyond what her contract covers — her yes first.

items.s: Posting a clip of her raw vocal on the studio's social feed
items.why: Her performance, her call — however short the clip.

items.s: The single's release date
items.why: The label owns the release under her contract.

items.s: The file format and loudness limit for delivery
items.why: Their delivery spec.

items.s: Whether review links are named, view-only and expiring
items.why: Custody of the files is the studio's.

items.s: How often every file share's access log is checked
items.why: The studio's policy — Hollis signs it.

M-1008.success: Every new use of her voice is hers; the release and the spec are the label's; how the files travel is the studio's.

T-1009.title: Five thousand for backups
T-1009.brief: Hollis can spend about $5,000 on backups this month (illustrative). Fund what retires the most risk to the album and the archive.

items.name: Two 8 TB drives rotated off-site weekly — Hollis takes one home every Friday
items.why: The off-site copy that can actually keep up.

items.name: An hourly versioned backup to a separate device, keeping deletions 30 days
items.why: The copy that survives a mistake.

items.name: Alerts when the off-site backlog passes one day, or a job fails
items.why: Nineteen silent days, never again.

items.name: A monthly restore test, timed and logged — Pim's hours
items.why: The only proof you have a backup.

items.name: A UPS for the recording computer and the session drive
items.why: A power blip mid-take corrupts files.

items.name: More cloud storage for the nightly upload
items.why: Useful for each day's new work — not the whole backlog.

items.name: A faster internet connection for a year
items.why: Helps the upload; doesn't replace the drives.

items.name: A bigger mirrored pair in the machine room
items.why: Still copies every mistake.

items.name: A second mirrored pair next to the first
items.why: Two copies of the same mistake, in the same room.

T-1009.success: Rotated drives, versioned backups, alerts, restore tests, a UPS and nightly cloud for the day's work — inside $5,000, and no more mirrors.

O-1010.title: The last night, in order
O-1010.brief: Seven moves between 01:40 and 09:00. Put them in the order that keeps the album safe and every decision with its owner.
items: Stop writing to the failing drive
Copy what exists only on it and verify the checksums
Switch recording to a fresh drive
Show Esme the comp sheet; whether she sings again is her call
Check the consent log before anything new leaves the building
Deliver the album with a checksum manifest
Ask the label to confirm the checksums on arrival, and rotate the new drive off-site
why: Every write can make a failing drive worse.
Protect the only copy first — and prove the copy.
Then the work can go on.
Evidence to the person who owns the voice.
A phone call isn't consent.
Proof travels with the files.
Proven where the files arrive.
O-1010.success: Stop, copy, switch, her call, the log, the manifest — and proof it arrived intact.

F-1101.title: Where did the morning go wrong?
F-1101.brief: Eight dark mornings and a flooded underpass. One step per row — tap the earliest one that's wrong.

stages.name: Integrator's set-up
stages.reading: Update window typed as ‘12:00’ — meant local noon; nobody approved it
stages.why: The first failure: an unapproved change window, in an unchecked time zone.

stages.name: Wall controller
stages.reading: Keeps UTC; restarts at 12:00 UTC = 07:00 local
stages.why: Doing exactly what it was told.

stages.name: Shift change
stages.reading: 07:00 — both shifts brief in front of the wall
stages.why: A second weakness: the handover depended on one screen.

stages.name: Handover
stages.reading: 250 s dark; the Mill Road sandbag request not passed on
stages.why: The consequence of the first two.

stages.name: Mill Road underpass
stages.why: Where it landed.

F-1101.ask: Tap the earliest step that's wrong.
F-1101.success: The set-up came first: a change nobody approved, in a time zone nobody checked. The handover's dependence on the wall made it cost something.

O-1102.title: Stop a flapping failover
O-1102.brief: Seven steps to take a flapping link off an operations room's back. Put them in the order that restores service fastest and keeps each change with its owner.
items: Log every switch — times, direction, what dropped
Take the evidence to the network owner
The network owner pins traffic to the stable path for the activation
The network owner adds a hold-down: fail back only after minutes clean, manually during activations
The carrier repairs the flapping path
Watch the repaired path clean for a day before failing back
Check the two paths' routes for shared conduit and fund a separate one
why: Evidence first — how often, which way, what it cost.
His network, his timers.
Stop the bleeding.
Fail back slow.
Their plant, their repair.
Trust earned, not assumed.
Two paths that can fail together are one.
O-1102.success: Evidence, owner, pin, hold-down, repair, a day's proof — then the question nobody had asked: are they really two?

M-1103.title: Whose is it?
M-1103.brief: Six things that came up in the radio room this week. Sort each by who decides it.

items.s: Moving public works' loaner repeater to another site
items.why: Transmitters, sites and licenses are his.

items.s: Adding a filter on the mast's shared antenna system
items.why: The mast and what's on it.

items.s: What fire's talkgroup is called and who is on it
items.why: Each agency owns its talkgroups.

items.s: Who speaks for public works on the joined channel
items.why: Their people, their voice.

items.s: Which patch runs during a flood activation
items.why: The room's plan — the director signs it.

items.s: Which dispatcher is net control in an activation
items.why: Named in the EOC plan she owns.

M-1103.success: Transmitters and sites: the radio systems manager. Talkgroups and voices: the agencies. Which patch, and who runs it: the director's plan.

O-1104.title: Relay a warning
O-1104.brief: Seven steps from the moment a warning arrives. Put them in the order that gets the owner's words to everyone, fastest, unchanged.
items: Confirm the warning came from the issuing agency's own feed
Relay it verbatim, with the agency's name and time
Publish the approved Spanish template for that warning, with the same details
Check captions show the words as issued
The director adds any county instruction — in a separate, labeled message
Confirm it published on every channel
Log what went out, when
why: Only the owner's warning is relayed.
Their words, attributed.
Prepared by qualified translators before the storm.
Captions carry the warning too.
Evacuation language is the director's.
Everyone, not most people.
The record for the after-action review.
O-1104.success: Source, verbatim, both languages, captions, the director's words kept separate — everywhere, logged.

M-1105.title: Keep, shed or never?
M-1105.brief: Eight loads in the EOC. Which stay on the UPS, which go first when it's shed, and which should never be on it at all?

items.s: Radio consoles and the interoperability gateway
items.why: The interagency voice path.

items.s: The operations network core
items.why: Everything rides on it.

items.s: The public-information stream encoder
items.why: The public's lifeline.

items.s: Half of the video wall
items.why: Keep half the picture; save the rest of the minutes.

items.s: The GIS workstations beyond the two on duty
items.why: Useful, not critical.

items.s: Printers
items.why: Nothing prints during a transfer.

items.s: The break-room coffee machine
items.why: A heater for water, on a battery meant for radios.

items.s: Space heaters under the desks
items.why: Big loads, zero operational value.

M-1105.success: Voice, network and the public stream stay; half the wall, spare workstations and printers go first; heaters and the coffee machine never belonged on it.

F-1106.title: Where did the Spanish go?
F-1106.brief: The Spanish channel carries English. One step per row, from the interpreter to the viewer — tap the earliest one that's wrong.

stages.name: Interpreter's microphone
stages.why: Fine.

stages.name: Interpretation console
stages.why: Fine.

stages.name: Stream template · audio 2 source
stages.why: The first failure: channel two was told to carry English.

stages.name: Encoder
stages.reading: Encodes two tracks it was given
stages.why: Doing its job.

stages.name: Viewers' app
stages.why: The symptom.

F-1106.ask: Tap the earliest step that's wrong.
F-1106.success: The interpreter and the console were fine. The template sent a copy of the program to channel two; everything after it faithfully carried the mistake.

O-1107.title: A handover at hour twelve
O-1107.brief: Seven steps for handing over an operations role at the end of a shift. Put them in the order that leaves nothing in your head.
items: Write the handover brief before your relief arrives
Read it aloud to your relief
Walk the room together: every pending item, every open patch
Your relief repeats back what they're taking
Both sign the brief
Tell the director the handover is done
Go home and rest
why: Written while you still remember everything.
Heard, not skimmed.
Pending items are where handovers leak.
What they heard, not what you said.
Two names on one picture.
The roster is hers — she knows who's on.
The last step of the job.
O-1107.success: Written, read, walked, repeated, signed, reported — and home.

M-1108.title: Which network?
M-1108.brief: Seven devices and files in the EOC. Where does each belong?

items.s: The radio interoperability gateway
items.why: The room's own critical system.

items.s: The county's GIS workstations
items.why: County-managed, on the operations network.

items.s: The dispatch consoles
items.why: Critical, county-managed.

items.s: The state flood-model contractor's laptop
items.why: A partner's device: internet only.

items.s: The utility liaison's own company laptop
items.why: Their device, their network — not ours.

items.s: A visiting journalist's phone
items.why: Internet access, nothing more.

items.s: A USB stick with the flood model on it
items.why: Unknown media goes through the scanned transfer service, not into a desk.

M-1108.success: County systems on the operations network; every visitor's device on the partner network; files through the scanned transfer service.

T-1109.title: Two hundred and fifty thousand
T-1109.brief: The state's first tranche is about $250k (illustrative). Fund what retires the most risk before the flood season; whatever you don't fund goes on the register for the director to accept in writing.

items.name: A separate licensed microwave path to the hilltop (the shared-conduit finding)
items.why: Two carriers, one bridge.

items.name: UPS batteries and the transfer switch's control relay, retested under load
items.why: Twelve minutes and a dead switch.

items.name: Written handovers and roster enforcement, trained for every shift lead
items.why: The wall and hour sixteen.

items.name: The gateway runbook, and two trained people per shift
items.why: The only one who knew.

items.name: Approved warning templates in Spanish, and a live interpreter contract
items.why: Verbatim, in every language.

items.name: Port security, partner jacks and new-device alerts
items.why: Thirty-eight open doors.

items.name: Weekly three-agency patch tests and the written plan's upkeep
items.why: A plan, not a patch.

items.name: Failback hold-down and path monitoring on the router
items.why: Fail over fast, fail back slow.

items.name: A second video wall
items.why: More glass; not a fix.

items.name: New chairs for the operations floor
items.why: Comfortable, and not a risk.

T-1109.success: The separate path, backup power, handovers, the gateway, templates, ports, patch tests and failback — $216k, 140 of 143 risk points. The wall and the chairs go on the register, signed.

M-1110.title: Whose move is it?
M-1110.brief: Ten moves from the night before the crest. Which are Maya's to make, which does she ask an owner for — and which are never anyone's?

items.s: Work out how long the UPS carries the room
items.why: Knowing the minutes is engineering; the UPS itself is facilities'.

items.s: Write the handover brief and read it to Kit
items.why: Her open items, her brief — and her way off shift.

items.s: Point the partner's laptop to the PARTNER jack
items.why: The fast path and the right path are the same path.

items.s: Move traffic onto the hilltop microwave path
items.why: Routing is Wendell's; the link is the radio shop's.

items.s: Shed load before the generator overheats
items.why: The director's go, facilities' hands.

items.s: Order the lower valley out
items.why: Evacuations are the director's; Maya brings the facts.

items.s: Answer the dam rumor
items.why: The dam operator's facts, in the PIO's words.

items.s: Soften the warning so people don't panic
items.why: Warnings are relayed verbatim.

items.s: Free the generator's stuck louvre
items.why: The generator is facilities' — running, hot and not hers.

items.s: Stay past hour sixteen because only you know the gateway
items.why: The roster is the director's; ‘only me’ is a single point of failure.

M-1110.success: Three moves Maya makes, four she asks an owner for, three nobody makes. That's the mission room.

M-1201.title: Back, owned — or promoted?
M-1201.brief: Seven differences the scan found. What happens to each?
classes: Test it, then take it to the change board

items.s: Valmera's automatic mic-mixing template — a third of the complaints
items.c: Test it, then take it to the change board
items.why: Better than the standard: promote it, with evidence.

items.s: Singapore room: fire-alarm mute input disabled ‘temporarily’
items.why: Life safety: facilities and the fire-alarm contractor.

items.s: A room PC with a shared local admin password written on the panel
items.why: Access is security's.

items.s: A second display added in a room with a blind corner
items.why: A sensible local fix: owned and dated, reviewed at expiry.

items.s: A regional head's favorite wallpaper on every screen
items.why: Harmless; still recorded, still dated.

items.s: Three rooms on an older touch-panel layout awaiting refresh
items.why: Expires at the refresh.

items.s: An Tahvara ceiling-mic layout that beats the standard in low rooms
items.c: Test it, then take it to the change board
items.why: Evidence first, then the owner's decision.

M-1201.success: Record most, escalate what crosses a boundary, promote what works better — nothing just forced back.

T-1202.title: Five hundred and twenty thousand
T-1202.brief: This year Rashida can find about $520k (illustrative) for the rooms. Fund what retires the most risk; what you don't fund is deferred with her written acceptance.

items.name: Migrate the 34 rooms' control processors before vendor support ends
items.why: After end of support, every fault and security hole is yours.

items.name: Replace the 8 highest-fault rooms from the six-year-old wave now
items.why: Starts flattening the cliff where it hurts most.

items.name: The yearly one-page lifecycle report and the reserve policy
items.why: The board sees it coming every year.

items.name: A spare-parts kit for the old wave
items.why: Useful — if the money's there.

items.name: Higher-resolution displays for the boardroom
items.why: Nice. Not a risk.

items.name: New wall graphics in every room
items.why: Not a risk at all.

T-1202.success: Control processors, the eight worst rooms and the report — $511k. Spares, displays and graphics wait, and the deferral is accepted in writing.

O-1203.title: From one room to sixty
O-1203.brief: Eight steps for putting new firmware on sixty rooms. Put them in the order that keeps the blast radius small.
items: Read the release notes — which hardware revisions does it support?
Raise a change ticket; the change board approves the plan
Apply it to the lab room and test camera, audio and controls
Soak the lab room for 24 hours
One room in each region; soak and check
Ten percent of rooms; watch faults and complaints
All rooms, in the agreed window
Record it: version, date, rooms, owner
why: The revision question would have caught this on paper.
The owner approves the plan, not the panic.
One room you can afford to lose.
Some faults take a day to appear.
Different rooms, different surprises.
A tenth is a signal, not a catastrophe.
Only now, and never before a big meeting.
The next person needs to know what's where.
O-1203.success: Read, approve, lab, soak, one per region, a tenth, all — then record. Three days, and never eighteen rooms dark at once.

F-1204.title: Which step failed?
F-1204.brief: Runbook RB-07, as Pim followed it. Every step worked — until one didn't. Tap the earliest step that's wrong in the runbook itself.

stages.name: 1 · Confirm
stages.reading: Stream-health alert confirmed on the monitor at 11:12
stages.why: Worked: the alert fired and he checked it.

stages.name: 2 · Encoder
stages.reading: Primary encoder's status page: not responding
stages.why: Worked: the fault found.

stages.name: 3 · Uplink
stages.why: Worked: ruled out the network.

stages.name: 4 · Switch
stages.reading: Event moved to the backup encoder path at 11:18
stages.why: Worked: the tested backup.

stages.name: 5 · Verify
stages.reading: Picture and captions checked at two remote offices, 11:19
stages.why: Worked: proof where the people are.

stages.name: 6 · Tell
stages.reading: Event producer told; stay on backup until the end
stages.why: Worked.

stages.name: 9 · Approve
stages.reading: ‘Call Tobin to approve failback’ — Tobin on leave
stages.why: The first wrong step: a name, not a role.

F-1204.ask: Tap the earliest step that's wrong in the runbook.
F-1204.success: Steps one to six were right because a drill had fixed them. Step nine named a person; the rota has roles.

M-1205.title: Covered, single — or no reason on file?
M-1205.brief: Seven items from Maya's list. What does each one need?
classes: Covered — two or more can do it
Coverage of one — train a second person
Record the decision — the why is missing

items.s: Restore the room platform from backup — only Tobin has done it
items.c: Coverage of one — train a second person
items.why: One person; train and sign off a second.

items.s: Rebuild a DSP template from scratch — only Maya
items.c: Coverage of one — train a second person
items.why: The architect's own task — hand it off first.

items.s: Renew the captions license — Lian and procurement both do it
items.c: Covered — two or more can do it
items.why: Two owners who know it.

items.s: Run the global event stream — Pim and Noor both have
items.c: Covered — two or more can do it
items.why: Covered, and drilled.

items.s: Why the glass-room template gates the ceiling mics — only in Maya's email
items.c: Record the decision — the why is missing
items.why: A reason nobody can find is a reason someone will undo.

items.s: Why the event stream uses two encoders — nobody wrote it down
items.c: Record the decision — the why is missing
items.why: Write it before someone ‘saves money’.

items.s: Rotate the room service account — only Tobin knows the order
items.c: Coverage of one — train a second person
items.why: Tobin teaches it; Noor signs off.

M-1205.success: Train where one person holds it, record where the reason is missing — and leave alone what's already covered.

F-1206.title: Nineteen days, from the start
F-1206.brief: How a room went unheard for nineteen days. Tap the earliest step that's wrong.

stages.name: Confidential meeting
stages.reading: ‘Privacy’ preset recalled: ceiling mics muted — the preset never clears itself
stages.why: The first failure: a preset with no way back.

stages.name: Touch panel
stages.reading: The mute button shows unmuted — it only reflects the table mics
stages.why: A second weakness: the indicator hides it.

stages.name: Device monitoring
stages.why: Watching devices, not whether the room can be heard.

stages.name: Users
stages.reading: The far end can't hear; locals switch to a laptop mic; nobody reports it
stages.why: People work around a broken room.

stages.name: Day nineteen
stages.reading: Noor notices on a firmware visit
stages.why: Found by luck.

F-1206.ask: Tap the earliest step that's wrong.
F-1206.success: It started with a preset that never cleared. It lasted nineteen days because the monitoring watched devices and the people worked around it.

O-1207.title: A fair decision, in order
O-1207.brief: Eight steps for deciding who gets scarce money. Put them in the order that keeps the loudest voice from choosing the answer.
items: Agree the question — and who decides
Agree the criteria with the owner
Agree the weights with the owner
Collect evidence for every option
Rate each option on each criterion
Work out the weighted scores
Show the owner the scores, how close they are, and what would change them
The owner decides and records why
why: Without an owner, the loudest voice decides.
What matters, before any option is named.
How much each matters — before anyone can see which way it tips.
Evidence, not advocacy.
Ratings from the evidence.
S = Σ (w × r).
Honest about closeness — without re-weighting.
A decision with its reasons, on file.
O-1207.success: Question, criteria, weights, evidence, ratings, scores, the honest picture — then the owner's decision, recorded.

O-1208.title: Retire a key that opens sixty rooms
O-1208.brief: Eight steps. Put them in the order that never locks every room out at once.
items: Security decides the plan and owns the new accounts
Find every room configuration that uses the old account
Security creates three regional accounts in the vault, with least privilege
Move the lab room; run its synthetic test
Move one room in each region; check overnight
Move the rest, region by region
Confirm from the logs that no room still uses the old account
Security disables the old account; record it
why: Access is theirs.
Map every door before you change the lock.
A third of the estate per key, and no more power than needed.
One room you can afford to lose.
Different regions, different surprises.
Staged, checked.
Evidence before you pull it.
Retired by its owner, on the record.
O-1208.success: Owner, map, smaller keys, lab, one per region, the rest, evidence — then retire. Never all sixty at once.

T-1209.title: Ninety thousand for access
T-1209.brief: Lian has about $90k (illustrative) this year for the gaps. Fund what closes the most — the first item is a requirement of the standard.

items.name: Caption licenses and configuration for the 22 rooms
items.why: The standard's first promise.

items.name: Assistive listening in the 9 large rooms, installed by each site's facilities
items.why: Large rooms, many people.

items.name: Caption and loop testing with the people who use them
items.why: Tested by users.

items.name: Lower touch panels in six rooms for wheelchair users
items.why: Real — and next on the list.

items.name: Larger displays in the boardroom
items.why: Not an access gap.

items.name: New room-name signs
items.why: Not a gap at all.

T-1209.success: Captions, assistive listening and user testing — $89k. The lower panels are next, recorded with a date.

M-1210.title: Held by the year — or by Maya?
M-1210.brief: Seven moments from the last week. Which were held by what was built, which by someone trained — and which still depended on Maya?

items.s: Captions ran in all sixty rooms from the first minute
items.why: Funded in the year; nothing to save.

items.s: Pim switched the town hall to the warm backup path from RB-07
items.why: A drilled runbook and a warm path.
