items.why: Stop-work authority in the standard.

items.s: Noor restored Valmera's template using DR-07
items.why: Signed off, with the reason on file.

items.s: A room-booking integration only Maya had ever configured
items.why: Coverage of one — the architect's own.

items.s: Synthetic tests heard the echo before any user did
items.why: Monitoring aimed at people.

items.s: A vendor contact whose number was only in Maya's phone
items.why: Move it to a role and the records before the last day.

M-1210.success: Built, trained — and two last things that still had Maya's name on them. Those are the last week's work.

SM-01.title: Stream audio drops every 40 seconds
SM-01.page: People at home lose the audio every 20–60 seconds. The room sounds fine. Doors open soon.
SM-01.brief: Baptism Sunday. Walter is watching from two states away.
SM-01.briefing: The private test stream drops audio every 20–60 seconds; the picture keeps moving; the room is fine. Last week the stream froze for five minutes and nobody found out why. You have until doors open.
SM-01.opening: Test stream up. Audio gaps every 20–60 s. Picture fine. Room fine.

after.l: After unplug: rx a few Mbit/s, no gaps

proof.l: 10 min on cellular in the parking lot

actions.why: Restarting changed many things at once and erased the one measurement that proves the cause.
actions.label: Restart the stream computer
actions.text: Sound comes back… for about three minutes. Then the gaps return. The computer's receive history is gone.

actions.why: Classify by path before touching anything.
actions.label: Walk the four paths
actions.text: Power: every light on. Signal: console stream meters steady. Control: settings unchanged. Network: the booth switch's lights are hammering.

actions.why: A measurement, not a hunch. Keep it.
actions.label: Open the stream computer's network monitor
actions.text: Receiving hundreds of megabits per second. The stream needs a few. It isn't broken — it's being shouted at.

calc.q: The stream computer's port is 1,000 Mb/s and it's receiving about 400 Mb/s of video nobody asked for. What percentage of the port is the flood using?

actions.why: “What changed?” answered by a record.
actions.label: Compare with last month's inventory photo
actions.text: Three cables last month. Five today. A new blue cable runs into the floor.

actions.why: Fast, and kind — you get the story, not a defense.
actions.label: Ask on the radio: “What changed?”
actions.text: Theo: “I added overflow video Saturday!”

actions.stop: Ray: “Whose network is that? It runs the door locks and the giving kiosks.” You don't own it.
actions.why: An authorization boundary. The office network belongs to Priya.
actions.label: Move the encoder onto the office switch

actions.why: Escalate to the owner; get a plan instead of a workaround.
actions.label: Call Priya, who owns the office network
actions.text: Priya: “Not on a Sunday and not without a plan. Unplug the encoder, use the lobby TV, I'll come Tuesday.”

actions.why: One reversible change, with a prediction that could have proven you wrong.
actions.label: Unplug only the encoder's network cable (predict first)
actions.text: Receive rate falls to a few Mbit/s. Two minutes of clean audio on the preview. The overflow room goes dark.

actions.why: Restore the people who lost something because of your fix.
actions.label: Put the livestream on the lobby TV for overflow
actions.text: The overflow room gets the service a few seconds behind. Imani tells them why.

actions.why: The weakest test: it shares the path you're trying to prove.
actions.label: Check the booth preview
actions.text: No gaps on the booth monitor. But the booth isn't where the viewers are.

actions.why: Proof where the people are, on an independent network, longer than the fault's 20–60 s pattern.
actions.label: Listen on cellular in the parking lot for 10 minutes
actions.text: Wi-Fi off, cellular on, earbuds in. Ten minutes. No dropouts.

actions.why: That's what happened last week: service back for a while, evidence gone, cause UNKNOWN.
actions.label: Power-cycle the booth switch
actions.text: Everything drops for a minute. When it comes back, so do the gaps. The switch's state is gone.

outcomes.proven: The stream is clean and you proved it on cellular in the parking lot. Walter will see Lily's baptism.
outcomes.partial: The stream is clean — but you never proved it where the viewers are. You believe it's fixed. You don't know.
outcomes.fail: The stream still drops.

expert: Walk the four paths (or ask what changed)
Read the stream computer's receive rate — keep that history
Call Priya instead of borrowing her network
Predict, then unplug only the encoder's network cable
Lobby TV for the overflow room
Ten minutes on cellular in the parking lot
rv: RV-01: the network mechanism is illustrative and needs expert review.

SM-02.title: Hum at 9:14
SM-02.page: The guest speaker's laptop hums through the room. Her video has sound. Doors in 16 minutes.
SM-02.brief: The one adapter that fits brought a hum with it.
SM-02.briefing: A low, steady hum fills the room whenever the laptop's channel is up. The speaker's talk depends on a video with sound. A helpful congregant is holding an “old trick”.
SM-02.opening: Laptop channel up: steady hum. Doors at 9:30.

mute.l: Hum only in the laptop channel

circuits.l: Stage and booth on different circuits

actions.why: Hiding a symptom for the whole room isn't finding its path.
actions.label: Turn the main down
actions.text: The hum gets quieter. So does the pastor's mic, and everything else.

actions.why: Shrink the problem to one path before changing anything.
actions.label: Mute and unmute the laptop channel
actions.text: Muted: silence. Unmuted: hum. It lives in that one channel.

actions.why: Ruled out one thing, but it cost half a minute you didn't need to spend.
actions.label: Swap the audio cable
actions.text: New cable, same hum.

actions.why: Changed many things, learned nothing, and made the speaker nervous.
actions.label: Restart the laptop
actions.text: Dr. Park waits. The hum returns with the slides.

actions.end: You defeated the protective earth on a device people touch. The hum might stop; the safety path is gone. The safety ground is never the fix. Incident ended.
actions.label: Use Gus's ground-lifting adapter

actions.stop: Imani: “That's electrician work. Not ours.”
actions.why: Building wiring belongs to a licensed electrician.
actions.label: Open the stage outlet to check the wiring

actions.why: Map the paths the hum could ride in on.
actions.label: Trace what the laptop connects to
actions.text: Charger in the stage outlet, video to the projector, audio cable back to the booth console.

actions.why: A safe, reversible test that points at the power connection.
actions.label: Unplug the charger; test on battery
actions.text: On battery: silence. Charger back in: hum. Every prong stays where it belongs.

actions.why: Fix it in the signal path, never the safety path.
actions.label: Put an audio isolator in the laptop's audio line
actions.text: Signal passes; the hum doesn't. Both safety grounds untouched.

actions.why: It works today, but nothing is fixed or recorded for next time.
actions.label: Run the talk on battery only
actions.text: Quiet for now at 80% battery.

actions.why: Proof with the real conditions: charger connected.
actions.label: Soundcheck: charger in, isolator in, listen in the room
actions.text: Quiet from the booth and from the middle of the room.

actions.why: The building question goes to the person allowed to answer it.
actions.label: Log it and request the electrician
actions.text: Change log #4. Andre booked to check the stage and booth circuits.

outcomes.proven: Quiet, proven with the charger connected, and every safety ground intact.
outcomes.partial: It's quiet — but you haven't proven it under real conditions.
outcomes.fail: The room still hums.

rv: RV-02 / SB-01: never defeat a protective earth. Building wiring belongs to a licensed electrician.

SM-03.title: Stage circuit trips before Easter
SM-03.page: Half the stage is dead fifteen hours before Easter. The breaker is in a locked room that isn't yours.
SM-03.brief: Twelve new fixtures, one circuit, one thunk.
SM-03.briefing: Sofia brought the Easter look to full and the stage-left outlets died, taking the keyboard and monitors with them. The breaker is in the locked electrical room.
SM-03.opening: Stage left: no power. Easter look: half dark.

actions.why: Stabilize first.
actions.label: Lights to zero; everyone off stage-left gear
actions.text: Nothing re-energizes by surprise. People clear.

actions.end: You reset a breaker in a room you don't own. If the overload was still there — or it was something worse — you just repeated it. Only the electrician resets it. Incident ended.
actions.label: Get the electrical room open and reset the breaker

actions.why: Moving an unknown load to an unknown circuit spreads the problem.
actions.label: Run a cord across the stage to the far wall
actions.text: Four minutes later the far circuit trips too. Now both sides are dark — and there's a cord across a dark stage.

actions.why: Classify before you act.
actions.label: Walk the paths
actions.text: Power: only the stage-left outlets are dead. Control: the lighting desk still answers. Signal: the keyboard is dead because its power is.

actions.why: Arithmetic from the outside of the equipment. You don't open anything.
actions.label: Read nameplates; build a load table
actions.text: 12 × 150 W fixtures + keyboard, monitors and pedals ≈ 2,700 W on one circuit. At 120 V that's about 22.5 A.

calc.q: Nameplates: 12 × 150 W fixtures plus 900 W of keyboard, monitors and pedals. At 120 V, how many amps on the circuit? (1 decimal)

actions.why: A vague escalation makes the expert spend time rediscovering what you knew.
actions.label: Text Andre: “breaker tripped, help”
actions.text: Andre, driving: “Which breaker? What's on it?”

actions.why: Escalation as competence: what, when, what's on it, your estimate, what you didn't touch.
actions.label: Call Andre with the load table
actions.text: Andre: “Most useful call I've had all week. Don't touch the panel. Thirty minutes.”

actions.why: The person allowed to open the door did the part behind it.
actions.label: Andre and Malik rebalance the load and reset the breaker
actions.text: Six fixtures move to circuit 5. The electrician resets circuit 3. Outlets labeled C3 and C5.

actions.why: A promise before proof.
actions.label: Tell Sofia “it'll hold now”
actions.text: Sofia is thrilled.

actions.why: Proof under the real load, measured by the person allowed to measure inside the panel.
actions.label: Full-look test: all twelve at full, band playing, Andre reads the current
actions.text: Thirty minutes at full. About 15 A on circuit 3 (illustrative). No trip.

outcomes.proven: Easter starts from a proof, not a hope.
outcomes.partial: Power is back and the look is full — but nobody has run it at full load yet.
outcomes.fail: Easter morning is still at risk.

expert: Build the load table from nameplates
rv: RV-26: load numbers are illustrative. Only a licensed electrician opens the panel or resets the breaker.

SM-04.title: Nobody could hear the reading
SM-04.source: S01E06 · Nobody Could Hear the Reading
SM-04.page: Receiver users hear the songs but never the scripture reading. Sunday is coming.
SM-04.brief: Two people assumed it was them. It wasn't.
SM-04.briefing: Dolores and Mr. Adeyemi hear music on their assistive listening receivers but nothing during readings. Nobody complained for years.
SM-04.opening: Listening system: songs yes, readings no.

actions.why: You tested the moment it works, not the moment it fails.
actions.label: Replace the receiver batteries
actions.text: The receiver works — during the song you tested with.

actions.why: Right device, wrong moment.
actions.label: Test a receiver at the booth
actions.text: Works fine during rehearsal music.

actions.why: Test at the moment it fails.
actions.label: Wear a receiver through the whole service order
actions.text: Worship: fine. SPOKEN WORD: silence. Worship: fine.

actions.why: What does that button change? It mutes AUX 4.
actions.label: Trace the transmitter's input
actions.text: Masking tape on the cable: “from AUX 4” — the band's monitor mix.

actions.why: Fixing one output by breaking another.
actions.label: Unmute AUX 4 in SPOKEN WORD
actions.text: Readings reach the receivers — and the band wedges, into open mics, during the sermon. A ring of feedback.

actions.why: It works; it isn't tuned for an ear an inch away.
actions.label: Feed the listening system from the main mix
actions.text: Readings come through, a bit boomy in the receivers.

actions.why: An output with its own intent and owner.
actions.label: Build AUX 6 for listening; save it in every preset
actions.text: Its own mix: speech and music, never muted by a scene.

actions.stop: Imani: “We're not doing that.”
actions.why: Excluding people is not a fix.
actions.label: Post a sign: “receivers: music only”

actions.why: The proof comes from the people it's for.
actions.label: Test with Dolores and Mr. Adeyemi in their seats, every scene
actions.text: “I heard the reading. I've been coming eleven years.”

outcomes.proven: Receiver users hear every reading — and told you so themselves.
outcomes.partial: It works at the booth. Nobody who uses it has confirmed it.
outcomes.fail: The readings are still silent, or you broke the sermon to fix them.

expert: Wear a receiver through every scene
Test with the users in their seats
rv: RV-11 / RV-21: no legal obligation is stated; representation needs review.

SM-07.title: Hollow seats, mid-sermon
SM-07.page: During the sermon, an usher says the middle rows sound hollow. The fill hangs three meters up.
SM-07.brief: The service version of the Upward Center Fill: you can't re-aim anything now.
SM-07.briefing: Mid-sermon. Rows 7–9 center sound hollow. You know there is a center fill aimed high. Nothing overhead can be touched during a service.
SM-07.opening: Usher: “Middle rows say it's hollow again.”

actions.why: A notch that moves between seats isn't an EQ problem.
actions.label: EQ the fill during the sermon
actions.text: Seat 13 changes; seat 12 gets worse. Still hollow, differently.

actions.end: Overhead work over an occupied room during a service. Never. Incident ended.
actions.label: Re-aim the fill from a ladder, now

actions.why: A before you can compare against.
actions.label: Slip into row 8 and listen (baseline)
actions.text: Hollow, doubled speech. Noted time and seat.

actions.why: Moved the problem to other people.
actions.label: Mute the fill entirely
actions.text: Center clears; side rows go thin.

actions.why: Small, reversible, logged. Not a fix — a mitigation.
actions.label: Trim the fill 6 dB (reversible)
actions.text: Notches shallower. Hollowness softens.

calc.q: A 6 dB trim multiplies the fill's voltage by how much? (2 decimals)

actions.why: Proof against a baseline, where people sit.
actions.label: Listen again from row 8
actions.text: Better. Not perfect. Measurably shallower than your baseline.

actions.why: The real fix belongs to a qualified crew, outside service hours.
actions.label: Log seats, time and trim; schedule Mateo's crew
actions.text: Change log entry; re-aim booked with a lift for Thursday.

outcomes.proven: Mitigated, measured against a baseline, logged, and the real fix is booked.
outcomes.partial: It sounds better, but you have nothing to compare it to.
outcomes.fail: Still hollow — or you made it worse for someone else.

expert: Log it and book the re-aim

SM-09.title: The heavy vocal, mid-set
SM-09.page: Worship set, second song. The lead vocal is heavy and crushed on every chorus.
SM-09.brief: The service version of Mix Rescue.
SM-09.briefing: The lead vocal sounds heavy and crushed on choruses. Last week, cutting 250–500 Hz “worked”. Devon is away.
SM-09.opening: Chorus two: vocal crushed and boomy.

chan.l: Heaviness is in the lead vocal

actions.why: Louder isn't cleaner, and it wins the first listen.
actions.label: Cut 250–500 Hz and nudge the main up
actions.text: Louder. Sounds “better” for a moment. Still crushed on the chorus.

actions.why: More of a clipped signal.
actions.label: Push the vocal up to cut through
actions.text: Heavier, and the clip light flashes more.

actions.why: Shrink the problem to one channel.
actions.label: Headphones: listen to one channel at a time
actions.text: Drums fine. Keys fine. Lead vocal heavy on choruses.

actions.why: The earliest stage you can reach.
actions.label: Watch channel 1's input meter on the chorus
actions.text: Red on every chorus peak — before the EQ.

actions.why: Fix at the source, keep the level the same.
actions.label: Lower the preamp gain; raise the fader to match
actions.text: Chorus peaks stay out of the red. Level unchanged.

actions.why: Handing your problem to the performer.
actions.label: Signal Marisol to sing softer
actions.text: She sings timidly. Less heavy, less alive.

actions.why: Proof that isn't just “louder”.
actions.label: Level-matched A/B in headphones: before vs now
actions.text: At matched level, the difference is obvious.

outcomes.proven: Clean vocal, same level, proven blind to loudness.
outcomes.partial: It sounds fine — but you never checked it against loudness bias.
outcomes.fail: Still crushed — or just louder.

expert: Watch the input meter on the chorus
rv: RV-25: gain and level numbers are illustrative.

SM-10.title: WORSHIP opens the wrong mics
SM-10.page: Soundcheck. The touch panel's WORSHIP button opens the lectern and mutes the vocal. Service in minutes.
SM-10.brief: The service version of Readiness / Preventive Maintenance.
SM-10.briefing: On Tuesday a crew tidied the rack. Today WORSHIP turns on the wrong microphones.
SM-10.opening: WORSHIP pressed: lectern live, vocal silent.

meters.l: Vocal lands on CH 7, lectern on CH 3

actions.why: Hides the patch change and leaves every other preset wrong.
actions.label: Re-save WORSHIP to match today
actions.text: WORSHIP works. SPOKEN WORD still opens the wrong mic.

actions.why: The panel was never the problem.
actions.label: Restart the touch panel
actions.text: It restarts. Same result.

actions.why: Did the panel act wrongly, or act correctly on a world that moved?
actions.label: Talk into each mic; watch the meters
actions.text: Vocal on CH 7. Lectern on CH 3.

actions.why: What changed?
actions.label: Read the change log
actions.text: #5 Rack tidy — done. Switch moved into rack. — M.

actions.why: A before-state makes the fix provable.
actions.label: Find Priya's before-photos
actions.text: A month-old photo shows every cable in place. Only 3 and 7 moved.

actions.why: Nobody knows what else moved.
actions.label: Swap 3 and 7 back by guess
actions.text: The meters look right for these two.

actions.why: Fix against the record.
actions.label: Move 3 and 7 back to match the photo
actions.text: One cable, check the meter. The other, check again.

actions.why: It works today and misleads the next person who trusts the labels.
actions.label: Remap the channels inside the console instead
actions.text: Presets work. The labels, drawing and console now disagree.

actions.why: Every preset, not just the one you care about.
actions.label: Press every preset and watch the right channels
actions.text: WORSHIP, SPOKEN WORD, BAPTISM, ALL OFF: right mics every time.

outcomes.proven: Right mics in every preset, fixed against the record.
outcomes.partial: It works — but the building's records no longer match it.
outcomes.fail: The service starts with the wrong microphones.

SM-05.title: Bands on the wall, eight minutes to Christmas Eve
SM-05.page: Rolling dark bands on the LED wall — on camera only. The first Christmas Eve service starts in eight minutes.
SM-05.brief: The rental forgot its settings. The room hasn't noticed. Four hundred homes are about to.
SM-05.briefing: The stream preview shows dark bands rolling up the LED wall on Cam 1, and rainbow ripples on Cam 2 when it zooms. In the room the wall looks perfect. It was fixed on December 10.
SM-05.opening: Cam 1: bands rolling. Cam 2 zoomed: ripples. Room: perfect.

text.l: Rental tech: factory reset at 2 p.m.

phone.l: Stream clean on cellular, both cameras

actions.why: Contain the damage without touching the wall or losing evidence.
actions.label: Contain: Cam 1 wide with the wall small, Cam 2 on people
actions.text: The program looks acceptable for now. The problem is still there — just smaller.

actions.why: A factory reset caused this. Another restart repeats it — in front of everyone.
actions.label: Restart the wall processor
actions.text: Ninety seconds of black wall in front of three hundred people. It boots to factory defaults: still 50 Hz. The status history is gone.

actions.why: Brightness isn't timing.
actions.label: Raise the wall to 100% to “burn through” the bands
actions.text: The room squints. The bands don't change.

actions.why: Read before you reset.
actions.label: Read the processor's status screen (touch nothing)
actions.text: IN: 50 Hz. Every camera in the building runs 59.94.

actions.why: What changed? A record of it was in your pocket.
actions.label: Check your phone
actions.text: A text from the rental tech: “swapped a tile at 2, did a factory reset.”

actions.why: Discriminate on preview, never on program: shutter-dependent means timing.
actions.label: On preview only, step Cam 1's shutter
actions.text: The bands change speed and thickness with every step. The ripples don't care.

calc.q: The wall refreshes at 59.94 Hz × 8. With a 1/60 shutter, how many refresh cycles fit in one exposure? (2 decimals)

actions.why: Zoom-dependent means spatial: moiré.
actions.label: On preview only, zoom Cam 2 in and out
actions.text: The ripples grow, shrink and swim with the zoom. The bands don't care.

actions.why: You broke the building's standard to match one misconfigured rental.
actions.label: Switch every camera to the 50 family
actions.text: Both cameras lose sync with the switcher. The stream preview flashes black twice.

actions.why: Fix against the record, not from memory.
actions.label: Re-enter the settings from the sheet taped to the processor
actions.text: Input 59.94, refresh multiple, brightness 40%, cameras 1/60. The wall doesn't blink. Cam 1: bands gone.

actions.why: Moiré is spatial: focus, zoom, angle.
actions.label: Cam 2: pull focus to the people, not the wall
actions.text: The wall softens behind the choir. The ripples vanish.

actions.why: Escalation is right when you can't fix it. Here the fix was taped to the box.
actions.label: Call the rental company's hotline and wait
actions.text: Hold music. Then: “A tech will call you back.”

actions.why: Proof on an independent path, where the viewers are.
actions.label: Lily: watch the stream on cellular in the parking lot, both cameras
actions.text: “Clean on my phone. Both cameras. Outside, on cellular.”

outcomes.proven: A clean wall on the stream, a perfect wall in the room, proven on a phone outside. Merry Christmas.
outcomes.partial: It looks clean at the booth. Nobody has looked where the viewers are.
outcomes.fail: The stream still shows the problem — or the room paid for your fix.

expert: Contain: wide frame, Cam 2 on people
Re-enter the settings from the sheet
rv: RV-03 / RV-29: timing and standards mechanics are simplified; processor menus and values are illustrative.

SM-11.title: Twelve minutes on the agenda
SM-11.page: The board gives AV twelve minutes. Tasha has one budget line and three good reasons to spend it.
SM-11.brief: No cables. Just evidence, honesty, and a clock.
SM-11.briefing: The roof repair came in high: the AV line is $6,000. The worship team wants to buy the LED wall. You have a debt register. The board needs a decision it can defend.: every figure is illustrative.
SM-11.opening: Tasha: “Don't tell me it's important. Tell me what happens if we don't.”

actions.why: Specifications answer questions nobody asked.
actions.label: Open with twenty slides of specifications
actions.text: Eyes glaze. Tasha checks the clock.

actions.why: One page the board can read in two minutes.
actions.label: Hand out the one-page debt register
actions.text: Each item: what it is, who owns it, what happens if we do nothing.

actions.why: History is evidence; it isn't a sales pitch.
actions.label: Show the change log: what actually broke this year
actions.text: Eight entries. Three touch the booth network.

actions.why: Risk made comparable — and arguable, which is the point.
actions.label: Score each item: likelihood × impact
actions.text: Network 4×4 = 16. Receivers 5×3 = 15. UPS 2×5 = 10. Balcony 5×2 = 10. Documentation 3×3 = 9.

actions.why: Popular isn't the same as risky. It retires no risk.
actions.label: Back the LED wall purchase to keep the worship team happy
actions.text: Tasha: “That's four and a half times the line.”

actions.why: Overclaiming spends trust you'll need later.
actions.label: Say “if we don't fund the UPS, the room will go silent”
actions.text: Tasha: “How likely?” You don't know. The room hears certainty you don't have.

actions.why: Calibrated: what you know, what you don't, and what would change your mind.
actions.label: Say “the UPS risk is rare and I can't size it yet”
actions.text: Tasha nods. “Then give me something that costs nothing for now.”

actions.why: When you can't fund the fix, reduce the damage and write it down.
actions.label: Offer a free mitigation: a written power-dip recovery card
actions.text: Imani: “Do it this week.” It goes in the register as DEBT-011's mitigation.

actions.why: Commitments first, then the most risk retired per dollar — and the rest named out loud.
actions.label: Recommend: receivers + network redesign ($5,400)
actions.text: The board votes yes. The UPS and documentation day are deferred, named, owned and dated.

actions.why: A plan the board can't pay for isn't a plan.
actions.label: Ask for everything, split across next year
actions.text: Tasha: “So nothing this year?” The vote is postponed.

actions.why: Deferred isn't forgotten if it has an owner and a date.
actions.label: Put owners and review dates on the deferred items
actions.text: UPS: Imani, review in April. Documentation day: Ray and Maya, before summer.

outcomes.proven: Funded, within budget, with every deferred risk named, owned and dated.
outcomes.partial: A decision was made — but the risks you didn't fund have no owner and no date.
outcomes.fail: The board ran out of time without a plan it could defend.

heads.proven: ✓ FUNDED · EVERY DEFERRED RISK NAMED, OWNED AND DATED
heads.partial: ◐ FUNDED · DEFERRED RISKS HAVE NO OWNER
heads.fail: ✕ NO DECISION · THE BOARD RAN OUT OF TIME

expert: Be honest about what you can't size
Owners and dates on the rest
rv: RV-30 / RV-34: budget figures invented; board depiction needs a fairness read.

SM-08.title: The phantom flicker
SM-08.page: Acceptance test. Fixtures 3 through 8 flicker at random. Elias leaves for another job in a few minutes.
SM-08.brief: It works. It isn't accepted. Those aren't the same.
SM-08.briefing: The new stage lighting passes the look test — until the full-look run, when fixtures 3–8 start flickering at random. The console output is steady. The vendor wants to swap fixture 3. Elias won't sign anything that isn't evidence.
SM-08.opening: Full-look run: fixtures 3–8 flicker. 1 and 2 steady.

console.l: Console output steady on a tester

touch.l: Flicker when the 2→3 cable is touched

cable.l: 2→3 link is a mic cable extension

term.l: No terminator at the end of the line

actions.why: Swapping parts at random moves the problem and erases the evidence.
actions.label: Let the vendor swap fixture 3
actions.text: New fixture 3. Still flickering — now with a fixture whose history you can't check.

actions.why: Clear the source before walking the line.
actions.label: Check the console output with a DMX tester
actions.text: Values steady at the console's port.

actions.why: Everything downstream inherits the fault.
actions.label: Walk the line: find the first fixture that misbehaves
actions.text: 1 steady. 2 steady. 3 flickers. 4–8 flicker.

actions.why: A physical fault at the first failure point.
actions.label: Gently flex the 2→3 cable while watching
actions.text: Fixture 3 stutters on every flex.

actions.why: The usual suspects are physical.
actions.label: Inspect the 2→3 link and the end of the line
actions.text: The 2→3 link is a microphone cable extension. The last fixture has no terminator.

actions.why: DMX is a line, not a tree.
actions.label: Split the line with a Y-cable to “balance” it
actions.text: Now stage right flickers too.

actions.why: A signature is a claim about evidence.
actions.label: Ask Elias to sign now; fix it next week
actions.text: Elias: “Sign what? I have a flicker and no cause.”

actions.why: Fix the cause you found, not the part you suspected.
actions.label: Replace the 2→3 link with rated data cable; add a terminator
actions.text: Steady. All eight fixtures, every look.

actions.why: Test under the stated condition — the one that failed.
actions.label: Rerun the full look for thirty minutes, band playing
actions.text: Thirty minutes at full. No flicker. Elias watches the whole time.

actions.why: The record is what the signature points at.
actions.label: Record requirement, condition, method, result, threshold, evidence
actions.text: Elias reads the sheet line by line, then signs.

outcomes.proven: Found at the first failure point, fixed, rerun under the failing condition, recorded — and signed.
outcomes.partial: Steady for now, but the evidence isn't on the sheet.
outcomes.fail: Elias leaves without signing.

expert: Walk the line to the first failure
rv: RV-04 / RV-31: DMX physical-layer teaching is simplified; the acceptance sheet is illustrative.

SM-06.title: Two seconds of dark
SM-06.page: Mid-sermon, the power dips for two seconds. The lights come back. The sound doesn't. The offering song is in four minutes.
SM-06.brief: Everything came back except the one thing everybody needs.
SM-06.briefing: A two-second power dip. The emergency lights flashed. The house lights are back; the console (on its own small UPS) is up; the room is silent, and so are the stream and the listening system. Ray is in row 12 with laryngitis.
SM-06.opening: Power dip, 2 s. Room silent. Stream silent. Receivers silent.

dsp.l: Processor: rebooted, preset 00 SAFE START, muted

pw.l: Processor password: only in Ray's notebook

actions.end: You overrode the hotel's interlock on a system you don't own, with a code you shouldn't have. Whatever happens next is on you, not the hotel. Incident ended.
actions.label: Get the panel's service code from a banquet server and force DIVIDED

actions.why: Escalate to the owner with what you know, what you didn't touch, and what you need.
actions.label: Radio the house tech with the evidence
actions.text: “Sensor lead's unplugged in the Room A pocket; panel says WALL OPEN; I haven't touched it.” — “Good. Don't. I'm on my way.”

actions.why: A temporary bridge, said out loud to the people it costs. It works; it isn't right.
actions.label: Bridge for the walk-on: feed plate B too; turn Room B's zone right down; Leah tells the captain
actions.text: The keynote reaches Room A through the only bus that works. In Room B it's a murmur under dessert. Leah is already at the captain's elbow.

actions.why: A state change is a change: make before break, counted in with the owner.
actions.label: At the video roll: house tech reconnects the sensor on your count; you mute plate B on the flip
actions.text: “Three, two, one.” Click. The panel turns green: DIVIDED. Room A: the video, clean. Room B: dessert, and nothing else.

actions.why: Your guessed patch met the real state. Fixing the state broke both rooms at once.
actions.label: House tech reconnects the sensor
actions.text: Click. DIVIDED. Your feed is only on plate B now — so the keynote vanishes from Room A mid-sentence and plays at full level into the sponsors' lunch.

actions.why: Undo the guess. The plate that belongs to the room.
actions.label: Move your feed back to plate A
actions.text: Room A: keynote. Room B: lunch only.

actions.why: Verify in every room — including the one you weren't working in.
actions.label: Walk both rooms; press each panel; listen
actions.text: Room A: keynote only. Room B: lunch only. Both panels: DIVIDED · WALL CLOSED.

outcomes.proven: Keynote only in Room A, lunch only in Room B, the state matching the wall — changed on the owner's count and verified in both rooms.
outcomes.partial: Both rooms sound right from where you're standing. Nobody has walked the other room.
outcomes.fail: A room is still hearing the wrong thing — or you changed a system that isn't yours.

Check your own feed to plate A
Radio the house tech with the evidence
Find the label and the sensor lead
Bridge the walk-on on plate B, Room B turned down, Leah tells the captain
Sensor back on the house tech's count at the video roll; mute plate B on the flip

SM-207.title: The mix nobody approved
SM-207.page: Hybrid product launch. The room sounds perfect. Online, the band is too loud and a mic in the wings is live. Four thousand viewers, and the CEO.
SM-207.brief: One mixer, two audiences, two different shows.
SM-207.briefing: 2:15 p.m. The stream carries a co-presenter's mic from the wings — the room engineer muted it ten minutes ago — and the band at a level nobody in the room approved. The stream vendor built the stems. The CEO is watching from an airport.
SM-207.opening: Stream: wings mic live, band pinned. Room: perfect.

mute.l: Devon's mute doesn't reach the stream

meters.l: Stream band stem ignores Devon's fader

proof.l: Leah, cellular + headphones: clean, in sync

actions.why: The whole stream for one bad input. The smallest move was one fader away.
actions.label: Pull all stream audio
actions.text: Four thousand people lose everything, including the presenter. Chat explodes.

actions.why: The problem was audio. You changed the picture.
actions.label: Cut the stream picture to a holding slide
actions.text: A pretty slide. The wings chatter carries on underneath it.

actions.why: The smallest move that stops the harm, on the path that's leaking.
actions.label: Mute the wings mic on the stream mixer
actions.text: The chatter stops online. The room never knew.

actions.why: A mute that doesn't reach the stream is a tap-point clue.
actions.label: Ask Devon to mute the wings mic
actions.text: “I did. Ten minutes ago.” He shows you the lit mute. The stream meter is still moving.

actions.why: The stream ignores the fader too: it's listening upstream of it.
actions.label: Watch the stream's band stem while Devon pulls the band down
actions.text: Devon's fader drops 10 dB. The stream's band meter doesn't twitch.

actions.why: The record says where the stream listens.
actions.label: Read the stream vendor's patch sheet
actions.text: STREAM STEMS · TAP: INPUT (PRE). Built for multitrack recording.

actions.why: The encoder was faithfully encoding the wrong mix.
actions.label: Restart the encoder to reset its audio
actions.text: Sixty seconds of black stream. It comes back with the same mix.

actions.why: A room mix isn't a stream mix.
actions.label: Move the stem sends to post-fader
actions.text: The stream now follows Devon's faders. His band fader is nearly down — the room hears them acoustically. Online, the band vanishes.

actions.why: Obey the mutes; keep the stream's own balance.
actions.label: Set the stem sends pre-fader, post-mute (after processing); balance the stems in headphones
actions.text: Mutes and gates now apply to the stream; Devon's faders don't. Band stem trimmed for headphones. The wings mic stays muted because Devon muted it.

actions.why: Pictures are late. Measure, then delay the audio to match.
actions.label: Clap test on camera; add the measured audio delay
actions.text: On the program feed the clap is heard about 40 ms before it's seen. Audio delayed 40 ms; it lands on the picture.

actions.why: The weakest test: it shares the path you're trying to prove.
actions.label: Check the booth confidence monitor
actions.text: Sounds fine at the booth.

actions.why: Proof on an independent path, where the viewers are.
actions.label: Leah listens on cellular with headphones, on the real stream, for a whole song
actions.text: “Clean. Band's back. Lips match. Nobody in the wings.”

outcomes.proven: The stream obeys the room's mutes, keeps its own balance, sits on the picture — and a second listener on cellular heard it that way.
outcomes.partial: It sounds right at the booth. Nobody has listened where the viewers are.
outcomes.fail: Four thousand people are still hearing a mix nobody approved — or nothing at all.

expert: Mute the wings mic on the stream mixer
Ask Devon: the mute was already on
Watch the band stem while Devon rides the band
Stems pre-fader, post-mute; balance in headphones
Second listener on cellular for a whole song

SM-208.title: Camera 2 is black
SM-208.source: S02E08 · Doors in Four Cues · CASE-009
SM-208.page: 6:05 p.m. The pre-show checklist finds camera 2 — the CEO's IMAG camera — black on the switcher. Doors at 7:00.
SM-208.brief: The checklist did its job. Now yours.
SM-208.briefing: The room flipped for dinner at 5:40. Camera 2 worked at the afternoon launch. The new reveal cue was just programmed. The CEO walks on at 7:28 and both IMAG screens need camera 2.
SM-208.opening: Switcher: CAM 2 black. Doors in 55 minutes.

walk.l: Field monitor: picture to the pocket, none after

all.l: Every source full screen after the fix

actions.why: It restarts the one part that was working, and erases work you needed.
actions.label: Reboot the switcher
actions.text: Every source goes black for ninety seconds. The unsaved reveal programming is gone. Camera 2 comes back black.

actions.why: Random swaps move parts, not causes.
actions.label: Swap camera 2 for the spare body
actions.text: A new camera, same black.

actions.why: The camera is fine: the fault is downstream.
actions.label: Ask the camera op what the viewfinder shows
actions.text: “Picture's perfect.”

actions.why: Clear the suspect everyone's already blaming.
actions.label: Read the router: is camera 2 on input 2?
actions.text: CAM 2 → IN 2. The new reveal playback is on IN 6. The new cue didn't do this.

actions.why: Last good, first bad.
actions.label: Walk a field monitor down the path: camera out, pocket (both sides), router
actions.text: Picture at the camera. Picture on the camera side of the pocket. Nothing on the house side.

actions.stop: Jordan: “That side's venue power. Electrician only.” The lid stays shut.
actions.why: Floor pockets can hold power. Not ours.
actions.label: Open the pocket's power side to check it too

actions.why: Fix at the first failure point.
actions.label: Lift the AV side of the pocket and inspect the connector
actions.text: The connector is crushed flat — a caster mark across it.

actions.why: A crushed connector isn't fixed by tape.
actions.label: Tape the crushed connector and push it back in
actions.text: Picture flickers on and off with every footstep.

actions.stop: Jordan: “That's the guest path from the doors. Not a chance.”
actions.why: A cable across a guest path is a trip hazard — and the next cart crushes it.
actions.label: Run the spare straight across the aisle, taped flat

actions.why: Built for a few meters, not forty.
actions.label: Use the 40 m consumer display cable from the truck
actions.text: Sparkles, then dropouts.

actions.why: Route outside traffic; stay inside the cable's reach.
actions.label: Run the spare SDI along the wall, under ramps, outside the guest path
actions.text: Eighty-five meters, taped under ramps at the service door. Camera 2 appears on the switcher.

actions.why: Prove it the way you found it.
actions.label: Rerun the checklist line: every source, full screen
actions.text: Cam 1, cam 2, playback, graphics, reveal, confidence feed: all clean.

actions.why: The client hears it from you, with evidence.
actions.label: Tell Graham: camera 2 was black, is fixed and checked, and why
actions.text: Graham: “An hour before doors. Not at 7:28.” He almost smiles.

outcomes.proven: Camera 2 found at the first failure point, rerouted outside the traffic, every source rechecked — fifty minutes before doors.
outcomes.partial: Camera 2 is up. Nobody has rechecked every source since the fix.
outcomes.fail: The CEO walks on to one camera — or none.

expert: Walk a field monitor down the path
Inspect the AV side of the pocket
Spare SDI along the wall, outside the guest path
rv: Q-004 · RV-54: the failure is the SIGNAL adaptation; floor-pocket power belongs to the venue's electrician.

SM-209.title: Gates at nine
SM-209.page: 12:58 a.m. The site team joined their network to ours and went home. Half the gate scanners are offline and the stream test is dropping. Gates open at nine.
SM-209.brief: Two networks, one range, two servers answering the same question.
SM-209.briefing: At 12:40 the site's network team patched our AV switch into theirs to share internet, then left. Half the ticket scanners show OFFLINE with full Wi-Fi bars; the stream encoder's test keeps dropping. The site lead's phone goes to voicemail until seven. Priya is asleep, probably.
SM-209.opening: Scanners: half OFFLINE. Stream test: dropping. Patch cable: SITE → AV.

dup.l: Encoder .50 answered by a second device

priya.l: Priya: one DHCP server, ours fixed at the top

proof.l: Every lane scans; stream clean on cellular

actions.stop: Imani: “That's the site's switch. And rebooting it wipes the table that shows what happened.”
actions.why: Not ours, and it erases the state you need.
actions.label: Reboot the site's switch

actions.why: Two gateways on one network: two servers answering.
actions.label: Read a failing scanner's network screen, and a working one
actions.text: Failing: 198.18.20.142, gateway .1. Working: 198.18.20.37, gateway .254. Our AV router is .1.

actions.why: Undo the change that joined them: one cable, reversible, on our side.
actions.label: Predict, then unplug the patch at our switch
actions.text: Prediction: scanners recover, our stream loses internet. Both happen. The ticketing lead reconnects her scanners; every one goes green.

actions.why: The stream drop and the scanners were the same fault.
actions.label: Read the encoder's log and our router's address table
actions.text: “Address conflict: 198.18.20.50.” A scanner was handed the encoder's fixed address.

actions.stop: Maya's hand stops. The password on the case isn't permission. It's their router.
actions.why: A network owner owns their network, even at 1 a.m.
actions.label: Log into the site's router with the password taped to its case

actions.why: The owner hears it first, in writing, even if they're asleep.
actions.label: Call the site network lead; text what you found and what you did
actions.text: Voicemail until seven. The text says: joined at 12:40, two DHCP servers, we unplugged our end.

actions.why: Escalate to someone who knows more than you do. Say what you know, not what you think.
actions.label: Call Priya
actions.text: Priya, from her kitchen: “Evidence first. Then tell it back to me.”

actions.why: Fixed addresses inside the busy part of someone else's pool collide immediately.
actions.label: Give our gear fixed addresses in the middle of the range and rejoin
actions.text: You pick .50–.90. The site's pool is already handing those to scanners — two conflicts before you finish typing. You undo it.

actions.why: One network, one server answering.
actions.label: Turn off our router's DHCP (ours)
actions.text: One DHCP server on the joined network from now on: the site's.

actions.why: Tonight, the pool fills from the bottom and there are sixty scanners. That's the fuse.
actions.label: Give our gear fixed addresses at the top of the range (.240–.249)
actions.text: Encoder .240, console .241, stage boxes .242–.245. Inside the site's pool — not excluded. It's not our server.

actions.why: The workaround, made on our side, reported to the owner.
actions.label: Re-join the networks; text the site lead exactly what changed
actions.text: Scanners stay green. The stream gets internet. The site lead has a text waiting at seven.

actions.why: Proof where the users are: the gates, and the viewers.
actions.label: Scan test tickets at every lane; stream to the private preview, checked on cellular
actions.text: Twelve lanes, twenty tickets each: green. Stream: clean on a phone outside the network.

actions.why: A workaround nobody wrote down becomes the design by accident. (In the story, nobody does.)
actions.label: Write it up now: what, why, what's wrong with it, who fixes it
actions.text: Four lines in the shared log. Imani sighs, then reads them. “Fine. Bed.”

outcomes.proven: Every lane scans, the stream is up, the owner has been told — and the workaround is working. Did you write it down? The story didn't.
outcomes.partial: It works. Nobody has scanned a ticket at every lane.
outcomes.fail: Three thousand people meet offline scanners at nine — or you changed a network that isn't yours.

expert: Read a failing and a working scanner
Unplug the patch at our switch (predict first)
Call and text the site lead
Our gear fixed at the top of the range
Scan every lane; stream on cellular

SM-210.title: Festival in the rain
SM-210.source: S02E10 · Festival in the Rain · MS-04
SM-210.page: 9:21 p.m. The headliner is on and the rain is early. Two wireless channels drop, FOH loses stage-box control for seconds at a time, and the generator shows an alarm.
SM-210.brief: Twelve thousand people, three faults, and a sky that gets a vote.
SM-210.briefing: Rain arrived twenty minutes ahead of the forecast. The headliner's vocal and a guitar drop out on wireless; FOH's control of the stage box drops for two or three seconds at a time; a red ALARM light shows on the generator. Ben has the weather plan. Hank has the generator. You have FOH.
SM-210.opening: RF: 2 channels dropping. Control: drops of 2–3 s. Generator: ALARM. Rain: getting heavier.

scan.l: RF scan: no new signals; antenna B low

corr.l: Control drops track rain bursts; one port flaps

photo.l: 8:40 photo: junction boot off, box on the ground

hold.l: Ben: hold per the weather plan (flash-to-bang 9 s)

ramp.l: Antenna B cable crushed under the truck ramp

proof.l: 10 min stable · RF walk test clean · Hank's sign-off

actions.why: Service first, with a move you can undo.
actions.label: Headliner to the wired backup mic on the stand; tell Devon
actions.text: She grabs the stand mic mid-line. The crowd sings the chorus back at her.

actions.why: No new interference was measured. Changing a coordinated plan mid-show creates the fault you feared.
actions.label: Blame the crowd's phones: rescan and re-coordinate every channel live
actions.text: Two more channels start dropping as the new frequencies land near each other.

actions.why: Rules out the crowd; points at one antenna's path.
actions.label: RF scan and per-antenna signal readout
actions.text: No new signals anywhere. Antenna A: healthy. Antenna B: signal well down.

actions.why: Recent isn't evidence, and the reboot wiped the drop log.
actions.label: Reboot the console — it updated last week
actions.text: Ninety seconds of silence for twelve thousand people. It comes back. The drops come back with the next burst of rain.

actions.why: Correlate with the weather, then find the one physical link.
actions.label: Line up control drops against the rain; read the switch port log; check Imani's walk photos
actions.text: Every drop sits on a burst of heavier rain. Port 7 — the stage-left junction — has flapped 23 times. Imani's 8:40 photo: the junction's rain boot hanging off, the box on the ground.

actions.why: Branch C: the planned local path, set up at soundcheck.
actions.label: Move monitor control to the local fallback mixer at the stage
actions.text: Devon takes the headliner's in-ears on the stage mixer. A drop at FOH can't reach her ears now.

actions.why: The power vendor's machine, the power vendor's call.
actions.label: Radio Hank about the generator alarm
actions.text: “Mine. Keep your loads where they are. Four minutes.”

actions.end: You reset an alarm on a machine that belongs to the power vendor, in the rain. It was a real fault; you just hid it. Incident ended.
actions.label: Reset the generator alarm yourself

actions.why: The hold belongs to the plan and the person it names. Your job is to make it easy.
actions.label: Ask Ben for the weather call
actions.text: A flash. Ben counts: nine seconds. “Hold. Weather plan, section three.” Rosa calls it; the headliner leaves the stage; the crowd moves to shelter.

calc.q: Flash to bang: 6 seconds. At about 343 m/s, how far away is the lightning? (km, 2 decimals)

actions.end: “Just one more song” overrides the weather plan's hold with twelve thousand people in the open. That is exactly what the plan exists to prevent. Incident ended.
actions.label: Tell Rosa to let them finish the song first

actions.end: Ben: “Stop.” You went for an energized connector sitting in water, next to a power distro, in a storm. Nothing about a show is worth that. Incident ended.
actions.label: Dry and re-seat the junction connector now — it's live and wet

actions.why: After the all-clear, the owners first, then one fix at a time.
actions.label: After the all-clear: Hank makes the distro beside the junction safe and signs the generator back in; the crew swaps in the spare jumper in a raised, booted box
actions.text: 10:31, all clear. Hank: “Distro's safe. Generator was a fuel filter — changed, signed.” The spare jumper goes into a booted box on a stand, off the ground.

actions.why: Fix the path the scan pointed at, then prove it where the performers walk.
actions.label: After the all-clear: trace antenna B's cable; replace the section crushed under the truck ramp; walk test with Devon
actions.text: The cable is flattened where the ramp has sat since 11:04 this morning. New cable, routed clear of the ramp. Devon walks every position with a handheld: solid.

actions.why: Proof, then facts to the person who decides.
actions.label: Watch control for ten minutes; report the facts to Rosa — restart is her call
actions.text: Ten minutes, zero drops. “Booth is ready: control stable ten minutes, RF walk test clean, Hank signed. Your call.” Rosa: “Restarting.” The crowd roars.

heads.proven: ✓ HELD SAFELY · RESTARTED · EVERY FIX PROVEN
heads.partial: ◐ RESTARTED · NOT ALL OF IT PROVEN

outcomes.proven: The show held when the plan said so, came back on Rosa's call, and every fix was proven: ten stable minutes, a clean walk test, Hank's signature.
outcomes.partial: The show is running again, but something was fixed on hope rather than proof.
outcomes.fail: The show didn't come back — or someone crossed a line no show is worth.

expert: RF scan per antenna (not the crowd)
Line up drops with the rain; port log; walk photos
Monitors to the local fallback mixer
After the all-clear: Hank first, then the junction in a raised, booted box
Replace antenna B's crushed cable; walk test
Ten stable minutes; facts to Rosa

SM-301.title: 8:55 Monday
SM-301.page: Twelve meeting rooms refuse to join calls. A client pitch starts at 9:00 in one of them. The rest of the fleet restarts tonight.
SM-301.brief: The rooms are healthy. They just aren't allowed in.
SM-301.briefing: At 8:55 on Monday twelve rooms on six floors show a sign-in error. Renata's client pitch is in the Summit Room at 9:00. You're new; the accounts belong to the identity team; Mei is on her way. ⚑ Figures illustrative.
SM-301.opening: Summit Room panel: SIGN-IN FAILED · PASSWORD EXPIRED. Eleven more like it.

ring.l: Panel: ring PILOT · last restart Sun 02:00

lap.l: Personal laptop joins from the same room

chg.l: Change: Fri 18:00 password expiry, people listed

mei.l: Mei: room accounts are in the default policy

pilot.l: Twelve pilot rooms signed in after restart

call.l: Real call from Summit to an outside far end

actions.why: The meeting happens and the evidence stays where it is.
actions.label: Contain: Renata joins from her laptop on the table input
actions.text: The room display takes the laptop. The client sees slides and faces at 9:01. The panel still says SIGN-IN FAILED.

actions.why: A restart is exactly what caused this. Repeating it teaches nothing and erases the panel's record.
actions.label: Restart the Summit Room
actions.text: Four minutes of boot. It signs in with the same expired password and fails again. The panel's sign-in log from Sunday is gone.

actions.why: Read before you reset: the error names the account, and the restart time says when it tried.
actions.label: Read the panel's info screen (touch nothing)
actions.text: SIGN-IN FAILED · PASSWORD EXPIRED. RING: PILOT. LAST RESTART: SUN 02:00.

actions.why: One test clears two suspects: the meeting service and the network.
actions.label: Join the same call from a personal laptop in the same room
actions.text: It joins instantly, video and audio. The service is up; the room's network path works.

actions.why: You'd be choosing a new secret for an account security owns — and locking rooms out while you try.
actions.label: Type the room password Sam knows into each panel
actions.text: Room 7-West: “Password expired. Choose a new password.” Room 18-North locks after three tries.

actions.why: What changed? A record exists — and it didn't list rooms.
actions.label: Search the change calendar for Friday
actions.text: CHG Fri 18:00 · Passwords older than 90 days must change at next sign-in. Impacted systems: staff accounts (from the people directory).

actions.end: The room accounts belong to the identity team, and the access decision belongs to security. You just set a new secret for three hundred rooms by yourself. Incident ended.
actions.label: Reset the room accounts yourself from Sam's help-desk console

actions.stop: Mei: “That policy closes an audit finding. Bring me what broke, not what to undo.”
actions.why: Undoing a security change to fix a symptom re-opens the risk it closed.
actions.label: Ask Mei to roll the policy back

actions.why: Escalation as competence: facts the owner can act on, no fix smuggled in.
actions.label: Bring Mei the evidence: twelve rooms, the error, the ring, Friday's change
actions.text: Mei: “Room accounts are in the default policy. Passwords set at install — some are three years old. My team can move them to a room-account policy today.”

actions.why: The owner made the access change; the fleet is covered before 02:00.
actions.label: Identity team moves the room accounts to the room-account policy (unique, managed credentials)
actions.text: 289 room accounts moved. Unique credentials, rotated by the identity team, sign-in limited to each room's device.

actions.why: It hides the trigger and leaves every room one restart away from failing, unpatched.
actions.label: Turn off the nightly restarts for the whole fleet
actions.text: The 277 rooms won't sign in tonight — and won't take tomorrow's security updates either.

actions.why: A small, known ring proves the change before the whole fleet depends on it.
actions.label: Restart the twelve pilot rooms and watch each one sign in
actions.text: Twelve panels: READY. Sign-in log: twelve successes with the new credentials.

actions.why: A panel saying READY isn't a meeting. A real far end on an independent path is.
actions.label: Real call from the Summit Room to Maya's phone, outside the building's network
actions.text: Maya, on cellular in the stairwell: picture, voice, content. Both ways.

outcomes.proven: The pitch happened, the twelve rooms are back, the fleet is protected before 02:00 — and you proved it with a real call to an outside far end.
outcomes.partial: The rooms say READY. Nobody has made a real call from one yet.
outcomes.fail: Rooms are still signed out, the fleet is still at risk — or you made an access decision that wasn't yours.

expert: Laptop on the table input for the pitch
Real call to an outside far end

SM-302.title: Hear yourself twice
SM-302.source: S03E02 · The Room That Hears Twice
SM-302.page: Remote participants hear their own voices echo back from the Harbor Room. An angry client calls into the same room at 14:00.
SM-302.brief: Two cancellers, one room, one client who thinks she's being recorded.
SM-302.briefing: Yesterday Helen Voss heard her own voice come back late from the Harbor Room and asked if she was being recorded. She calls back at 14:00, into the same room, with legal on the invite. Sam holds the keys to the room computer's profile.
SM-302.opening: Test call: far end hears itself ~0.5 s late, only when the room is quiet.

repro.l: Reproduced from the far end: ~0.5 s echo in silence

dsp.l: Processor AEC on, true reference; clean alone

proof.l: Far end on cellular: no echo in silence or double-talk

actions.why: Level isn't the path. You made the room harder to hear and left the echo.
actions.label: Turn the ceiling mics down 10 dB
actions.text: Everyone in the room gets quieter. The far end still hears itself, just a little softer.

actions.why: The new part was the obvious suspect and the wrong one.
actions.label: Replace the new ceiling microphone
actions.text: Forty-five minutes of ceiling tile and cable. Same echo.

actions.why: Hear it where the user heard it, and note when it happens.
actions.label: Reproduce: call in from the corridor on cellular and listen as the far end
actions.text: Your own voice comes back about half a second late, faint and warbly, only when the room is silent.

actions.why: The canceller nearest the mics is healthy. Look downstream.
actions.label: Read the room processor: canceller on? Reference?
actions.text: Canceller ON, reference = the exact signal to the loudspeakers. With the software's processing bypassed, no echo returns.

actions.why: Sam holds the keys to the room computer; you bring the question.
actions.label: With Sam, read the conferencing computer's audio settings
actions.text: Echo cancellation: ON. Noise suppression: HIGH. They were off at install.

actions.why: What changed? Sunday, again.
actions.label: Read the room computer's update history
actions.text: Updates installed Sunday 02:04. Settings restored to defaults.

actions.why: Restarting erased the one on-screen clue about what changed, and fixed nothing.
actions.label: Restart the room computer
actions.text: It comes back with the same settings — and the update notice that told you when is gone.

actions.why: You removed the canceller with the true reference and kept the one without it.
actions.label: Turn off the room processor's echo canceller instead
actions.text: Now only the software's canceller works — it can't see the room's loudspeaker path. The echo gets louder.

actions.why: Undo the change that made it worse.
actions.label: Turn the room processor's canceller back on
actions.text: Back where you were.

actions.why: It works today. Next Sunday the ghost is back.
actions.label: Turn off the software canceller locally on the room computer
actions.text: The echo stops — until the next update resets the setting.

actions.why: The setting now lives where updates can't quietly undo it.
actions.label: Sam turns the software canceller off in the managed room profile for Harbor
actions.text: Profile applied. Software canceller and noise suppression off; the processor does both. Survives updates.

actions.why: Proof from the far end, on an independent path, under the condition that failed.
actions.label: Far-end test on cellular: silence, then double-talk, then silence
actions.text: No echo in silence. Double-talk clean both ways.

actions.why: The client's fear was a recording. Explaining the mechanism is part of the fix.

SM-1001.title: The click that keeps time

CASE-001.title: The Upward Center Fill
CASE-001.hook: Ten seats. Two years. One loudspeaker pointed at the ceiling.
learn: What happened. A renovation hung a center-fill loudspeaker tilted up toward the balcony. Part of its sound bounced off the hard ceiling and reached rows 7–9 a few milliseconds after the direct sound from the mains.

Why it sounded hollow. Two arrivals of similar level add at some frequencies and cancel at others: comb filtering. The delay depends on the path difference, which changes seat by seat, so the notches move. No single EQ setting fixes all ten seats.

How it was proved. Ten-seat baseline before any change; the reflection predicted with the image-source method; a falsification test (trim the fill; the notches should get shallower); a re-aim by a qualified crew; verification in the seats under two conditions.
The honest tradeoff. The balcony front lost coverage. It went into the change log and to the owner (DEBT-010).
CASE-001.service: Mid-sermon you can't touch anything overhead. Take a baseline from the seats, make one small reversible change (trim), check it again from the seats, and log it for a qualified crew to fix properly.

engineer.intro: Work the geometry. Speed of sound c ≈ 343 m/s (dry air near 20 °C). The first notch for two equal arrivals is at 1 ÷ (2Δt); notches repeat every 1 ÷ Δt.
engineer.flag: Illustrative geometry, not a measured room.

steps.prompt: Seat 13: the reflected path is 1.7 m longer. What is Δt?
steps.hint: Δt = ΔL ÷ c. Divide 1.7 m by 343 m/s, then convert seconds to milliseconds.
steps.unitWhy: A delay is a time: milliseconds.

steps.prompt: Seat 13: where is the first notch?
steps.hint: f = 1 ÷ (2 × Δt). Use Δt in seconds.
steps.unitWhy: A notch is a frequency: hertz.

steps.prompt: Seat 13: how far apart are the notches?
steps.why: Notches repeat every 1/Δt.

steps.prompt: Seat 12: the path difference is 1.4 m. Where is its first notch?
steps.why: A different seat, a different notch: that's why EQ can't fix all ten.

CASE-003.title: Mix Rescue
CASE-003.hook: A muddy mix that “got better” last week — because it got louder.
learn: SIGNAL's adaptation. Maya cut 250–500 Hz and nudged the main up. It sounded better. Level-matched and blind, nobody could pick the cut: the improvement was loudness.
The real problem was upstream. Preamp gain was set at speaking level from arm's length; at full voice the chorus clipped. Up close, a directional mic also gains low end (proximity effect).
The fix. Lower the preamp gain, raise the fader to match, agree a consistent mic distance with the singer, rewrite the line check. Proved blind and level-matched, then live on Sunday.
The heuristic, reframed. “250–500 Hz is mud” is a place to look, not a rule.
CASE-003.service: Mid-set there's no time for a blind test at first: find the channel, read its input meter, fix gain at the source with a matched fader move — then confirm with a quick level-matched check in headphones.

engineer.intro: Headroom and level matching. Keep units honest: decibels are ratios.

steps.prompt: The chorus peaks would reach about 4 dB above full scale if they could. You want peaks 6 dB below full scale. How much should you lower the preamp gain?
steps.hint: From +4 above the ceiling down to −6 below it.
steps.why: Then raise the fader 10 dB to keep the same level in the room.
steps.unitWhy: A change of gain is in dB; dBFS names a level on the digital scale.

steps.prompt: In the A/B, version A measures 2 dB louder than version B. To match them, how much do you trim A?
steps.why: Now you're comparing the change, not the loudness.

steps.prompt: The singer moves from 5 cm to 10 cm from the mic. Roughly how much does the level at the mic change? (answer as a positive number of dB lost)
steps.why: About 6 dB — distance is a fader you can't see.

CASE-006.title: Readiness / Preventive Maintenance
CASE-006.hook: A neat rack, a missing label, and a preset that did exactly what it was told.
learn: SIGNAL's adaptation. A weekday rack tidy-up swapped two patch cables to make them hang straight. On Sunday, WORSHIP opened the lectern and muted the vocal.
The control didn't fail. A preset recalls channel numbers, not intentions. It acted correctly on a world that moved.
Readiness is a habit. Plan the change, photograph the before-state, label both ends, log before you leave, press every preset after, compare against the record.
The evidence that saved Sunday was a cable photo Priya took a month earlier for a drawing.
CASE-006.service: Minutes to service: measure which mic lands where, read the log, fix against the before-photo, then press every preset — not just the broken one.

engineer.intro: Design the check so it can't miss. Count what you must verify, then order the work.

steps.prompt: The panel has 4 presets. Each must be checked on 6 outputs (room, stream, wedges, listening, lobby, recording). How many checks is that?
steps.why: 4 × 6 = 24. Write them as a matrix and tick every cell.

steps.prompt: At about 20 seconds per check, how long does the full matrix take?
steps.why: Eight minutes — cheap next to a wrong mic on Sunday.
steps.unitWhy: 480 is in seconds; the question wants minutes.

CASE-004.title: Loose DMX: The Phantom Flicker
CASE-004.hook: New stage lighting “works”. During acceptance, fixtures flicker at random.
learn: SIGNAL's adaptation. During Elias's acceptance test, several fixtures on one line flicker intermittently. The console output is steady.

Find the first failure point. Every fixture downstream of a bad link inherits the fault. Walk the line: the first fixture that misbehaves marks the spot — the fault is at or just upstream of its input.
The usual suspects are physical: a damaged connector, cable not rated for data, a Y-split, or no terminator at the end of the line.
Acceptance is evidence. Requirement, condition, method, result, threshold, where the evidence lives — then sign, or don't.
CASE-004.service: Mid-service: stabilize the look (park the flickering fixtures on a safe state or take them out of the look), don't swap fixtures at random, and walk the line to the first failing fixture when you can.

engineer.intro: Addresses and footprints. One universe = 512 channels.

steps.prompt: A 14-channel fixture starts at address 1. What address should the next fixture start at?
steps.why: The next free channel is 15.

steps.prompt: Twelve 14-channel fixtures in a row starting at 1. What is the last channel used?
How many 14-channel fixtures fit in one universe?
steps.why: You can't use part of a fixture.

CASE-010.title: Video Standards Mismatch
CASE-010.hook: A rented wall from a 50 Hz tour, in a 59.94 building, on the biggest night of the year.
learn: SIGNAL's adaptation. A rented LED wall looked perfect in the room and showed rolling dark bands on camera. Its processor had arrived set to the 50 Hz family; every camera in the building ran 59.94. A factory reset on Christmas Eve afternoon put it back.

Two effects, one costume. Rolling bands are temporal: the wall's refresh sampled by the camera's exposure. Rainbow ripples are spatial: moiré between two pixel grids. Change one variable at a time — shutter for timing; zoom, focus or angle for moiré.

The fix. Put the odd device into the building's family, expose for whole light cycles (a shutter equal to the frame period is a common start), focus on people rather than the wall, and write the settings on the rental itself.
The habit. Anything you rent arrives with somebody else's defaults. After any service visit, re-check the settings sheet and look through a camera.
CASE-010.service: Minutes before doors: contain (wide frame, second camera on people), read the processor's status before touching it, find what changed, restore from the record, prove on a phone outside.

engineer.intro: Timing arithmetic. Frame period = 1 ÷ frame rate. A frame catches whole refresh cycles when exposure × refresh rate is a whole number.
engineer.flag: Illustrative values; real walls and cameras differ.

steps.prompt: At 59.94 frames per second, how long is one frame period?
steps.hint: Period = 1 ÷ rate, then convert to milliseconds.

steps.prompt: The wall refreshes at 16 × 59.94 Hz. How many refresh cycles fit in one 1/59.94 s exposure?
steps.why: A whole number: every frame gets the same light.

steps.prompt: With the processor mistakenly at 50 Hz × 16 = 800 Hz refresh, how many cycles fit in a 1/100 s exposure?
steps.why: 8 is whole — but the 50 Hz refresh and the 59.94 frame starts drift against each other, so each frame starts at a different point in the cycle. That drift is the roll.

steps.prompt: The 50 Hz and 59.94 Hz frame starts drift against each other. How often does the pattern repeat? (the beat frequency, in Hz)
steps.hint: Beat = difference between the two rates.
steps.why: A beat near 10 Hz: bands that visibly crawl. Same family, no beat.

CASE-002.title: Building the Room
CASE-002.hook: The room leaned left before the first note — and every fix made it lean harder.
learn: The Fieldbook case. In a sanctuary, the bass amp, the keyboard amp, the drums, the left sub and the left main loudspeaker all sat on audience-left. The room leaned left before the mix even started. Seats near the left were loud and boomy, the back rows lost punch, and the right side sounded thin.

Three fixes that made it worse. The bass amp was turned up on stage and began to “take over” services — roaring, distorted and beyond the console's control. The Fieldbook's lesson: mix the source, not just the board. The keyboardist said “I can't hear myself”, so a monitor was added, aimed at the left wall — and it became a mid and high booster for the side that was already too loud. The drummer's “distorted in-ear mix” turned out to be gain staging, not the monitor.
The hidden one. The subs overlapped in polarity and placement, so some seats got more bass and others got cancellation.

How it was fixed. Several seats were measured with the same material. Stage levels were agreed with the players, the wedge was re-aimed, the gain was restaged and the subs were aligned, one change at a time. Result: the left became a controlled, intentional low-end engine, a center fill kept the vocals clear, the right side was balanced, and the vocals sat on top.
Why Maya re-read it before the ballroom flip. Flip a room and the stack moves with it. The room is part of the signal chain.
CASE-002.service: Mid-event you can't rebuild a stage. Ask for stage amp levels down (the source), check each wedge's aim, trim the sub that is piling up if its owner agrees, and walk three seats before and after. One change at a time, logged.

engineer.intro: Room modes: f = c ÷ (2 × L). Inverse square: about 6 dB per doubling of distance. Two arrivals Δt apart first cancel at 1 ÷ (2 × Δt). c ≈ 343 m/s.

steps.prompt: The sanctuary is 18 m long. Where is its lowest length mode?
steps.why: Below most music — but its multiples (19, 29, 38 Hz …) are not.

steps.prompt: The room is 12 m wide. Where is its lowest width mode?
steps.hint: Same formula, width instead of length.
steps.why: Each dimension picks its own favorite notes.

steps.prompt: Seat L5 is 6 m from the left sub and seat R5 is 12 m from it. How much quieter is that sub at R5 (free field)?
steps.why: One doubling: the right side hears that sub about 6 dB lower.

steps.prompt: At the center seat the left sub arrives 3.5 ms after the right sub. Where is the first cancellation?
steps.hint: f = 1 ÷ (2 × Δt), with Δt in seconds.
steps.why: Right where the bass guitar lives — alignment matters.

CASE-005.title: One Dim Panel
CASE-005.hook: The rest of the wall was fine. One square wasn't — and everybody's eyes went straight to it.
learn: The Fieldbook case. One area of the LED wall went noticeably dim. At audience distances of 5–20 m the drop was obvious, because eyes judge a panel by contrast with its neighbors, not by its absolute brightness.

The likely causes, in the order to check them: a loose or partly seated data connection, or a failing receiving card; a failing power supply or driver on that module; overheating or blocked ventilation; the wrong brightness or calibration on that one module.

The method: identify (which module, since when, and does it follow the content?), understand (data, power, heat or calibration?), measure (brightness against its neighbors; the temperature and status in the wall processor), then fix — through the wall's owner.

SIGNAL's version, at Riverbend. It happens in the rain, so there's heat inside the cases and moisture outside. The weather plan and the vendor's safety plan own any physical work. Nobody opens the wall or works at height during the set.
“Every pixel carries a purpose.” Until the fix, move the lyrics and the captions away from the dim square.
CASE-005.service: During the set, don't touch the wall. Read the processor's status for that module, move critical graphics away from the square, and give the vendor a photo and the module's position. The physical fix waits for the weather plan and the vendor.

engineer.intro: Percent change = (neighbor − module) ÷ neighbor × 100. Pixels across = panel width ÷ pixel pitch. Pixel count = width × height.

steps.prompt: The dim module reads 220 nits; its neighbors read 1,000 nits. What percentage of brightness has it lost?
steps.why: The Fieldbook's example: a 78% drop is obvious at any audience distance.

steps.prompt: The module is 500 mm wide with a 3.9 mm pixel pitch. About how many pixels across?
steps.why: A common module size: 128 pixels across.

steps.prompt: The wall is 6 modules wide and 4 high, each 128 × 128. How many pixels in the whole wall?
steps.hint: Width in pixels × height in pixels.
steps.why: One module is 16,384 of them — about 4% of the wall, and 100% of the audience's attention.

CASE-011.title: The License That Expired
CASE-011.hook: Two renewals nobody was tracking. One Sunday morning. Fifteen percent of the stage lit.
learn: The Fieldbook case. During a service, the lighting software's subscription and the license on the lighting interface both expired. Control of the stage lights was lost, only one fixture could be brought up by hand, and the stage ran at about 15% of its usual coverage for the whole service.

What SIGNAL changes. In the Fieldbook account someone climbed to switch on a front-truss light. SIGNAL does not show that as a fix. Nobody climbs during a live event; overhead work belongs to trained crew with the right equipment and a plan. The safe live fallback is on the ground: house lights at a readable level, and a console or hardware preset if one exists.
The fix. The license and subscription were renewed and the software was brought up to a current, supported version — after the service, with a known-good fallback — and control was restored.

The real lesson, and why Ray brought it to the budget meeting. Track every software and device license in the asset register with its expiry date, send renewal reminders to two people, and keep a non-software fallback that is tested every quarter. The license fee is small next to one dark service.
CASE-011.service: Mid-service: don't climb, and don't reinstall while people are watching. Tell the TD, bring the house lights to a safe readable level, and use any preset that doesn't need the software. After the service: renew, update, test, and add every license to the register.

engineer.intro: Percentage = part ÷ whole × 100. Total = a × b.

steps.prompt: The stage normally reads 600 lux at the lectern; during the outage it read 90 lux. What percentage of normal is that?
steps.why: The Fieldbook's number: about 15% of normal coverage.

steps.prompt: The register lists 14 licenses, and 3 expire within 60 days. What percentage need action now?
steps.why: One in five, which is a budget line, not a surprise.

steps.prompt: A subscription costs $240 a year. What does it cost over a 5-year plan?
steps.why: Put it in the lifecycle budget, with its renewal date beside it.

CASE-021.title: The Camera That Leaves
CASE-021.hook: Thirty-seven tickets closed as “user error.” The user was the one fixing it.
learn: What happened. In the Studio Room the camera vanished from calls “randomly.” Last month's room image had set a power plan that suspends idle USB devices after ten minutes. When a presenter paused her video for a long stretch, the camera went idle.

Why it didn't come back. The long USB extender between the camera and the credenza didn't pass the wake-up cleanly, so the camera re-enumerated as a new device, and the conferencing software kept looking for the old one.

The twist that changed the question. The log showed the camera leaving at 10:14:03 and the manager's replug at 10:16:40. She wasn't causing it; she was fixing it. Fourteen other rooms with the same extender had 37 “camera missing” tickets, all closed as user error.

The fix and the proof. A managed room profile (no USB suspend on room computers; the software selects the room camera by type), rolled out in rings, and an idle-share test that reproduces the failure before the fix and not after.
CASE-021.service: During the call, a replug brings the camera back — that's the workaround, so log the time. Afterwards, pull the device log, match the drop time against idle time, and test the fix by reproducing the idle, not by waiting for a complaint.

engineer.intro: Time arithmetic from the logs, and the scale of a pattern. Percentage = part ÷ whole × 100.
engineer.flag: USB power behavior simplified; the log times are the episode's.

steps.prompt: The camera dropped at 10:14:03 and the replug came at 10:16:40. How many seconds apart is that?
steps.why: The drop came first. The user was fixing it, not causing it.

steps.prompt: Of 15 rooms with the same extender, 14 had tickets. What percentage is that?
steps.why: That's a pattern, not bad luck — a problem record, not 37 incidents.

CASE-023.title: The Backup That Followed
CASE-023.hook: Two references, one failure. The backup did exactly what it was told: follow the main.
learn: What happened. A contractor's cart damaged the roof cable to the facility reference clock's antenna, so the clock went into holdover and began to drift. The roof belongs to facilities; the fix at the antenna was theirs.

Why the backup didn't help. The backup reference was configured to follow the main, so both drifted together. The old video gateway had a tight lock range and dropped a camera and the program return every few seconds.
The fix. Cal's card inside rack 4 said: gateway → house reference B (the independent black-burst generator). The change was made with a second person checking, then ten stable minutes before air.
The lesson. A backup that depends on the thing it backs up isn't a backup. Independence has to be designed, written down and tested.
CASE-023.service: An hour to air: don't touch the roof. Move the gateway to the independent reference, watch ten stable minutes, and tell facilities about the antenna cable with a photo.

engineer.intro: Clock drift: a clock off by p parts per million gains or loses p microseconds every second. Frame period = 1 ÷ fps.

steps.prompt: At 29.97 fps, how long is one frame?
steps.why: Drift that adds up to a frame is visible.

steps.prompt: A clock in holdover drifts 10 ppm. How many milliseconds does it drift in one hour?
steps.why: More than a frame in an hour — and both references moved together.

CASE-007.title: Wireless Drop-Outs
CASE-007.hook: Same song, same bar, three shows running. Everyone blames the batteries.
learn: SIGNAL's adaptation. A lead singer's wireless dropped for about eleven seconds at the same bar of the same song, three shows in a row. The RF scan was clean; batteries, phones and the crowd were all blamed and all cleared by evidence.

The mechanism. At load-in, the receiver antennas had been moved behind an LED wall's steel frame to make room for a riser.
