At that bar the singer stood at the downstage-right lip, turned upstage: steel and her own body between transmitter and antennas. The signal fell into the noise at that one position.
Why diversity didn't help. Both antennas stood behind the same steel. A diversity receiver picks the better of two signals; two weak signals are still weak.

The fix and the proof. Antennas to line of sight on a stand the head rigger approved; a walk test with the singer at every position, before and after. The workflow fix: load-in changes that touch RF get logged — the as-built photo had become the next city's plan.
CASE-007.service: Mid-show, don't touch the frequency: hand over the pre-planned spare. Next day: read the drop log, scan, watch the show video, compare the load-in photos with the plan, walk the real path with a meter, move antennas through their owner, and walk it again.

engineer.intro: Radio budget arithmetic. Wavelength λ = c ÷ f with c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Margin (dB) = received signal − noise floor. Losses in dB add.
engineer.flag: Every frequency and level is illustrative; no band is named as legal.

steps.prompt: Channel 7 sits at an illustrative 600 MHz. What is its wavelength?
steps.hint: λ = c ÷ f. Use 3 × 10⁸ m/s and 600 × 10⁶ Hz.
steps.why: Half a meter: about the width of a person — which is why bodies matter.

steps.prompt: How long is a quarter-wave antenna at that frequency?
steps.hint: A quarter of λ, then convert to centimeters.
steps.why: A small whip for a big job.

steps.prompt: At the booth the receiver reads −68 dBm; the noise floor is −98 dBm. What is the margin?
steps.why: Thirty dB of room before the audio drops.
steps.unitWhy: A difference of two dBm levels is a ratio: dB.

steps.prompt: At the lip, the steel frame costs about 15 dB and her body about 12 dB more (illustrative). How much margin is left?
steps.hint: Losses in dB simply add. Subtract both from the margin.
steps.why: Three dB is nothing: any fade drops it into the noise. Line of sight gives most of the 15 back.

CASE-012.title: Event-Day Control Update Disaster
CASE-012.hook: A “recommended update” at 2 p.m. Press night at 7:30. Nobody tested the file in between.
learn: SIGNAL's adaptation. A lighting-console update was installed on the afternoon of opening. At the top of Act 1, some fade times and some fixture positions differed from rehearsal. Nobody had tested the show file after the update, and there was no rollback copy on the console.

Consistent, not random. Only cues that used the show's default fade time ran fast (the update reset the default), and only one fixture type was off in position (the update replaced its profile, so the same stored values meant different angles). The network, the dimmers and the operator were all cleared by evidence.

The live decision. A skilled operator ran Act 1 by hand from the rehearsal video; the stage manager was told the facts and held the decisions. At intermission, a rollback needed more time than the interval and the older file lost the day's notes, so Act 2 ran by hand as well. Fly and scenery cues were never improvised.
The proof and the rule. A full cue-to-cue against the rehearsal record before the next show, then a show-day change freeze and a pre-show verification checklist.
CASE-012.service: During the show: don't reboot, don't roll back, don't improvise anything that moves. Give the operator the rehearsal record, tell the stage manager the facts, run by hand, read the change log without touching the show, and make the fix after the house is empty — then prove it cue-to-cue.

engineer.intro: Profiles, defaults and the intermission window. A stored position is a fraction of a fixture's range; change the range and the same number points somewhere else.
engineer.flag: Pan/tilt ranges, fade times and task durations are illustrative.

steps.prompt: The old profile mapped the full tilt value to 270°; the new one maps it to 240°. Cue 14 stores tilt at 50%. How many degrees lower does the mover now point?
steps.why: Same stored value, different meaning: every mover off by the same amount at that value — consistent, not random.
steps.unitWhy: An aim difference is an angle.

steps.prompt: The show's default fade was 8 s; the update reset it to 2 s. How many times faster do default-timed cues now run?
steps.why: A sunrise becomes a light switch.

steps.prompt: A rollback at intermission needs: reload 3 min, re-enter 6 notes at 1.5 min each, and check 12 key cues at 20 s each. How long in total?
steps.why: Sixteen minutes of work in a fifteen-minute interval, with no margin for a surprise. Don't.

steps.prompt: Tomorrow's cue-to-cue: 96 cues at about 45 s each. How long should Rosa book?
steps.why: About an hour and a quarter — cheap next to another press night.

CASE-008.title: Livestream Transport and Stems
CASE-008.hook: The room sounded perfect. Four thousand people online heard a different show.
learn: SIGNAL's adaptation. At a hybrid product launch, the stream vendor fed the stream from input-tapped stems: sends taken at each channel's input, before processing, mutes and faders. Online, the band was too loud, a muted co-presenter's mic stayed live, and a joke from the wings went out to four thousand people.

Why the room didn't notice. In the room, the engineer's mute and faders did their jobs, and the small room heard the band acoustically. The stream heard none of that. One mixer, two audiences, two different shows.

The fix that made it worse. Moving the stems post-fader made the stream follow the room's balance — which barely included the band. The right tap was pre-fader, post-mute (after processing), with the stream balanced on its own for headphones.

Transport and sync. Video through the switcher and frame sync arrived about three frames after the audio; a clap test measured it and the audio was delayed to match. Proof came from a second listener on cellular with headphones, on the real stream.
CASE-008.service: Mid-show: mute the leaking input on the stream mixer (not the whole stream); read the send's tap point before changing anything; set pre-fader post-mute; balance the stems in headphones; clap-test the sync; prove it with a second listener on an independent path.

engineer.intro: Latency and bandwidth for a stream feed. At 59.94 fps, one frame = 1 ÷ 59.94 s.
engineer.flag: Illustrative latencies and rates; real systems differ.

steps.prompt: The switcher and frame sync delay the picture by 3 frames at 59.94 fps. How much is that?
steps.unitWhy: A latency is a time: milliseconds.

steps.prompt: The audio stems reach the encoder with 10 ms of their own latency. How much delay do you add to the audio?
steps.why: Now sound and picture leave the encoder together. Confirm with a clap test.

steps.prompt: Four mono stems at 48 kHz, 24-bit travel uncompressed to the stream mixer. What bit rate is that?
steps.hint: Stems × sample rate × bits per sample, then ÷ 1,000,000.
steps.why: About 4.6 Mbit/s — small next to video, but plan it on the network.
steps.unitWhy: Bits per second, not bytes: MB/s would be eight times smaller.

CASE-009.title: One SDI Cable Took Out the Camera
CASE-009.hook: An hour before doors, the CEO's IMAG camera goes black. The camera is fine.
learn: SIGNAL's adaptation. At an evening corporate show, the pre-show checklist's line “every source on the switcher” found camera 2 — the CEO's IMAG camera — black at 6:05. The viewfinder was fine; the router was correct.

First failure point. A field monitor walked down the path showed picture at the camera, picture on the camera side of a floor pocket, and nothing on the house side. The connector in the pocket had been crushed by a cart's caster during the dinner flip. One cable, one camera: the classic one-cable failure.

The fix. A spare SDI run along the wall, under ramps, outside the guest path — not across the aisle, and not on a consumer display cable built for a few meters. The pocket's power side stayed closed: it belongs to the venue's electrician.
The habit. Checks prove the room at the time you ran them. Run source and floor checks after the last room change, then freeze.
CASE-009.service: An hour before doors: don't reboot or swap at random. Ask what the viewfinder shows, read the router, walk a field monitor down the path, fix at the first failure point, reroute outside traffic, then rerun the checklist line and tell the client what happened.

engineer.intro: Cable paths and check budgets. Treat reach figures as typical, not specification.

steps.prompt: Original path: camera to floor pocket 20 m, pocket to the switcher 45 m. The spare runs along the wall: 85 m. How much longer is the spare?
steps.why: 20 m longer — the price of staying out of the traffic lane.

steps.prompt: Take about 100 m as a typical good-cable reach for this SDI rate (illustrative). How much margin is left on the 85 m spare?
steps.why: 15 m of margin. A longer detour would need a different transport (fiber, or a reclocking step).

steps.prompt: The checklist line “every source on the switcher, full screen” takes about 45 s per source. Six sources: how long is the line?
steps.why: Four and a half minutes to find the fault that would have ended the CEO's walk-on.
steps.unitWhy: 270 is in seconds; the question wants minutes.

CASE-013.title: The Room That Hears Twice
CASE-013.hook: One room, one client, her own voice coming back half a second late — and she thinks it's a recording.
learn: SIGNAL original. Remote participants heard their own voices come back from one meeting room only. A client heard herself late and assumed she was being recorded and played back.: proposed SIGNAL-original case.

Two cancellers, one path. The room processor canceled echo with the true loudspeaker reference. Sunday's update on the conferencing computer switched the software's own echo cancellation and noise suppression back on. The second canceller kept re-learning a signal the first had already cleaned and leaked bursts of echo.

Who hears it isn't who causes it. Remote people hearing themselves points at your room. During the follow-up call, the Harbor Room heard itself — the leak was in the client's room, and the kind fix was a headset on their side.

A fix that survives Sunday. The software canceller went off in the managed room profile for rooms with a processor, a post-update echo test joined the checklist, and nobody blocked updates — that would have made Harbor an exception room.
CASE-013.service: Mid-call: reproduce from the far end, read which cancellers are on, leave the one nearest the mics with the true reference, and prove it from the far end in silence and double-talk. If YOUR room hears itself, the leak is theirs — contain it kindly on their side.

engineer.intro: Echo arithmetic. Speed of sound c ≈ 343 m/s. Echo reduction is a level difference in dB. The far end hears its echo after a full round trip.

steps.prompt: The nearest ceiling microphone is 3.4 m from a loudspeaker. How long after the far-end voice leaves the loudspeaker does it reach that mic?
steps.hint: t = distance ÷ c, then convert seconds to milliseconds.
steps.why: About 10 ms for the direct path — reflections keep arriving for hundreds of ms after, which the canceller must also learn.
steps.unitWhy: A delay is a time: milliseconds.

steps.prompt: The far-end reference plays at −20 dBFS. The leftover echo leaving the room measures −52 dBFS. How much echo reduction is the room achieving?
steps.hint: The difference between the two levels.
steps.why: A level difference is in dB; dBFS names a level on the digital scale.
steps.unitWhy: A difference between two dBFS levels is a plain dB ratio.

steps.prompt: One-way delay between Helen and the Harbor Room (network plus processing) is 160 ms. How late does Helen hear her own echo?
steps.hint: Her voice goes there, and comes back.
steps.why: A third of a second: late enough to sound like a recording being played back.

CASE-014.title: The Dashboard Is Green
CASE-014.hook: Every tile green for eight weeks. Two hundred and twelve room tickets. Both can't be true.
learn: SIGNAL original. Aldermoor's room dashboard showed every room healthy for eight weeks while the help desk logged 212 room tickets (illustrative).: proposed SIGNAL-original case.

A metric with no user behind it. “Green” meant a room controller answered a ping. Failed polls kept their last color, so some tiles were days stale — and the healthiest room, 14-East, was a controller in a box in the mail room.

What the dashboard couldn't see. It drew only rooms in the inventory: 289 of 300. Eleven hand-configured “exception” rooms — the boardroom among them — never had a tile, and every fleet fix scoped by the inventory skipped them. That was the Monday Ghost.

The fix. Last-heard age on every tile, stale tiles grayed, the eleven rooms registered as exceptions with an honest owner (“unknown — investigate”), and a user-outcome metric on top: meetings that started clean within two minutes.
CASE-014.service: When the dashboard and the help desk disagree: freeze one window, line up snapshots, tickets and call logs, show data age instead of deleting it, count coverage against an independent list, and register what you can't see before anyone “fixes” it.

engineer.intro: Telemetry arithmetic. Coverage = monitored ÷ real. Staleness = tiles older than the threshold ÷ tiles. Outcome = clean starts ÷ meetings. Reporting rate = tickets ÷ failures.

steps.prompt: The inventory lists 289 rooms; facilities lists 300 bookable rooms. What is the dashboard's coverage?
steps.why: 96% sounds fine — until you learn which 4% is missing.

steps.prompt: 23 of the 289 tiles were last heard more than 24 hours ago. What share of tiles is stale?
steps.why: About one tile in twelve was showing the past as the present.

steps.prompt: Last Monday 8–10 a.m., 212 meetings were scheduled in rooms and 40 failed to start clean within two minutes. What share started clean?
steps.why: The first honest number on Priya's slide.

steps.prompt: Of those 40 failures, 17 produced a ticket. What is the reporting rate?
steps.why: Most people who hit a broken room didn't tell anyone.

CASE-016.title: Ticket Closed
CASE-016.hook: Nine tickets. Nine “Resolved.” One box everyone thought was gone.
learn: SIGNAL original (proposed). A meeting room's display was on the wrong input most weekday mornings. The service desk restored it nine times in two months — good incident work — and nobody owned why it kept happening.

The evidence was already there. The display's own log recorded every input change with a time and a source: 07:00:00, a network control command. Rebooting or factory-resetting it would have erased that. Nine tickets opened between 07:02 and 07:55, weekdays only.

The record lied. The command came from a legacy room scheduler the inventory listed as decommissioned two years earlier. It was still powered in a riser closet, running an old configuration's 7:00 wake job against twelve addresses — including a lobby sign on a reused address and a projector in a room that no longer existed.

Incident, problem, change. Restore the meeting; link the incidents to one problem with an owner; catch the cause with the network's owner; publish the known error; remove the cause through a change with a rollback; verify at 07:00, then decommission properly.
CASE-016.service: Before 7:00: read the display's log without touching it, line up the tickets, and ask the network owner to capture at the switch port. Watch it happen, look up the source, restore the room, open the problem record — and don't touch the box until a change says so.

engineer.intro: The cost of a problem nobody owns. Every figure is illustrative.
engineer.flag: Invented rates and minutes, for arithmetic practice only.

steps.prompt: Nine incidents in eight weeks. What is the rate per week?
steps.why: Just over one a week — easy to shrug off one at a time.

steps.prompt: Each incident costs about 12 minutes of Sam's time plus a 6-person meeting delayed 8 minutes. How many person-minutes per incident?
steps.why: An hour of people's time, every time — most of it not Sam's.

steps.prompt: At that rate for 52 weeks, how many person-hours does the problem cost?
steps.hint: Incidents per year × 60 person-minutes, then convert to hours.
steps.why: About a working week and a half of people's time, per year, for one room.

steps.prompt: The problem work took about 6 person-hours. After how many weeks does it pay for itself?
steps.hint: Hours invested ÷ hours saved per week (1.125 incidents × 1 h).
steps.why: Five and a bit weeks — and that ignores the lobby sign and the ghost projector.

CASE-015.title: The CEO Room
CASE-015.hook: The room joined. The cameras worked. The investors saw a blank window.
learn: SIGNAL original (proposed), based on MS-02. At the start of a board meeting with investors dialed in, the CEO shared her screen. The local display showed it; the panel said Sharing; the far end saw a blank content window.

Two paths, one symptom. The local display was fed from the table input through a switcher. The far end got content from the room computer's capture device — which an overnight update had pointed at “the first input detected”: the boardroom's second, empty table-cubby input.

Why the test ring missed it. The update passed five standard rooms, each with one content input, where “first detected” is always right. The boardroom was an exception room, off the inventory and out of the ring. The exception had never been recorded — only labeled, five years earlier, by the installer.

Seconds, then a week. In the meeting: read the far-end view, find the labeled input (or use the documented laptop fallback), confirm from the far end — never roll back mid-meeting. In the week: an exception register, representative rings, a pinned capture input, a fleet query, and a proof on five rooms including every exception type.
CASE-015.service: In the meeting: glance at the local display, the panel and the far-end view; split the path; try the labeled second input or the laptop-join fallback; confirm with one remote person on their own screen. Don't reboot, don't interrupt, and never roll back an update mid-meeting.

engineer.intro: Ring arithmetic and the cost of a failure class. Every figure is illustrative.
engineer.flag: Invented fleet sizes and minutes, for arithmetic practice only.

steps.prompt: Ring 1 has 5 rooms out of a 400-room fleet. What percentage of the fleet is that?
steps.why: Small on purpose — so it must be representative, not random.
steps.unitWhy: A share of the fleet: percent.

steps.prompt: Ring 2 is 10% of the rooms left after ring 1. How many rooms, to the nearest whole room?
steps.why: Big enough to see rare problems, small enough to roll back in an evening.

steps.prompt: Suppose the bad default had reached 14 multi-input rooms, each holding 4 meetings before anyone noticed, each losing 3 minutes to reboot-and-rejoin. How many meeting-minutes lost?
steps.why: Nearly three hours of meetings — and every one of them in front of someone who noticed.

steps.prompt: The 30-second fallback card turns a 3-minute recovery into 30 seconds. How many minutes does it save per affected meeting?
steps.why: Two and a half minutes of dead air, gone — for the price of a laminated card.

CASE-017.title: Five Frames
CASE-017.hook: The anchor's lips arrive after his voice — only on the stream, only since Tuesday.
learn: SIGNAL original. A regional station's stream showed the anchor's voice about five frames before his lips. The broadcast output was in sync. The stream's video path adds processing latency; its audio path had carried a matching delay — until someone careful removed it because nothing said why it was there.

The mechanism. Video processing (scaling, graphics insertion, frame synchronizers, encoders) delays pictures by whole frames. Audio doesn't wait unless you make it. Uncompensated, sound arrives early — the direction audiences notice fastest.
The fix. Measure with a flash-and-beep clip at the viewer's end; compensate the audio by the measured amount; re-measure; label the reason next to the setting; check weekly where viewers watch.
The habit. A setting without its reason is a trap for the next careful person. Blame the missing label, not the person who read it honestly.
CASE-017.service: Measure at the viewer's end, compare broadcast and stream, read the change log, talk to the person without blame, compensate by a measurement, prove it again, label it.

engineer.intro: Frame arithmetic. One frame = 1000 ÷ fps milliseconds. Delay to add = video latency − audio latency.

steps.prompt: At 29.97 fps, how long is one frame?
steps.why: One frame ≈ 33.4 ms.
steps.unitWhy: A frame period is a time.

steps.prompt: The stream's video path is 5 frames late. How many milliseconds?
steps.why: About 167 ms.

steps.prompt: Suppose the audio path already carries 33 ms of its own latency. How much delay do you add?
steps.why: Add only the difference.

steps.prompt: After an encoder update the video path grows to 7 frames. What's the new video latency?
steps.why: Updates change latency — which is why the weekly check exists.

CASE-018.title: Twelve Minutes
CASE-018.hook: Perfect captions on air. None on the stream. Twelve minutes of a road-closure bulletin that deaf viewers never saw.
learn: SIGNAL original. A station's live captions were present on broadcast and missing on its stream for twelve minutes during an emergency road bulletin. The captioner had sent every word.
The mechanism. Captions travel as data inside the video signal. A stream transcoder profile applied for a weekend test discarded that data. Picture and sound were perfect; captions silently vanished.
The fix. Roll the stream back to a profile that passes caption data, verify from a phone off the network with the captioner, and monitor caption presence on every output — not just broadcast.
The habit. Test profiles roll back automatically; change records say what they touch, including access. For deaf viewers, captions are the audio.
CASE-018.service: Clear the captioner with her log, compare broadcast and stream, find the profile that changed, roll it back, verify with the person who knows, monitor every output.

engineer.intro: Scale arithmetic. How much was missed, how small captions are, and what monitoring costs.

steps.prompt: Live speech runs about 160 words per minute. How many words did stream viewers miss in 12 minutes?
steps.why: A whole bulletin, and then some.

steps.prompt: Caption data is about 9.6 kbit/s inside a 6,000 kbit/s stream. What share of the stream is that? (%, 2 decimals)
steps.why: Captions cost almost nothing to carry. Dropping them saves nothing.

steps.prompt: A caption check on 4 outputs takes about 3 minutes each. How long is the nightly check?
steps.why: Twelve minutes of checking, against twelve minutes of silence.

CASE-019.title: Fourth Quarter
CASE-019.hook: A stadium full of phones, a fixed bit rate, and a reporter who hears herself two seconds late.
learn: SIGNAL original. A regional station's live remote from a packed stadium kept dropping, and the sideline reporter kept stumbling. The bonded cellular kit was healthy; the network was full.

The mechanism. Each cellular link's capacity falls as crowd noise rises. A fixed-rate encoder can't fit; an adaptive one lowers quality to stay on. The reporter's earpiece carried the program return, two seconds late.
The fix. Adaptive bit rate with a floor, program prioritized, enough bonded links; a mix-minus for the reporter — studio and cues, never her own voice or the late return — tested with her talking.
The habit. Plan remotes for the crowd, not the empty stadium. Bend, don't break.
CASE-019.service: Read the modem stats, read the preset, switch to adaptive, check the earpiece source, build the mix-minus, test with the reporter talking.

engineer.intro: Capacity arithmetic. C = B × log₂(1 + S/N) per link; you can count on about half; round the links up.

steps.prompt: One link: B = 5 MHz, S/N = 1.58 (2 dB). Capacity C?
steps.why: In the empty stadium S/N was far higher.

steps.prompt: You can count on about 50% of that. Usable per link?
steps.why: Shared networks never give you the whole limit.

steps.prompt: The encoder needs 8 Mb/s. How many links?
steps.why: Always round up — half a link doesn't exist.

steps.prompt: The adaptive floor is 4 Mb/s out of a normal 12. What share of normal is the floor? (%, 1 decimal)
steps.why: Soft but on beats sharp and gone.

CASE-020.title: Crest
CASE-020.hook: A flood, a station in the flood zone, and a valley that can only hear one channel.
learn: SIGNAL original. On the night a river crested, a regional station stayed on air through a power cut and an evacuation of its own building by moving master control to a drilled backup across the valley.
The job. Relay official forecasts and alerts word for word, sourced and repeated; route unverified reports to officials; captions and second-language audio on every output.

The boundaries. The emergency manager orders evacuations; the news director pulls field crews back; the power vendor and electrician own the generator; the agencies own forecasts. The backup exists so nobody has to stay.
The habit. Rehearse the bad night on a good night — and know that a drill only tests the hours it runs in.
CASE-020.service: Relay and repeat, plan internally from the agency's numbers, route reports, keep your hands off the power, obey the order, check every output at the backup, confirm with the emergency manager.

engineer.intro: Planning arithmetic — for the team's timing only. On air, only the agency's words.

steps.prompt: The crest passed Cedar Row at 9:40 p.m.; the Old Mill is 6 km downstream at about 3 km/h. Hours until the Old Mill?
steps.why: Enough to move master control before the order, not after it.

steps.prompt: The forecast is repeated every 15 minutes for 6 hours. How many repeats?
steps.why: Say less, more often.

steps.prompt: Of 40,000 valley households, the EM estimates 12,000 are without internet tonight. What share can only get the broadcast? (%)
steps.why: Nearly a third of the valley, on one channel.

steps.prompt: Hank's generator has fuel for 14 hours from 11:10 p.m. When does it run out if nothing is delivered? (24-h clock, e.g. 13.1 for 1:10 p.m.)
steps.why: A planning number for Hank's fuel delivery — his call, not yours.

CASE-025.title: Lecture Capture, Silent
CASE-025.hook: Twenty-two rooms. Three days. Every tile green. Every recording silent.
learn: What happened. A vendor firmware update meant for four pilot rooms went to all 22 Engineering rooms, because the ring list used the wildcard ENG*. The new firmware changed each capture appliance's default audio input from the room DSP's line out to USB — with nothing plugged into USB.
Why nobody noticed. The rooms sounded normal; only the recordings were silent. The dashboard checked that each appliance answered the network, not that its recordings had sound.
How it was proved. Capture status (INPUT: USB), a recording played from the student portal, the vendor's change record. One room fixed and proven with a test recording, then 21 more, each proven.
What changed for good. An audio-level outcome check on every capture appliance; rings defined by explicit room lists; a plain message to the students who missed lectures.
CASE-025.service: Before the next lecture: fix one room and prove it with a test recording from the portal. Then roll out, proving each room. Don't reboot the evidence away, and don't touch the vendor's server.

engineer.intro: Percentage = part ÷ whole × 100. A time budget is Σ (count × time each). Monitoring coverage = outcome checks ÷ devices × 100.

steps.prompt: 22 of 400 rooms were affected. What percentage?
steps.why: Small as a percentage; enormous for the students in those rooms.

steps.prompt: Each proof takes 6 minutes. How long to prove all 22 rooms?
steps.why: Just over two hours — plan it before you promise a time.

steps.prompt: Before the fix, 0 of 400 capture appliances had an audio check. After, all 400. What coverage is that?
steps.why: Every silent recording now turns a tile red.

CASE-026.title: The Clinical Room
CASE-026.hook: Three rooms. Weekday mornings. The wall said CLINICAL. The switch didn't agree.
learn: What happened. After a renovation, three clinic rooms' wall ports were re-terminated and relabeled. The ports marked CLINICAL were patched to the GUEST VLAN.

Why only mornings. The guest network has no priority for video and caps each device at 4 Mb/s, and its uplink is shared with the waiting room's Wi-Fi, which peaks 9–11 a.m. A 3.8 Mb/s consult runs at 95% of its cap; every spike froze it.
How it was proved. The cart's own network page, a morning vs afternoon bitrate graph, and a test call with a training manikin — never a real patient's consult.

The fix. The network owner moved the ports to the clinical video VLAN; a test call at the 10:30 peak proved it; the ports were relabeled from a verified map. Every renovated room now reopens only after a test call.
CASE-026.service: Patient first: the phone fallback. Then evidence from outside the room: the cart's page, the graph, a manikin test call. Bring it to the network owner. Prove at the peak.

engineer.intro: Link use (%) = traffic ÷ link speed × 100. Headroom = cap − traffic.

steps.prompt: A 3.8 Mb/s consult under a 4 Mb/s cap: how full is the cap?
steps.why: Five percent headroom: any spike freezes the picture.

steps.prompt: The guest uplink carries 470 Mb/s of 500 at 10 a.m. Utilization?
steps.why: A shared uplink at its limit during clinic hours.

steps.prompt: How much headroom does the consult have under the cap?
steps.why: A fifth of a megabit: nothing.

CASE-027.title: Hearing Loop Dead Zone
CASE-027.hook: The sign said everyone. Row ten got half of every lecture — and blamed her own ears.
learn: What happened. Hall B's hearing loop passed acceptance in July, measured at one point, front center. In September facilities added a steel-framed platform under rows 8–12. The steel soaked up about 12 dB of the loop's field (illustrative), and the amplifier had been left 3 dB low.
Who it hurt. A student using hearing aids with a telecoil sat in row 10 all semester and heard about half of each lecture. She assumed her hearing was getting worse.
How it was proved. The acceptance file (one point), a seat-by-seat field survey, facilities' change log, and a telecoil listening test with volunteers after the repair.

The fix. A portable receiver the same day, her choice; a supplementary loop segment by the installer with facilities' approval; levels set to reference; an honest interim sign; and a rule: any metal change near the seating triggers a re-test.
CASE-027.service: Today: offer a portable receiver and let the student decide. This week: survey every seat, find the later change, book qualified hands, and prove it with the people who use the loop.

engineer.intro: Loop level L = 20·log₁₀(H ÷ H_ref), with H in mA/m and H_ref the target (400 mA/m here). Percent = part ÷ whole × 100.

steps.prompt: Row 10 reads 100 mA/m against 400 mA/m. What level?
steps.why: A quarter of the field: speech falls apart.

steps.prompt: After the repair row 10 reads 360 mA/m. What level now?
steps.why: Within a decibel of the reference.

steps.prompt: 60 of 240 seats sat over the platform. What share of the hall is that?
steps.why: A quarter of the room behind a promise it couldn't keep.

CASE-029.title: Exam Week
CASE-029.hook: Every day at four o'clock, the microphones in four exam rooms lost an argument with twelve cameras.
learn: What happened. Twelve security cameras were plugged ‘temporarily’ into the AV floor switch. By day they fit its 370 W PoE budget with 24 W to spare.

Why four o'clock. At 4:00 the cameras' night mode switched on their infrared: 25 W each instead of 13. The switch was asked for 490 W, and it shed its lowest-priority ports — the exam rooms' microphones.
How it was proved. The switch's PoE log, the cameras' schedule, the change record and a watched 4:00 the next day with night mode back on.

The fix. Handheld mics for the proctors; Delgado held day mode during exams; Tomas moved the cameras to security's own switch from a budget plan. Every temporary change now gets an owner and an end date.
CASE-029.service: Students first: announcements that don't depend on the switch. Then the switch's log, the minute it fails, and the change record. Bring each owner the numbers.

engineer.intro: PoE: P_used = Σ P_port; headroom = P_budget − P_used. Percent = part ÷ whole × 100.

steps.prompt: At night: 190 W plus 12 cameras at 25 W on a 370 W budget. Headroom?
steps.why: Negative headroom: the switch must shed something.

steps.prompt: What percentage of its budget is the switch being asked for at night?
steps.why: A third more than it has.

steps.prompt: By day (13 W per camera), what's the headroom?
steps.why: Fine by day — which is when the contractor tested it.

CASE-028.title: The Green Dashboard, Again
CASE-028.hook: For three years a professor said his recordings faded. For three years the dashboard said everything was fine. Both were right about different things.
learn: What happened. Hall D's recordings faded whenever Professor Grant walked to the whiteboard, 4 m from the lectern lobe — 12 dB quieter, under the auto-mixer's gate.

Why nobody saw it. The dashboard checked proxies — microphone online, file exists — and an hour-average audio level added in the spring (CASE-025). All true. An average hides ten-minute fades. (Compare CASE-014.)
How it was proved. A walk test with Grant, the dashboard's check list, the commissioning file (‘lobe 3 OFF — revisit after HVAC balance’) and facilities' rebalance date.
The fix. Lobe 3 enabled from the walk test, proven by a second walk test; a speech-level check on every recording, levels only, agreed with the teaching office. It found 37 more rooms.
CASE-028.service: Believe the person reporting the outcome. Test it with them, find what the monitor measures, close the revisit, and teach the monitor to check what people actually get.

engineer.intro: Inverse square: ΔL = 20·log₁₀(d₂ ÷ d₁). Open mics: ΔGBF = −10·log₁₀(N). Percent = part ÷ whole × 100.

steps.prompt: Lectern lobe at 1 m; whiteboard at 4 m. How many dB quieter at the board?
steps.why: Two doublings: 6 dB each.

steps.prompt: With two lobes open instead of one, what's the change in gain before feedback?
steps.why: Why you don't open every lobe.

steps.prompt: The new check flags 37 of 400 rooms. What percentage?
steps.why: Nearly one room in ten, invisible to the old dashboard.

CASE-030.title: The Missing Conduit
CASE-030.hook: The AV sheet promised two floor boxes. The electrical sheet had never heard of them.
learn: What happened. Courtroom 3's AV floor boxes were drawn on an old electrical background. The architect had moved the counsel tables to keep a wheelchair turning space clear; the electrical revision followed; the AV sheet didn't.
Why it mattered. Two AV boxes sat in the turning space with no conduit, and the conduit that did exist was too small: 41% fill for four cables.
How it was proved. An overlay of the latest sheets with every clash clouded, the revision history, and a fill calculation per box.
The fix. The engineer of record resized and added the conduits; the AV boxes moved to the architect's layout; a final overlay proved the sheets agreed.
CASE-030.service: Before any issue: refresh every background, overlay, cloud the clashes, attach the numbers — and send each clash to the person who owns the fix.

engineer.intro: Conduit fill = Σ cable area ÷ conduit internal area × 100 (usual limit 40% for three or more cables).
engineer.flag: Illustrative cable areas; conduit areas are typical internal areas.

steps.prompt: 228 mm² of cable in a 1 in conduit with 557 mm² inside. Fill?
steps.why: Just over 40%.

steps.prompt: The same cables in a 1¼ in conduit, 965 mm² inside?
steps.why: Room for the cable pull — and for next year's extra cable.

steps.prompt: What's the most cable area a 1¼ in conduit can take at 40%?
steps.why: The budget for everything that goes to that table.

CASE-032.title: The Beam at Nine Meters
CASE-032.hook: The throw calc and the spec picked different lenses. The architect's new beam picked a fight with both.
learn: What happened. The throw calculation used a 1.5:1 lens (9 m for a 6 m image). The specification called a 0.8:1 lens. The architect's revision C moved a new steel beam to 9 m from the screen.
Why it mattered. The projector was drawn inside a structural beam, and the two documents a contractor would price from disagreed about the lens.
How it was proved. Throw re-run for every lens the family offered, the projection cone drawn on the latest section, and the architect's check of the booth sightlines.
The fix. A 1.8:1 lens at 10.8 m on the existing booth rail; one lens schedule referenced by the calc and the spec.
CASE-032.service: Before promising a projector position: one lens schedule, the cone on the latest section, and the architect and structural engineer asked about anything they own.

engineer.intro: Throw distance D = throw ratio × image width.
engineer.flag: Invented lens family; real lenses publish exact ranges.

steps.prompt: 6 m image, 1.5:1 lens. Distance?
steps.why: Inside the beam zone.

steps.prompt: 6 m image, 1.8:1 lens. Distance?
steps.why: The booth rail.

steps.prompt: A projector 4.8 m from a 6 m screen: what throw ratio?
steps.why: The spec's short-throw — which would need a new ceiling mount.

CASE-031.title: The Duplicate
CASE-031.hook: The cost list called it a duplicate. It was the only thing between the court's record and a failed UPS.
learn: What happened. A value-engineering item deleted court recorder B as ‘a duplicate’ and proposed a file copy of recorder A instead.
Why it mattered. B was the official record's only independent copy — on its own UPS with its own inputs. The file copy shared everything with A.
How it was proved. The court's recording standard, a dependency trace (power and inputs), and availability arithmetic: ≈ 52 h a year down with one recorder, ≈ 0.3 h with two independent ones.
The fix. The court put the requirement in writing, the owner rejected VE-14 and found the saving elsewhere, and B stayed on UPS 2 fed from a passive split.
CASE-031.service: Every VE item goes back with a function statement: what it does, what depends on it, the numbers, and who decides.

engineer.intro: A = MTBF ÷ (MTBF + MTTR); A_pair = 1 − (1 − A)² only if the two fail independently.

steps.prompt: MTBF 8,000 h, MTTR 48 h. Availability? (3 decimals)
steps.why: Very good — and still 52 hours a year.

steps.prompt: Hours a year down for one recorder? (h)
steps.why: Roughly two days of testimony.

steps.prompt: Two independent recorders: hours a year with neither? (h, 1 decimal)
steps.why: Twenty minutes — if nothing is shared.

CASE-033.title: The Witness Who Couldn't Hear the Question
CASE-033.hook: Every seat in the courtroom had assisted listening except the one where a person is sworn to answer questions.
learn: What happened. A courtroom design covered the gallery, jury and counsel with assisted listening — not the witness box. The touch panel sat above the reach range, and the sign-language interpreter stood in an unlit corner.
Why it mattered. A hard-of-hearing witness, a wheelchair-using lawyer and a deaf juror could each be shut out of the proceeding.
How it was proved. A position-by-position list, reach measured against the reviewer's table, light and sightlines checked at the interpreter's spot — then a mock-up test with disabled users.
The fix. Coverage at all four positions, controls within reach plus a second control, and the interpreter moved and lit — agreed with the architect and the court.
CASE-033.service: List every position and every person who might sit there; check coverage, reach and sightlines for each; test with disabled users before you call it done.

engineer.intro: percent = part ÷ whole × 100 — but access is judged position by position.
engineer.flag: Reach tables differ by jurisdiction; illustrative.

steps.prompt: Assisted listening at 3 of 4 positions. Percent?
steps.why: Most — and the missing one is the witness.

steps.prompt: The panel's top control is 1.52 m; the table allows 1.22 m. How far too high? (m)
steps.why: A hand's length out of reach.

steps.prompt: The interpreter's corner reads 30 lx; the court's target for her face is 300 lx. What fraction of the target? (%)
steps.why: Seen in shadow, if at all.

CASE-034.title: Equal to What?
CASE-034.hook: The contractor offered an ‘equal’ amplifier with half the channels. The spec never said what equal meant.
learn: What happened. An amplifier submittal offered two 240 W channels and no fault relay as equal to a specified four-channel amplifier.
Why it mattered. The building's 70 V zones need 526 W of taps; two channels at 80% carry 384 W. And a failed channel would have gone unreported.
How it was proved. The tap schedule summed zone by zone, the usable capacity at 80%, and a re-read of our own spec: ‘or equal’, with no criteria.
The fix. Revise and resubmit with the arithmetic; an addendum listing salient characteristics; a four-channel resubmittal with a balanced riser.
CASE-034.service: Write ‘or equal’ with its salient characteristics; review every submittal with the arithmetic that proves conformance — or not.

engineer.intro: P_taps = Σ P_tap ≤ 0.8 × P_amp (a common design margin).

steps.prompt: Twenty loudspeakers at 6 W. Taps? (W)
steps.why: Courtroom 3's ceiling.

steps.prompt: Usable taps on a 240 W channel at 80%? (W)
steps.why: The margin.

steps.prompt: Two 240 W channels: most taps at 80%? (W)
steps.why: Short of the 526 W the building needs.

CASE-035.title: Forty Sites, Forty Standards
CASE-035.hook: A dashboard counted every difference as a failure. A contractor erased a required design to raise the number — and a boardroom began to echo.
learn: What happened. Corvane's conformance scan flagged 228 of 600 rooms (62% conforming) against the HQ template. A contractor began pushing the template onto flagged rooms. In Valmera it moved the echo canceller's reference onto the hearing-loop feed.
Why it mattered. Every HQ–Valmera call echoed — and 96 of the flagged rooms were recorded regional designs that the push would have broken too.
How it was proved. A test call, the site design file, the canceller's reference; then a sample of every flagged room against its site file: 96 designs, 132 drift.

The fix. The reference returned to the loudspeaker mix through the region's change window; the dashboard now measures drift (22%), and a difference becomes design only when recorded, owned and approved.
CASE-035.service: Before ‘fixing’ a non-conforming room: open its site file. If the difference is recorded and approved, it's design. If not, it's drift — give it an owner.

engineer.intro: Conformance and drift, as shares of all rooms.

steps.prompt: 372 of 600 rooms match the template. Share?
steps.why: The number that counted differences.

steps.prompt: Add the 96 recorded regional designs. Working as designed?
steps.why: Design counts as conforming.

steps.prompt: 132 rooms with unrecorded differences. Drift?
steps.why: The number worth shrinking.

CASE-036.title: The Firmware Island
CASE-036.hook: Every report said 100%. One region had been left out of every update for fourteen months — and the reason it stopped was a good one.
learn: What happened. Tahvara's update ring selected region=TAHV; the inventory had renamed the tag region=THV. The ring matched nothing; the dashboard reported 100% of targeted devices.
Why it mattered. 154 devices missed a security fix for 300 days — 46,200 device-days of exposure — and nothing looked wrong.
How it was proved. The ring's target count (zero), the inventory (154), and the firmware read from the devices themselves (7.1). Sam's desk explained the original pause.

The fix. A staged ring under security's risk decision, with the interpretation test in the pilot; rings built from the inventory; ‘devices in no ring’ on the dashboard; every pause recorded with an owner and an end date.
CASE-036.service: When a report says 100%, ask ‘of how many?’ — and ask which devices are in no ring at all.

engineer.intro: Exposure in device-days: E = N × t.

steps.prompt: 154 devices, 300 days behind a fix. Exposure?
steps.why: The number security weighs.

steps.prompt: A staged rollout takes 7 days. At most how much more?
steps.why: The price of doing it safely — about 2% more.

steps.prompt: Tahvara's 154 of the estate's 1,150 devices. Share?
steps.why: A whole region, invisible.

CASE-037.title: License Cliff
CASE-037.hook: Twelve hundred licenses, one renewal date, one bounced order — and the grace period ending the night before the AGM.
learn: What happened. 1,200 room licenses were co-termed to 31 March. The order bounced on new cost-center codes into a leaver's mailbox. The grace period ended at 00:00 UTC on 15 April, the AGM's day.
Why it mattered. Forty sites' viewing rooms, the AGM stream and its captions would have stopped working fifteen hours before the meeting.
How it was proved. The bounced order traced; the license list reconciled against the room inventory (290 ghosts); the AGM rehearsed from every viewing room on 14 April.

The fix. Emergency approval for the AGM path and a reconciliation that pays back in five months; an extension for the rest via procurement; an owner, a deputy, alerts and quarterly checks. CASE-011, forty sites wide.
CASE-037.service: For any renewal date: who owns it, who is the deputy, who gets the 90/60/30-day alerts — and when was the list last matched to real rooms?

engineer.intro: License cost and payback: years = one-off cost ÷ savings per year.

steps.prompt: 290 ghost licenses at $150 a year. Waste per year?
steps.why: Paid for rooms that don't exist.

steps.prompt: A $18,000 reconciliation stops it. Payback in years?
steps.why: About five months.

steps.prompt: Grace ends 00:00 UTC; the AGM starts 10:00 at UTC−5. Hours between?
steps.why: The margin nobody knew about.

CASE-038.title: The Telemetry Lie
CASE-038.hook: Sampled every fifteen minutes, failing for eight. For a month the dashboard said 100% — because it never once looked at the right moment.
learn: What happened. Eighteen Valmera training rooms restarted at five past every hour for eight minutes. The monitor polled on the quarter hour and never saw it.
Why it mattered. Every class lost eight minutes an hour — about 13% of teaching time — while every report said 100%.
How it was proved. Complaint times against the clock, the codecs' own logs, the monitor's poll times, and the reset task's schedule: ‘5 * * * *’ from a blank template field.

The fix. The schedule corrected in the rooms and the template (sixty queued rooms held); a monitoring requirement — see any outage of 5 minutes or more — met by 5-minute polls, event alerts and class-hour test calls.
CASE-038.service: Before you trust an uptime number: how often does it sample, and could an outage hide between two samples?

engineer.intro: Polling as sampling: P = min(1, d ÷ T).

steps.prompt: An 8-minute outage, 15-minute polls at random times. Chance it's seen?
steps.why: A coin toss — and phase-locked, zero.

steps.prompt: 600 devices polled every 5 minutes. Polls per hour?
steps.why: Inside a 12,000 budget.

steps.prompt: 8 minutes lost in every 60-minute class hour. Availability?
steps.why: The number the dashboard should have shown.

CASE-039.title: Vendor Lock
CASE-039.hook: One integrator's password opened 740 devices in 31 sites — and the booking panels depended on it too.
learn: What happened. Ferrant Systems set one administrator password on every device it installed from 2019: 740 of Corvane's 1,150. Fourteen people knew it; four had left.

Why it mattered. Management logins were reachable from the whole user network and Ferrant's VPN pool. Corvane couldn't revoke one person's access — and rotating the password would have blanked every booking panel.
How it was proved. The audit, who knew the key, what could reach the logins, and everything that logged in with it (740 scheduled scripts).

The fix. Reach first (MGMT VLAN behind a security-owned jump host), a least-privilege service account for the integration, unique vaulted credentials site by site, and a contract that makes Corvane the owner of every key and configuration.
CASE-039.service: For any installer-managed system: who owns the credentials, who can reach the logins, and what breaks if you change them?

engineer.intro: Share of devices on one credential: % = part ÷ whole × 100.

steps.prompt: 740 of 1,150 devices share the password. Share?
steps.why: Most of the estate behind one key.

steps.prompt: Four of fourteen key holders have left. Share?
steps.why: A key you can't take back.

steps.prompt: After the pilot, 310 devices are on unique credentials. Share of the estate?
steps.why: Progress, site by site.

CASE-040.title: Fiber Through the Wrong Wall
CASE-040.hook: The backbone was pulled neatly, labeled and tested — through a wall the architect had already moved on paper.
learn: What happened. The MER-to-stage backbone was pulled through the east dock wall. Bulletin 14 had moved that wall two meters; the low-voltage sub was missing from the distribution list.
Why it mattered. The bay was due for demolition on Tuesday; the stage rack needed the backbone for commissioning three weeks later.
How it was proved. A walk of the route, the bulletin's distribution list, and a loss budget for each reroute — then an OTDR trace and a witnessed loss test.
The fix. The south pathway the drawings already carried (4.28 dB of margin); demolition held two days; a distribution matrix every trade acknowledges.
CASE-040.service: When a trade's work is in the wrong place, ask first whether they ever received the change — then fix the distribution, not only the work.

engineer.intro: Optical loss: L = α·d + n_c·L_c + n_s·L_s; margin = budget − L.
engineer.flag: Planning allowances, not a product's figures.

steps.prompt: North riser: 0.39 km × 0.4 + 4 × 0.75 + 2 × 0.3. Loss?
steps.why: Four connectors cost the most.

steps.prompt: Against 6.2 dB, the north route's margin?
steps.why: Under the spec's 3 dB.

steps.prompt: South route margin (loss 1.92 dB)?
steps.why: The route the drawings promised.

CASE-041.title: Temporary Power, Permanent Problem
CASE-041.hook: Four racks ran for a week on power the electrician didn't know about. The lighting preheat told her every morning at seven.
learn: What happened. AV rack burn-in was plugged into temporary circuits planned for construction tools. At 07:00 the lighting preheat switched twelve washes on at once on the same overloaded circuit, and it tripped.
Why it mattered. Burn-in restarted every morning, and the suggested shortcut — a cord from an unreleased permanent panel — would have put people and equipment at risk.
How it was proved. What was on the circuit (from its owner), the running and surge currents, and the console's 07:00 cue.

The fix. The electrician's decision: a new AV circuit from a load schedule and a staggered preheat; every trade now sends a load schedule before using temporary power. Electrician-owned; Maya documented.
CASE-041.service: Before you plug anything into temporary power: send the electrician a load schedule. When a breaker trips, tell its owner what's on it — and reset nothing.

engineer.intro: Running current I = P ÷ V; switch-on surge I_peak ≈ n × k × I_run.

steps.prompt: Racks A and B: 2,000 W at 120 V. Current?
steps.why: Already over the 16 A line.

steps.prompt: Twelve washes at 0.8 A. Running current?
steps.why: Added on top at seven.

steps.prompt: Each surges to 20× for a few ms. Rough peak?
steps.why: Why staggering works.

CASE-042.title: The Ceiling Went Up First
CASE-042.hook: A ceiling closed two weeks early over missing loudspeaker supports — and one hatch opened onto a loudspeaker that no longer existed.
learn: What happened. The GC resequenced the studio theater ceiling to recover time. The AV supports weren't in. An old value-engineering RFI had deleted S-9 without updating the hatch schedule.
Why it mattered. Sixteen panels had to be reopened, a hatch served nothing, S-8 had no access, and rows F–H sat in a coverage hole.
How it was proved. Every position checked against the latest RFI log; coverage without S-9 worked out (5.0 m from the nearest loudspeaker vs a 3.8 m reach); a survey after closing.
The fix. Closure stopped and resequenced by the GC; S-9 restored by RFI while open; hatch schedule re-issued; ceiling closure now a hold point every above-ceiling trade signs.
CASE-042.service: Before a ceiling closes: every trade above it signs, and the hatch schedule matches the latest RFIs.

engineer.intro: Ceiling coverage at ear height: D = 2 × (H_c − H_e) × tan(θ ÷ 2).

steps.prompt: Ceiling 5.0 m, ears 1.2 m, 90°. Coverage diameter?
steps.why: Radius 3.8 m.

steps.prompt: Largest square-grid spacing with no holes?
steps.why: The 5.0 m grid was fine — with S-9.

steps.prompt: Sixteen of 120 panels reopened. Share?
steps.why: The price of closing early.

CASE-043.title: Pull Test
CASE-043.hook: Forty-eight links passed on paper. Eleven were never tested, and a winch had stretched fourteen more past their rating.
learn: What happened. The certification report showed 48 PASS. Eleven were one measurement saved under eleven IDs; a sample retest failed five of twelve links pulled by winch at about 3.6 times the cable's rated tension.
Why it mattered. The lobby displays, cameras and broadcast room would have run on untested and damaged links — failing later, when they're behind finished walls.
How it was proved. Identical lengths and timestamps, the tester's raw files, a witnessed sample retest, and the pulling log.
The fix. Every link retested, witnessed; the over-pulled group replaced within its rating; raw files and a witnessed sample written into the spec.
CASE-043.service: Never accept a certification summary on its own: ask for the raw files and witness a sample.

engineer.intro: How far over its rating, and how bad the sample: ratio = A ÷ B; % = part ÷ whole × 100.

steps.prompt: 400 N applied, 110 N rated. Ratio?
steps.why: More than three and a half times.

steps.prompt: 5 failures in a sample of 12. Share?
steps.why: Not a termination problem.

steps.prompt: 11 of 48 never tested. Share?
steps.why: Almost a quarter of the proof was paper.

CASE-044.title: Heat
CASE-044.hook: The mechanical design was right — for two kilowatts. Nobody had told it about the other ten point eight.
learn: What happened. The MER's cooling was sized for 2 kW from an old equipment list. The racks drew 12.8 kW. The AV heat schedule had never been issued to the mechanical engineer.
Why it mattered. 38 °C at half load, throttling racks, and a first re-selection (two units) that would fail the moment one unit did.
How it was proved. A logger in the room, the basis of design, the missing transmittal, and a full-load test with one cooling unit switched off.
The fix. Heat schedule issued and acknowledged; N+1 cooling (three 7 kW units) sized by the mechanical engineer; a coordination register for every number another discipline sizes from.
CASE-044.service: If your equipment makes heat, draws power or hangs weight, someone else sizes something from it — send them the numbers and get them acknowledged.

engineer.intro: Heat load Q = P × 3.412 (BTU/h); N+1: C × (N − 1) ≥ Q.

steps.why: The number the cooling needed.

steps.prompt: Two 7 kW units, one out. Capacity?
steps.why: Not N+1.

steps.prompt: Three units, one out?
steps.why: Covers 12.8 kW.

CASE-045.title: Integrator's Remote Account
CASE-045.hook: It was made for three weeks of commissioning. Ninety days later, nine people could still use it.
learn: What happened. A shared ‘ext-support’ login created for commissioning was never removed. Nine people knew the password; two had left the integrator; the handover said ‘removed’.
Why it mattered. Nobody could say who did anything with it — including a legitimate 03:12 fix — and anyone who once knew it could still get in.
How it was proved. The account list, the login record, the integrator's staff list and a handover tick that didn't match the building.
The fix. Named accounts through security's jump host, approved and recorded; the shared account disabled by security after the new path worked; an offboarding clause; a quarterly access review.
CASE-045.service: Every account on a system you look after needs an owner, a reason and an end date. If one doesn't, take it to whoever owns access.

engineer.intro: Share = part ÷ whole × 100; exposure E = N × t.

steps.prompt: Two of nine have left. Share? (%)
steps.why: People who can still get in and shouldn't.

steps.prompt: Nine people, ninety days. Person-days?
steps.why: The size of the exposure.

steps.prompt: Eleven accounts, three orphaned. Share? (%)
steps.why: What the review found.

CASE-046.title: Signage Says Evacuate
CASE-046.hook: It was a drill slide, a default date and a banner that fell off the screen. The real fault was that the screen could say it at all.
learn: What happened. A drill template reading ‘EVACUATE’ went live on the lobby wall for 40 s. The ‘DRILL’ banner fell off the wall's canvas; the date defaulted to today; nobody had to approve it.
Why it mattered. 90 of 620 people began moving on a false message; the duty manager held the stairs. The signage system had become an emergency channel nobody accepted.
How it was proved. The fire panel's log, the CMS log, the template on a 32:9 canvas, and a commissioning note that said ‘alternate emergency channel — per GM request’.
The fix. Emergency templates removed; a read-only fire-panel relay drives one fixed slide, reviewed by the marshal; two-person approval; no default dates; no blame.
CASE-046.service: If a screen, a speaker or an app can tell people to evacuate, ask who accepted that — and make it repeat the real system instead of starting its own.

engineer.intro: Δt = t₂ − t₁; share = part ÷ whole × 100.

steps.why: How long the lie was up.

steps.prompt: 90 of 620 moved. Share? (%)
steps.why: People put at risk on stairs.

steps.prompt: The relay slide appears 1.2 s after the panel alarms; the sequence allows 10 s. Margin? (s)
steps.why: Inside what the marshal accepted.

CASE-047.title: Shared Admin
CASE-047.hook: The log said ‘admin’. Fourteen people were admin. The real culprit was a missing button.
learn: What happened. The hearing loop was off through a whole cabaret after someone recalled ‘Rehearsal’ as ‘admin’. Fourteen people knew the admin password; five had left.
Why it mattered. Loop users heard nothing, and nobody could be accountable for a change because the account named nobody.
How it was proved. The DSP log, a count of who knew the password, a blameless conversation with the stage manager, and a field-strength meter in row M.
The fix. Five named roles set up by security; an operator panel with ‘Rehearsal’ and ‘Show’ (which always restores the loop); the loop back at its reference; a loop check before every show.
CASE-047.service: When people borrow a password, find the button their job needed. Then give it to their role — and give every change a name.

engineer.intro: Share = part ÷ whole × 100; loop level L = 20·log10(H ÷ 400 mA/m).

steps.prompt: Five of fourteen gone. Share? (%)
steps.why: Accountability with a shared key.

steps.prompt: 280 mA/m against 400. Level? (dB)
steps.why: Low, after the fix.

steps.prompt: A pre-show loop check takes 3 minutes; the venue runs 250 shows a year. Hours a year?
steps.why: What the check costs — about a day and a half a year.

CASE-048.title: The Paging Path
CASE-048.hook: Paging had priority. The packets never got as far as the priority.
learn: What happened. On full-lobby nights, paging broke up. The paging stations shared a VLAN with 900 guests on Wi-Fi, ‘for now’ since the lobby expansion.
Why it mattered. The emergency plan uses paging for the duty manager's ‘stay where you are’. A message that must get through was sharing a queue with everyone's video.
How it was proved. The VLAN map, the uplink graph at 108%, the DSP's priority working only on what arrived, and a check that the fire alarm's own voice system was separate.
The fix. Paging on its own VLAN with priority queuing on the uplinks; guests isolated and capped — Raffa's change; twenty clean test pages on the next full night.
CASE-048.service: For any message that must always get through, ask what path it takes — and who else is on that path.

engineer.intro: Load = n × rate; utilization = load ÷ link × 100.

steps.prompt: 900 guests × 1.2 Mb/s. Load? (Mb/s)
steps.why: What the uplink was asked to carry.

steps.prompt: On 1,000 Mb/s. Utilization? (%)
steps.why: Past full — so something gets dropped.

steps.prompt: After the cap, guests use 710 Mb/s. Utilization? (%)
steps.why: Room for paging to never wait.

CASE-049.title: The Commissioning Record That Wasn't
CASE-049.hook: Forty-eight PASS lines, thirty test files, and a summary with Maya's name on it.
learn: What happened. A commissioning record claimed 48 amplifier channels passed; only 30 had tests. The other 18 were typed at design values on handover eve. Maya had signed the summary.
Why it mattered. The warranty claim needed real data, and two real faults were hiding behind typed PASS lines.
How it was proved. Files against lines, the tester's session memory, identical design values, and the dates.
The fix. Maya owned her signature in writing; a witnessed retest of 18 channels; the record re-issued with every line linked and exceptions listed; honest data to the manufacturer.
CASE-049.service: Before you sign a summary, open what it summarizes. If you've signed one you didn't check, say so first.

engineer.intro: Share = part ÷ whole × 100; time = count ÷ rate.

steps.prompt: 30 of 48 with files. Share? (%)
steps.why: How much of the record was evidence.

steps.prompt: 18 channels at 6 an hour. Hours?
steps.why: The witnessed retest.

steps.prompt: The retest found 2 faults in 18. Share? (%)
steps.why: What the typed lines were hiding.

CASE-050.title: Two Clocks
CASE-050.hook: Both clocks were good. That was the problem.
learn: What happened. A converter set to its own clock fed a network interface running on another. Every 66.7 seconds the interface's buffer spilled and a take clicked.
Why it mattered. Only takes longer than a minute clicked, so the fault hid in exactly the performances that mattered most — and it looked like a ghost, a cable or a singer.
How it was proved. Ten minutes of tone on every input, clicks timed to a fixed interval on one device's channels only, and the clock source read on every device.
The fix. One leader, every other device following it; lock status watched; a lock warning treated as evidence.
CASE-050.service: When a fault keeps time, time it. Then find the two things that disagree about what time it is.

engineer.intro: Mastery: choose the relationship from the reference and say why.

steps.prompt: Two clocks 20 ppm apart at 48 kHz. Samples of drift per second?
steps.why: How fast the buffer fills.

steps.prompt: The buffer holds 64 samples. Seconds between clicks?
steps.why: The fingerprint of a two-clock fault.

steps.prompt: With a 256-sample buffer instead, seconds between clicks?
steps.why: A bigger buffer makes the fault rarer, not gone.

CASE-051.title: The Mix That Only Sounded Good Here
CASE-051.hook: Thirty years of good ears — sitting in the one chair where the room swallowed the bass.
learn: What happened. A new desk moved the mix chair to the exact middle of a 4.3 m room, where the first and third length modes cancel. For two years every mix carried extra deep bass to fill holes only that chair heard.
Why it mattered. The mixes sounded perfect where they were judged and wrong everywhere they were played.
How it was proved. Measurements at the chair and around it, the 2019 mixes against the 2023 ones on other systems, and a +10 dB boost that changed everything except the chair.
The fix. The chair moved off the center line and re-measured; the boost removed; one gentle cut; corner trapping designed by the acoustician; a translation routine.
CASE-051.service: Before you trust a room, find out what it does at the spot where you sit — and check the result somewhere else.

engineer.intro: Mastery: choose the relationship from the reference and say why.

steps.prompt: Room length 4.3 m, c = 343 m/s. First length mode? (Hz)
steps.why: The note the chair can't hear.

steps.prompt: Third length mode? (Hz)
steps.why: Odd modes also cancel on the center line.

steps.prompt: The new chair at 38% of 4.3 m from the front wall. Where? (m)
steps.why: A common starting point off the center line — then measure.

CASE-052.title: Phase at the Drum Kit
CASE-052.hook: Four good microphones on one drum — adding up to a cardboard box.
learn: What happened. A snare's bottom mic was left in opposite polarity after a template rebuild, and the overheads sat at different distances, the nearer still 1.15 m further than the close mic.
Why it mattered. The cancellation landed around 150 Hz — the snare's body — and the new drum head got the blame.
How it was proved. Each mic alone and then added one at a time, the polarity switch read, the distances measured with a tape, the comb's notches calculated.
The fix. Polarity flipped, overheads equal, close mics delayed to line up, a mono check, and the drummer's ears.
CASE-052.service: When a sound gets worse as you add microphones, suspect the microphones' relationship before the instrument.

engineer.intro: Mastery: choose the relationship from the reference and say why.

steps.prompt: Overhead 1.20 m, close mic 0.05 m from the snare. Delay between them? (ms)
steps.why: The delay that makes the comb.

steps.prompt: First notch of that comb? (Hz)
steps.why: Right where a snare's body lives.

steps.prompt: The 3:1 rule: spill at three times the distance is how many dB down? (1 decimal)
steps.why: Why the hi-hat mic moved.

CASE-053.title: Latency You Can Feel
CASE-053.hook: Twenty-seven milliseconds nearly replaced a singer on her own album.
learn: What happened. A singer's headphone feed went round the recording computer: two 512-sample buffers, the converters and a lookahead limiter — 27.3 ms.
Why it mattered. She heard herself late and hollow, sang behind the beat, and the fault was blamed on her.
How it was proved. A clap recorded against the headphone feed; every buffer and plug-in on her path read and added up.
The fix. Direct monitoring through the cue mixer, no lookahead on her path, the vocal recorded dry, the buffer left for mixing — and the decision left with her.
CASE-053.service: When a performer says something feels wrong, measure what they hear before anyone judges how they perform.

engineer.intro: Mastery: choose the relationship from the reference and say why.

steps.prompt: 2 × 512 samples at 48 kHz. Buffer delay? (ms)
steps.why: Most of the delay.

steps.prompt: Plus 1 ms of converters and 5 ms of lookahead. Total? (ms)
steps.why: What she was hearing.

steps.prompt: The same delay as standing how far from a speaker? (m)
steps.why: A way to explain it to the label.

CASE-054.title: The Archive
CASE-054.hook: Ten years later, the sessions wouldn't open, a third of the tracks were on a dead drive, and two ‘finals’ disagreed.
learn: What happened. An album's session files belonged to a program that had retired; 9 of 24 tracks per song lived on a scratch drive that no longer spun; two DVD sets disagreed and nothing recorded which was released.
Why it mattered. A reissue — and a piece of the artist's history — depended on files nobody could open or prove.
How it was proved. Read-only images and checksums, a list of what each session expected, recovery logged file by file, and a pencil track sheet plus the artist's memory to settle the conflict.
The fix. Broadcast WAV exports from bar 1, a readme and scans, a checksum manifest, three copies, a yearly fixity check and a five-year migration.
CASE-054.service: Archive for someone who wasn't there, can't ask you, and doesn't own the program you used.

engineer.intro: Mastery: choose the relationship from the reference and say why.

steps.prompt: 24 tracks × 48 kHz × 24-bit × 240 s. One song? (MB)
steps.why: The size of what you're rescuing.

steps.prompt: Nine of 24 tracks missing. Share? (%)
steps.why: How big the hole is.

steps.prompt: Three of 99 recovered files unreadable. Share? (%)
steps.why: What you tell the label, plainly.

CASE-055.title: The Wall Went Dark at Shift Change
CASE-055.hook: Noon, somewhere — and seven o'clock in the one room that couldn't afford it.
learn: What happened. An integrator typed ‘12:00’ as the video wall's update window, meaning local noon. The controller keeps UTC; at UTC−5 that is 07:00 — shift change.
Why it mattered. Both shifts handed over in front of the wall. On a dark morning, a sandbag request was never passed on and an underpass flooded first.
How it was proved. The exact time of the outage on eight mornings, the controller's log and time zone, and the dispatch liaison's account of what was lost.
The fix. Updates in a change window the director approves, never during an activation, tested first; a written handover brief for every operational period.
CASE-055.service: If something breaks at the same time every day, find whose clock it's keeping — then find what else happens at that time.

engineer.intro: Mastery: choose the relationship from the reference and say why.

steps.prompt: 12:00 UTC at UTC−5. Local hour?
steps.why: Why it hit shift change.

steps.prompt: 250 s dark on each of eight mornings. Total seconds?
steps.why: What the room lost.

steps.prompt: 8 of 16 handovers fell at 07:00. Share? (%)
steps.why: Half the handovers ran blind.

CASE-056.title: Failover That Failed Over Too Much
CASE-056.hook: The backup worked perfectly — sixty times an hour.
learn: What happened. A waterlogged cabinet made carrier A drop for fifteen seconds in every minute. The router failed over after three seconds and failed back the instant A answered — two switches a minute, each costing twelve seconds of radio and video.
Why it mattered. The emergency operations room was off the air 45% of the time during a flood; on the backup alone it would have been fine.
How it was proved. The router's log timed against session drops, the arithmetic of the cycle, and the carriers' route maps laid over the county's conduit records.
The fix. Pinned to the stable path, a hold-down for failback, the cabinet repaired and watched for a day — and a separate path funded because the two carriers shared a bridge.
CASE-056.service: A backup should be quick to use and slow to leave. Then check whether it shares anything with what it's backing up.

engineer.intro: Mastery: choose the relationship from the reference and say why.

steps.prompt: Heartbeats every 1 s, three missed to fail over. Detection time? (s)
steps.why: Fast to fail over — that part was fine.

steps.prompt: Every 60 s: 3 s undetected plus two 12 s rebuilds. Share of time lost? (%)
steps.why: The backup was the outage.

steps.prompt: Two truly independent 99.9% paths. Pair availability? (%)
steps.why: Only if nothing is shared.

CASE-057.title: Radio Interop
CASE-057.hook: Two transmitters made a third, and the patch lived in a retired dispatcher's head.
learn: What happened. A loaner repeater on the EOC's mast mixed with the EMS repeater and put a third-order product on fire dispatch's receive frequency; and the flood patch pointed at a talkgroup public works no longer used.
Why it mattered. In a flood, fire couldn't hear public works, and fire dispatch was losing weak calls under the hiss.
How it was proved. Listening with each transmitter keyed and unkeyed, the intermod arithmetic, and the gateway's patch read against each agency's current talkgroups.
The fix. The loaner moved by the radio systems manager, under license, with a certified crew; a written flood patch plan with net control and a weekly test, signed by the director.
CASE-057.service: When two systems that each work can't work together, look for what they make together — and for the plan that's supposed to join them.

engineer.intro: Mastery: choose the relationship from the reference and say why.

steps.why: Fire's receive frequency.

steps.prompt: 2f₂ − f₁? (MHz)
steps.why: The other product — check it isn't anyone's receive.

steps.prompt: 49 of 52 weekly patch tests pass. Share? (%)
steps.why: A plan that's tested, measured.

CASE-058.title: Verbatim
CASE-058.hook: ‘Move to higher ground now’ became ‘flooding possible, stay alert’ — and then became Spanish.
learn: What happened. A flash flood warning was rewritten by the county's public information officer to avoid panic, approved, posted seven minutes later — and machine-translated from the rewrite.
Why it mattered. A family at a low-water crossing waited. A warning's words are its instruction; softening them changed what people did.
How it was proved. The relay chain timed from the logs, the agency's text beside the county's, and the Spanish post and captions checked against both.

The fix. Verbatim, attributed relay with the county's guidance separate; evacuation wording only from the director; pre-approved Spanish templates by qualified translators; a live interpreter; captions verbatim.
CASE-058.service: When you relay someone else's warning, you are a wire, not an editor. Say your own piece separately.

engineer.intro: Mastery: choose the relationship from the reference and say why.

steps.prompt: Received 16:12:05, posted 16:19:00. Delay in seconds?
steps.why: What the rewrite cost.

steps.prompt: Verbatim path: check 20 s + relay 30 s + captions 6 s. Total? (s)
steps.why: The same warning, unchanged, in under a minute.

steps.prompt: Nine standard warnings in two languages. Templates?
steps.why: Prepared before the storm.

CASE-059.title: Generator Test Friday
CASE-059.hook: Three skipped tests hid a transfer switch that would not transfer.
learn: What happened. Monthly load tests were skipped because they caused a blip. Meanwhile the room's load grew to 9 kW, the batteries aged to about 60%, and the transfer switch's control relay failed.
Why it mattered. In a real outage the UPS would have carried the room for about twelve minutes and then dropped it — with the generator running and nothing connected to it.
How it was proved. The UPS's load and battery health, the runtime arithmetic, and a planned load test on a Friday afternoon that found the dead relay.
The fix. The relay repaired by facilities, new batteries funded, a load-shed plan rehearsed, and a monthly test on the calendar.
CASE-059.service: The test that annoys people is the one that finds the fault on your schedule instead of the storm's.

CASE-060.title: The Exception Register
CASE-060.hook: Twelve exceptions on paper. Forty-one in the rooms. And the rooms breaking the rules were the best ones.
learn: What happened. A register listed 12 exceptions to the room standard; a scan found 41 of 60 rooms that differed. Most exceptions had no expiry, and one hid a disabled fire-alarm mute input.
Why it mattered. Differences nobody records can't be managed — and the ones that cross a safety boundary can hurt people. Meanwhile the best-performing rooms were the ones breaking the standard.
How it was proved. A conformance scan, the register's own dates, and complaint rates per room by region — not totals.
The fix. Every difference recorded with an owner, reason, risk and expiry; life-safety issues to their owners the same day; the better template tested and taken to the change board.
CASE-060.service: Before you enforce a standard, ask what the differences are telling you — and who owns each one.

CASE-061.title: Lifecycle Report
CASE-061.hook: Sixty rooms, one wave, one cliff — and a report nobody would read past page one.
learn: What happened. The board set aside $120k a year for sixty rooms with no basis. Twenty-six rooms bought in one wave were about to reach end of life in the same year, and a vendor's end-of-support notice sat in procurement's files.
Why it mattered. A $1.09M year arriving unseen means rooms failing without money to replace them — or a panic purchase.
How it was proved. An inventory with install dates and replacement costs, the reserve (R = C ÷ L) and a chart of the year each wave ends.
The fix. A reserve with a basis; a staggered refresh with the deferral accepted in writing; the migration before end of support; a one-page lifecycle report every year.
CASE-061.service: When someone asks if the budget is enough, find every thing's birthday before you answer.

CASE-062.title: The Junior Who Stopped It
CASE-062.hook: One click would have reached sixty rooms. The most junior person on the rota said no.
learn: What happened. A regional head pressed a senior technician to push new camera firmware to every room overnight; the senior told the junior on the night rota. She put it on the lab room first. The lab camera died.
Why it mattered. Eighteen of sixty rooms have the same camera revision. A push to all would have left them without a camera at the board's meeting.
How it was proved. The lab room's log, the camera revisions across the estate and the platform's permissions.
The fix. The junior backed in writing; a blameless review; stop-work authority in the standard, signed by the CIO; a ticket and staged groups built into the platform.
CASE-062.service: When someone junior says ‘not like this’, the first thing to protect is their right to say it.

steps.why: The blast radius.

steps.prompt: Soaks of 24 h after the lab, the regional stage and the 10% stage. Hours before ‘all’?
steps.why: What slow costs.

steps.prompt: The 10% stage: how many rooms of 60?
steps.why: A signal, not a catastrophe.

CASE-063.title: The Runbook Worked
CASE-063.hook: Three in the morning at headquarters. A stream died in front of twelve offices. Nobody woke the architect — and that was the point.
learn: What happened. The primary encoder crashed during Tahvara's all-hands. A junior on the rota followed runbook RB-07 and restored the stream on the backup path in nine minutes.
Why it mattered. Twelve offices lost their all-hands for nine minutes instead of an hour — without waking anyone in another time zone.
How it was proved. The junior's timed log, the stream records, and the notes from the March drill that had fixed three wrong steps.
The fix. The one failing step named a person on leave: every runbook now names roles on the rota; the backup path is tested monthly; juniors drill runbooks every quarter.
CASE-063.service: The best sign a runbook works is that nobody needed its author.

CASE-064.title: What Survives You
CASE-064.hook: Halfway through a year spent building something that shouldn't need her, the architect counted — and found herself on the list.
learn: What happened. Of 24 critical tasks, 11 could be done by only one person: seven by the senior technician, four by the architect. And a junior nearly undid a key design decision because its reason lived only in an email.
Why it mattered. Every single-person task is an outage waiting for a holiday, and every unwritten reason is a decision waiting to be reversed by someone tidying up.
How it was proved. A list of tasks with a count of who can do each unaided — including the architect — and one near-miss with the glass-room template.
The fix. A second person for each, signed off by doing it; decision records for the key decisions; a week without the architect to prove it.
CASE-064.service: Ask ‘who else can do this?’ about every critical task — starting with yours.

gain.name: Gain needed
