where: gain to add, dB (negative means cut)
gain.ex: Arriving at −30 dB, target −18 dB: G = −18 − (−30) = +12 dB.
gain.when: Use it for any level correction: target minus what arrives.

dbsum_equal.name: Summing equal sources
dbsum_equal.note: Two equal sources add about 3 dB; four add about 6 dB.
dbsum_equal.when: Use it when several equal, unrelated sources combine — doubling the sources adds about 3 dB, not double the level.

dbsum.name: Summing unequal levels
dbsum.note: Convert each level to power, add, convert back.
dbsum.when: Use it when two unrelated sources of different level play together — decibels don't add like ordinary numbers.

db_to_ratio_v.name: Decibels to a voltage ratio
where: how many times larger the voltage or sound pressure is
db_to_ratio_v.ex: A 6 dB increase in voltage or sound pressure: 10^(6/20) ≈ 2 times.
db_to_ratio_v.when: Use it for field quantities: voltage, sound pressure, microphone level. Divide by 20, not 10.

db_to_ratio_p.name: Decibels to a power ratio
db_to_ratio_p.ex: A 3 dB increase in power: 10^(3/10) ≈ 2 times the power.
db_to_ratio_p.when: Use it for power quantities: amplifier watts, RF power, signal-to-noise as a power ratio.

db_diff.name: Level difference
db_diff.ex: A mic at −18 dB and another at −24 dB: −18 − (−24) = 6 dB difference.
db_diff.when: Use it whenever you compare two levels — meters, readings, before and after.

headroom.name: Headroom change
where: where the peaks are (or would be), dBFS
how much to lower the gain, dB
headroom.ex: Peaks at −2 dBFS, target −10 dBFS: lower the gain by 8 dB.
headroom.when: Use it to set gain so peaks stay clear of clipping with a known margin.

inv_sq.name: Inverse-square law
inv_sq.note: About 6 dB per doubling of distance in a free field.
inv_sq.ex: Moving from 2 m to 8 m: 20·log₁₀(8 ÷ 2) ≈ 12 dB quieter.
inv_sq.when: Use it to predict level changes with distance from a small source in open space.

doublings.name: Distance from a level drop
doublings.note: Free-field estimate: about 6 dB per doubling.
doublings.ex: A 12 dB drop: 12 ÷ 6 = 2 doublings, so 1 m × 2² = 4 m.
doublings.when: Use it outdoors to estimate distance from a level change, or level from a distance change (free field, about 6 dB per doubling).

gbf_mics.name: Open microphones and gain before feedback
where: how many times more mics are open
change in gain before feedback, dB
gbf_mics.note: Each doubling of open mics costs about 3 dB.
gbf_mics.ex: Going from 1 open mic to 4: −10·log₁₀(4) ≈ −6 dB of gain before feedback.
gbf_mics.when: Use it when feedback starts as more mics open — mute unused mics before reaching for EQ.

loop_growth.name: Loop gain over many laps
loop_growth.ex: +2 dB per lap for 5 laps: 10^(5 × 2 ÷ 20) ≈ 3.2 times louder.
loop_growth.when: Use it to see why feedback runs away — small gains per lap multiply fast.

margin.name: Signal margin
margin.ex: Received −65 dBm, noise floor −95 dBm: margin 30 dB.
margin.when: Use it to judge how much fade a link can survive before it drops.

loss_add.name: Losses in dB add
where: level with a clear path, dBm
loss_add.ex: −40 dBm clear, minus 3 dB and 6 dB of losses: −49 dBm.
loss_add.when: Use it to build a link budget — in decibels, losses simply subtract.

erl.name: Echo return loss
erl.eq: ERL = L<sub>speaker at mic</sub> − L<sub>echo at mic</sub>
where: loudspeaker level at the mic position, dB
erl.ex: Loudspeaker at the mic 70 dB, echo picked up 50 dB: ERL = 20 dB.
erl.when: Use it when a conference room's far end hears itself — it tells you how much echo the mic collects before any processing.

loudness_gain.name: Loudness correction
where: integrated loudness of the program, LUFS
gain to apply, dB (1 LU = 1 dB)
loudness_gain.ex: Measured −19 LUFS, target −23 LUFS: G = −23 − (−19) = −4 dB.
loudness_gain.when: Use it to bring a program or spot to the loudness target — target minus measured, from a loudness meter, not a peak meter.

time_of_flight.name: Travel time of sound
where: speed of sound, about 343 m/s in air at 20 °C
time_of_flight.ex: A delay speaker 17.15 m farther away: 17.15 ÷ 343 = 0.05 s = 50 ms.
time_of_flight.when: Use it to align speakers or explain echoes — distance divided by the speed of sound.

distance_of_flight.name: Distance traveled
where: speed of sound, about 343 m/s in air at 20 °C
distance_of_flight.when: Use it to turn a measured delay into distance — how far a speaker, reflector or stage really is.

echo_distance.name: Echo distance (there and back)
where: one-way distance to the reflector, m
speed of sound, about 343 m/s in air at 20 °C
echo_distance.ex: An echo 0.1 s after the clap: 343 × 0.1 ÷ 2 = 17 m to the wall.
echo_distance.when: Use it when a sound goes out and comes back — divide by 2, because the sound traveled there and back.

flash_bang.name: Flash-to-bang distance
where: speed of sound, about 343 m/s in air at 20 °C
distance to the strike, m (÷ 1,000 for km)
flash_bang.note: About 3 seconds per kilometer. Distance informs the weather plan; the stop call belongs to the person the plan names.
flash_bang.ex: 15 s from flash to thunder: 343 × 15 ≈ 5,145 m ≈ 5.1 km.
flash_bang.when: Use it to estimate lightning distance for the weather lead's decision — the decision itself belongs to the plan's owner.

speed_temp.name: Speed of sound and temperature
speed_temp.when: Use it outdoors or in hot venues where delay settings drift with temperature.

comb_notch.name: First comb-filter notch
where: speed of sound, about 343 m/s in air at 20 °C
comb_notch.ex: Two arrivals 1 ms apart: 1 ÷ (2 × 0.001) = 500 Hz is the first notch.
comb_notch.when: Use it when a seat or mic sounds hollow and the same sound arrives twice — speakers, reflections, two mics.

comb_spacing.name: Notch spacing
comb_spacing.ex: Arrivals 2 ms apart: notches every 1 ÷ 0.002 = 500 Hz.
comb_spacing.when: Use it to predict how dense the comb is once you know the first notch.

round_trip.name: Round-trip delay
round_trip.ex: One-way delay 150 ms: the echo returns 300 ms later.
round_trip.when: Use it when someone hears themselves on a link — the echo is twice the one-way delay.

harmonic.name: Harmonics
harmonic.ex: Hum at 50 Hz: the 3rd harmonic is 3 × 50 = 150 Hz.
harmonic.when: Use it when a buzz has several tones — the fundamental times 2, 3, 4… tells you where they sit.

octave.name: Octaves
octave.note: One octave up doubles the frequency.
octave.when: Use it to read EQ and analyzer bands, which are spaced in octaves or fractions of one.

wavelength.name: Wavelength
where: speed of the wave: 343 m/s for sound, 3 × 10<sup>8</sup> m/s for radio
wavelength.when: Use it to see why low sounds bend around pillars and why antenna size depends on frequency.

quarter_wave.name: Quarter-wave antenna
quarter_wave.when: Use it to check that an antenna element suits the frequency it's supposed to receive.

sabine.name: Sabine reverberation time
where: time for sound to fall 60 dB, s
sabine.ex: A 500 m³ room with 50 m² of absorption: 0.161 × 500 ÷ 50 ≈ 1.6 s.
sabine.when: Use it to predict how long a room rings and how much absorption would tame it.

fft_bin.name: FFT bin to frequency
fft_bin.when: Use it to turn an analyzer's bin number into a real frequency you can notch or name.

q_factor.name: Filter Q
q_factor.ex: A cut centered at 2,000 Hz, 500 Hz wide: Q = 2,000 ÷ 500 = 4.
q_factor.when: Use it to set a notch narrow enough to kill one ring without hollowing the voice.

samples.name: Samples and time
samples.eq: N = t × f<sub>s</sub> · t = N ÷ f<sub>s</sub>
samples.when: Use it to convert between delay in samples (what a DSP shows) and time (what people hear).

nyquist.name: Nyquist limit
nyquist.ex: Sampled at 44,100 Hz: the highest frequency is 22,050 Hz.
nyquist.when: Use it to choose a sample rate — anything above half of it folds back as distortion.

bits_dr.name: Dynamic range per bit
bits_dr.note: Rule of thumb; for a full-scale sine wave the theoretical figure is 6.02 × b + 1.76 dB. Dither and converter noise make real figures lower.
bits_dr.ex: A 16-bit recording: 6.02 × 16 ≈ 96 dB of dynamic range.
bits_dr.when: Use it to decide whether a bit depth leaves enough room between the noise floor and full scale.

bitrate.name: Uncompressed bit rate
bitrate.ex: Two channels at 48,000 Hz and 24 bits: 2 × 48,000 × 24 = 2,304,000 bit/s ≈ 2.3 Mbit/s.
bitrate.when: Use it to size a link or storage for uncompressed audio before you choose a network or a recorder.

bits_fraction.name: Fraction of full scale
bits_fraction.ex: An 8-bit value of 64: 64 ÷ 255 ≈ 0.25, a quarter of full scale.
bits_fraction.when: Use it to turn a raw channel value into a percentage — DMX levels, video code values.

entropy.name: Password entropy
entropy.ex: A 12-character password from 26 lowercase letters: 12 × log₂(26) ≈ 56 bits.
entropy.when: Use it to compare password choices — length and randomness add bits; clever substitutions barely do.

shannon.name: Shannon capacity
where: most data a channel can carry, bit/s
signal-to-noise ratio as a plain ratio (10<sup>dB/10</sup>)
shannon.ex: B = 5 MHz, S/N = 3 (≈ 4.8 dB): C = 5 × log₂(4) = 10 Mb/s.
shannon.when: Use it to know a channel's hard ceiling. No encoder beats it — when the noise rises, the ceiling drops.

percent.name: Percentage
percent.when: Use it to report scale in a way owners can compare.

rate.name: Rate
rate.ex: 12 tickets in 4 hours: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 tickets per hour.
rate.when: Use it to turn a pile of events into a trend you can compare over time.

product.name: Counting combinations
where: the two things being multiplied (e.g. presets × outputs)
product.when: Use it to count a test matrix before you promise to test 'everything'.

time_budget.name: Time budget
where: minutes or seconds per task — keep units the same
time_budget.ex: 3 checks of 5 min + 2 of 10 min: 15 + 20 = 35 min.
time_budget.when: Use it to test whether a plan fits the time you actually have before doors or air.

ratio.name: How many times
ratio.ex: Old wait 30 min, new wait 6 min: 30 ÷ 6 = 5 times faster.
ratio.when: Use it to say 'how many times' — better or worse — in one number.

difference.name: Difference
difference.when: Use it whenever you compare a reading to a target or to a second reading.

cost_per_incident.name: Cost of one incident
cost_per_incident.ex: A fixer spends 20 min while 10 people wait 15 min each: 20 + 10 × 15 = 170 person-minutes.
cost_per_incident.when: Use it when deciding whether a recurring small fault is worth a permanent fix — count everyone's time, not just the fixer's.

payback.name: Payback time
payback.eq: weeks = hours invested ÷ hours saved per week
payback.ex: 8 hours of work that saves 2 hours a week: 8 ÷ 2 = 4 weeks to pay back.
payback.when: Use it to argue for fixing the root cause of a recurring nuisance.

ring_size.name: Update ring size
where: fleet minus rooms already in earlier rings
ring_size.ex: 200 rooms left, 25% ring: 200 × 0.25 = 50 rooms in this ring.
ring_size.when: Use it to stage updates so a bad change hits a few rooms, not all of them.

frame_period.name: Frame period
frame_period.ex: At 25 fps: 1 ÷ 25 = 0.04 s = 40 ms per frame.
frame_period.when: Use it to convert between frames and milliseconds before any timing fix.

frames_to_time.name: Frames to time
frames_to_time.when: Use it to turn a measured frame offset into a delay you can set.

refresh_cycles.name: Refresh cycles per exposure
where: LED refresh rate, Hz (frame rate × multiplier)
refresh_cycles.note: A whole number of cycles per exposure means no banding.
refresh_cycles.ex: A 3,840 Hz LED wall and a 1/50 s shutter: 3,840 × 0.02 = 76.8 cycles.
refresh_cycles.when: Use it when an LED wall shows bands on camera — whole cycles per exposure keep it clean.

beat.name: Beat frequency
beat.ex: Two tones at 440 Hz and 443 Hz: |440 − 443| = 3 beats per second.
beat.when: Use it when two nearly equal rates interfere — tuning, flicker between a camera and lights, a wobble in a tone.

av_delay.name: Audio delay to match picture
where: latency of the picture path, ms
latency already in the audio path, ms
av_delay.ex: Picture path 120 ms, audio path already 20 ms: add 120 − 20 = 100 ms of audio delay.
av_delay.when: Use it when the sound runs ahead of the lips and you know both path latencies. Delay the faster path by the difference, not by ear.

lipsync.name: Lip-sync offset
where: positive = sound late, negative = sound early
lipsync.ex: Audio path 40 ms, video path 100 ms: offset = 40 − 100 = −60 ms (sound early).
lipsync.when: Use it after measuring both paths; the sign tells you whether sound is early (negative) or late (positive).

focus_distance.name: Distance to the subject
where: how far the subject stands in front of that wall
focus_distance.ex: Wall 6 m from the camera, presenter 1.5 m in front of it: focus at 4.5 m.
focus_distance.when: Use it when autofocus hunts or the wall is sharp and the face isn't — set focus to the subject, not the background.

thin_lens.name: Thin-lens equation
where: image distance behind the lens, mm
thin_lens.when: Use it to reason about focus: close subjects need the image farther behind the lens.

wheel_freeze.name: When a wheel looks frozen on camera
wheel_freeze.ex: A 30 fps camera and a 6-spoke wheel: 30 ÷ 6 = 5 rev/s looks frozen.
wheel_freeze.when: Use it to explain strobing on camera — motion that matches the frame rate appears to stop.

mired.name: Mired scale
mired.when: Use it to reason about color correction — gel and filter shifts add in mired, not in kelvin.

pixels.name: Pixel count
pixels.when: Use it to compare resolutions or to size a video processor.

aspect.name: Aspect ratio
aspect.when: Use it to check whether a picture will fill a screen or get bars or cropping.

ntsc_rate.name: The 1.001 rates
where: the offset introduced with NTSC color in 1953
ntsc_rate.when: Use it to explain why timecode and frame counts drift against wall-clock time at 29.97.

throw_width.name: Beam width at a distance
throw_width.ex: A 20° beam at 10 m: 2 × 10 × tan(10°) ≈ 3.5 m wide.
throw_width.when: Use it to choose a fixture or position so light covers the area you need.

lux_fc.name: Foot-candles and lux
lux_fc.when: Use it to compare a lighting spec written in foot-candles with a meter that reads lux.

dmx_last.name: Last channel a fixture uses
dmx_last.when: Use it to check that the next fixture doesn't overlap — the last channel is start + count − 1.

dmx_next.name: Next free start address
dmx_next.ex: A fixture at 101 using 16 channels: the next free address is 117.
dmx_next.when: Use it when patching fixtures back to back without overlaps or gaps.

dmx_fit.name: Fixtures per universe
dmx_fit.ex: Fixtures using 14 channels: ⌊512 ÷ 14⌋ = 36 fixtures per universe.
dmx_fit.when: Use it when planning how many fixtures a universe can carry before you need another.

dmx_universes.name: Universes needed
dmx_universes.when: Use it early in planning to size the lighting network.

dmx_levels.name: Levels per channel
dmx_levels.when: Use it to understand why a DMX value of 255 is full and 128 is about half.

angle_map.name: Value to angle
angle_map.ex: A pan channel stored at 25% on a fixture that maps 100% to 540°: angle = 0.25 × 540 = 135°.
angle_map.when: Use it when a control value is a fraction of a range and you need the physical position — pan, tilt, a fader throw.

subnet_hosts.name: Usable hosts in a subnet
where: network and broadcast addresses can't be hosts
subnet_hosts.when: Use it to check whether a subnet is big enough for every device before you address it.

subnet_last.name: Last usable address
subnet_last.ex: Network .64 with /26: .64 + 64 − 2 = .126 is the last usable address.
subnet_last.when: Use it to find the edges of a subnet so fixed addresses land inside it — and outside the automatic range.

range_count.name: Addresses in a range
where: the range's first and last numbers
range_count.when: Use it to count addresses, channels or seats in an inclusive range — add 1.

link_use.name: Link utilization
link_use.when: Use it to tell whether a link is busy or full before blaming the network.

current.name: Current from power
current.note: A planning estimate to hand the electrician. Only the electrician works on the panel.
current.when: Use it to plan loads on a circuit — as a planning number for the electrician, never as permission to touch the panel.

power.name: Power
power.when: Use it to estimate power draw for planning — a number for the electrician, not a procedure.

derate.name: Continuous-load planning line
derate.ex: A 15 A breaker: 0.8 × 15 = 12 A planning line.
derate.when: Use it to plan continuous loads with margin. It's a planning number for the electrician's decision, never a procedure.

imd3.name: Third-order intermodulation
imd3.note: Keep every wireless channel off these products.
imd3.ex: Transmitters on 600 and 601 MHz: 2 × 600 − 601 = 599 MHz and 2 × 601 − 600 = 602 MHz.
imd3.when: Use it when coordinating several wireless channels — products land near your carriers and can land on one.

fspl.name: Free-space path loss
fspl.when: Use it to estimate how much signal a radio link loses to distance alone before you add walls, rain and cables.

rain_fade.name: Rain fade
where: specific attenuation for this rain rate and frequency, dB/km
path length through the rain, km
rain_fade.ex: 0.5 dB/km of rain over 20 km: A = 0.5 × 20 = 10 dB.
rain_fade.when: Use it to predict whether a microwave link survives a storm: compare A with the fade margin.

fresnel.name: First Fresnel zone radius
fresnel.note: Keep at least 60% of this radius clear of obstacles.
fresnel.ex: A 10 km, 6 GHz hop, at mid-path (5 km each side): 17.32 × √(25 ÷ 60) ≈ 11.2 m.
fresnel.when: Use it to check whether hills, trees or buildings intrude on a microwave path — clearance is about more than line of sight.

clock_drift.name: Clock drift
clock_drift.ex: A clock 5 ppm fast for one hour: 5 × 10⁻⁶ × 3,600 s = 0.018 s = 18 ms.
clock_drift.when: Use it when a clock has lost its reference and you need to know how far it wanders over time.

drift_frames.name: Drift in frames
drift_frames.ex: 0.1 s of drift at 30 fps: 0.1 × 30 = 3 frames.
drift_frames.when: Use it after clock_drift to express the error in frames — the unit people see on screen.

lever.name: Beam support reactions (moments)
where: load's distance from the left support, m
lever.note: An illustration of why ratings matter. Only a qualified engineer rates a structure.
lever.ex: A 100 kg load 1 m from the left support on a 4 m span: right support carries 100 × 1 ÷ 4 = 25 kg.
lever.when: Use it to understand how load shares between supports. Rigging decisions belong to the rigger and engineer.

ohm.name: Ohm's law
ohm.note: Planning math for low-voltage runs and meters. Only a licensed electrician works on panels and mains wiring.
ohm.ex: A 2 A load through a cable with 1.5 Ω of total resistance: V = 2 × 1.5 = 3 V lost in the cable.
ohm.when: Use it when you know two of voltage, current and resistance and need the third — a low-voltage run, a meter reading, a battery rig.

cable_drop.name: Cable voltage drop (DC)
where: resistance per length of one conductor, Ω/ft or Ω/m
cable_drop.ex: 24 V at 2 A over 100 ft of cable with 0.0064 Ω/ft per conductor: 2 × 2 × 0.0064 × 100 = 2.56 V lost.
cable_drop.when: Use it for long low-voltage DC runs (LED tape, sensors, small lights) before you blame the device at the far end.

battery_runtime.name: Battery runtime
battery_runtime.note: Ideal figure; real runtime is shorter (age, temperature, cut-off voltage).
battery_runtime.ex: A 2 Ah pack feeding 0.25 A: 2 ÷ 0.25 = 8 h, ideally — real packs give less.
battery_runtime.when: Use it to know whether a pack can make it through — then fit fresh batteries before every service anyway.

room_mode.name: Axial room mode
where: speed of sound, about 343 m/s in air at 20 °C
distance between the two parallel surfaces, m
room_mode.note: For each axial mode the pressure is highest at the walls. Odd modes (n = 1, 3, 5 …) cancel in the middle of the room — so a chair on the center line hears a hole in the bass.
room_mode.when: Use it before you touch an EQ: find which bass notes the room itself is adding or removing, and where.

spl_distance.name: Loudspeaker level at a distance
where: sensitivity, dB SPL at 1 W and 1 m
spl_distance.note: Free-field estimate for one loudspeaker; rooms, arrays and limiters change it.
spl_distance.ex: Sensitivity 90 dB (1 W, 1 m), 100 W, 10 m: 90 + 20 − 20 = 90 dB.
spl_distance.when: Use it to check whether a loudspeaker can reach a seat at the level you need before you buy, aim or turn up.

comp_out.name: Compressor output above threshold
where: output level before makeup gain, dB
comp_out.ex: Threshold −20 dB, ratio 4:1, input −8 dB: −20 + 12 ÷ 4 = −17 dB, so 9 dB of gain reduction.
comp_out.when: Use it to predict how hard a compressor will pull a peak down before you trust the meter or your ears alone.

shutter_rule.name: Shutter rule of thumb
shutter_rule.note: Natural motion blur; change it to match lights or LED walls that flicker.
shutter_rule.when: Use it to set a natural starting shutter, then adjust to stop LED walls or lights from banding.

latency_sum.name: Total latency
where: the delay each stage adds, ms
latency_sum.ex: Mic DSP 2 ms + encoder 150 ms + network 80 ms + decoder 60 ms + display 30 ms = 322 ms.
latency_sum.when: Use it to find which stage owns most of the delay before you try to shrink it.

light_inv_sq.name: Inverse-square law for light
where: illuminance at the first distance, lux
illuminance at the new distance, lux
light_inv_sq.note: Small fixture, far compared with its size. Double the distance → a quarter of the light.
light_inv_sq.ex: 800 lux at 4 m; move the fixture to 8 m: 800 × (4 ÷ 8)² = 200 lux.
light_inv_sq.when: Use it when a fixture moves farther from the subject — double the throw, a quarter of the light.

video_bw.name: Uncompressed video rate
video_bw.eq: R = W × H × fps × b × s
video_bw.note: Active picture only; the cable format adds overhead.
video_bw.ex: 1920 × 1080 × 60 fps × 10 bits × 2 (4:2:2) ≈ 2.49 Gb/s of active picture.
video_bw.when: Use it to see why uncompressed video needs a fast link — and why IP video is often compressed.

loop_field.name: Hearing-loop field level
where: level relative to the reference, dB
loop_field.note: Loop systems are commonly set so speech peaks sit near the reference level; check local standards (illustrative).
loop_field.ex: Measured 200 mA/m against a 400 mA/m reference: 20·log₁₀(200 ÷ 400) = 20 × (−0.301) ≈ −6 dB.
loop_field.when: Use it to compare a hearing-loop reading with its target, seat by seat — a dead zone shows up as a big negative number.

poe_sum.name: PoE power budget
poe_sum.eq: P<sub>used</sub> = Σ P<sub>port</sub> · headroom = P<sub>budget</sub> − P<sub>used</sub>
where: power drawn at each port, W
what's left, W (negative means ports get shut off)
poe_sum.ex: A 370 W switch feeding 20 ports at 15.4 W: 20 × 15.4 = 308 W used; 370 − 308 = 62 W headroom.
poe_sum.when: Use it before plugging in anything powered by the network — when the budget goes negative, the switch starts shutting ports off.

fail_rate.name: Failure rate
fail_rate.eq: λ = failures ÷ (units × years) · expected = λ × units × years
fail_rate.ex: 12 failures among 140 projectors over 2 years: 12 ÷ (140 × 2) ≈ 0.043 per projector per year.
fail_rate.when: Use it to turn a pile of tickets into a replacement plan you can defend with numbers.

conduit_fill.name: Conduit fill
where: cross-section area of each cable, mm²
internal area of the conduit, mm²
percent of the conduit the cables occupy
conduit_fill.note: For three or more cables the electrical code's usual limit is 40%; the engineer of record sizes and signs the conduit. Bend radius and pull length matter too.
conduit_fill.ex: Four cables of 50 mm² in a 490 mm² conduit: 4 × 50 ÷ 490 × 100 ≈ 41% — just over a 40% limit.
conduit_fill.when: Use it before you promise a floor box can carry a camera, a mic and a display link — then hand the numbers to the engineer of record.

throw_dist.name: Projector throw distance
where: throw ratio of the lens (distance ÷ image width)
throw_dist.note: Use the maker's published throw range for the exact lens; a zoom lens has a minimum and maximum ratio, and lens shift changes where the projector can sit.
throw_dist.ex: A 6 m wide image with a 1.5:1 lens: 1.5 × 6 = 9 m. With a 0.8:1 lens: 4.8 m.
throw_dist.when: Use it to place a projector before the ceiling, the beams and the booth decide for you.

availability.name: Availability — one unit and a redundant pair
where: fraction of time a unit works
fraction of time at least one of two works
availability.note: The pair formula assumes the two fail independently. Shared power, a shared rack, shared software or the same firmware bug break that assumption — and the real figure is worse.
availability.ex: MTBF 8,000 h, MTTR 48 h: A = 8,000 ÷ 8,048 ≈ 0.994. Two independent units: 1 − 0.006² ≈ 0.99996.
availability.when: Use it to show what a ‘duplicate’ recorder buys — and remember it only holds if the two can't fail together.

tap_load.name: 70 V line loading
where: the tap setting on each loudspeaker transformer, W
the amplifier channel's rated power, W
tap_load.note: A common design practice, not a code rule; the maker's data, line losses and the program's peaks set the real limit.
tap_load.ex: A 240 W channel: 0.8 × 240 = 192 W. Twenty loudspeakers tapped at 10 W = 200 W — over the margin.
tap_load.when: Use it when checking an amplifier submittal or adding loudspeakers to a line.

spk_spacing.name: Ceiling loudspeaker spacing
where: spacing for edge-to-edge coverage at ear height, m
spk_spacing.note: Edge-to-edge spacing (= D) leaves holes between every four loudspeakers on a square grid; spacing ≤ D ÷ √2 (minimum overlap) covers every point. Closer still gives smoother level. Check the angle at the frequencies that carry speech.
spk_spacing.ex: Ceiling 4.2 m, ears 1.2 m, 90° coverage: 2 × 3.0 × tan 45° = 6.0 m.
spk_spacing.when: Use it to lay out a ceiling grid — then check the jury box, the witness box and the lectern sit inside the pattern.

exposure.name: Exposure in device-days
exposure.note: A way to compare risks and the cost of delay — not a probability. Security owns the risk decision.
exposure.ex: 154 devices × 300 days = 46,200 device-days. Every extra day of delay adds 154 more.
exposure.when: Use it to compare the cost of waiting with the cost of a careful rollout — then let security decide.

utc_offset.name: Local time from UTC
where: the time in Coordinated Universal Time
the zone's offset from UTC, hours (negative west of Greenwich)
local clock time — add or subtract 24 h, and change the date, if it crosses midnight
utc_offset.note: Many places shift their offset for daylight saving time; the invented countries here don't. Write handovers in UTC with the customer's local time beside it.
utc_offset.ex: 09:00 in Tahvara (UTC+8) = 01:00 UTC = 20:00 the evening before in Harrowmere (UTC−5).
utc_offset.when: Use it whenever a time crosses a desk, a border or a handover — and write the UTC time down.

poll_detect.name: Catching an outage by polling
where: chance one outage is seen, if polls fall at random times
polling interval, same units as d
poll_detect.note: If T ≤ d every outage is seen, whatever the timing. An outage locked to the clock (a scheduled job) can be missed every time. Event-driven alerts see it as it happens.
poll_detect.ex: An 8-minute outage polled every 15 minutes at random: 8 ÷ 15 ≈ 53%. Polled every 5 minutes: 100%.
poll_detect.when: Use it to choose a polling interval from the shortest outage that matters — not from habit.

flicker_shutter.name: Flicker-free shutter
flicker_shutter.eq: f<sub>flicker</sub> = 2 × f<sub>mains</sub> · no bands when t<sub>s</sub> × f<sub>flicker</sub> is a whole number
where: how often the light's output pulses, Hz
flicker_shutter.note: Holds for lights whose output follows the mains waveform. Many LED drivers flicker at other rates or hardly at all — check with the camera, or a flicker meter.
flicker_shutter.ex: 50 Hz mains → 100 Hz flicker. A 1/100 s shutter holds exactly one pulse: no bands. 1/60 s holds 1.67: bands.
flicker_shutter.when: Use it when a camera profile moves between 50 Hz and 60 Hz regions.

payback_money.name: Payback time (money)
payback_money.eq: years = one-off cost ÷ savings per year
payback_money.note: Simple payback ignores interest and risk. Finance owns the spending decision; you bring the numbers.
payback_money.ex: $18,000 once, saving $43,500 a year: 18,000 ÷ 43,500 ≈ 0.41 years — about five months.
payback_money.when: Use it to show finance what a fix buys back, in their units.

heartbeat_timeout.name: Heartbeat timeout
where: heartbeats that may be missed before an alarm (often 3)
how long the monitor waits before calling the device down
heartbeat_timeout.note: A timeout shorter than the interval raises an alarm on every gap between heartbeats — an alarm flood.
heartbeat_timeout.ex: Heartbeats every 120 s, three may be missed: timeout ≥ 3 × 120 = 360 s.
heartbeat_timeout.when: Use it when moving devices to a new monitoring system — carry each site's interval with them.

ups_runtime.name: UPS runtime (rough)
ups_runtime.note: A first estimate only: real runtime falls faster at high loads and as batteries age — use the maker's runtime chart. The UPS is facilities'.
ups_runtime.ex: 2,400 Wh × 0.9 ÷ 1,200 W = 1.8 h (108 min). Shed the load to 700 W and the same energy lasts longer.
ups_runtime.when: Use it to give facilities a countdown in minutes — then let them decide what to shed.

fiber_budget.name: Optical loss budget
fiber_budget.eq: L = α × d + n<sub>c</sub> × L<sub>c</sub> + n<sub>s</sub> × L<sub>s</sub> · margin = budget − L
where: mated connector pairs and the loss allowed for each, dB
splices and the loss allowed for each, dB
the transceiver's allowed channel loss, dB
fiber_budget.note: Common planning allowances: single-mode about 0.4 dB/km at 1310 nm, 0.75 dB per mated connector pair, 0.3 dB per splice. Also check the transceiver's reach — multimode links hit a distance limit before a dB limit. Illustrative; certify with an OTDR and a loss test.
fiber_budget.ex: 300 m of single-mode: 0.3 × 0.4 = 0.12 dB; 2 connectors × 0.75 = 1.5 dB; 1 splice × 0.3 dB. Total 1.92 dB; against a 6.2 dB budget, 4.28 dB of margin.
fiber_budget.when: Use it before you promise a fiber route — and again after the route changes.

inrush.name: Switch-on surge
where: each load's inrush multiple (from its data sheet)
inrush.note: The surge lasts milliseconds; whether it trips a breaker depends on the breaker's trip curve. Staggering switch-on is the electrician's usual answer — the circuits are theirs.
inrush.ex: 12 fixtures × 20 × 0.8 A ≈ 192 A for a few milliseconds — against 9.6 A running.
inrush.when: Use it to explain to the electrician why a circuit trips at switch-on but not while running — then let them stagger it.

heat_load.name: Equipment heat load
where: electrical power the equipment draws, W
heat released into the room, BTU per hour
heat_load.note: Nearly every watt a rack draws ends up as heat in the room. Mechanical engineers size cooling from this number — so it has to reach them.
heat_load.when: Use it to send the mechanical engineer the heat your equipment makes, in their units.

n_plus_1.name: N+1 cooling
where: capacity of one cooling unit, kW
n_plus_1.note: With one unit failed or in maintenance, the rest must still carry the load. The mechanical engineer of record sizes and selects the units.
n_plus_1.ex: Three 7 kW units: with one failed, 2 × 7 = 14 kW ≥ 12.8 kW. Two units: 7 kW < 12.8 kW.
n_plus_1.when: Use it to ask whether a room still copes when one cooling unit is down.

risk_score.name: Risk score
risk_score.note: A way to rank risks against each other, not a probability. The risk's owner decides what to do about it. Illustrative.
risk_score.ex: A shared admin password: likely (4) × severe (5) = 20. A scuffed cover plate: 1 × 1 = 1.
risk_score.when: Use it to put a remediation list in order before the money runs out.

log_storage.name: Log storage
where: average size of one event, bytes
log_storage.note: Retention is security's and the privacy owner's decision; this only tells you what it costs to keep. Illustrative.
log_storage.ex: 20,000 events a day × 500 bytes × 365 days ≈ 3.65 GB.
log_storage.when: Use it to tell security what a retention period costs to keep.

slip_interval.name: Time between sample slips
where: samples the receiver's buffer can absorb before it must drop or repeat a block
how far apart the two clocks run, as a fraction (ppm × 10<sup>−6</sup>)
slip_interval.note: Two free-running clocks drift apart by f<sub>s</sub> × Δ samples every second; a buffer hides it until it fills. The fix is one clock leader, not a bigger buffer. Illustrative.
slip_interval.ex: 48,000 Hz × 20 ppm = 0.96 samples a second; a 64-sample buffer fills in 64 ÷ 0.96 ≈ 67 s.
slip_interval.when: Use it when clicks arrive on a schedule: a regular interval points at two clocks, not a cable.

rtl.name: Round-trip latency
where: buffer size, samples (one buffer in, one buffer out)
converter delay in and out, s
extra delay from plug-ins such as lookahead, s
what the performer hears between singing and hearing herself, s
rtl.note: Several milliseconds of your own voice arriving late can feel like singing behind the beat or sounding hollow. Direct monitoring skips the computer entirely. Illustrative.
rtl.ex: 2 × 512 ÷ 48,000 = 21.3 ms, + 1 ms of converters + 5 ms of lookahead ≈ 27 ms.
rtl.when: Use it when a performer says they sound late or hollow in their headphones.

transfer_time.name: Transfer time
where: how much data, in bytes (or bits)
the rate, in the same unit per second — 8 bits make a byte
transfer_time.note: The same relationship tells you how long a restore takes and how much an upload can move overnight (S = r × t). Mixing bits and bytes is the classic eight-times mistake.
transfer_time.when: Use it before you promise a restore time, or an off-site copy that ‘keeps up’.

audio_size.name: Size of uncompressed audio
audio_size.note: 24-bit audio is 3 bytes a sample. Headers and metadata add a little; the audio is almost all of it.
audio_size.ex: 24 tracks × 48,000 × 3 bytes × 240 s ≈ 829 MB for one four-minute song.
audio_size.when: Use it to size storage and backups from the way you actually record.

annual_reserve.name: Replacement reserve
where: what it costs to replace everything in the estate, $
what to set aside every year, $
annual_reserve.note: A reserve spreads a replacement across the years the equipment lives. If everything was bought at once, the average hides a cliff — look at the year each thing ends, too. Illustrative.
annual_reserve.when: Use it to turn the age of an estate into a number the people with the money can plan for.

weighted_score.name: Weighted score
where: the weight agreed for each criterion — they add up to 1
the rating each option gets on that criterion, e.g. 1–5
weighted_score.note: Agree the criteria and the weights before anyone rates an option. Changing the weights after seeing the scores is choosing the answer and then building the reasons.
weighted_score.when: Use it when several people want the same money and each is sure they're first — agree the weights first.

mean_detect.name: Average time to detect
where: average time from a failure starting to a test catching it — the worst case is T
mean_detect.note: A failure can start any time between two tests, so on average it waits half the interval. Halve the interval and you halve the wait — and double the tests.
mean_detect.ex: A test every 30 min: on average 15 min to detect, 30 at worst.
mean_detect.when: Use it to decide how often to test, and to be honest about how long users wait before you know.

jitter_buffer.name: Receive buffer for a jittery path
where: safety multiple chosen for the link (here 3)
peak jitter measured on the path, seconds
jitter_buffer.note: A deeper buffer adds delay but stops late packets from tearing the picture. Illustrative rule of thumb (MD-01).
jitter_buffer.ex: Peak jitter 0.2 s with a multiple of 3: B ≥ 3 × 0.2 = 0.6 s.
jitter_buffer.when: Use it when packets arrive unevenly — a buffer trades a little delay for a picture that doesn't tear.

estimate.name: Project estimate
where: sales tax on equipment, as a decimal
estimate.note: Contingency pays for what you can't see yet on a live job; it isn't profit and it isn't optional. Illustrative (BOSS-02).
estimate.when: Use it to price a turn-key job before you promise a number to anyone.

tco.name: Total cost of ownership
where: running cost per year — support and licenses, $
one-off costs later in the life, such as a refresh, $
tco.note: A board funds the whole life of a system, not just the day it's installed. Illustrative (BOSS-02).
tco.ex: Build $85,250 plus support $4,200 a year for 3 years: 85,250 + 12,600 = $97,850.
tco.when: Use it when the client is paying for years of ownership, not just the installation.

s04e03_perceived.name: Perceived loudness (rule of thumb)
where: how many times louder it sounds
s04e03_perceived.note: About twice as loud for every 10 LU — a rough guide, not a law.
s04e03_perceived.ex: A spot 10 LU above the program: 2^(10 ÷ 10) = 2 times as loud to the ear.
s04e03_perceived.when: Use it to explain complaints: a 10 LU jump feels about twice as loud, even when the peaks look fine.

s04e06_links.name: Links needed
where: bit rate the encoder must send, Mb/s
share of each link's capacity you can count on, Mb/s
s04e06_links.ex: Need 10 Mb/s, each link gives 3 Mb/s usable: ⌈10 ÷ 3⌉ = 4 links.
s04e06_links.when: Use it to size a bonded cellular kit — round up, and plan for the crowd, not the empty stadium.

travel_time.name: Travel time at a steady speed
where: speed — keep units consistent (km and km/h give hours)
travel_time.note: Internal planning only: on air, relay the agency's forecast word for word.
travel_time.ex: A crest 12 km upstream moving 3 km/h: t = 12 ÷ 3 = 4 hours.
travel_time.when: Use it for internal planning on an agency's own numbers — the forecast itself always belongs to the agency.

glossary.d: The path a signal takes from its source to where people receive it — every box, cable and setting in between, in order.
The earliest point along the signal flow where the signal is wrong. Everything after it is a symptom.
Something you observed or measured, labeled with how sure you are (observed, measured, verified …), kept before you change anything.
An evidence state: you saw or heard it yourself, but haven't measured it.
An evidence state: a meter, log or instrument gave you a number.
An evidence state: a conclusion you reasoned from other evidence. Useful, but not yet proven.
An evidence state: proven where the people are — the fix checked from the audience's side.
Checking a fix at the audience's end — a phone off the network, an off-air receiver, a seat in the room — instead of on the operator's monitor.
alias: prove it where the people are

glossary.d: A change you can undo quickly and exactly. Make one at a time, so you know which change did what.
Returning a system to its last known-good state by a planned step.
Conditions written before a test or change that say exactly when you stop and go back.
The underlying reason a fault happened, as opposed to the symptom people noticed.
What people notice — the hum, the frozen picture — which may be far downstream of the cause.
A clue that looks important but leads away from the real cause.
A temporary way around a problem. Useful tonight; dangerous if nobody writes it down and replaces it.
Shortcuts and workarounds that keep working until the day they fail — recorded in SIGNAL as DEBT items.
Written, tested steps for running or recovering a system, kept where the next person can find them.
A log entry saying what changed, when, by whom — and ideally why.
Looking at what the system allowed to happen, not at who to punish, so people keep reporting mistakes.
Hand a decision to the person who owns it, with your evidence attached.
The person or team responsible for a system and its decisions. You ask; they decide.
A line you don't cross because a system or decision belongs to someone else — power, rigging, towers, security, evacuations.
Deciding what to do first when you can't do everything, by weighing risk, people affected and time.
An unplanned interruption or degradation of a service, run under a clock until it is restored and proven.
One part whose failure takes the whole service down.
A second way to do the same job, so one failure doesn't stop the service.
Switching a service from a failed or at-risk system to its backup.
A planned rehearsal of a failover, run when failing is cheap, with rollback criteria written first.
A tracked item for the underlying cause behind repeated incidents, with an owner and a fix.
A list of every room or system that doesn't follow the standard, each with an owner and a reason.
A logarithmic way of comparing two levels. Useful because ears and signals cover huge ranges. Written dB.
Decibels relative to digital full scale. 0 dBFS is the loudest value a digital system can represent; everything else is negative.
Sound pressure level — how loud a sound is in the air, in dB.
How much a stage amplifies (positive dB) or reduces (negative dB) a signal.
Setting each stage's gain so the signal stays well above the noise and well below clipping all the way through.
The space between normal peaks and the point of clipping.
Distortion when a signal tries to go beyond the maximum a stage can pass; the tops of the wave are cut off.
The level of background noise in a system or a radio channel; signals must sit above it.
A howl when a microphone picks up its own loudspeaker and the loop gain reaches 0 dB or more.
How loud you can make a mic before it starts to ring. Fewer open mics means more of it.
A pattern of regularly spaced notches when the same sound arrives twice with a small delay — it sounds hollow.
A deep dip at one frequency — from a comb filter, or cut deliberately with EQ.
Equalization — boosting or cutting ranges of frequencies.
How narrow a filter is: center frequency divided by bandwidth. High Q is narrow.
How many cycles per second a wave makes, in hertz (Hz).
The length of one cycle of a wave in space.
A frequency that is a whole-number multiple of the fundamental.
A low buzz at the mains frequency and its harmonics, usually from a grounding problem.
Two or more paths to ground that let a small mains current flow in audio cables, heard as hum.
A feed that contains everything except the listener's own voice, so they don't hear themselves late.
Interruptible foldback — the feed in a presenter's earpiece: program or a mix-minus, with the director able to talk into it.
A loudspeaker or earpiece that lets performers hear themselves and each other.
Delay a stage adds to a signal.
How many times per second a digital system measures a signal.
How many bits each digital sample uses; sets the dynamic range.
The span between the quietest and loudest a system can handle, in dB.
Sound persisting in a room after the source stops, from many reflections.
A distinct, delayed repeat of a sound.
Processing that removes the far end's voice from a room's microphones in conferencing.
How loud a program seems to people over time, measured in LUFS — not the same as its peak level.
Loudness units relative to full scale: the unit of measured loudness. 1 LU = 1 dB.
A meter showing the highest instantaneous level — good for clipping, poor for how loud something feels.
A box that keeps programs near a loudness target automatically.
Whether a speaker's voice and lip movement arrive together.
Level from a small source falls about 6 dB each time the distance doubles, in open space.
About 343 m/s in air at 20 °C; faster when warmer.
A loudspeaker farther from the stage, delayed so its sound arrives just after the main speakers'.
An assistive listening system that sends audio magnetically to hearing aids.
How many pictures per second a video system shows, in fps.
One still picture in a video sequence.
Locking video equipment to a common reference so every frame starts together.
The master timing source a facility locks to.
A classic analog video reference signal used to lock equipment.
When a reference loses its source and keeps time on its own oscillator, slowly drifting.
A label on every frame giving hours, minutes, seconds and frames.
Parts per million — how far a clock's rate is off, one millionth at a time.
The room where a station's program is assembled and sent to air, and where it is monitored. Also MCR.
A second master control, somewhere else, able to take the station's program.
The finished output a station sends to air.
A receiver that picks up the station the way viewers do — the only proof of what actually arrived.
A static card put on air when there's no program — 'Please stand by'.
Text graphics across the lower part of the picture — names, titles, alerts.
The ordered list of stories and segments for a show.
A screen that shows the presenter's script in front of the camera lens.
The desk that cuts between cameras and sources to make program.
A box that compresses video and audio for a stream or link.
A saved set of encoder settings — change it and you can change what survives, including captions.
A converter between two kinds of video systems, e.g. older cameras and an IP network.
Width divided by height of a picture.
How many pixels a picture has across and down.
How many times per second an LED wall redraws.
How long a camera exposes each frame.
Adjusting the lens so the subject is sharp.
The warmth or coolness of white light, in kelvin.
Image magnification — live camera shots of the stage on big screens.
Text of what's spoken and heard, shown with the picture for deaf and hard-of-hearing viewers.
The device that inserts caption data into the video signal.
Extra data carried inside a video signal alongside the picture — captions travel there.
An extra audio channel carrying the program in another language.
Designing so everyone can use the service — including people who are deaf, blind or use other assistive tools.
A device's number on a network, like 198.18.0.5.
A block of addresses that can talk to each other directly, written with a prefix like /24.
The automatic service that hands out addresses from a range.
An address typed into a device by hand, not handed out automatically.
A DHCP entry that always gives one device the same address.
A block of addresses the automatic service is told never to hand out.
Two devices using the same address; both misbehave.
A virtual network: ports grouped so traffic stays separate on shared switches.
Separating networks so a problem or attack in one can't reach another.
A network device that connects devices on the same network.
Sending one stream to many receivers at once; floods a network unless managed.
How much data a link can carry per second.
How full a link is, as a percentage of its capacity.
Variation in packet arrival times.
Storage that holds data briefly to smooth out uneven arrival, at the cost of delay.
Several cellular modems combined into one contribution link.
An encoder that lowers or raises its bit rate to fit the link, instead of breaking.
The maximum error-free data rate of a channel, set by bandwidth and signal-to-noise.
A second route that fails for different reasons — different carrier, different conduit, different building.
A group of systems updated together, smallest and least critical first.
Automatic checks that alert you when something is wrong — only as good as what they check.
Radio frequency — wireless signals, from wireless mics to microwave links.
New unwanted frequencies created when several transmitters mix in a receiver or amplifier.
Choosing wireless channels so they don't interfere with each other or with intermodulation products.
Power in decibels relative to 1 milliwatt; received signals are usually negative dBm.
How many dB a link can lose before it drops.
Extra loss on microwave links caused by rain.
How much signal a radio wave loses just by spreading over distance.
The football-shaped region around a radio path that must stay mostly clear.
Studio-to-transmitter link: the path carrying program from the studio to the transmitter site.
The equipment that broadcasts the station over the air. Only a licensed engineer operates it.
The element that sends or receives radio waves.
Electrical pressure, in volts (V).
Flow of electricity, in amperes (A).
Rate of energy use, in watts: volts × amps.
A switch that trips when current is too high, protecting the wiring. Resetting it is the electrician's call.
A fuel-driven power source for when utility power fails. It belongs to facilities and the power vendor.
The switch that moves a building from utility power to a generator.
Uninterruptible power supply — batteries that carry equipment through a short power interruption.
The safety ground connection. Never defeat it.
Hanging equipment overhead. Belongs to the rigger and structural engineer.
The most a piece of rigging hardware is rated to hold in use.
Stopping outdoor work or a show because of wind or lightning, called by the weather/safety lead.
The written plan that says when field crews pull back. The news director owns it at Kestrel Valley.
An order from the emergency manager to leave a building or area. Nobody stays against it.
An emergency message from an agency, relayed word for word, captioned, never edited.
The control protocol for stage lighting: 512 channels per universe.
One DMX line of 512 channels.
The first DMX channel a fixture listens to.
A lighting instrument.
How wide a light's beam spreads.
Illuminance: light falling on a surface, lumens per square meter.
One login used by many people — impossible to trace or revoke for one person.
A login for one person, with only the access they need.
Giving each account only the access its job needs.
A fake message that tricks people into giving away passwords or clicking a harmful link.
How unpredictable a password is, in bits.
The written specification every meeting room follows.
The team and system that take and track tickets.
Software and panels that operate a room's devices together.
Where a signal starts: a microphone, a camera, a laptop, a console output.
Where a signal is supposed to end up: a loudspeaker, a screen, a recorder, the stream.
The final stretch to the people — the loudspeaker, the display, the stream return. Verify there, not at the meter.
The Fieldbook's live-fault routine: stay calm, identify, isolate, check the path, fix or work around, communicate.
Planned small care (weekly, monthly, quarterly, yearly) so failures don't choose their own moment.
A list of every device: location, age, serial, firmware, license and expiry dates — the start of every budget conversation.
A period before an event when nothing gets updated or reconfigured.
A software or firmware version proven to work, kept so you can go back to it.
Labeled both ends, power and signal kept apart, coiled over-under, strain-relieved, no trip hazards.
Support that keeps a cable's weight off its connector, so the joint doesn't work loose.
Coiling a cable with alternating loops so it lies flat and uncoils without twists.
The person who leads the production team, aligns roles and removes blockers during a show.
Passing responsibility from one person or system to another — an interface that can fail like any cable.
The minute-by-minute order of a service or event, shared before the day.
A microphone the operator uses to speak to the stage or crew without going to the audience.
A device that converts one form of energy into another — a microphone (air pressure → voltage), a loudspeaker (the reverse).
A rugged mic that uses a coil moving in a magnetic field; handles loud sources.
A sensitive, detailed mic built as a capacitor; needs phantom power.
About 48 V sent down a balanced mic cable to power condenser microphones.
The directions a microphone hears from.
A heart-shaped pickup pattern: hears the front, rejects the rear.
A pickup pattern that hears equally all around.
The tiny signal a microphone makes — millivolts — before the preamp.
The stronger signal level between devices after the preamp — about +4 dBu in professional gear.
A decibel scale for voltage, referenced to 0.775 V. Professional line level is about +4 dBu.
The first amplifier stage: raises mic level to line level. Gain is set here.
A stage that neither raises nor lowers the level — 0 dB on a fader.
The slider that sets how loud a channel or bus comes out — volume after the gain stage.
One input's controls on a console, in signal order: input, gain, phantom, polarity, filter, dynamics, EQ, sends, fader.
The small display or label above a fader showing the channel's name.
A box on stage that converts mic inputs to digital and sends them to the console over one cable.
A cable carrying the signal twice, one copy inverted, so noise picked up on the way cancels at the input (e.g. XLR, TRS).
A direct box: turns an unbalanced instrument signal into a balanced mic-level one, and can isolate ground.
Which way up a waveform is. Swapping pins 2 and 3 flips polarity; a flipped copy cancels a correct one.
Where a wave is in its cycle. In-phase copies add; copies 180° apart cancel.
Signal-to-noise ratio: how far the signal sits above the noise floor, in dB.
A way of averaging a changing level that tracks energy — closer to perceived loudness than a peak reading.
A mix sent somewhere — a wedge, in-ears, a recorder, the stream.
The control that sets how much of a channel goes to a bus.
A send taken before the channel fader, so fader moves don't change it (monitors).
A send taken after the channel fader, so it follows the fader (effects).
A remote volume control for many channels that doesn't change their sends.
A bus that mixes channels together and processes them as one (e.g. a vocal group with a compressor).
A set of outputs built from mixes of other mixes — for zones, delays and feeds.
A saved snapshot of a console's settings, recalled to repeat a setup.
A setting that protects chosen channels from being changed when a scene is recalled.
A filter that lets frequencies above its cutoff pass and removes rumble below it.
A filter that lets frequencies below its cutoff pass and removes content above it.
EQ that lifts or lowers everything above or below a point, gently.
EQ with adjustable frequency, gain and width (Q) for each band.
How steeply a filter cuts beyond its cutoff, in dB per octave.
A doubling of frequency — 100 Hz to 200 Hz is one octave.
Turns down signal above a threshold by a ratio, making levels more consistent.
The level above which a compressor (or below which a gate) starts working.
How strongly a compressor turns down signal above threshold — 4:1 means 4 dB in gives 1 dB out.
How quickly a compressor or gate reacts once the threshold is crossed.
How quickly a compressor or gate lets go after the signal drops.
Gain added after compression to restore the level.
A compressor with a very high ratio — a ceiling that stops peaks passing a set level.
A processor that closes (turns down) a channel when its level falls below a threshold, cutting bleed.
A processor that tames harsh “s” sounds (around 5–8 kHz).
A short gap before a reverb starts, keeping the dry words clear.
A single short echo (about 80–120 ms) that thickens a voice or instrument.
Separate recordings of groups of sources (vocals, band, drums) for mixing later.
A mix built for online listeners, separate from the room mix.
Loss of accurate hearing judgment after loud or long listening; mix at moderate levels and take breaks.
A loudspeaker that covers the front-center seats the main loudspeakers miss.
A loudspeaker for the lowest frequencies.
How evenly a sound system (or lighting) reaches every seat.
Real-time analyzer: shows level across frequency, live.
A calculation that turns a waveform (level over time) into a spectrum (level across frequency).
A bass frequency a room's dimensions reinforce: f = c ÷ 2L along each dimension.
Reverberation time: how long sound takes to fall by 60 dB after it stops.
A surface soaking up sound energy instead of reflecting it (carpet, curtains, people).
Sound bouncing off a surface and arriving again, later.
Scattering sound in many directions so reflections are spread out.
Waves bending around objects — long bass waves do it easily.
How easily speech can be understood.
The level a loudspeaker makes with 1 W at 1 m, in dB SPL.
Video that draws every line of each frame at once (the “p” in 1080p).
Video drawn as two half-frames (fields) captured at different moments (the “i” in 1080i); combs on motion.
The one resolution, frame rate and scan type every device in a venue is set to — written down.
False patterns when a camera's pixel grid and an LED wall's grid beat against each other.
A professional video connection over 75-ohm coax with locking BNC connectors; reliable over long runs.
A common consumer video-and-audio connection for short runs.
Digital signals work perfectly until they suddenly fail, with little warning in between.
The method that compresses (encodes) and rebuilds (decodes) audio or video.
How many bits per second a stream uses. Too low for the content shows as blocky, soft artifacts.
Storing color at lower resolution than brightness (4:4:4, 4:2:2, 4:2:0) to save data.
A light on a camera showing it is live on program.
A camera you pan, tilt and zoom remotely, often over the network, with saved presets.
One screen showing many sources at once, so the operator can see everything.
The switcher output showing the next shot, before it goes to program.
The lens opening (f-stop). A lower f-number lets in more light and gives shallower depth of field.
Camera sensor sensitivity (or gain). Higher is brighter and noisier.
How much light the camera records — set by aperture, shutter and ISO together.
Telling a camera what “white” is under the current light, so colors are right.
How much of the scene, front to back, is in focus.
The lens setting that decides field of view: short is wide, long is narrow (telephoto).
A video display built from modules of LEDs.
The card inside an LED module that receives the video data for that module.
Distance between LED pixel centers, in mm. Smaller pitch means finer detail up close.
A device that changes a video signal's resolution to fit a display.
A graph of how many pixels sit at each brightness — an exposure check.
How bright a light is, from 0 to 100%.
The main light on a subject, often about 45° in front.
A softer light from the opposite side of the key that fills shadows.
Light from behind that separates the subject from the background.
Light that covers an area evenly, with soft edges.
Light that picks out one subject, with a defined edge.
A simple fixture giving a soft-edged wash.
A fixture with a stepped lens giving very soft, natural light.
A profile fixture with a sharp, shapeable edge; takes gobos and shutters.
A motorized fixture that pans, tilts and changes color and shape remotely.
A small pattern placed in a fixture to project a shape.
A fine mist that makes light beams visible in the air.
A saved lighting look, with timing, that the operator plays back.
A sequence of looks that steps automatically.
A timed change from one look or source to another.
Total visible light a source emits.
How intense a light is in one direction (1 cd = 1 lm per steradian).
An illuminance unit: 1 fc = 10.76 lux.
Color rendering index: how faithfully a light shows colors (0–100). TLCI rates the same for cameras.
Pulse-width modulation: dimming an LED by switching it on and off very fast. Low frequencies band on camera.
Rapid brightness pulsing, often invisible to eyes but visible on camera.
A resistor at the end of a DMX line that stops the signal reflecting back.
Devices connected one after another on a single line — DMX works this way.
Remote Device Management: two-way messages over DMX to read and set fixtures remotely.
Seven layers from physical cables up to applications, used to troubleshoot bottom-up.
OSI layer 1: cables, connectors, light, radio.
OSI layer 2: MAC addresses, switch ports and VLANs on the local network.
OSI layer 3: IP addresses and routing between networks.
OSI layer 4: getting data there — TCP (reliable) or UDP (fast).
OSI layer 5: starting and keeping a conversation going — logins, stream sessions.
OSI layer 6: data format — resolution, codec, encryption.
OSI layer 7: the app people actually use.
A transport that confirms delivery and resends lost data — reliable but slower.
A transport that sends without waiting for confirmation — fast, suited to live media.
A hardware address built into a network device.
A device that connects different networks and forwards traffic between them.
The service that turns names into IP addresses.
Quality of service: priorities so live audio and video go first on a busy network.
A switch feature that sends multicast only to ports that asked for it (needs a querier).
Power over Ethernet: power and data on one network cable, within the switch's power budget.
Every device cabled back to a central switch — preferred over daisy chains for AV networks.
Opposition to current, in ohms (Ω).
V = I × R: voltage equals current times resistance.
Alternating current: changes direction many times a second (e.g. 60 Hz).
Direct current: flows one way, as from a battery.
A path with almost no resistance, so current becomes dangerously high and the breaker trips.
A broken path — no current flows.
A surge when equipment switches on — why systems are powered up in sequence.
Voltage lost along a cable because of its resistance.
The processor — the part of a computer that does the thinking.
A computer's short-term working memory for running programs.
Software built into a device (a console, a switch, a camera).
Multi-factor authentication: a second proof besides the password.
One button that runs a recorded series of actions.
The path that carries commands to a device, separate from the audio/video it handles.
The path the actual audio and video take, separate from control.
A monitoring check that asks whether the user got the result — a recording with sound, a call that connects — not just whether the device answered.
A monitoring check that asks only “is the device answering?” It can stay green while users fail.
A separate network for visitors' devices, usually with lower priority and a per-device bandwidth cap.
How strong a hearing loop's magnetic field is at a seat, in milliamps per meter (mA/m).
A place where a signal (a loop field, a radio signal, a microphone's pickup) is too weak to use.
The total power a network switch can supply to powered devices at once. Past it, ports get shut off by priority.
A switch setting that decides which powered ports keep power when the PoE budget runs out.
The copy of the far-end audio an echo canceller compares against the microphone so it can remove the echo.
A mixer that turns up the microphone nearest the talker and turns the others down automatically.
The area a microphone (or a steered ceiling array) listens to; a talker outside it is heard weakly or not at all.
The system that puts an emergency message on screens, speakers and phones. Its words and its activation belong to the emergency manager and security.
A small computer behind a display that plays scheduled content — often by checking a server for updates every so often (polling).
Network Time Protocol: how computers and devices on a network learn the time from a time server.
Precision Time Protocol: a much tighter way to share time over a network, used for audio and video that must stay in step.
A schedule for replacing equipment before it fails, based on age, failure rates and the cost of each failure.
How often a kind of device fails: failures per unit per year.
The date after which a product gets no repairs, parts or security fixes from its maker.
The device or software that compresses program audio and video into a stream for viewers online.
The numbered sheets (plans, sections, details, schedules) that tell every trade what to build. AV sheets must agree with the architectural, electrical and structural sheets.
Checking that the disciplines' drawings agree — that the AV floor box has conduit on the electrical sheet, and that nothing sits where a beam is.
The licensed engineer who signs a discipline's drawings (electrical, structural, mechanical) and is responsible for them. An AV designer shows intent; the engineer of record decides.
A box set into the floor with power and signal connections — under a courtroom table or a lectern.
How much of a conduit's inside area the cables take up. Codes limit it (commonly 40% for three or more cables) so cables can be pulled without damage and heat can escape.
A projection lens's distance-to-image-width ratio. A 1.5:1 lens 9 m away makes a 6 m image; a 0.8:1 lens makes it from 4.8 m.
Moving a projector's image up, down or sideways optically, so the projector doesn't have to sit dead-center on the screen.
Changing a design to cut cost while keeping its function. Done well it saves money; done blindly it removes the thing that made the function reliable.
The fraction of time a system works: MTBF ÷ (MTBF + MTTR). Redundancy raises it only if the parts can't fail together.
Mean time between failures: the average running time before a device fails.
Mean time to repair: the average time to get a failed device working again, including getting the part and the person.
A system (loop, infrared or radio) that sends program sound straight to people's hearing aids or receivers. Codes set how many receivers and where.
The heights and depths a person using a wheelchair can reach — where controls, touch panels and outlets must go. Accessibility codes set the numbers.
The unblocked line from a viewer's eyes to what they must see — a screen, an interpreter, a witness.
A formal check of drawings against requirements by people who will use or operate the space — including disabled users and accessibility reviewers.
The written half of the design: what each product must do, how it must be installed and tested. Drawings show where; specifications say what and how well.
The contractor's proposal of the exact products and drawings they intend to install, sent to the designer for review before anything is bought.
Specification wording that lets a contractor offer a different product that meets the same requirements. Without stated criteria, ‘equal’ is an argument.
A loudspeaker distribution system where many loudspeakers hang off one amplifier channel through small transformers, each set to a power tap.
The power setting on a 70 V loudspeaker's transformer (for example 2.5, 5 or 10 W). The taps on a line add up.
How well listeners can understand speech in a space; long reverberation, noise and poor coverage reduce it.
The angle over which a loudspeaker's level stays within about 6 dB of its on-axis level at a given frequency.
A loudspeaker mounted in the ceiling, aimed down. Spacing depends on ceiling height, ear height and coverage angle.
The height of listeners' ears — about 1.2 m seated, 1.7 m standing. Coverage is designed for it, not for the floor.
Request for information: a contractor's formal question to the designer. The answer becomes part of the contract — so it must be checked like a drawing.
Drawings updated to show what was actually installed. Also called record drawings. Everything after handover depends on them being true.
A formal change to the construction contract — its cost and time. The later a design error is found, the bigger the change order.
A network that carries many channels of live audio between devices, usually as multicast streams that need managed switching (IGMP snooping and a querier).
All of an organization's sites and rooms, managed as one system — here, forty sites in three countries.
An unrecorded, unapproved difference between what a room is and what its standard or design says it should be. Drift has no reason on file, no owner and no end date.
A recorded, approved difference in a standard for one region — 230 V power, 50 Hz camera settings, a required hearing loop, a second language. Design, not drift.
How closely a room matches its standard. A conformance scan is only as good as the rule it checks: counting every difference as a failure counts good design as drift.
A group of devices left behind on old firmware — often because an update ring never selected them — while every report says the estate is up to date.
A measure of exposure: the number of devices at risk times the number of days they stay at risk. 154 devices for 300 days is 46,200 device-days.
Aligning many licenses or contracts to one renewal date. It can earn a discount and simplify paperwork — and it concentrates every renewal into one day's risk.
The days a lapsed license keeps working before features switch off. A grace period is a countdown, not a safety net.
Support handed from one region's desk to the next as each working day ends, so someone awake always owns an open problem.
Coordinated Universal Time: one reference clock for the world. Local time = UTC + the local offset. Writing handovers in UTC stops ‘9 o'clock’ meaning three different times.
What one desk gives the next: the owner, the state, the evidence, the next action and when — with every time in UTC and the customer's local time.
The timer a service agreement runs on. If it counts business hours in the wrong time zone, a ticket can be ‘within SLA’ while the customer has waited a day.
How often a monitoring system asks a device how it is. An outage shorter than the interval can fall between two polls and never be seen.
Monitoring where the device reports a change the moment it happens (a log message or alert), instead of waiting to be asked. It catches short outages polling misses.
A five-field schedule (minute, hour, day, month, weekday). ‘5 2 * * *’ runs at 02:05 every day; ‘5 * * * *’ runs at five past every hour.
A single, hardened computer that administrators must log into, with their own named account, before they can reach device management. Every session is recorded.
A separate VLAN that carries only device administration traffic, reachable only through approved paths such as a jump host.
A system that stores credentials, gives each person or service only the ones it needs, rotates them and records every use. It belongs to the security team.
When the only way to change, support or even log into your systems runs through one supplier — because they hold the credentials, the configurations or the knowledge.
How many times a second the power supply alternates: 50 Hz in some countries, 60 Hz in others. Lights on mains power flicker at twice that rate.
Exposure time expressed as a fraction of the frame period × 360°. At 59.94 fps a 1/100 s shutter is about 216°.
A transformer that lowers voltage (230 V to 120 V, say). Choosing, installing and loading one is the electrician's call; it is never an improvised fix for equipment from another region.
Interpreters in sound-proofed booths turning a speaker's words into another language as they speak; listeners choose a language channel.
When a booth can't understand the language on the floor, it interprets from another booth's output instead — a pivot language.
A sound-proofed booth where interpreters work, with a clean, undelayed feed of the floor, a view of the speaker, and their own output channel.
Communication Access Realtime Translation: a trained human captioner writing live captions. Many access policies require it for live events where accuracy matters.
A statement of what a room must achieve and how that will be proved — ‘join a call from the panel in 60 s or less, 19 attempts in 20’. It can pass or fail.
A choice someone likes — a color, a brand, a model — written as if it were a requirement. Preferences belong in guidance, not in the rule that decides pass or fail.
The group that approves changes to a standard or a shared system — here the regional leads, security, accessibility and the standard's owner.
The moment a service moves from the old system to the new one. A good cutover has checkpoints, rollback criteria and a way to run old and new side by side.
Running the old and new systems side by side, comparing what each sees, before switching the old one off.
Far more alarms than people can read — often from one wrong threshold. Real alarms hide inside the flood, and the temptation is to mute everything.
How long a UPS can carry its load on battery: usable battery energy ÷ load. A countdown the facilities team needs in minutes, not adjectives.
Speech transmission index: a measured score from 0 to 1 for how well a room and its sound system carry speech. Around 0.60 or more is usually rated good.
The moment the last structural beam goes onto a new building — often marked with a small ceremony. The shell is up; the fit-out begins.
A formal change to the drawings issued by the architect during construction. Every trade whose work it touches has to receive it — or they build the old design.
The order the general contractor schedules the trades in. Change it — ceiling before loudspeaker supports, say — and someone has to undo work.
The main cables between equipment rooms — usually fiber — that everything else hangs from.
Optical fiber with a very thin core that carries one path of light — low loss (about 0.4 dB/km at 1310 nm) and long reach. Used for backbones.
Optical fiber with a wider core that carries many paths of light — cheaper optics, but higher loss and a short reach at high speeds (about 400 m at 10 Gb/s on OM4).
How much light a fiber link may lose between transmitter and receiver: attenuation per kilometer plus every connector and splice, compared with what the optics allow.
Two fiber ends melted together with an arc — a permanent joint with a small loss (a few tenths of a dB).
Optical time-domain reflectometer: sends pulses down a fiber and plots every connector, splice and break by distance. The fiber's X-ray.
Power the electrician provides during construction, before the permanent panels are inspected and energized. It's sized for a plan — tell the electrician what you'll plug in.
A panel in a finished ceiling that opens so equipment above it can be reached. Its position has to follow the equipment — including changes.
The enclosure and support a ceiling loudspeaker mounts into, installed before the ceiling closes.
A handheld tester's measurement of an installed cable link against a standard (length, loss, crosstalk). The report is evidence only if it belongs to the link it names.
Near-end crosstalk: signal leaking from one pair into another at the same end of a cable. Damaged or over-pulled cable fails it first.
How hard a cable may be pulled during installation. Over it, the pairs stretch and the cable fails its tests — sometimes years later.
An independent person who verifies, on the owner's behalf, that the systems do what the design says — by watching the tests, not reading the paperwork.
The heat equipment gives off — nearly all the electrical power it draws. Measured in watts or BTU per hour; it sizes the cooling.
Enough units that one can fail and the rest still carry the load: N needed, plus one spare.
The engineer's written assumptions — loads, occupancy, equipment lists — that a design was sized from. If the inputs change, the design must be checked again.
A separate network segment where devices are updated or configured before they join the live production network.
Audio and video sent as streams over a standard network — hundreds of encoders and decoders, each running firmware that has to match.
A place designed by the structural engineer to carry a suspended load, with a rated capacity. A catwalk is not a hang point unless the engineer says so.
Loudspeakers set on the floor or the stage instead of flown — a safe temporary option while the hang is being designed and installed.
The panel that runs a building's fire alarm system. It belongs to the fire alarm contractor and the authority; other systems only receive signals from it.
The fire alarm designer's written list of what every connected system must do when an alarm happens — including muting AV program audio.
A fire alarm circuit the panel watches for faults: a cut or loose wire shows as TROUBLE at the panel instead of failing silently. Only the fire alarm contractor works on it.

A contact that is closed in normal operation and opens to signal. An AV mute input wired this way fails safe: a cut wire looks like an alarm and the program mutes, instead of the interface failing silently.
The versions a device has to pass through, in order, to reach a target firmware. Skip one and the device may land in recovery mode — so read the release notes and update one device first.
People assigned to patrol a building for fire while part of its protection is incomplete or out of service — often a condition of a temporary certificate of occupancy.
A fire alarm system that plays spoken evacuation messages. AV program audio mutes so those messages can be understood.
The list of unfinished or wrong items found near the end of construction. Closing an item means someone has verified it, not that someone has ticked it.
The authority's permission for people to use a building. It can depend on life-safety tests passing — with the fire marshal watching.
The official body — here the fire marshal — whose acceptance a life-safety system needs. Their decision isn't negotiable on opening night.
A login that lets someone outside the building reach its systems — usually an integrator or vendor doing support. It needs an owner, a reason and an end date.
Removing a person's access when they leave a team, a firm or a contract. If nobody owns it, old accounts outlive the people who used them.
A regular check of every account on a system: who it belongs to, what it can do, and whether it should still exist. Security owns it.
A system's record of who did what, and when. It is evidence only if the account names a person and the clock is right.
A record of who collected a piece of evidence, when, and everyone who handled it since — so nobody can say it was changed along the way. Security runs it.
A ready-made emergency slide or message. It belongs behind an approval — or wired read-only to the fire alarm — never in a library anyone can publish from.
A rule that a second named person must approve content or a change before it goes live.
The server and software that schedule what appears on signage screens. Here: the CMS.
An account used by software rather than a person — a booking integration, say. It gets only the rights that job needs, and a named owner.
The one person in charge during an incident — here, the duty manager. Everyone else brings facts and options; the incident commander decides.
The venue manager on shift. In an emergency they are the incident commander: they decide whether people move or stay, and what staff say.
A rehearsal around a table: people walk through a realistic incident, decision by decision, to find the gaps before a real one does.
A new piece of information the exercise leader drops into a tabletop exercise — a second screen, a social-media post, a demand from the CEO.
A short, true public message issued early in an incident — what happened, what people should do, when there'll be more — owned by communications.
A single, documented permission for one kind of traffic between two network segments. Everything not on the list is blocked.
The list of known risks, each with an owner, a score and a decision: fix, accept, transfer or watch.
A named owner's written decision to live with a risk for now. Only the person who owns the risk can make it.
