Announcements from a microphone or a recorded message to parts of a building — staff calls, ‘please take your seats’. In an incident it carries the incident commander's words; the fire alarm's own voice system is separate.
A table of who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed for each task. Its job is to stop ‘I thought that was yours’.
A dedicated clock signal that tells digital audio devices exactly when to take each sample. One device leads; every other device follows it.
The one device whose clock every other digital device in a system follows (older manuals say ‘master’). Two leaders means two clocks — and slips.
When two devices run on clocks that differ very slightly, the receiver's buffer eventually runs over or under and a block of samples is dropped or repeated — heard as a click at a regular interval.
A room mode between one pair of parallel walls. The first sits at the speed of sound ÷ twice the distance; its pressure is highest at the walls and cancels in the middle of the room.
A spot where two or more arrivals of the same sound cancel, so a frequency almost disappears. EQ can't fill a null: boosting feeds the cancellation too.
Where the engineer's head sits when judging a mix. In a small room, moving it tens of centimeters can change the bass by many decibels.
How well a mix keeps its balance on other systems — cars, earbuds, phones. A mix that only sounds right in one room doesn't translate.
A finished, well-known recording in a similar style, played at matched loudness so your ears can calibrate to a room.
Delaying one microphone or loudspeaker so that two arrivals of the same sound line up in time, which moves or removes comb-filter notches.
A rule of thumb for spaced microphones: keep two mics at least three times as far from each other as each is from its own source, so the spill is roughly 9 dB down and comb filtering stays mild.
The delay from a sound entering the converter, through the computer's input and output buffers and any plug-ins, back out to the headphones.
Sending a performer's own microphone to their headphones before it reaches the computer, so they hear themselves with almost no delay.
The headphone mix a performer hears while recording — their own, separate from the mix in the control room.
A processor delays the audio by a few milliseconds so it can react to a peak before it arrives. Fine on a master; poison in a performer's headphones.
The project document a recording program saves: which audio files go where, edits, fades and plug-in settings. Without a program that can read it, it is instructions nobody can follow.
A plain, widely readable audio file with room for metadata — who, when, and where the file starts in the song. The safest thing to leave for the future.
A short fingerprint computed from a file's bits. If a copy's checksum matches the original's, every bit survived the copy; checking them on a schedule is called a fixity check.
Moving an archive onto newer storage — and, when needed, newer formats — on a schedule, before the old media or software can't be read.
The highest level a waveform actually reaches between its samples once it is turned back into sound, in dBTP. It can be higher than the highest sample, and lossy encoding can push it higher still.
A playback service measures each track's integrated loudness and turns it up or down to a common target, so a louder master is not played louder.
The loudness of a whole song or program in LUFS, measured with gating so that silence doesn't drag the number down.
A switch, usually on a DI box, that disconnects the audio cable's shield at one end to break a ground loop in the signal path. It never touches the mains protective earth.
The artist's own yes — in writing — to a specific use of her performance: who gets which files, for what, and until when.
A mark added to a review copy so that a leaked file can be traced to the person it was sent to.
Three copies of anything that matters, on two different kinds of storage, with one of them kept somewhere else.
A backup that keeps earlier versions of each file, so a deletion or a bad save can be rolled back instead of copied over every copy.
Actually bringing files back from a backup and opening them. Until you have restored, you have a hope, not a backup.
Two drives that hold the same data at the same time (RAID 1). It survives one drive dying — and copies every mistake instantly, so it isn't a backup.
A composite take: the best phrases from several takes edited into one performance.
A drive's own health report — for example a rising count of reallocated or pending sectors. A rising count means copy now, not later.
The room where a county's agencies work side by side during a disaster — sharing one picture, deciding together, each keeping its own authority.
The block of time — often twelve hours — that one shift's plan covers. Each ends with a written handover to the next.
A written summary passed to the incoming shift: the situation, what's pending, resources, hazards and who's who. A handover that lives only on a screen or in a head fails.
The shared view of an incident everyone in the room works from — on the wall, the status board and the situation report.
An agreed, approved time when a system may be updated or changed — never in the middle of the work it supports.
A link or service that keeps going down and coming back. Automatic failover that follows every flap can be worse than no failover.
A rule that keeps traffic on the backup until the main path has stayed healthy for a set time, so a flapping link can't drag everything back and forth.
Two things that look independent but can fail together — two carriers in the same conduit across the same bridge.
Different agencies' radios able to talk to each other when a plan says they should — through a patch, a shared talkgroup or a gateway.
A named group on a trunked radio system: everyone in it hears everyone else. Agencies own their own talkgroups.
A connection, usually through a gateway, that joins two radio channels or talkgroups so their users hear each other.
The one dispatcher who runs a shared radio channel — who talks when — so a patch doesn't turn into everyone talking at once.
A receiver losing sensitivity because strong unwanted energy — often an intermodulation product — lands on or near its frequency.
Passing on an official warning in exactly the issuing agency's words, with its name and time — the county adds its own guidance separately.
Checking an unconfirmed report with the people who would know, then telling the public plainly what is and isn't true.
The switch that moves a building's load from the mains to the generator (and back). It belongs to facilities, and it has to be tested under load.
Running the generator and transfer switch with the real load on them, on a schedule — the only way to know they'll carry the room.
Switching off the least important loads so a UPS or generator can carry the ones that matter for longer.
The rising chance of mistakes as a shift goes on. Rosters and written handovers manage it; working past the limit doesn't make anyone safer.
A separate network segment for visiting agencies and contractors — internet access, nothing on the operations network.
A structured look back after an activation: what was supposed to happen, what did, why, and an improvement plan with owners and dates.

The date an approved exception to the standard ends — when the room is brought back to standard, the exception is renewed on purpose, or the standard changes. An exception without an expiry is drift with paperwork.
Taking a recorded exception that works better than the standard and making it the new standard, through the change board — instead of forcing every room back to the old way.
A one-page yearly report for the people who hold the money: how old everything is, what it will cost to replace and when, and which risks that creates. It lets owners decide before things fail.
Money set aside every year so equipment can be replaced when it wears out: the replacement cost divided by its planned life.
The date after which a manufacturer stops fixing, patching or selling parts for a product. It still works the next morning — but every fault and every security hole after that is yours.
When a lot of equipment bought in the same year all reaches the end of its life in the same year — one enormous bill and one enormous risk. Staggering replacements flattens it.
Changing a small number of systems first (a canary), watching them for a set time, then widening in steps — so a bad change hurts a few rooms instead of all of them.
How much a single change or fault can break at once — as a count or a share of everything. Architecture keeps it small on purpose.
The written right of anyone — including the most junior person — to stop work they believe is unsafe or unapproved, without being punished for it. It only exists if leaders back it when it's used.
How long from the start of a failure until people have service again: detecting it, working out what's wrong and restoring it, added together.
A named duty — ‘Tahvara on-call engineer’ — that a rota fills, instead of one person's name and phone number. People leave; roles stay.
A short note written when an architecture decision is made: what was decided, why, what else was considered and who owns it. It tells the next person why — so they don't undo it by accident.
For each critical task, how many people can do it unaided. A task only one person can do has a coverage of one — a single point of failure with a name.
Monitoring that checks what people actually experience — can a meeting start, is there audio, are captions on — instead of whether each device answers a ping.
An automatic, scheduled test that behaves like a user — starting a call in an empty room, listening for audio, checking captions — and raises an alert to a named role if it fails.

Ranking options against criteria agreed in advance, each with an agreed weight: score = Σ (weight × rating). Agreeing the weights before anyone scores keeps the loudest voice from choosing the answer.
An emergency admin account kept sealed for when normal access fails. Its use is logged, alarmed and reviewed — and its password is changed after every use.
A place where the standard promises access — captions, assistive listening, reachable controls — and a room doesn't deliver it. Recorded, owned and dated like any other defect.
Planning for the day a key person leaves: who takes each duty, what they need to know and how you'll prove they can do it before it matters.
